A PROCLAMATION,

For Dissolving this present Parliament, and declaring the Calling of another.

GEORGE R.

WHEREAS We have thought fit, by and with the Advice of our Privy Council, to difl'olvc this present Parliament, which now (lands prorogued to day the Twelfth Day of May next; We do for that end publish this our Royal Proclamation; and do hereby difi'olve the said Parliament accordingly: And the Lords Spiritual and Temporal, and the Knights, Citizens, and Burgertes,.and the Commissioners for Shires and Burghs, of the House of Commons, are discharged from their Meeting and Attendance, oh Tuesday the said Twelfth Day of May next: And we being desirous and resolved,

as loon as may be, to meet our People, and have their

Advice in Parliament, do hereby make khown to all our loving Subje<fls our Royal Will and Pleasure, to call a new Parliament; and do hereby further declare, That, with the Advice of our. Privy Council, we have this Day given Order to our Chancellor of Great , to ifi'ue

out Writs in due Form for calling a new Parliament; which Writs are to bear Teste on Tuesday the Twenty-eighth Day of this Instant Apr, and to be returnable on Thursiay the Twenty-fifth Day of June next.

Given at our Court at St. James's, the Twenty-seventh Day of April 1741, in the Fourteenth Year of our Reign.

GOD lave the KING.

Message to attend his Majesty.

ON which Day, being the First Day of the Meeting of this Parliament for the Dispatch of Business, pursuant, to a Proclamation hereunto annexed, and also to the Writs which had issued for that Purpose, the most noble Lionel Duke o&'Dorset, Lord Steward of his Majesty’s Houshold, came, about Nine of the Clock, into the Rooms belonging to the Clerk of the House of Commons, called the Inner Court of Wards, where the Oath4; appointed to be taken by the Members returned to serve in Parliament are usually administered;. and Nicholas liardinge Esquire, Clerk of the House of Commons,' and Mr. Naylor, Clerk Assistant,~and the other Clerks, attending, according to their Duty; the Lord Steward did himself, in Person, administer the Oaths appointed, to several of the Members who appeared; and afterwards made a Commission, or Deputation, under his Hand and Seal, hereunto also annexed, impowering fe- . veral of the Members, who had before been sworn, to administer the said Oaths to the rest of the Members returned, some of which Commissioners administered the same accordingly to such other Members as appeared: Which being done, the Members repaired to their Seats in the House of Commons. After which,

A Message was delivered from the King, by Sir Charles Dalton, Gentleman-U(her of the Black Rod:

Gentlemen,

The King commands this Honourable House, to at-, tend his Majesty, immediately, in the House of Peers.

Accordingly, the House went up to attend his Majesty in the House of Peers: Where the Lord High Chancellor of Great Britain, by his Majesty’s Direction, said.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

I have it in Command from his Majesty to acquaint you, that he is pleased to defer declaring the Caules of calling this Parliament, till there shall be a Speaker of the House of Commons.

It is, therefore, his Majesty’s Pleasure, that you. Gentlemen of the House of Commons, do immediately repair to the Place where the Commons usually fit, and there chcofe a fit Person to be your Speaker; and that you present the Person, who shall be To chosen, to his Majesty here, for his Royal Approbation, on Friday next, at Two of the Clock.

And the House being returned;

The Right Honourable Henry Pelham Esquire, One of his Majesty’s most Honourable Privy Council, Knight of the Shire for the County of Sussex, addressing himself to the Clerk (who, (landing up, pointed to him, and then fat down), said to this Effect:

Mr. Hardinge,

Mr. Onslow We are met, by his Majesty’s gracious Order, in a new chosen Parliament; and, agreeably to the Custom of former Speaker. Times, we are directed, in the First place, to choose a proper Person to fill the Chair of this House.

Vol. 14.

Lord

Chancellor’s

Speech.

This is an Affair of the greatest Importance to the Being of Parliaments.'

And it becomes us Feriously to consider wrhom we elect into an Office, that requires a Man of the greatest Ability, the greatest Integrity, and the greatest Application.

It is^with Pleasure I fee many Persons, under these various Deft:riptions, who deserve to be called to this Honour.

But when I fee one particular Person, who has already discharged this Employment so much to his own Hpnour, and so much to the Interest of this House; when I fee Ofie of this distinguished Capacity, it will not be derogatory to their Merit thus publickly to express rpy Thoughts of his.

It was in the early Days of his Life, when, by theuna-. nimous Consent of this House, he was placed in that high Station, in which he succeeded a Person of great Honour, whose Authority gave Weight to the Proceedings of this House: And it was an evident Mark of publick Esteem, and a convincing Proof of Merit, to be thus appointed his Successor.

I believe all Mankind fees the Situation of Affairs Abroad and at Home; so that it is probable, that Matters of the greatest Importance may come under the Consideration of this Housej which ought to induce us the more willingly to place in that Chair One, whose Principles, Experience in the Laws of his Country, and particular Application to the Proceedings of Parliament, do so well qualify him to preside in this Assembly.

When I consider (what recommends him to me, and is, in my Opinion, not the least of his Virtues) his constant and firm Zeal for his present Majesty, his Father, and the Succession in his illustrious House — When I consider (what also weighs with me, and I doubt not with every one who hears me) his steady Adherence to the Rules of Parliament — When I consider his Candour and Impartiality, his Temper and Resolution — Temper to indulge the young and unexperienced Members, and Resolution to correct the oldest — When I consider thele Qualifications, by which he has gained a general Esteem, I: mud conclude, that it will be always incumbent upon us, as long as he is able, to desire his acceptance of this important Office.

When I have said this, I am persuaded every Gentleman has already in his Thoughts the Person whom I mean to propose — Mr. Onslow.

And I make no doubt, but that all Gentlemen, those especially with whom I have fat in former Parliaments, will unanimously concur with me in the Choice of the Person whom I now offer.

If I should not offend his Ears, I could fav, that his Behaviour in private as well as in publick Life is an amiable Part of his Character; of which his Neighbours ami Countrymen have shewn their Opinion, by unanimously lending him to Parliaments

A. 1741:;

Let us ftiew our Sense of him, by calling (I should rather say tiefiring) him to undertake this laborious Task, that our Choice may soon be spread through, and approved by, the whole united Kingdom.

I am sorry I am not able to set forth his Qualities in abetter Manner than I have done; but Gentlemen, by their private Thoughts, will do him more Justice.

Therefore I shall move you, That the Right Honourable Arthur Onslow Esquire do take the Chair as Speaker.

Then Thomas Clutterbuck Esquire, Burgess for the Borough of Plympton, in the County of Devon, addressing himfeit likewise to the Clerk (who, (landing up, pointed to him, and then fat downj, laid to this Effect:

What I rife up for, is to l'econd the Honourable Gentleman’s Motion, and not, by any thing I can say, to add Weight to it.

It is not necessary for me to enlarge upon the Merits of the Person proposed, or to commend his Temper and Prudence, his Knowledge of the Laws and Constitution of this Kingdom, and of the Forms and Rules of this House, upon which the Honour thereof so much depends. ' These his Endowments we have seen in Two successive Parliaments; and, added to these, the strictest Regard to the Interest of the Publick, his. Zeal for the Liberties of this House, his Zeal Tor his Majesty, and his Family} . it is no Wonder, that any Person who has these Qualifications, should be called upon to so high an Office.

I congratulate this House, that there is a great Number of Gentlemen of Rank and Ability in it; yet I shall still be excused in the Preference which I h^ve given. And I cannot but look upon it as a fortunate Circum-

Clock, for the Presentment of their Speaker to his Majesty, in the House of Peers, for his Royal Approbation moved, That the House would adjourn till Friday next.

A Message was brought from his Majesty, by Sir Charles the

Dalton, Gen tleman-U AVer of the Black Rod:

Mr. Speaker,

The King commands this Honourable House to attend him, immediately, in the House of Peers.

Accordingly, Mr. Speaker elect, with the House, went up to attend his Majesty: Where he spake to the Effedk following:

May it please your most Excellent Majesty,

The Commons of Great Britain, in Parliament assembled, have, in pursuance of your Majesty’s Commands, and according to their ancient Right to make Choice of One of their Members to be their Speaker, once more elected me to this high and painful Office; but how properly for me, for themselves, and for the Publick, is now with your Majesty to judge: And to your Royal

Judgment, Sir, I do, with all Humbleness and Resigna-stance in the present Situation of Affairs, that we are abje. tion, submit myself; being well assured, that, should to fix our Choice upon a Perfom whom, by Experience your Majesty think fit to disapprove of this their present

Choice, your Commons will have no Difficulty to find some other Person among them, to be presented to your Majesty on this Occasion, to whom none of those Objections can be made, which I fear may too justly, from my Imperfections, arise in your Royal Breast, upon my being again the Subject of your Majesty’s Confutation for this important Charge.

we know to be equal to any Difficulty.

I could say much more; but I fear it may give Un-ealiness to one Person who hears me; and therefore I second the Honourable Gentleman, That Mr. Onslow do take the Chair.

And the House calling Mr. Onslow to the Chair, he flood up in his Place, and said,

Mr. Hardinge,

I cannot make Acknowledgments enough of what I owe to the Honourable Persons who have made this Motion to the House: I am very sensible, Sir, of my own DefeCls; and although I have, from the great Candour and Indulgence of Gentlemen in the Two lad Parliaments, twice gone through this difficult Trust, yet am I sensible too, that will not make the Repetition of it in me now either less hazardous to myself, or of less Danger to the publick Affairs: But, however, Sir, I will not trouble Gentlemen with the Arguments of Disability in myself, which I might, perhaps ought to use at this time; but shall submit myself intirely to the Judgment.of the House, to dispose of me in whatever Manner they shall think proper, on this and every other Occasion.

And the House a^ain calling Mr. Onslow to the Chair, he was taken out of his Place by Mr. Pelham and Mr. Clutterbuck, who led him from thence to the Chair, where, upon the First Step, he said,

It is my Duty to inform Gentlemen, that they have yet an Opportunity to reconsider what they have done, by differing me to go back to the Place I have just now left: But the Members cried " No ! No!"

Whereupon Mr. Onslow ascended the upper Step; and, Handing the re, said,

Since Gentlemen have commanded me to this Eminence, I have now only to return them my humbled Thanks for this particular Instance of their Favour to me; the Sense of which I hope I shall always retain with that Respect and Gratitude to the House, this Mark of their Esteem will ever claim from me.

And thereupon he fat down in the Chair;

Then the Lord Chancellor, receiving Directions from his Majesty, said,

Mr. Onslow,

The King has had so manjf eminent Proofs of your Ability and Zeal for the Service of himself, and of your Country (which is always the fame), in the high Station to which you are now a Third time called, that his Majesty has commanded me to let you know, that he intirely approves the Choice, which his faithful Commons have made; and therefore allows and confirms you to be their Speaker.

Then Mr. Speaker said,

Since your Majesty has been pleased to ratify the Choice your Commons have made of me to be their Speaker, it is my Duty, Sir, to submit myself to your Royal Determination, and to return your Majesty my humbled Thanks for this Mark of your Royal Grace and Favour to me; and to assure you, Sir, of my bell Endeavours to discharge, as I ought, this great Trust, which the Commons have committed to, and your Majesty has now confirmed upon me: And, for my Encouragement therein, suffer me, great Sir, to hope for your Majesty’s Pardon of my Failings and Infirmities; at lead, that your Majesty would not impute them in anywise to your faithful Commons -. The Lord Chancellor, receiving further Directions from his Majesty, laid,

Mr. Speaker,

The King has an intire Confidence in the Prudence and Temper of this House of Commons, as well as in their Duty and AffeXion to his Person and Government; and his Majesty does most readily grant to them all their Privileges, in as full and ample Manner as they have at any time been heretofore granted, or allowed, by his Majesty, or any of his Royal Predeceftbrs.

As to the Suit, which you. Sir, have made on your own Behalf, your former Conduct is the cleared Evidence how little you stand in need of it; but, for your greater Encouragement and Support in the execution of so important a Trust, his Majesty, agreeably to his wonted Gocdness, has commanded me to allure you, That he will always put the most favourable ConstruXion both upon your Words and Actions.

The House being returned;

Mr. Speaker reported, That the House had attended his Majesty, in the House of Peers: Where his Majesty was pleased to approve the Choice they had made of him to be their Speaker; and where he, in the Name and Behalf of the House of Commons, by humble Petition to his Majesty, did lay Claim to all their ancient Rights and Privileges; particularly, That themselves, their Servants, and Estates, might be free from Arrests, and all Molestations — That they might enjoy Freedom of Speech in their Debates, and have Liberty of Access to his Royal Person, whenever Occasion should require it — And that all their Proceedings might receive from his Majesty the most favourable ConstruXion: Upon which, his Majesty did grant to them all their Privileges, in as full and ample a Manner as ever were granted, or allowed, by his Majesty, or any of his Royal Predeceftbrs.

And now. Gentlemen, he laid, he hoped, would give him Leave to renew his humble Thanks to them, for the Honour they had done him, in raising him to that exalted Station; He said. The best Return he could make, was to allure Gentlemen of his constant Endeavours to discharge his Duty in that Place, so as to render his Services acceptable to the House, and every Member in it; which to do, he said, would be the Pride of his Life: And that they might all be the better enabled to perform their Duty, he laid. He must exhort Gentlemen to a ftrieband steady Observance of the Rules and Orders of the House ;to avoid all personal Altercations and Reflexions in their Debating; and, for the better and quicker Dispatch of Business, to come down early in a Morning ro it: And he hoped, Gentlemen would make it a Point of Honour, to dedicate that which is the best Fart of the Day to the Service of their Country.

Resolved, That no Peer of this Realm hath any'Right to give his Vote in the Election of any Member, to serve in Parliament.

Resolved, That where the House shall judge any Petition, touching Elections, to be frivolous and vexatious, the House will order Satisfaction to be made to the Person petitioned against.

Resolved, That if it shall appear, that any Person hath procured himself to be elected, or returned, a Member of this House, or endeavoured so to be, by Bribery, or any other corrupt Practices, this House will proceed with the utmost Severity against such Person.

Resolved, That if it shall appear, that any Person hath been tampering with any Witness, in respect of his Evidence to be given to this House, or any Committee thereof, or directly, or indirectly, hath endeavoured to deter, or hinder, any Person from appearing, or giving Evidence, the same is declared to be a high Crime and Mit demeanor; and this House will proceed with the utmost Severity against such Offender.

Resolved, That if it shall appear, that any Person hath given false Evidence, in any Case, before this House, or any Committee thereof, this House will proceed with the utmost Severity against such Offender.

Resolved, That it is an high Infringement of the Liberties and Privileges of the Commons of Great Britain, for any Lord of Parliament, or any Lord Lieutenant of any County, to concern themselves in the Elections of Members to serve for the Commons in Parliament.

House did, on Friday last, attend his Majesty, in the House of Peers, his Majesty was pleased to make a most gracious Speech from the Throne to both Houses of Parliament; of which, Mr. Speaker said, he had, to prevent Mistakes, obtained a Copy: Which he read to the House; and the same is as follows; viz.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

It is always a great Satisfaction to me to meet you assembled in Parliament, and especially at this time, when the Posture of Affairs makes your Counsel and Af-, fiftance lb necessary; and when, by means of the new Elections, I may have an Opportunity of knowing the more immediate Sense and Disposition of my People in general, from their Representatives chosen during a Sea-Ion, which has been attended with great Variety of Incidents of the highest Consequence and Expectation, and during the Course of the War in which we are engaged against the Crown of Spain; a War in itself just and necessary, entered into by the repeated Advice of both Houses of Parliament, and particularly recommended to me to be carried on in America; which has been my principal Care: I can therefore make no doubt, but that you are met together fully fenlible of our present Situation, and prepared to give me such Advice as shall be most conducive to the Honour and true Interest of my Crown and Kingdoms.

You cannot but have observed, with an Attention suitable to the Occasion, the impending Dangers that threaten Europe, and more immediately such Parts of the Continent, as shall withstand or refill the formidable Powers which are confederated for the Subversion, or Reduction, of the House of Austria. The Apprehension of these Things was communicated to the last Parliament, when both Houses expressed their great Concern for the Troubles which were then broke out in the Attftrian Dominions, and came to the strongest Resolutions, in favour of the Queen of Hungary, for the Maintenance of the Pragmatick Sanction, and for the Preservation of the Balance of Power, and the Peace and Liberties of Europe: And had other Powers, that were under the like Engagements with me, answered the just Expectations they had so solemnly given, the Support of the common Cause had been attended with less Difficulty.

I have, pursuant to the Advice of my Parliament, even

) since the Death of the late Emperor, exerted myself in

I the Support of the House of Austria: I have endeavour-

ed, by the most proper and early Applications, to indure other Powers, that were equally engaged with me, and I VoL. 24.

the King’s Speech.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

I have, during the Course of my Reign, had so much Experience of the Duty and Affection of my Parliaments to my Person and Government, and of their Zeal for the Good of their Country, and the Support of the common Cause, that I do, with the greatest lleafon, rely upon the Continuance of them in the present Conjuncture. There never was a Time, in which your Unanimity, Vigour, and Dispatch, were necessary to so many great Ends as those which are now before you. I will do my Part; let it appear, by your Proceedings and Re(b-lutions, that you have that just and hearty Concern for them, which their Importance requires.

Sir,

The Angular Honour done me, in being thought deserving of the unanimous Thanks of the House of Commons, for my Endeavours to discharge my Duty to ids Majesty in these Seas, is what I can’t find Words futfi-ciently to express niv grateful Sense of; but I shall ever retain a just Acknowlegement of the great Honour done me by the House, in their Approbation of my Services to his Majesty, and my Country, and thinking them deferring of their Notice in this publick manner.

As the publick Approbation of so augtift an Assembly is the highest Honour a Subject can receive, I must beg the Favour of you, Sir, to assure the House, that a grateful Sense of it will never be effaced out of my Memory, and that I shall endeavour, in all my future Conduct, by a continued Diligence, and faithful Discharge of my Duty to his Majesty, in the Execution of his Orders, lor the Honour of the Crown, and Service of my Country, to study to preserve the Continuance of their Efteein. I am, Sir,

Your most obedient, and most humble Servant,

E. Vernon.

Ireland, Sir Charles Water, Knight, Edward Vernon, Esquire, Vice-Admiral of the Blue, and Charles Edwin, Esquire, having, on the Second Day of May 1741, been nominated Candidates at the late Election of Members to serve in this present Parliament, for the City and Liberty of W 1flminster,a Poll was then demanded, and proceeded upon in the Porch of the Parish Church of St. Paul, Covent-Garden, within the said City and Liberty; that it was previously agreed between the said Lord Sundon, Sir Charles Wager, Charles Edwin, and John Lever, Esquire, High-Bail iff and Returning Officer of the said City and Liberty, that Cheque-Books should be kept on Behalf of the said Edward Vernon and Charles Edwin, at the said Election, during the Continuance of the said Poll;, that the said John Lever was determined, at all Events, to return the said Lord Sundon and Sir Charles Wager-, that during the first Three Days of taking the Poll, the said John Lever contentedhimlelf barely with doing Insultice, under Colour of exercising his Judgment, and under that Dilguile refuled the Votes of several Persons duly qualified, and delirous to Vote for the said Edward Vernon and Charles Edwin; and, at the same time, admitted others to poll for the said Lord and Sir Charles Wager,

who had no Right of voting: That the said John Lever, being conscious of his own gross Partiality, with a; View to suppress the proper Evidence of it, on the

-Sixth of May 1741, arbitrarily refused to fuller tire said Cheque-Books to be continued on behalf of the said Edward Vernon and Charles F.dwitt, notwithstanding his own previous Agreement, and the Consentofall the Candidates present: That the said John Lever, not satisfied with Insultice and Partiality only, had recourse to Violence; and, in Coiyun&ion with Arthur Rawlin/on, the High Constable of the said City and Liberty, and others, did hire and pay a great Number of loose and dilfolute Persons, and furnish them with Clubs, Bludgeons, and other offensive Weapons;: and did direct the Persons, lb armed, to attend the Place of Poll, and insult the Friends and Voters of the said Edward Vernon and Charles Edwin-, and the said hired Persons did accordingly attend, and prevent many legal Voters from polling at the said Election: That the said John Lever being determined at lall.to make a Return, without observing so much as the Form of gping through the Poll, did, on the 8th Day of May 1741, in Defiance of Law and Justice, without any Notice to the Voters, without the Consent of the Candidates, or any Person in their Behalf, and contrary to the express Protell of the said Charles Edwin against that Proceeding, even while several Persons were then polling, and others demanding to be polled for the said Edward Vernon and Charles Edwin, finally closed the Poll: That a Body of Soldiers, to the Number of Fifty and upwards, headed by Officers, marched, with Drums beating, to the Place of Polling; and, being the re drawn up in a military manner, the said John Lever did, under the Shew of their Protection, most unjustly declare the said Lord Sundon and Sir Charles Wager duly elected Members for the said City and Liberty of , while many

Hundred legal Voters, deCrous to vote, remained unpolled: That the Petitioners, thus deprived of the Right of being represented in Parliament by Member* of their Vol. 24.

A Petition of John Hylton Esquire, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth. That at the general Election of Citizens to serve in this present Parliament for the City of Carlisle, in the Chunty of Cumberland, the Honourable Charles Howard Esquire, John Esquire, and the Petitioner, stood Candidates: That the undoubted Right of Election of Citizens to serve in Parliament for the said City is in the Mayor, Aldermen, Bailiffs, and Freemen thereof; and that the Mayor of the said City, for the Time being, is’ the Returning Officer: That Richard Coultharwas, at the time of the said Election, Mayor of the said City, and presided at taking the Poll at the said Election; That the said Election began at the Town-hall of the said City upon the 13th Day of May last; and the Petitioner and the said Charles Howard, and John then attended as

Candidates; and several Votes were then given by Freemen of the said City for the Petitioner, and also for the said Charles Howard and John respectively j

That, about Twelve of the Clock, at Night of the said 13th Day of May, until which time the said Poll had continued, the said Richard Coulthard did, with the Con-lent of the Petitioner, and also of the said other Candidates, adjourn the further Taking of the said Poll till Nine of the Clock next Morning, being the 14th Day of the said Month of May j at or about, which time the said Richard Coulthard, and also the Petitioner and the said other Candidates, met at the said Town-hall, and several Freemen, to the Number of 250, and upwards, who had not voted at the said Election, also then and there attended, in order to give their Votes at the said Election; but the said Richard instead of pro-

ceeding to take the Votes of such of the Freemen of the said City, as had not before voted at the said Election, but Were ready to vote, and many of whom then tendered

their Votes for the Petitioner, called to' his Clerk for the Numbers of the Votes which had been given tite Day before, and being informed by his laid Clerk, that there were for the said Charles Howard 109 Votes, lor the said John Stamvix 90, and for the Petitioner 3; Votes; the said Richard Coulthard immediately ordered his Clerk to close the Poll-Books; which was accordingly done; and, in an arbitrary and illegal Manner, declared the said Charles Howard and John Stanwix duly elected; though, at the same time the said Charles Howard, the Petitioner, and many Persons who had a Right of voting, protested against such Declaration, and infilled upon the said Richard Coulthartf s proceeding in the said Poll;

and the said Richard Coulthard, soon after such Declaration made by him, withdrew himself from the said Town-hall, without taking the Vote of any one Freeman of the said City, upon the said 14th Day of That, immediately after the said Mayor had thus illegally withdrawn himself, a great Number of Persons, having an undoubted Right of Voting, and, who had nor voted before at the said Election, gave their Votes in the Town-hall in the Manner following; to wit, for the said Charles Howard 252 Votes, for the Petitioner 256 Votes, and for the said John Stanwix27 Votes; winch Votes were taken down by Beufon Highmore and Thomas the

younger, Two of the Clerks appointed to take the Poll at the said Election for the said Charles Howard and the Petitioner; by which it appears, that the said Charles Howard and the Petitioner were duly eletfted by a great Majority of legal Voles, and ought to have been returned; but the Cud Richard Coulthard hath unduly returned the said John Stanwix, together with the said

Charles Howard, as Citizens to serve in this present Parliament for the said City, in jmanifeft Prejudice to the Petitioner, and in Violation of the'Rights of the said City:

And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and to give the Petitioner such Relief as to the House fhalffeem meet.

A Petition of the several Persons, whose Names are Denbigh thereunto subscribed, being Freeholders of the County of Ek&u« Denbigh, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth. That, on the 26th Day of May last came on the Election of a Knight of the Shire to serve in this present Parliament for the County of Denbigh, at which Sir Wi-kin Williams Wynn Baronet, and John Myddelton Esquire, were Candidates: That, upon casting up the Poll, it appeared that there was a Majority of 419 Votes for Sir Watkin Williams Wynn, as the Numbers were declared and published by William Myddelton Esquire, the Sheriff and Returning Officer of the said County, and delivered ‘ in Writing by him to the said Sir Watkin Williams Wynn; the Numbers upon the Poll being for the said Sir Watkin Williams Wynn 135a, and for the said Mr. Myddelton 933; and a Scrutiny being thereupon demanded by Mr. Myddelton and his Friends, the Sheriff declared the whole 17 Poll

i 5 Geo. II. 14° Decembris, 1

Poll had been a Scrutiny; and that he did not know, that Mr. Myddelton had any Right to demand a Scrutiny, or he to grant one, or to that Effect; but that, notwithstanding this Majority and Declaration in favour of the said Sir Watkin Williams Wynn, the said Sheriff, in order to give a Colour for returning the said John Myddelton, hath presumed, privately and clandestinely, without hearing any one Party or Witness, to disallow near 600 Votes that were polled for the said Sir Watkin Williams Wynn;in which Number the Petitioners, who have long had very considerable Freeholds in the said County, and were everyway qualified to vote at the said Election, to their great Surprize find themselves included: That the Petitioners apprehend, the said William Myddelton was emboldened to commit this Injustice by Hopes of Impunity from the Numbers of those he had injured; imagining, that the House could not spare Time from the publick Business to examine into the Rights of near 600 Freeholders, and knowing that no Action could safely be brought against him at Law, nor any Prosecution by way of Indictment or Information, without first: obtaining the Leave of the House: And therefore praying the House to appoint a short Day for hearing the Petitioners, by their Counsel, and to give them such Relief as the Nature of their same requires, and as to the House shall seem meet. elected, and returned, a Burgess for the said Shire-Town; by which undue Means, the said Sir George Wynne has procured himself to be returned: That Evan Lloyd Esquire, and Edward Ellis Gentleman, then Bailiffs of the said Shire Town, and to whom the Precept for the said last Eiedion was directed, proceeded in taking the Poll with the utmost Partiality against the said Mr. Williams; rejeding several good Votes duly tendered for him, and admitting others for the said Sir George Wynne, contrary to the last Kesolution of the House of Commons; whereby the Right of Eiedion of a Burgess to serve in Parliament for the said Shire-Town of Flint is settled and declared; which Proceedings the Petitioners conceive not only to be to the apparent Wrong of the said Mr. Williams, but themselves and others, who, as Inhabitants of some one of the said several Boroughs, and paying Scotland Lot within the same, have an undoubted Right to a free and legal Election of a Burgess to serve in Parliament for the said Shire-Town of Flint: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and give the Petitioners such Relief as to the House shall seem meet.

but the Majority of the said Meeting, in an irregular Manner, rejected and excluded some Persons from the Rolls, who produced sufficient and legal Titles, and thereby deprived them of their Right of voting; and, not with {landing the Objections made by the Petitioner, several Persons were inrolled by the said Meeting, and thereby admitted to vote at that Eiedion, who had no legal Titles, nor the Qualifications necessarily required by Law: That particularly, Charles Ross, of Ballnagown, Esquire, was then admitted to vote, although it was objected by the Petitioner, and well known by many of the Freeholders present, that the said Charles Ross was then under the Age of 21 Years; and therefore, by an express Provision of an Act of Parliament, declared neither capable of eleding, or of being elected, a Member of Parliament: That the said Barons and Freeholders having afterwards proceeded to make choice of a Member to represent them in Parliament, the Petitioner was duly elected by the Majority of legal and unexceptionable Voters, and was the only Person capable of being chosen, for whom any of the said Freeholders voted; and therefore ought to have been returned by the Clerk of the said Meeting; but, notwithstanding this, to the great Injury of the Petitioner, by the aforesaid and other illegal Practices, the said Charles Ross, of Balnagoivn, has procured himself to be returned, although he was neither elected by the Majority of legal Voters for the said Shire of Ross, nor was capable of being so: And theie-fore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and to grant the Petitioner such Relief as to the House shall seem most proper.

And the Counsel were called in:

And the Counsel for the fitting Members examined a Witness, and procured Evidence, in order to prove, that, for some Days before the final Closing of the Poll, the Numbers each Day for each of the Candidates gradually decreased:

Then they examined several Witnesses, in order to prove, that an Agreement was made on the Second Day of the Poll, that such Persons as were Inhabitants within the Liberty of the Duchy of Lancaster should not be admitted to vote; and that, in consequence of such Agreement, several, who offered to vote for the Sitting-Members, were refused, as well as several who offered to vote for th* other Candidates:

Then they examined several Witnesses, in order to prove how often, and for what Intervals of Time, the Poll was discontinued the last Day thereof, by reason that no Persons having a Right to Poll, did, at those Intervals, offer their Votes; and also in order to prove in what Manner, and for what Reason, the Poll was closed by the High Bailiff:

And having examined several Witnesses, in order to prove when, and how often, Declarations were made of the High Bailiffs Intention to close the said Poll, and how many Proclamations were made before the same was closed; and by whom, and what was the Purport of those Proclamations, and what Intervals of Time were between each Proclamation so made:

They examined several Witnesses, as to a Number of Persons assembled in the Church-yard of St. Paul, Covent-Garden, near the Vestry-Room of the said Church, after the Poll was finally doled; and as to the Behaviour and Menaces of those Persons:

A Petition of the Trustees, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, appointed to put in Execution Two Acts of Parliament, One of the Eighth Year of the Reign of her late Majesty Queen Anne, for repairing the Highways between the House, commonly called the Horseshoe-house, in the Parish of Stoke Goldington, in the County of Bucks, and the Town of Northampton; and the other, made in the Ninth Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the First, for enlarging the Term granted by the aforesaid Ad, and for repairing the Road from the North Bridge of Newport PagueI, in the said County of Bucks, to the said Horseshoe-house, was presented to the House, and read; letting forth, That, by the said Acts, several Tolls were granted, continued, and made payable, for the several Terms therein mentioned, for repairing the said Roads, containing in Length about 1'wclve Miles: And that the Trustees, finding the same in a very ruinous Condition, and the annual Income not being sufficient, they were obliged to borrow a considerable Sum of Money, in order to put and keep the same in Repair; which Money, so borrowed, together with tilt

Vol. 24.

Tolls collected by virtue of the said Acts, has been duly laid out, and applied, according to the Directions thereby given; and that the Petitioners find the Money, now due and owing on the Credit of the said Acts, cannot be repaid, nor can all the said Roads, during the subsisting Term, be effectually amended, and kept in good Repair for the future: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for enlarging the Term and Powers by the said former Acts granted, for such Time, and in such Manner, as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

And it is referred to Mr. Compton, Sir John Rufhout, Dr. Lee, Mr. Vernon, Lord Dupp/in, Earl of Granard, Mr. Bance, Mr. Walker, Mr. Stanhope, Mr. Carezv, Col. Bladen, Mr. Wright, Sir Wm. Mr. Francis Fane, according to Order, reported from the Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred to consider of the Supply granted to his Majesty, the Resolutions which the Committee had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same were read; and are as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That Forty thousand Men be employed for the Sea Service, for the Year 1742, beginning from the First of January 1741.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum not exceeding Four Pounds per Man, per Month, be allowed for maintaining the said Forty thousand Men, for Thirteen Months, including the Ordnance for Sea-Service.

The First; Resolution being read a Second time, was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House, Nemine contradicente.

The Second Resolution being read a Second time, was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

Resolved, That this House will. Tomorrow Morning, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider of Ways and Means for raising the Supply granted to his Majesty.

The other Order of the Day being read;

The House proceeded to the Hearing of the Matter of the several Petitions of the Honourable Alexander Hume Campbell Esquire, and Sir John Sinclair Baronet, severally complaining of an undue Election, and double Return, for the Shire of Berwick, and of the Matter of the said double Return.

And the Counsel were called in;

And the said Petitions were read:

And the Handing Order of the House, made upon the Sixteenth Day of January 1735, for restraining the Counsel at the Bar of this House, or before the Committee of Privileges and Elections, from offering Evidence touching the Legality of Votes for Members to serve in Parliament, for any County, Shire, City, Borough, Cinque-Port, or Place, contrary to the last Determination in the House of Commons, was also read:

And it appearing, from the said double Return (with which the Clerk of the Crown attended according to Order), that the Indenture of Return of the Honourable Alexander Hume Campbell Esquire, was immediately annexed to the Writ;

The Counsel for the Honourable Alexander Hume Campbell Esquire were first: heard:

And having infilled, that Sir Robert Pringle Baronet, was duly elected Praefes, and James Pringle Clerk to the Meeting of Freeholders for the Election of a Commissioner to serve in this present Parliament for the Shire of Berwick, by a Majority of the said Freeholders, called

A. 1741*

over, by the Roll last made up, at the Michaelmas Head--Court; and that the Honourable Alexander Hume Campbell Esquire, was duly returned by the said Clerk.

They offered to call the said James Pringle, to produce the original Poll, taken at the Election of the said Pnefes and Clerk;

Which being objected to by the Counsel, for the Petitioner Sir John Sinclair;

The Counsel on both Sides were directed :o withdraw. The Counsel were again called in:

And the said Poll being produced by the said James Pringle;

The Counsel for the Petitioner Alexander Hume Campbell Esquire, examined the said James Pringle, and an--other Witness, as to the said Poll, and to the Proceedings at the Election of the said Prafes and Clerk:

Then the said Poll was brought up, and read:

Then the Counsel for the Petitioner Sir John Sinclair were heard, and produced Evidence, and examined a Witness, in order to prove, that the said Praefes and Clerk were not duly elected, but that Sir John Home Baronet, was duly elected Praefes, and John Sinclair Clerk of the said Meeting:

Then they offered to examine Witnesses, in order to disqualify several Persons who voted at the Election of the said Praefes and Clerk, and to whose Right of voting at such Election, the said Sir John Sinclair then objected, as not then having sufficient Freeholds to qualify them to vote at the said Election, although their Names were inserted in the Roll last made up, at the Michaelmas Head-Court:

And the Counsel for the Petitioner Alexander Hume Campbell Esquire, having objected to the Admission of that Evidence:

The Counsel on both Sides were directed to withdraw': Then Part of the Act of Parliament of Scotland, made September the 17th 1681, intituled, Act concerning the Election of Commissioners of Shires, was read:

And the Resolution of the House, of the 1 ith Day of May 1733, upon the Report from the Committee of Privileges and Elections, touching the Election and Return for the Shire of Peebles (that the Right of Election of a Praxes and Clerk is in such Persons as (land upon the Roll last made up by the Freeholders at the Michaelmas Head-Court, or at the last Election of a Member to serve in Parliament), was read:

And the Act, made in the Seventh Year of the Reign of his present Majesty, for the better regulating the Election of Members, to serve in the House of Commons, for that Part of Great Britain called Scotland, was read.

Resolved, That the Counsel be called in, and directed to proceed, according to the Resolution of this House, of the nth of May 1733: Which Resolution is, That the Right of Election of a Praefes and Clerk, is in such Persons as Hand upq%the Roll last made up by the Freeholders at the Michaelmas Head-Court, or at the last Election of a Member to serve in Parliament.

The Counsel were accordingly called in; and acquainted therewith:

And the Counsel for the Petitioner Sir John Sinclair, were further heard as to the Election of the said Prajfes and Clerk:

And the Counsel for the other Petitioner having been heard by way of Reply;

The Counsel on both Sides were directed to withdraw. Resolved, That Sir Robert Pringle, Baronet, was duly elected Pnefes of the Meeting of the Freeholders of the Shire of Berzvicky for electing a Commissioner to serve in this present Parliament for the said Shire.

Resolved, That Mr. James Pringle was duly elected Clerk to the Meeting of the Freeholders of the Shire of Berwick, for electing a Commissioner to serve in this present Parliament for the said Shire.

The Counsel were again called in, and acquainted with the said Resolutions:

Then the Counsel for the Petitioner Alexander Hume Campbell Esquire, produced Evidence, in order to prove*

Esquire, was tendered to him: And the 'Petition of the said Alexander Hume Campbell Esquire, having been again read:

The Counsel on both Sides were directed to withdraw. They were again called in:

And the Counsel for the Petitioner Alexander Hume Campbell Esquire, examined several Witnesses, as to the Objections made- by the said David Home, against accepting the Return, tendered to him, of Alexander Hume Campbell Esquire:

Then the Counsel on both Sides were directed to withdraw.

Resolved, That the Honourable Alexander Hume Campbell Esquire, is duly returned a Commissioner to serve in this present Parliament for the Shire of Berwick.

Resolved, That the Honourable Alexander Hume Campbell Esquire, is duly elected a Commissioner to serve in this present Parliament for the said Shire.

Countrymen, while their Families at home have been reduced to the greatest Want and pistress; and, at the same time, the Spanish Prisoners here have been treated with the utmost Lenity and Humanity; several of whom have been permitted to lie in private Lodgings, and to walk the Streets in publick; or which some have abused the Indulgence shewn them, and made their Escapes: That these Things tend greatly to the encouraging our Enemies, and must naturally check that ancient British Bravery, for which our Soldiers and Sailors have been ever famous, and of which they have given signal Proofs, in every Opportunity, since the Commencement of the present War: That the greatest Part of these Captures have been made in and near the British Channel and Soundings, at a time when' the Naval Force of Great Britain was greater than ever was known; a few Ships whereof might have blasted the Projects of the Adventurers in the said Privateers, and occasioned their being totally ruined, instead of amassing such prodigious Wealth as they have, at the Expence of these Nations: That these Things being of the highest Importance to his Majesty, and his Subjects, and particularly to their Trade and Commerce, the Petitioners humbly hope the same will not be thought unworthy the Enquiry of a British Parliament: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into their serious Consideration, and to prepare such Laws as shall be thought most effectual for appointing a sufficient Number of Convoys and Cruizers to be properly stationed, for securing the Ships of these Nations, and to be subject to such Examination and Inspection, as shall best answer the Ends designed; and that the Petitioners, and the Trading Part of these Nations, may have such further and other Relief, as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the said Committee of the whole House, to whom the Petition of the subscribing Merchants and Traders of the City of London, in behalf of themselves, and of the Trade of these Kingdoms, is referred.

A Petition of the Merchants of the Port of Liverpool, whose Names are subscribed, on behalf of themselves, and many others trading to and from that Port, was presented to the House, and read; representing to the House, That the Trade of that Port having of late been greatly obstructed, and Navigation discouraged, not only by their Sailors being impressed, and taken out of their outward-bound Ships, even when cleared out and ready to fail, notwithstanding the great Charge and Expence Which the Merchants and Owners have been at in fitting out such Ships, hiring of Seamen, and obtaining Protections for the Security of their Men (whereby their Voyages have been often greatly retarded); but also by their homeward-bound Ships being forced to come to Anchor ih very improper and dangerous Places, and their Sailors impressed, and carried over-board, before their Ships are got into Safety 5 and likewise by the ill Usage of them, when taken Prisoners by the Spanish Privateers (which; through the great Succels they have met with, in taking so many Prizes even in the Entrance and Soundings of the British Channels, and on the Coasts of the British Colonies, are of late become very numerous, for want of a competent Number of small Men of War being properly stationed, which, as the Petitioners conceive, might in a great measure prevent it); and likewise by the Prisoners

from complaining of such Inconveniencies and Losses as must be the unavoidable Consequence of a War so just and necessary, in order to secure the future Freedom of Trade, and the undoubted Rights of Navigation; but apprehend, these Inconveniencies and Losses may be prevented, if the Commanders of his Majesty’s Ships of War, and their Tenders, were strictly retrained from obliging the homeward-bound Ships to drop Anchor in improper Places, and from stripping them of their Hands, without seeing them first in Safety, and from impressing Sailors out of outward-bound Ships, when ready for Sea, and provided with proper Protections; and that the Ships may be better secured, by having regular Convoys appointed from time to time, with Orders to take care of the Ships under their Charge, and not to desert them when in the greatest Danger of becoming a Prey to the Enemy: And therefore praying the House to take their same into Consideration, and grant them such Provision for the future Encouragement and Security of their Trade and Navigation, as shall be thought fit and necessary.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the said Committee of the whole House, to whom the Petition of the subscribing Merchants and Traders of the City of London, in behalf of themselves, and of the Trade of these Kingdoms, is referred.

A Petition of the Merchants, and others, trading from Annoyance the Port of Lancaster, was presented to the House, and of Trade by read; setting forth. That, since the Commencement of Pri*

the just and necessary War against Spain, the Spanish Privateers have already taken Four of their Ships, with their Cargoes; which they can justly remonstrate are a Fifth-part thereof concerned in foreign Trade, and which, together with their Seamen made Captives, and flibjected to long and tedious Imprisonments, has greatly distressed their Trade and Navigation; and that they apprehend, these Calamities are very much owing to the Want of a sufficient Number of Ships of War being properly stationed, which might probably, with the assiduous Care and Vigilance of their Commanders, have prevented a great many Ships (which have had the Misfortune to be taken) from falling into the Enemies Hands; and also might have retaken others: That it is with the greatest Concern they fee the Commerce of these Kingdoms so much interrupted by the many other Instances of Captures of the Ships of his Majesty’s Subjects by the Spanish Privateers; and that so little Care has been taken to flop the Progress of these growing Evils: And therefore praying the House to take the Petition into Consideration, and concert such Measures for the future Preservation of the Navigation and Commerce of these Kingdoms, as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the said Committee of the whole House, to whom the Petition of the subscribing Merchants and Traders of the City of London, in behalf of themselves, and of the Trade of these Kingdoms, is referred.

A Petition of the Merchants, Traders, and principal Ditto; Inhabitants of the City of Exeter, was presented to the

House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioners have been considerable Sufferers in their Trade and Navigation, since the Commencement of the War with Spain t That their Misfortunes have been Chiefly owing to the great Numbers of Spanish Privateers that appeared in the Channel and Soundings, soon after the Declaration of War on the Part of Spain, who made Prize of leVeral Vessels belonging to that Port: That the Peti. ioners apprehend, that moll of these Captures might have been prevented, had a few Ships of War been timely stationed to cruize between the Coast of Ireland and UJhant, and a few more between UJhant and Cape Finisterre, and near the Spanish Ports, in the Bay of Biscay: That the Petitioners have also sustained considerable Losses in their Trade to our Colonies in America, occasioned chiefly by the Neglect of the Captains of those few Ships of War stationed there:

That the Petitioners are not a little alarmed, not only at the Increase of the Number and Size of the Privateers lately equipped by the Enemy, but also at the unexpected great Strength the Court of Spain have lately shewn in the Mediterranean, by which our Trade to the Strain mull now become much more precarious than ever: That the Petitioners beg Leave to assure the House, that it is far from their Design to complain of Captures that may be reasonably looked on as unavoidable, much less would they be understood to be influenced by any Uneasiness on Account of the present War, both just in itself, and thought necessary by the Wisdom of the Nation, for the Security of our Commerce, and the Rights and Freedom of our Navigation: And praying the House to rake the Premises into Consideration, and to make speh Provision for the future Protection of the Trade and Navigation of these Kingdoms as the House shall think fit.

Ordered, That the Is^d Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Petition of the subscribing Merchants and Traders of the City of London, in behalf of themselves, and of the Trade of these Kingdoms, is referred.

A Petition of the Merchants of the City of Glasgow, in behalf of ihemselves, and many others, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the preserving and proteding the Trade and Commerce of his Majesty’s Subjects, is of theutmoftConsequence to the Prosperity of this Island: That, since the Commencement of this just and necessary War with Spain, such numerous Fleets being employed, and the Naval Force of Great Britain so much superior to our Enemies, the Petitioners flattered themselves with Hope of the greatest Care and Attention in guarding and protecting the Persons and Effects of his Majesty’s trading Subjects; and representing to the House, that, for want of a sufficient Number of Men of War, and Cruizers, being properly stationed in the Channels, and on the Coasts of America; and through the Commanders, especially in the latter Parts, not doing their Duty, the Number of Spanish Privateers is greatly multiplied, and, by reason of their Success, likely more and more to increase, whereby our Navigation is rendered most infeciire, our Merchants (tripped of their Properties, our Sailors of their Liberties, an$l by barbarous Usage, and want of a Cartel, forced into the Spanish Service: That a further Hardship the Petitioners labour under, is, the impressing their Seamen on their homeward Voyages, at a considerable Distance from their Ports of Discharge, and putting careless and insufficient Hands on board, in their Place, whereby the Ships*of the Petitioners have been endangered, and their Cargoes considerably damaged: And therefore praying the House to consider the Premises, and give such Relief as to the House shall seem meet*

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Petition of the subscribing Merchants and Traders of the City of London, in behalf of themselves, and of the Trade of theft Kingdoms, is referred.

Mr. Francis Fane according to Order, reported, from the Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred to consider of Ways and Means for raising the Supply granted, to his Majesty, the Resolution which they had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table; where the same was Tead; and is as folio weth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, towards 'railing the Supply granted to his Majesty, the Duties on Malt, Mum, Cyder, and Perry, which, by an Act of Parliament of the Fourteenth Year of his Majesty’s Reign, have Continuance to the Twenty-fourth Day of June 1742, be further continued, and charged upon all Malt which shall be made, and all Mum which shall be made or imported, and all Cyder and Perry which shall be made for Sale, within the Kingdom of Great Britain, from the 23d Day of June 1742, to the 24th Day of June 1743.

The said Resolution being read a Second time, was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the Houft.

Ordered, That a Bill be brought in upon the said Resolution: And that Mr. Francis Fane, Mr. Scrope, Mr. Chan^lorof the Exchequer, Mr. Earle, Mr. Treby, Mr. Qlutteriyck, Mr. Attorney-General, and Mr. Legge, do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

Prayers.

AJA T HAN IE L Blacker by yGeorgc Howardy and Thomas Lediard, Esquires, attending according to Order, were brought to the Bar; and, upon their Knees, reprimanded by Mr, Speaker, as the House had directed. The Reprimand was as follows , viz.

Mr. Blacker by, Mr. Howard, M r. Lediard:

You having, at the Bar of this House, Yesterday, confessed, that you did fend for, and cause to come, on Friday the Eighth Day of May last, a Body of armed Soldiers, headed by Officers, in a military manner, who did take Possession of the Church-yard of St. Paul, Covent-Garden, near the Place where the Poll (for the Election of Citizens to serve in this present Parliament for the City

of Westminster) was taken, before the find Election was ended, and you having acknowledged your Offence therein, the floufe did order you to attend this Morning, to be brought to the Bar, to be reprimanded, on your Knees, by me, for the said Offence:

I cannot better describe to you the Nature of this Offence you have been guilty of, than in the Words of the Resolution this House came to, upon their Examination into that Matter; which aFe:

" That the Presence of a regular Body of armed Soldiers at an Election of Members to serve in Parliament, €t is an high Infringement of the Liberties of the Subject, " a manifest Violation of the Freedom of Elections, and " an open Defiance of the Laws and Constitution of this u Kingdom."

And it is impossible, if you well consider the Terms of this Resolution, but that you mud have in your Breads the deeped Sorrow and Remorse for this rash Act of yours, which, if it had not been animadverted upon, might have given the most dangerous Wound to the Constitution of this free Country, that perhaps it had ever felt: — This Country, free, becausethis House is so; which this House can never be, but from the Freedom of Elections to it; and amidst the too many Ways for violating that, none can be more pernicious, because none more quick, decisive, and permanent, than what you might unhappily have set a Precedent for, and which might have grown to an Extremity, under the specious and ready Pretences of Fears and Necessity, that supersede all Law; a Precedent that would have received an Authority from the Place it began in the Seat of the Government and Legislature of this Kingdom:

Necessity, which is to take Place of Law, must be left to the Circumstances of every particular Cafe; the Ad must be presumed to be wrong, inquired into as such, and excused only by the cleared Proofs, that the Necessity of it was real:

What you have done, is against one of the most essen-tiai Parts of the Law of the Kingdom: Has any real Necessity been shewn for it ? There might be Fears, there might be some Danger, but did you try the Strength of the Law todifpel those Fears, and remove that Danger ? Did you make use of those Powers the Law has inverted you with, as Civil Magistrates, for the Preservation of the publick Peace ? — No- — you deserted all that, and wantonly, I hope inadvertently, resorted to that Force, the most unnatural of all others, in all Respects, to that Cause and Business you were then attending, and for the Freedom of which every Briton ought to be ready almost to suffer any thing — More might be said — but you have acknowleged your Offence, and have asked Pardon for it: This has disposed the House to Lenity: Use it not to lessen the sense of your Crime, but to raise in your Hearts that Sense of Gratitude you owe to the House, for the gentle Treatment you have met with on this Occasion, in Expectation of which you are discharged, paying your Fees.

Ordered, That the said Nathaniel Blackerby, George Howardy and Thomas Lediardy Esquires, be discharged, paying their Fees.

Resolved, That the Thanks of this House be given to Mr. Speaker, for the Speech by him made upon reprimanding the said Nathaniel Blacker by, George Howardy and Thomas Lediard; and that he be desired to print the fame.

A Petition and Representation of the Merchants trading in the Port of Poole, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioners apprehend themselves under a Necessity of applying to the House for proper Redress, under the manifold Hardfnips that their Commerce and Navigation have differed from the SpanifJt Privateers, since the Commencement of the War, and that they are yet like to sustain more and greater Miffortunes, to the great Lossof his Majesty’s Subjects, and the Ruin of their Trade: That, since the Commencement of the War, the Petitioners have loft Eighteen of their best capital Ships, some of them richly laden, and of great Consequence to the Spaniards, who have carried them into Si. Sebafiians, and -other adjacent Ports, whereby a great Number of our Mariners are carried into Spanish Prisons, and so inhumanly treated as to put some of them under the hard Necessity of entering into the Spanish Service: That the Petitioners are humbly of Opinion, that most of their Losses might have been prevented had Ships of Force been properly stationed, from the Beginning of the War, and the Commanders kept to the strictest Duty, whereby most of the Privateers from St. Sebajlians, which are daily increasing, would have been disappointed of those Prizes, which unavoidably fell into their Hands (most of them in the Mouth of our Channel); and as our Trade to Newfoundland, and other his Majesty’s Colonies in America, is pretty large, and of great Consequence to the Nation in general, expressing their Hope, that the House will think of some proper Measures for the Security of our Commerce, and the Rights and Freedom of our Navigation: And further representing to the House, That the Petitioners are well feiisfied some Losses will be sustained, and several Captures of our Ships, during the Course of this War, which the Petitioners arc of Opinion his Majesty has, with great Justice, declared against Spain, as abfohately necessary to the Security of our Trade; but such Losses as are unavoidable in the Course of War, the Petitioners arc apprehensive would have been fewer, had such Care been taken as they might reasonably have hoped for, but as yet have been neglected: And therefore praying the House, to take the Premises into Consideration, and to make such Provision in future for the Protection and Security of our Trade, as to the House shall appear fit.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Petition of the subscribing Merchants and Traders of the City of London, in behalf of themselves, and of the Trade of these Kingdoms, is referred.

Ordered, That the proper Officer do lay before this House, Copies of the Returns which have been received since the Commencement of the present War, from such Persons as are, or have been, impowered to pay his Majesty’s Bounty to the British Subjects, Prisoners in the Ports of Spain, in Europe and Africa; distinguishing the Number of Men paid each Month, and what Ships or Vessels they belonged to, when taken by the Spaniards, respectively.

Annoyance The House being informed, that the Sheriffs of the

City of London attended at the Door;

Privateer*. They were called in; and, at the Bar, presented to the House, a Petition of the Lord Mayor, Aldermen, and Commons, of the City of , in Common Council assembled:

And then they withdrew.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read 5 setting forth, That, at a Time when a feeble Enemy holds our Naval Power inDerifion, and the Conduct and Distribution of our Ships of War are the Subject of universal Censure, to remain unconcerned and (ilent would ill become the representative Body of this great Metropolis, which so sensibly shares in every publick Misfortune: That the Petitioners therefore beg Leave humbly to represent to the House, that it is with the utmost Grief they have seen the Navigation and Commerce of these Kingdoms so constantly interrupted on our own Coasts, and almost in Sight of our late powerful Naval Armaments, by the Privateers of Spain, to the Ruin of our Trade, the Enriching of the Enemy, and the Disgrace of the British Name: That the Losses hereby sustained, the Manner in which Applications for Redress have been often evaded, and other numerous lnllances of Negligence and Disregard of the commercial Interest of these Kingdoms (whilll a neighbouring Nation is every Day converting these Errors to their own Advantage), have given the Petitioners the most dreadful Apprehensions, left our Trade, the Foundation of our Wealth and Power, and which has formerly enabled us to maintain the Liberties of Europe, should be transferred into the Hands of our potent and dangerous Rival: That the Petitioners cannot but observe with Concern, that those Ships of War, which they might reasonably have expected would have been employed inprotedingourTrade, have not contributed either thereto, or to the Interest or Honour of this Nation , and that the Petitioners have seen a powerful and well provided Fleet remaining inactive in our own Ports, or more ingloriously putting to Sea tvii hout the Appearance of any Enterprize in View, or even the Possibility of meeting an Enemy worthy of its Attention, whilst our trading Vessels have been daily exposed in the British Channel and Soundings, to the Privateers of a Place so inconsiderable as St. Sebastians; and that, notwithstanding these various Subjects of Complaint, the Petitioners beg the House to believe, that they do not hereby intend to signify the lead Desire of a Peace with until his Majesty shall, by a vigorous Prosecution of the War, have obtained from the Enemy an ample Acknowlegement of his People’s just Rights, and the Possession of such a Pledge as may effectually secure the Freedom of Navigation to our iateft Posterity: And therefore intreating the House to take the calamitous State of Trade, occasioned by the Grievances complained of, into their Confederation; and that the House would be pleased to make such a Provision for the future Security of the Navigation and Commerce of these Kingdoms, as they shall think fit.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Petition of the subscribing Merchants and Traders of the City of London, in behalf of themselves, and of the Trade of these Kingdoms, is referred.

A Person Ordered, That Gabriel Lloyd, of Pettus, do attend this House, upon Thursday the 4th Day of February next.

The other Order of the Day being read;

Carlisle The House proceeded to the Hearing of the Matter

file&ian. of the Petition of Joh Hylton Esquire, complaining of

an undue Election and Return for the City of Carlisle, in the County of Cumberland:

And the Counsel were called in:

And the Petition of John Hylton Esquire, was read:

And the (landing Order of the House, of the 16th Day of January 1735 (for restraining the Counsel at the Bar of this House, or before the Committee of Privileges and Elections, from offering Evidence touching the Legality of Votes for Members to serve in Parliament, for any County, Shire, City, Borough, Cinque-Port, or Place, contrary to the last Determination of the House of Commons), was also read:

And one of the Counsel for the Petitioner was heard, and proposed to produce Evidence, in order to prove that the Petitioner was elected by a Majority of legal Votes:

Whereupon the Sitting Member, in his Place (no Counsel appearing for him), acquainted the House, that he was satisfied that the Petitioner had a Majority of legal Votes; and that he himself had no Right to fit in this House:

And then he withdrew.

And then the Counsel were directed to withdraw'.

A Petition of the Right Honourable James Earl of Moreton was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That by an Act, passed in the Parliament of Scotland, upon the 12th Day of February 1707, her late Majesty Queen Anne, with the Advice and Con lent of the Estates of the said"Parliament, in Consideration of the faithful Service of James then Earl of Moreton, and his Ancestorsrand;for other the Confederations therein recited, did dissolve from the Crown, and the Patrimony thereof, the whole Earldom of Orkney, and the Lord ship of Jet-land, with the whole Jurisdictions, Rights, Casualties, and Privileges thereunto belonging (except the Right of Admiralty thereof), thereby refeinding and voiding certain other Acts of the said Parliament of Scotland, whereby the said Earldom and Lordship were annexed to the Crown, and made Part of the Patrimony and Demesnes thereof, to the End that her Majesty might convey and make over the same to the said Earl, and his Heirs; subject never* theless to a Power of Redemption by her said Majesty, and her Royal Successors, on Payment of£. 360,000 Scots, or £. 30,000 Sterling; to be held by the said Earl, and his Heirs, of her Majesty, and her Royal Successors, in Fee-Farm, paying a yearly Rent of £. 6,000 Scotch, or £. 500 Sterling, in the Name of Few-Duty, by half-yearly Payments, till such time as such Redemption should be made, and double the said annual Rent or Few-duty, at the Entry of every Heir, and administring Justice to the Lieges in the several Offices of Jurisdiction thereby granted, the said Earl, his Heirs and Successors, paying also the yearly Sum of £. 1,600 Scotch, to the Ministers of the Gospel jn Orkney, or such other Sums as were or should be modified, by way of Augmentation to the said Ministers, out of the Tythes, by the said Act disponed; which laid yearly Payments were to be in lieu of all other Burden, Exaction, Question, Demand, or Service, which could be any-ways asked or required out of the said Earldom, Lordship, Illes, Lands, Offices, Juriididi ms, and other Tilings in the said Act mentioned, during the Non-redemption of the said Premises/reservingallHaufks belonging to her said Majesty, with the Fa.ulkners Salaries, and Vox* 24,

other Casualties to them belonging, conform to former Custom; and by the said Act all former and other Acts annexing the fiiid Earldom of Orkney, and Lord ship of Zetland, with the Appurtenances to the Crown, were repealed; with a Reservation nevertheless, of the Right and Jurisdiction of Admiralty, which was not to be comprehended therein: That, in pursuance of the said Act of Parliament, her laid late Majesty Queen Anne was, by her Royal Charter, bearing Date 18th Day of February, in the same Year 1707, graciously pleated to grant and convey, in Fee, to the said James Earl of Moreton, and his Heirs male, and in Default thereof, to his Heirs general (fub-jed nevertheless to such Right of Redemption in the Crown, as contained in the said recited Act of Parliament), the said Earldom of Orkney, and "Lordship of Zetland, with all and every the Lands, Lordships, Royalties, Offices, Jurisdictions, Duties, Rights, Powers, and Privileges, thereto belonging (redeemable always by her Majesty, and her Royal Successors, upon Payment of the Sums mentioned in the said recited Act, to be holden by the said Earl, and his Heirs, in manner and upon Payment of such yearly Duties as in the said Act expressed); and that by another Act of the Parliament of Scotland, patted upon the Twenty-first Day of March, in the same Year 1707, the said Royal Charter of her Majesty Queen Anne was ratified and confirmed, and the said Earl, and his Heirs, were thereby enfeoffed of the Premises, according to the usual Form: That the annual Rents and Profits arising from the Premises, so comprised in the said Royal Grant, and Acts of Parliament, to the said James, Earl of Moreton, the Petitioner’s Ancestor, after deduding the Few-Duty, thereby made payable to the Crown, and the other Charges and necessary Out-gbings, do not amount, one Year with another, to£. 1,350 Annum; which, supposing the same to be duly and regularly received, would not be sufficient to answer and discharge the legal interestof the said £. 30,000 Sterling; and the said Rents are so ill paid, that there is now in Arrear £. 6,000 Sterling, and upwards, notwithstanding the utmost Care in collecting the same; so that it can never become the Interest of the Crown to redeem the same: That the said Estate and Premises are capable of confiaerable Improve- menrs, by draining and cultivating several Tracts of marlhy and barren Grounds* which now lie wholly useless, and uncultivated; and by building Houses, and setting up Stands, on Convenient Parts of the Sea Coasts, adjacent thereto, for the Purposes of carrying on of a Fishery; and which Undertaking the natural Situation of the Estate, as well as the several Ports, Creeks, and Havens, belonging thereto, seem in a particular manner to invite and call for; and which, being an Undertaking of a publick Nature, mud necessarily, if it succeeds, redound to the Benefit and Advantage of the Kingdom in general.; but as the Accomplishment thereof cannot be effected But at a very great Charge and Expence, and at the Rilque and Hazard of the Petitioner, the Petitioner is discouraged from Undertaking the fame, in regard to the precarious Nature of his present Title to the said Estate and Premises, by reason of the said Right of Redemption, which will at all times (land out against the Petitioner, though the Petitioner hath no Method, in the ordinary Course of Proceedings, to compel such Redemption of the Premises, or the Payment of the saidjf. 30,000. And therefore, and as the Income of the said Estate is not near sufficient todischargeeventhe interestof the said £. 30,00 o, and as what the Petitioner is now applying for will not prejudice ordiminish any Branch of the Royal Revenue, but, on the contrary, tend to increase and enlarge -the fame, if his intended Undertaking be attended wirh Success y praying, that Leave may be given to bring in a Hill for diflbiving and disannexing from the Crown,^nd the Patrimony thereof, for ever, the said Earldom of Orkney, and Lordship of Zetland, with all Lands, Jurisdictions, Rights, Privileges, and Appurtenances thereto belonging, and for veiling the same irredeemable in the Petitioner, and his Heirs, discharged from any Power or Right of Redemption whatever, iu his Majesty, his Heirs, or Successors*

A Petition of the Merchants, Masters, and Owners of Ships, belonging to the Town of Whitehaven, in the County of Cumberland, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioners carry on a cori-siderable Trade to America, and other Places, which has been greatly interrupted by Numbers of Spanish Privaw teers, lying in and about the Latitude of Cape Clear, a Head-Land, which all Ships from the West Indies, that intend for the South Channel, endeavour to make in their Return Home, whereby several of the Petitioners, Ships have been taken, and carried into St. Sebastians and other Spanish Ports: That the Petitioners have alro greatly suffered by the Negligence of Men of War, stationed in America, and particularly in Virginia, upon which Coast many Ships have been taken by the Spanish Privateers, and some in Sight of the Man of War, at her Moorings* And that the Petitioners have likewise been great Sufferers by having their Seamen impresstrd in Virginia, by which, fi veral of their Ships have been disabled from returning Home: And therefore praying. That the House will takfc the Premises into Consideration, and that such Provisions may be made for the future Protection of the Trade and Navigation of these Kingdoms, as to the House shall seem meet.

A Message from the Lords, by Mr. Elde and Mr. Sawyer:

Mr. Speaker,

The Lords have passed a Bill, intituled, An Act to enable Sir Clement Cottrell Knight, and other the Devi-fees of the real Estate of Lieutenant-General James Dormer, deceased, to take and use the Surname of Dormer, pursuant and according to the Tenor and Purport of the Will of the said James Dormer: To which the Lords desire the Concurrence of this House: And also.

Oldfwinsford, in the County of IVtorcester, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Town of Stowerbridge is a populous Market-Town, and inhabited by great Numbers of Persons employed in the Woollen, Iron, and Glass Manufactures in the said Town and Parish; and that the said Town of Stozver bridge, in the said Pariflb, is a Mile distant from the Parish-Church of Old-fwinsford, which is not sufficient to contain Half the Inhabitants, who would willingly have attended Divine Service there; and that, by the voluntary Contributions of several Inhabitants of the said Town and Parish, and Places near the fame, a Church hath been lately built in the said Town, in which Divine Service is performed, according tcJ the Usage of the Church of England; and that the Inhabitants of the said Town have for several Years maintained the Poor of the said Town by a separate Levy from other Parts of the said Parish, under the Care of different Overseers; and that the Petitioners are desirous that the Town of Stowerbridge may be afeparate Parish in all respectrs, except being liable to the Tythes in the said Town ship, and a Levy for repairing the said Mother-Church; and that Part of the Common called the Short Heath, about Fifteen Acres, and Twenty Acres of Common, near the said Town, on the South Side of a Pool called the Gigmill-Pool, may be inclosed, and exempt from Tythes and Parochial Taxes, as a Glebe to the said new Church, and that Two Shillings a Kneeling in the bed Seats, being Half the present Kate, and the like Half Rate of the other Kneelings, may be payable to the Minister; and that the Inhabitants, who, for their Dwelling-houses, shall be assessed at the greatest Rates towards the Parochial Levies, may, from time to time, have the first Choice of Seats; and that the Presentation may be in the Right Honourable the Lord Foley: And therefore praying the House to give Leave that a Bill may be brought in for the Purposes aforesaid.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House:
