2d February,) IN Obedience to the Directions of an Act, passed in the Eighth Year of his Majesty’s Reign, inti* 1741. 3 tuled, An Act for the Application of the Rents and Profits of the Estates forfeited by the Attain*

ders of James late Earl of Dervoentwater and Charles;

Requiring the Commissioners or Governors of the Royal Hospital for Seamen at , to contract and agree

with able and sufficient Tradesmen, Artificers, or other Persons, for finishing and completing the said Royal Hospital in a Workman-like and substantial manner, on the easiest and most realOnableTerms, according toja Plan laid before the Honourable House of Commons, and to lay their Proceedings therein before his Majesty, and both Houses of Parliament, respectively.

THE Commissioners or Governors of the said Hospital do humbly report as followeth:

There has been received, between the 1 ft of December 1740, and 30th November 1741, out of the Rents of the Estate -

As to their Proceedings, in carrying on the Building

In King Charles's Court;

The Governor’s Apartment is completely finished, likewise the Board-Room and Waiting-Room adjoining; greatest Part of the Chimneys are examined, and secured from Fire, and the Water is laid into the said Court, from the great Reservoir.

In Queen Ann's Court;

South Pavision, the Stair-Cafe, and Paving of the Gallery, are done; the Apartments, One Pair of Stairs, Mezzanine and Attick Stories, are quite finished. Painting and Cleaning excepted.

In Queen Mary's Court;

The Tower and Dome, at the End of the Chapel, are up to the Lanthorn, the Colonade is quite covered in, and the Vaulting of the said Colonade is finished; the Communication-Passage between King William's and Queen Mary's Court is made; the Vaulting of the First Floor of the East Building is finished, and Stone Steps carried up near the Top of the Building; the Frames and Salhes in the First Floor and One Pair of Stairs are made, put in, and glazed; great Part of the Mezzanipe Floor is laid, and all the Floor of the Attick Story, and the Upper Story, in the Roof for the Boys Apartment, and School-Room, is finished.

The Brew-house, and Brewing Utensils, are likewise finished, and all set up.

The Works done this Year, and brought to Account, amount to the Sum of Eight thousand Fifty-three Pounds Seventeen Shillings and Six Pence -

The ordinary Works done this Year, amount to the Sum of Two thousand One hundred Sixty-four Pounds Seven Shillings and Nine Pence ——

Five Miles at least below Brandon Ferry: Thar, by Length of Time, and other Accidents, the Navigation of the said River is greatly damaged, and in Danger of becoming useless, although the Petitioners, within these Thirty Years last pad, have expended considerable Sums of Money, in order to preserve the fame: That the Petitioners are advised, that it is necessary for Two new large Sluices to be creded or built, and one of them to be placed between Brandon Ferry and aforesaid; which,

with other necessary Repairs, will be so great a Charge to them, that they are not anle to go through with, unless the Tolls or Rates for Carriage of Goods be extended below Brandon Ferry to IVkite house aforesaid; and as the Town of Brandon has an equal, if not a superior, Benefit with the Town of Thetford by the said Navigation, it is hoped they shall contribute towards making the same more effectual, by paying some Toll or Rate for all Goods pairing between Btandon and the Place called the Whitehouse aforesaid: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for the maintaining and supporting the Navigation of the said River; and that the present Tolls may be extended from Thetford down to the -Vol. 24.

A Petition of the Gentlemen, Matter-Clothiers, and WooSm others, Inhabitants of the Town of Shepton Mallet, in the Trad* County of SomerJel, vi2& presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Woollen Manufacture, which hath, for a long Series of Years, been esteemed the Staple Trade of this Nation, hath, by Experience, been found to be the Source of our Wealth and Power, as well as to yield a comfortable Support to vail Multitudes of our Poor; and that, notwithstanding the Vigilance and Attention of the Legislature to guard against all Irregularities, which might arise in this Trade, and to protest and encourage this useful Manufacture, by good Laws, several great Abuses have been of late introduced, to the great Loss of our national Trade, Injury of the Poor, and Distress of the Fabricators, or Master-Clothiers, whereby the Trade is in a languishing Condition; which, if not timely remedied, may have very pernicious Consequences, and end in the Ruin of the Manufacture, sinking the Value of the Lands, Loss of great Part of our Commerce, and the Dcllruftion of our Country: That, among the many Abuses which have crept into the Trade, the Petitioners apprehend the illicit and destructive Licence many Persons have taken of late Years to set up the Trade, and exercise the Art and Mystery, of Mallei -Clothier, without having either served a lawful Apprenticeship to the fame, or having a proper Skill in the Manufacture, and oftentimes without having any S ub-stance or sufficient Stock to carry it on, have been the great Source and Spring of these Calamities and Miffortunes: And further representing, Thar those Men of little Skill, and low Fortunes, who have engaged in the;

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Number of Land Forces, for Guards, Garrisons, and other Services (including Two thousand Three hundred and Twenty-three Invalids), amounting to Thirty-five thousand Five hundred and Fifty-four effective Men, Commission and Non-Commission Officers included, be employed for the Service of the Year 1742.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That aSum, not exceeding One million and Four thousand Nine hundred and Forty-seven Pounds and Ten Pence, be granted to his Majesty, for defraying the Charge of the Voi. 24.

said Thirty-five thousand Five hundred and Fifty-four effective Men, for Guards and Garrisons, and other Services, in Great Britain, West Indies, Guernsey, and Jersey'y for the Year 1742.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That Eleven thousand Five hundred and Fifty Marines (Commission and Non-Commissioni Officers included); employed for the Year 1741, be continued for the Service of the Year 1742.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Two hundred and Six thousand Two hundred and Fifty-three Pounds and Fifteen Shillings, be granted to his Majesty, for defraying the Charge of the said Eleven thousand Five hundred and Fifty Marines, Commission and Non-Commission Officers included, for the Service of the Year 1742.

Resolved, Thajt it is the Opinion of this Committee; That a Sum, not exceeding Fifty-three thousand Nine hundred and Ninety-five Pounds Thirteen Shillings and Four Pence, be granted to his Majesty, for maintaining a Regiment of Foot raised in America, for the Service in the West Indies, for the Year 1742.

Kejolved, That William Myddelton Esquire, High-Sheriff of the County of Denbigh, at the last Election of a Knight of the Shire to serve icr Parliament for the said County, having taken upon himself to return John Myddelton Esquire, as Knight of the Shire to serve in this present Parliament for the said County, contrary to the Majority of Votes received by him upon the Poll, and to his own Declaration of the Numbers at the Close of the Poll, without any publick subsequent Examination Into the Rights of the Voters, previous to such Return; and having afterwards presumed to alter the said Poll, in order to give a Colour to such Return, has acted partially, arbitrarily, and illegally, in Defiance of the Laws, in manifest Violation of the Rights of the Freeholders of the said County, and in Breach of the Privilege of this House.

Ordered, That the said William Myddelton Esquire be, for his said Offence, committed Prisoner to his Majesty’s Gaol of Newgate; And that Mr. Speaker do issue his Warrants accordingly.

Resolved, That an humble Address be presented to his Majesty, That he will be graciously pleased to give directions for removing the said William Myddelton Esquire, from being Receiver-General of the Land-Revenue ir> North Wales', and also from being one of his Majesty’s Justices of the Peace for the County of Denbigh, and for die County of Flint.

by an Act passed in the Ninth of Queen Anne, the Sum of Four thousand Pounds per Annum, for a certain Term of Years, was granted to the said Commissioners towards repairing and finishing the Collegiate Church of St.

Peter Westminster, and the Chapels of the fame; and, in order to the Finiftiing thereof, as directed by Parliament, Sir Christopher Wren, the then Surveyor, formed a Design of erecting a Spire on the middle Tower; a Model of which he then prepared, and a Draught of which, with the rest of the intended Building, has been laid before this House: That, by several Acts passed in the Reign of his present Majesty King George the Second, several Sums of Four thousand Pounds have been issued and applied towards carrying on the said Work, and a considerable Progress has been made therein, and an Account how the Money has been expended, has been annually laid before this House: That, to facilitate the said Repairs, Two of the Prebendal Houses, and Three Leasehold Tenements, lately {landing in St. Margaret's Churchyard, have been taken down, and thereby the whole North Side of the Church, from the North to the West Gate, has been laid open; but that the Monies already granted being nearly expended, the said Works will soon be at a Stand: That the said Dean and Chapter are highly sensible of the Favours already conferred on the said Collegiate Church, and hope that the good Work, so far advanced by the Aid of former Parliaments, will meet with the like Encouragement and Assistance from the present: And praying for the Continuance thereof.

The Counsel for the Sitting-Members insisted, that it was not conformable to the Methods of Proceeding, to determine the Merits of the Return, exclusive of the Merits of the Election, except in Cafes where feme Irregularity appeared upon the Face of the Return, or Where the

the same was not executed by the proper Returning-

That the Poll is not Part of the Return; and that the Return cannot be justified without entering into the Merits of the Election (which, they observed, the Petitioners Counsel had in some degree entered into): That this was not the First Instance of a Return made contrary to a Majority upon the Face of the Poll; the like being the same in the Election for the County of Flint in the last Parliament; and that, on the Hearing of the Merits of that Election, the 24th of March 1736, the House did not allow, that the Counsel for the Sitting-Member should be directed to proceed, in order to juf-tify the Return, before the Merits of the Election were proceeded upon:

That though there may be an apparent Majority upon the Poll, the same may not be a legal Majority; and as the Returning Officer is impowered by Law, as well as bound by Oath, judicially to determine upon the Legality of Votes, according to the last Determination of the House of Commons, his Return is presumed to be the Result of that Judgment:

And they alleged. That, pursuant to the Resolution of the House, read at the Opening of the Hearing of this Election, the Votes of several Freemen, made contrary to that Resolution, who offered to Poll, were rejected, and others, though admitted, were polled with Queries.

They further alleged,

That the Petitioners Agents had no Right to infill upon the Scrutiny’s being put off, when the Sitting-Members Agents were ready to proceed:

And that thereupon Serjeant , who was legally deputed to act as Returning Officer, did afterwards disallow the Votes of the Freemen made in 1728 and 1729, and declared a Majority for the Sitting-Members.

In Reply to which, the Petitioners Counsel answered. That the Poll is conclufiye Evidence } and that the same cannot; be altered but by a Scrutiny; which, in the present Cafe, was. not proceeded in, by reason the Sitting-Members Agents infilled upon an unreasonable Preliminary i and that though they admitted a Returning Officer had a Right to exercise his Judgment in reconsidering the Poll, yet it did not appear such Judgment had been exercised in this Instance.

And it being the Opinion of the Committee, that the Counsel should be called in; and that the Counsel for the Sitting-Members should be directed to proceed to justify the Return, without entering into the Merits of the Election;

The Counsel for the Sitting-Members were so directed; and they proceeded to open the Matter, which they intended to offer in Justification thereof:

And being directed to withdraw j The Committee were informed, that the Sitting-Members did not desire to give the Committee, or the Petitioners, any further Trouble as to the Return. Whereupon the Committee Came to the following Resolutkons:

A Petition of the Mayor, Aldermen, Gentlemen, TrtW Tradesmen, and principal Inhabitants, of the Borough Navigatloo> of Newark upon Trent, in the County of Nottingham, was presented to the House, and read; setting torth.

That the said Town of Newark is a considerable Town of Trade for Corn, Coal, Wool, and other Merchandize; and that the River Trent divides into Two Branches, or Channels, from above the Place called the Upper Wear, in the Parish of Averham, in the said County of Nottingham, being upwards of Two Miles from the said Borough; one of which Branches, or Channels, runs under the Borough and Castle of the said Town of Newark, and joins again with the other Branch below a Place commonly called the Crankleys, in the Parish of South kam, in the said County of Nottingham, being near Two Miles below the said Town of Newark: That the Navigation through the Branch of the said River under the Borough of Newark, by reason of Mills erected, and by several Dams made across the same >n the Time of the late civil Wars, is quite obstructed; and the Petitioners, of late Years, by reason of several Sands and Snoals formed in the said Branch, have been obliged to land their Goods and Merchandize in the Meadows (the Property ol divers Perf ms) upwards of a Mile dillant from the said Town; and what Goods or Merchandize the Petitioners have Oc-calion to convey up the Trent, they are obliged to lend Two Miles by Land-Carriage, and there leave them exposed to the Weather on the Banks of the said River; and as the Petitioners are discharged from landing any more Goods or Merchandize in the said Meadows, the Petitioners are quite destitute of either Navigation or Wharf: And therefore praying, That a Bill may be brought in for making that Branch, or Channel, of the River Trent navigable from below the Place commonly called the Crankleys, in the Parish of South Mufiam, to above the Upper Wear, in the Parish of Averham aforesaid.

The Lord Mayor of London reported from the said Committee, the Resolutions which they had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same were read, and are-as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee, That, notwithstanding the repeated Applications of the Merchants for Cruizers to be properly Rationed for the Protection of the Trade of this Nation from the Privateers of the Enemy, the due and necessary Care has not been taken to keep a proper Number of his Majesty’s Ships em- . ployed in that Service, more especially in and near the Channel and Soundings; for want of which, many Ships have been taken by the Enemy, some of them of considerable Value, to the great Loss of many of his Majesty’s Subjects, the great Advantage and Encouragement of the Enemy, and the Dictionour of this Nation.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Detcntion of the Fleet of Merchant Ships botmd to Portugal, for near Twelve Months, by the Refusal of Protections for some time, and the Delay of Convoy afterwards, gave our Rivals in Trade an Opportunity of introducing new Species of their'Woollen Manufactures into Portugal, to the great Detriment of this Kingdom.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the House be moved for Leave to bring in a Bill for the better protecting and securing the Trade and Navigation of this Kingdom in Times of War.

The First Resolution of the (hid Committee being read a Second time, w.as, upon the Question put thereupon* agreed to by the House,

The Lord William Manners reported from the Com- Trent mittee, to whom the Petition of the Mayor, Aldermen, Navigation, Gentlemen, Tradesmen, and principal Inhabitants, of the Borough of Nezvark upon Trent, in the County of Nottingham, was referred, That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House:

And he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was* read; and is as followeth $ viz.

i! 2 5* — 8° Martiu A

To prove the Allegations of the Petition, Mr. Robert Sprigging, Agent for the Petitioners, called

Mr. Robert Hall, who said, That he was born in, and knows, the Town of Newark very well: That the same is a considerable Town of Trade for Corn, Coals, Wool, and other Merchandize; which Commodities, when they are to be sent or brought by Water up or down the Trent, must be carried about Two Miles to and from the said Town by Land; and that Waggons and other Car-gages, that bring Corn to the said Town, and load back with Coals, which is a large Branch of Commerce there, are obliged to go Two Miles to fetch them; which might be avoided, by making that Branch of the River navigable from the Parting of the Stream at the upper Wear, to its joining again at the Crankleys, which at present is prevented by Sands and Shoals,

The Reverend Mr, Matt hew Bradford, being examined, confirmed the aforesaid Evidence, so far as the same relates to the Trade of the Town, and the Difficulty of navigating that Part of the River before-mentioned.

Then he laid before the Committee, a Plan of the Two Branches of the River, from their Dividing at the upper Wear, and their Joining again at the Crankleys.

He allb laid before the Committee a Weekly Paper, published according to Order of Parliament, dated March 13th, 1646, and intituled, Perfect Occurrences of both Houses of Parliament, and Martial Affairs; by which it appeared, that, at the time, there was a Design of turning the Stream of that Branch of the River which runs near Newark.

He further said, That he, by the Proprietors Order, had given Notice to the Inhabitants of Newark, and all other Persons, that no more Goods should be laid in the Meadows, where Goods are now laid, to be sent or brought by the Barges, the Meadows being much prejudiced by that Practice; he having fcen Twenty Horses feeding in the Meadows at one time, while the Carriages were loading and unloading with Commodities that were brought there, and were to be carried by Water; and the different Tracts the Carriages made in coming to the Wharfs; notwithstanding which, he had granted a Liberty fbr Persons to lay their Goods as before, till an Act of Parliament could be obtained this Session, for making the aforesaid Branch of the River navigable, which runs through Newark, as appeared to your Committee by a Paper laid before them, signed M. Bradford, Rector of Colling ham, dated July 15th, 1741.

Mr. Robert Hearne and Mr. Robert Spraggirg severally confirmed the Evidence of Robert Hall; and further said. That, by the aforesaid Notice, if an Act of Parliament for making the aforesaid Branch that runs near Newark navigable could not be obtained, the Inhabitants would have neither Wharfs nor Navigation;

That great Quantities of Goods are sent from Newark to Derby, Nottingham, and other Places of great Trade, by Water; and the Navigation being at present Two Miles from Nnvark, the Traders are obliged iometimes to leave their Goods exposed to the Weather a Day, Day and Half, or Two Days, for an Opportunity of Barges, as they go sooner or later, as the Wind serves; by which Delays, Goods are often damaged, to the great Loss of the Owner.

They were severally asked, If any Alteration was de-(igned to the upper Wear ? They said, Not as to the Dimensions; and that the Course of the River would not be at all prejudiced, as they thought and believed, by the intended Navigation.’

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for making the Branch or Channel of the River Trent navigable from the Dividing of the Stream at a Place called the Upper Wear, in the County of Nottingham, to their Joining again at a Place called the Crankleys, in the same County: And that the Lord William Manners and Mr. Charlton do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

A Petition of the Trustees, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, fot putting in Execution an Act of Parliament, passed in the 7th Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the First, intituled, An Act for repairing the several Roads leading from the Town of Led-? bury, in the County of Hereford, to the several Places therein mentioned, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That several Tolls were granted and made payable by the Laid Ad, for the Term therein mentioned, for repairing several Roads leading from the said Town of Ledbury; which,'computed together, amounted in Length to upwards of Thirty Miles; which Roads, at the Time of passing the said Act, were in a very ruinous Condition; and that although the Petitioners have caused the Money arising by the said Tolls to be justly applied towards repairing the said Roads, pursuant to the said Act, yet, by reason of the Length and Badness'of the Road directed to be repaired, and the Smallness of the Income arising yearly from the said Tolls, the Petitioners have not been able to repair all the said Roads; and that such Parts of the said Roads as have already been amended, unless constant Care be taken to look after the fame, and keep them in Repair (being in a deep Soil, and heavy Carriages frequently passing over them) will, in afhort time, become ruinous, and almost impassable; nor can the said Roads be effectually amended, and kept in Repair, without an Enlargement of the said Term: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for enlarging the Term and Powers by the said Act: granted, for such time, and in such manner, as to the House shall seem meet.

Were severally produced to the Committee, and read.

Then the Petitioners called,

Mr. John Chambers, and Mr. John Inman, who feve-' rally laid, That the Poor of the said Town are very much increased within these Ten Years, inso much that the yearly Sums, which the said Corporation are, by both the before-mentioned Acts, impowered to raise, are not sufficient to maintain the Poor under their Care; and that the said Corporation, by supplying their Necessities, are become greatly indebted: To remedy which, the Corporation are desirous that a Bill may be brought in for the Purposes expressed in the Petition.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for explaining, amending, and making more effectual, Two Acts, one passed in the Ninth and Tenth Years of the Reign of his late Majesty King William the Third, for erecting Workhouses, and Houses of Correction, in the Town of Kingston upon Hull, for the Employment and Maintenance of the Poor there, and the other passed in the Eighth Year of the Reign of her late Majesty Queen Anne, for the more effectual Provision of the Poor in the said Town: And that Mr. CroColonel Bladen, and Mr. Carter, do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

Woollen A Petition of the Gentlemen and Clothiers of the Manufacture. County of Wilts, in behalf of themselves, and many Thousands, Manufacturers, employed in the Woollen Ma -i nufadory, in the said County, was presented to the House, and read; representing to the House, That, notwithstanding the Care of the Legislature to guard against the Irregularities which might arise in the Mystery of Clothmaking, several great Abuses have of late crept into the lame, to the great Loss of the Nation, Distress of thp Poor, and Injury of the Mailer Clothiers, whereby the said Trade is reduced to a languishing Condition; which, if not timely remedied, the Petitioners conceive will be attended with the moll pernicious Consequences, and end in the Ruin of the Manufacture, to the great Loss of our national Commerce; and that among these, the Petitioners apprehend, the illicit Liberty many Persons have taken of late Years, to let up this Trade, without having either served a lawful Apprenticeship to the lame, or having proper Skill in the Manufacture, hath been one great Source of the Evils and Abuses which have been introduced into it, and a great cause of the Decay of this valuable Manufacture; and that by this destrudive Liberty upon every little Motion of Trade, Persons of little or no Skill have rulhed into this Occupation, debauched the labouring Hands, and thereby occasioned these Goods to be made in a scandalous and deceitful manner, to the great Discredit of this Commodity at foreign Markets; and at the same time raised the Price of Labour, by their Imprudence, to such an exorbitant Height, as the Nature of the Manufacture will not bear, whereby Clothiers of Skill and Reputation have not been able to carry on their Trade, as formerly, and many of them have been forced to abfoond, and become Bankrupts, and others to leave off Trade: And that this pernicious Practice, instead of being advantageous to the Poor, tends apparently to their Injury, by drawing many raw and unexperienced labouring Hands into the Trade, more than the Manufacture, in the greatest Extent, could ever support, they having, for many Years, been employed in an uncertain manner, having Work only at particular Seasons of the Year, being sometimes over-paid for their Voi. 24.

Martiu 117

Labour, and other times under-paid, and often without any Work at all; from whence, at one time they arc insolent, idle, debauched, and mutinous, through the extravagant Wages they receive; and at another time languishing in distressed Circumstances, and thereby become a Burthen upon the Parishes: And further, that these Men of little or no Skill, who have suddenly engaged in the Trade, to compensate for the extravagant Wages they give, have often paid the Poor in Truck, in lieu ot Money, and used other oppressive Methods, which have brought an Odium upon the Reputation of the Clothiers in general, though without any Foundation: And that, by an Act, made in the Fourth and Fifth Years of the Reign of King Philip and Queen , it is, amongst other things, enacted, " That no Person shall make any " Woollen Cloths, or Kerseys, to be sold, unless such Persons shall have been Apprentices to the Oecupation of making and rowing of Cloth, or Kerseys, or " have been exercised therein by the space of Seven " Years before, upon the Pain of Forfeiture of such " Cloth, or the Value thereof," in order, as the Petitioners apprehend, to prevent unskilful Persons from entering into the Trade; which Ad has proved ineffectual to produce this good End; praying, therefore, the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and that Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for the better regulating of the Cloathing-Trade; or that the Petitioners may have such other Relief as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

Ways The House resolved itself into a Committee of the and Means. wh0je House, to consider further of Ways and Means for raising the Supply granted to his Majesty,

Mr. Speaker left the Chair.

Mr. Francis Fane took the Chair of the Committee,' Mr. Speaker resumed the Chair.

Mr. Francis Fane reported from the Committee, That they had come to a Resolution; which they had directed him to report, when the House will please to receive the same. '

Ordered, That the Report be, received upon Monday Morning next.

Mr. Francis Fane also acquainted the House, That he was directed by the Committee to move. That they may-have Leave to lit again.

Resolved, That this House will, upon fVednesday Morning next, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider further of Ways and Means for raising the Supply granted to his Majesty. '

And then the House adjourned till Monday Morning next, Nine of the Clock.

Woollen A Petition of the Gentlemen and Clothiers of the Maftufrdure* county of Gloucester, in behalf of themselves, and many Thousand Manufacturers employed in> the Woollen Manufactory in the said County, was presented to the House, and read; representing to the House, That, notwithstanding the Care of the Legislature to guard again!! the Irregularities and Evils which might arise in the Mystery of Cloth-making, several great Abuses have of late crept into the fame, to the great Loss of the Nation, Distress of the Poor, and Injury of the Mailer-Clothiers, whereby the said Trade is reduced to a Ianguishing Condition, which, if not timely remedied, will, as the Petitioners conceive, be attended with the mofi pernicious Consequences, and end in the Ruin of the Manufacture; and that, among these, the Petitioners apprehend, the illicit Liberty many Persons have taken of late Years to set up this Trade, without having either served a lawful Apprenticeship to the fame, or having proper Skill in the Manufacture, hath been one great Source of the Evils and Abuses introduced into it, and a great Cause of the Decay of this valuable Manufacture; and that, by this destructive Liberty, upon every little. Motion of Trade, Persons of little or no Skill have rushed into this Occupation, debauched the labouring Hands, and thereby occasioned these Goods to be made in a scandalous and deceitful manner, to the Discredit of this Commodity at foreign Markets, and at the same time, raised the Price of Labour to such an exorbitant Height, as the Nature of the Manufacture will not bear; whereby' Clothiers of Skill and Reputation have not been able to carry on their Trade as formerly, and many of them have been forced to abscond, and become Bankrupts, and others to leave off Trade; and that this pernicious Practice, instead of being advantageous to the Poor, tends apparently to their Injury, by drawing many unexperienced Hands into the Trade, more than the Manufacture, in its greatest Extent, could ever support; they having, for many years, been employed in an uncertain Manner, having Work only at particular Seasons, being sometimes over-paid for their Labour, and at other times under-paid, and often without any Work at all; from whence, at one time they are insolent, idle, debauched, and mutinous, through the extravagant Wages they receive, and another time in distressed circumstances, and a Burthen upon the Parishes: And further, that these Men of little or no Skill, who have suddenly engaged in the Trade, to compensate for the extravagant Wages they give, have often paid the Poor in Truck, in lieu of Money, and used other of-preffive Methods, which have brought an Odium upon the Reputation of the Clothiers in general, though without any just Foundation: And further representing to the House, That, by an Act made in the 4th and 5th Years of the Reign of King Philip and Queen Mary, it is, amongst other things, Enacted, " That no Person shall " make any Woollen Cloths, or Kerseys, to be sold, M unless such Person shall have been Apprentice to the

Occupation of making and rowing of Cloth and Kerleys, or have been exercised therein by the Space

of Seven Years before, upon Pain or Forfeiture of " such Cloth, or the Value thereofin order, as the Petitioners apprehend, to prevent unskilful Persons from entering into the Trade; but that the said Act has proved

ineffectual to produce this good End: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration; and that Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for the better Regulating of the Clothing-Trade; or that they may have such other Relief, as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Gentlemen and Clothiers of the County of Wilts, in behalf of themselves, and many Thousands, Manufacturers employed in the Woollen Manufactory in the said County, is referred: And that they do examine the Matter of this Petition; and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House.

A Petition of Elizabeth Rogers Spinster, Daughter and Rogett,i foie Executrix of George Rogers Esquire, deceased, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That Company, the Petitioner’s late Father was a Subscriber for Five hundred Pounds Stock, in the Fourth Money Subscription, into the South Sea Company, in the Year 1720, and paid in the Sum of One thousand Pounds thereon; and the Petitioner’s laid Father was a great Sufferer by the Miffortunes of that Year, went abroad, and died in or about the Year 1735 That the Petitioner, for upwards of Five Years past, has made Application to the Sub-Governor, Deputy-Governor, and Court of Directors, of the said Company to have Credit allowed her for the fame; and had Hopes of Success, as nothing of that kind had been refused till lately, when the Petitioner’s Agent was told by the Court of Directors, that the Statute of the 9th of King George the First was a Bar to the Petitioner’s Demand; which the Petitioner conceives, and is advised, could not be the Intention of that Act, as the Petitioner's Father was abroad, and ignorant thereof: And therefore, as Sir Charles Vernon, and others, have been relieved in a like Cafe, praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for farther Time to be allowed for making good such Claim on the said Company, or as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of John Byrom, M. A. and F. R. S. was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioner, by long and diligent Application, hath invented a new Method of Shorthand; thereby that Art, peculiar to our Country, and remarkably applicable to our Language, may be rendered much more serviceable upon many Accounts, being reduced to an easy, beautiful, and regular Sydem, for general Use, as several Gentlemen, who have experienced the Utility and Perfection thereof, are ready to atted: That the Petitioner is willing to publish the same for that Purpose; but an Attempt having been lately made to deprive the Petitioner of the Benefit of this his said Invention, the Petitioner is apprehensive, that the like or other Devices may be used, to his Injury, and to the Loss of that general Conveniency, which uniform Practice in a thing of this Nature mud produce; and that the Petitioner is informed, that he cannot effectually secure to himself the foie Right and Property therein, whereby to render his Discovery more extensively fer-

A Petition of the late Mayor, Aldermen, Assistants, and Common-Council, and of the free Burgesses, and Inhabitants, of the Town of Colchester, in the County of Essex, whose Names are thereupto subscribed, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That King Charles the lid, by his Letters-Patent, dated the 3d of August, in the 15th Year of his Reign, confirmed to the said Borough all their Rights, Franchises, and Privileges, Before that Time granted, or otherwise belonging to the said Borough, and incorporated the same anew, by the Name of the Mayor and Commonalty of the Borough of Colchester, in riie County of Essex, therein preferring the Methods they shall take for Time to come, in the Choice of Mayor, Aldermen, Assistants, Common-Council, and other Officers, for the Service of the said Corporation: That King William and Queen Mary, by their Letters-Patent, dated on the 27th Day of July, in the 5th Yoar of their Reign, reciting the said Letters-Patent of King Charles the lid, did confirm the fame, and all the Ffan-chises, Grants, and Directions, therein contained: That, by the Inattention or Mistake of the Officers belonging to the said Borough, the Mayors, Aldermen, Assistants, and Common-Council, and other Officers of the said Corporation, have been chosen into their respective Offices, in a manner not exactly consonant to the Directions in the aforesaid Charters contained; which Mistake having been lately- discovered, and Informations, in the Nature of Q^tto Warrant os, having been thereupon brought against the last Mayor and all "the Aldermen of the said Borough now living, they have all disclaimed upon Record, ih his Majesty’s Court of King’s Bench, their Rights of acting as Aldermen of the said Borough, and in consequence thereof, there is no Person or Persons, now acting as Mayor or Aldermen of the Borough aforesaid: That by the aforesaid Charters, the Mayor and Recorder for the Time being, the Mayor of the preceding Year, and Two of the other Aldermen, nominated by the free Burgesses of the said Town, are appointed to be Justices of the Peace within the said Borough-, and die Liberties thereof, which extend some Miles about the said Town , and the late Recorder of the said Town being now dead, and there being np*Maydr 6r Aldermen now acting as Justices of the Peacedn the &id Town, there is. a total Failure of that Part of the Administration of Justice there, to the unspeakable Detriment and Danger of the Petitioners^and all others, the Inhabitants of the said Town and Liberties, occasioningalfo great Difficulties with regard toquartering Soldiers, and many other Inconveniencies: That, by other Mistakes made in the framing and executing of By-Laws, many Years since made in the said Corporation, certain of the.Members thereof have had Judgments^ajflfed against them, which, may incapacitate the said Officers From acting as Magi-

monalty of the said Borough, at several times, in many Years past; the Titles to which may probably be precarious, by means of the Incapacity or improper Choice of the aforesaid Officers: That, by an Act of Parliament, made i-n the Reign of King James the First, for the Paving of the said Town, and the Mainteftlrice of the Pavements thereof, certain Powers Were invested in the Magistrates, and other Officers of the same Town, for the due Execution of the said Act, and there not being at this Time any of those Magistrates, by reason of the Inabilities and Incapacities aforesaid; and the said Act being also now become defective in other respects, the Pavements of the said Town are in so ruinous a Condition as to incommode and endanger not only the Inhabitants thereof, but all Travellers passing through the lame: And therefore praying, That the said Charters may be confirmed, that all the said late Aldermen* and all other Officers now living, may, by the Assistance of an Act of

Parliament to be made for that Purpose, be restored to their Offices Within the said Borough, according to the Direction of the said Charters, and all their Incapacities remitted and removed; and that they, and the rest of the free Burgesses of the said Town, may have Power to elect new Officers, in the room of those that are dead, in such manner as the said Charters prescribe, that the said Leases, Mortgages, and Grants, may be confirmed: That the said Act for the Maintenance of the Poor may be confirmed, and continued; and that the said Act for Paving the said Town may be amended and continued* or that the Petitioners may have such other Relief in the Premises as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Oswald reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Provost, Baillies, and Town-Council, of the Burgh of Kirkcaldy, was referred, That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as follows; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, the Agents for the Petitioners called,

Mr. James Millet and Mr. John Baird, and they, being severally examined, said, That the Town of Kirkcaldy is very well situated for carrying on a foreign Trade; and that there are many Coal Works adjoining to, and near to, the said Town; and that there are Salt Works therein; and that the Trade in Coal and Salt, and other things, might be improved, and made very beneficial, not only to the Town but to the Country, if some Money could be raised for repairing the Harbour belonging to the said Town, which Harbour is now so much out of Repair, that it will cost One thousand Pounds and upwards to put the same into such Repair that Ships and Vessels may fail into, and out of, the Harbour with Safety:

And the said Mr. Miller laid before the Committee an Account of the Revenue and Expence or the said Town, for some Years past, by which it appeared, that the yearly Expence in and about the publick Works of the Town, exceeded the Revenue Sixty-six Pounds Eighteen Shillings and Four Pence.Sterling.

Then the Petitioners called,

Thomas Hanbttry Esquire, and Mr. Robert Bright, who being severally examined, said, That the Monies arising by the said Tolls and Duties, have been duly laid out and applied towards repairing the said Roads, which, the Witnesses said were computed together, to be in Length Thirty Miles, and upwards: And they further said. That although the Money collected had been justly laid out, according to the Directions given by the said Act; yet, by reason of the Length of the said Roads, and the Bad-ness thereof, and the Smallness of the Income arising annually by the present Act (which is near expiring), all the said Roads (being in a deep Soil, and heavy Carriages frequently passing over them) cannot be effectually amended and kept in Repair, unless the Term and Powers granted by the former Act be enlarged, and the same Act made more effectual.

A Petition of the Mayor, Aldertnen, Matter Clothiers, Wo^Uen and other Inhabitants, of the Borough of Wilton, in the County of Wilis, was presented to the House, and read; representing to the House, that many of the Laws to protect and encourage the Woollen Manufacture, have been evaded, and many Abuses have of late Years found means to introduce themselvesinto it, to the visible Decay there-of, the Misery of the Poor, the great Distress of the Master Clothier, the fi nking the Value of Lands, and the manifest Hurt of the Trade of this Kingdom in general:

And that although the illegal Practice of running Wool from Great Britain and Ireland into foreign Parts, must be allowed, above all others, to be a Practice of the most pernicious Consequerice, yet the Petitioners apprehend the Liberty which many Persons of late Years have affutned, of setting up the Trade of a Master Clothier, and exercising his Art, without havingferved a lawful ApprCntice-ffiip to it, or having proper Skill therein, hath had Effects very fatal to the Manufacture; and that such Persons unfki lied in the Trade, and imposed on in alhiofl: every Branch of it; do not only manufacture their own Goods in general, after a scandalous and deceitful mcm-ner, but do likewise thereby corrupt the Hhnds of the labouring Poor, to the Di it red it of our Markets at home and abroad, and the great Injury of the whole Trade in general; and not only so, but thatmanyevii-disposed Persons among them;under the Cover of buying fma'li Quantities:

140 22° Martii. A. 1741.

Tamworth qualified according to the Terms expressed in the Refo-Election. iution, had constantly voted in all Elections for this Borough, before and since the Commencement of the Act of Parliament, which declares the last Resolution final; and that several voted at this Election, as well for the Petitioner, as for the Sitting-Member:

That this being the Custom of the Place, becomes the Law of the Place:

That the Gaining of a Settlement is a Qualification not required by the Resolution; and that Persons residing by Certificate, if they contribute to the publick Expences of the Place where they reside, have a Right to be repre-fented in that Place; otherwise it would be manifestly unjust, as they can be only there represented at alii and that this Right they had by Law, before the Statute made in the 13th and 14th Year of King Charles the Second: That the Provisions made by that Statute, as well as fub-sequent Laws, were in order to remedy particular Inconveniencies, without any View or Tendency to what concerned the Right of voting in Elections:

And, in order to prove, that Certificate-Men had always voted at Elections for this Borough, they called J ' '

John Kendall and Francis Wilcox; who being severally examined, said, That they had known the Borough, the first 26, and the other 30 Years: That they were present at the Elections in the Years 1722, 1727, and 1734; and that during the times they we.re so present, Certificate-Men were admitted to vote, without being objected to by any of the Candidates: And the last Witness added. That they1 were always looked upon as legal Votes, though he remembered the Votes of Freeholders being disallowed; and that many of those Pprfons are the:most substantial Inhabitants of the Town, and, contribute to act publick Expences.

Then the Counsel for the Sitting-Member referred to that Part of the Report from the Committee of Privileges and Electrons, touching the Election for this Borough,-made the 19th Day of April 1729, where the Evidence is Rated, which was given in order to.teqyalify the Votes of several Persons objeCjied to by the then Petitionef, as. well ds the Sitting Member, under the Head of Cenificate-Persons, by proving them to be Householders, and to pay Scotland Lot; from which the Counsel inferred, that those Persons were then considered as Inhabitants within tire Meaning of the Resolution; and had they not been so considered, the Sitting-Member could not then have maintained a Majority.

In Answer to this, the Petitioner’s Counsel admitted, that many Certificate-Persons were Householders within the Borough, and paid Scotland Lot; but they infilled, that, unless they Lad rented a House of 10/. a Year, or otherwise gained a legal Settlement in the Borough, they could not be deemed Inhabitants within the Resolution, either by Construction of Law, or by the Law and Usage of Parliaments:

That personal Residence is not sufficient to create Inhabitancy; and, by the Statute-Law, every Certificate-Man is deemed an Inhabitant, not of the Place where he re-fides, but of that from whence he came; and that the Purport of the Certificate itleif implies as much: ,

That by the Law and Usage of Parliament, in all Cases where Scotland Lot creates the Right of voting, the De-: terminations, with regard to Certificate-Persons, have always been against allowing their Votes, particularly the same of Wendover, in the Year 1702, in the

Year 1705, and Reading in the last Session of the last Parliament:

That had the contrary been the Sense of the House in the same of Reading, the Counsel, as they alleged, would have been restrained from offering Evidence upon that Point by tbfc Standing Order; as they likewise would have been in the Year 172a, when the Resolution, touching the Right of Election for this Borough, was made, if at that time Certificate-Men had been allowed to be legal Votes within the Meaning thiereof; but as they were objected to on both Sides, the very Instant after the Resolu-

tion was made, it was, they said, evident from thence, that the Objection rnuft have been allowed good; for though the Act of the Second Year of his present Majesty, and the Standing Order, in consequence of that Act, were made long after, yet the Practice before in this Particular, after any immediate Decision of the Right of Election, was always conformable to the Restriction now imposed by the Standing Order; and that, in 1729, the Objection was virtually admitted by the.Sitting-Member against the Votes of such of the Certificate-Men whom he did not requalify:

That if the Construction were otherwise, it would be attended with manyInconveniencies, and give an Opportunity of introducing Numbers of occasional Votes at the time Elections are known to come on.

The Counsel for the Sitting-Member, in their Reply, alledged, that the Precedents of Wendover and were long before the Act of the 2d Year of his present Majesty; and though binding as to those Two Boroughs, yet could be no-ways applicable to; especially

as it did not appear, that Certificate-Persons had voted in either of those Boroughs before; and that they had been, proved to have voted formerly in this Borough:

That the Reason for contending the Point at this time,-is much stronger than it was formerly, in regard the De-t termination now to be made is binding by Law upont the House of Commons itself.

But it being the Opinion of the Committee, that the Counsel for the Petitioner should be admitted to; give Evidence todifqualify the Votes of such Persons as were resident in the Borough by virtue of, the Certificates j They produced the Certificates as to 28 of these Voters:

As to the Seven Persons objected to, as not being Householders;

John Woodcock gave Evidence as to Two of the said Persons, viz. ‘Thomas Farr and Richard Gent: That Farr quitted his House at Lady-day before the Election, which came on the Sixth of May following; and at that time boarded with his Uncle; and that Gent rented only a Shop in the Borough, and boarded with his Son Two or Three Years before the Election.

Joseph Clijjord gave Evidence as to Three others of the said Persons; viz. fore the Election: That the Son is the HoulholJer; and that both he and the Father voted for the same House.

Then, in order to prove Bribery on the Petitioner, George Moore, being examined, said. That he had not taken the Oath against Bribery: That the Sunday before the Election, the Petitioner asked the Witness fir his Vote; to whom he made Answer, That he thought he could not give it him: That he owed Samuel Princep 12 s.4 d.for Physick; and that if the Petitioner would

pay that Debt, and give the Witness a Pair of Buck-(kin Breeches, he should have his Vote: Which the Petitioner promising to do, the Witness accordingly voted for him.

Being asked. How he came to mention the Debt he owed to Princep ? He answered. That he had been ill, and was willing, if he could, to get it paid by his Vote; and that had he voted on the other Side, it would not have cleared his Debt:

That this Debt is not paid, to his Knowledge, nor hath he yet received the Breeches: That there was no Agreement for any Money to be in the Breeches; but the Witness owned he was corrupted by the Promise before-mentioned.

Being further examined, he said. That he never had any Conversation with Princep about disposing of his Vote; but that he hath paid him some Part of the Debt (ince the Election; and that Princep never made him any Offer to induce him to vote for the Sitting-Member:

But, upon further Examination, he owned, that Princep told him, one Night, when drunk, he would forgive him the Debt he owed him, provided he would vote for Mr. Flayer-, but that Princep did not mention it as the Desire of Mr. Floyer, only proposed it as his own Motion: And being asked, Whether Princep did not like-wile offer him a Pair of Breeches? He said, he did not.

THE Clerk of the Crown attending, according to Order, amended the Return for the Borough of Tamu'orth, in the Counties of Stafford and Warwick; and also the Return for the County of Cardigan-, and likewise the Return for the Borough of in the County of Flint.

Resolved, That the said Committee be a Committee of Secresy.

Resolved, That the Number of the said Committee be One-and-twenty.

Resolved, That the Committee be clioten by way of Balloting.

Ordered, That the Members of this House do, upon Friday next, at Twelve of the Clock, prepare Lifts, to be put into Glasses, of One-and-twenty Persons Names, to be the said Committee.

Ordered, That the said Glasses be placed upon the Table; and the said Lifts held up between the Finger and Thumb, be put into the Glasses, at the Table, by the Members called over for that Purpose, according to the Counties and Places they serve for, as the said Counties and Places are entered in the Return-Book.

Resolved, Nemine contradicente. That an humble Address be presented to his Majesty, to adore him of the Fidelity, Zeal, and Affection of this House, to his Royal Person, Family, and Government; and that his faithful Commons will take every Opportunity, in this critical Conjuncture, to shew how sensible they are of the present dangerous Situation of Europe, by the Distrefies to which the Queen of Hungary has been reduced; and as the late favourable Turn of Affairs affords reasonable Grounds to hope, that if (he is timely and properly assisted by those Powers who are engaged by Treaties, and bound by Interest, to support her, the Balance of Power may be again restored, and the Tranquillity of Europe re-established; this House will therefore proceed, with Unanimity, Vigour, and Dispatch, to support his Majesty in all such Measures as shall be necessary to attain these great and desirable Ends; having, front a just Sense of their Duty the highest Regard for the Honour and Safety of his Majesty, and the truest Concern for the Freedom, Peace, Trade, and Welfare of these Kingdoms.

Resolved, That the said Address be presented to his Majesty by the whole House.

Ordered, That such Members of this House, as are of his Majesty’s most Honourable Privy-Council, do humbly know his Majesty’s Pleasure, when he will be attended by this House.

And then the House adjourned till Tomorrow Morning, Nine of the Clock.

Mr. Speaker reported, That the House attended his Answer to Majesty Yesterday with their Address; to which his Ma- Ad<hef». jesty was pleased to give this most gracious Answer;

Gentlemen,

I thank you for this dutiful and loyal Address. Youf Unanimity on this Occasion will, 1 am persuaded, be attended with the happiest Consequences both at Home and Abroad. I reeonynend to you the laying aside all Heats and Divisions. I desire nothing more than to reign in the Hearts and Affections of all my People, which I look upon as the greatest Security to my Government, and their Liberties.

And then the Committee came to the following Resolutions:

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the said John Tuite has invented an Engine for railing Water, different from any thing of that Sort heretofore used in this Kingdom.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the said Engine may prove more useful for the Purposes in the Petition mentioned, than any other Engine now used in this Kingdom.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the House be moved for Leave to bring in a Bill for.veiling the sole Property of the said Engine in the said John Tuite, his Executors, Administrators, and Assigns, for such Term of Years, as to the House shall seem meet.

And a Debate arising in the House thereupon; thereof, for the Year 1742, be referred to the said

Mr. Speaker said. That it was the First time it had ever Committee.

come to him to determine any thing in the Chair by his Voice; and though he was under a Difficulty in this Cafe, and should not exercise any Right in it willingly; yet he had no Pain about giving his Voice openly; having ever disliked the Method of Ballot, except in Cafes of Necef-lity; the Openness of acting here, being, in his Opinion, one of the great Pillars of Security to the People, for a proper Behaviour of their Representatives: He said, he would never give up the Right of the Chair s yet he de-stred to be excused from declaring his Sentiments, as to the Point of Order in this Matter, and submitted himself to the Sense and Commands of the House.

Mr. Speaker being then desired to exercise the ancient Right of Speakers, in case of Equality of Voices, without putting a Question: And it being asserted, that upon the Report, in the same of Equality of Voices, the then Speaker desired to be excused from determining.

And it being the Sense of the House, That Mr. Speaker should now give his Determination;

Mr. Speaker gave his Voice for Sir Henry Liddel Baronet, and the Honourable John Talbot Esquire.

Ordered, That Five be the Quorum of the Committee of Secresy, appointed to enquire into the Conduct of Robert Earl of Orford, during the last Ten Years of his being First Commissioner of the Treasury, and Chancellor and Under-Treasurer of his Majesty’s Exchequer.

Ordered, That the said Committee have Power to fend for Persons, Papers, and Records.

Ordered, That the said Committee have Power to examine, in the most solemn manner, such Persons as they shall th;nk'proper to examine upon the Subject-Matter of their Enquiry.

Ordered, That the Estimate of the Charges of the Royal African Company of England, for the Maintenance of the several British Forts and Settlements belonging to the said Company on the Coast of Africa, for the Year 1742, be referred to the said Committee.

Ordered, That the Establishment of the Royal African Company of England, for their several Forts and Settle-

ments on the Coast of Africa, with the Charges thereof, for the Year 1741; distinguishing how much of the same is on Account of Trade, and how much for the Maintenance and Defence of the said Forts and Settlements; and also, an Account how the Money granted in the last Session of Parliament, towards the Maintenance of the said Forts and Settlements, hath been disposed of, be referred to the said Committee.

Then the House resolved itself into the said Committee.

That by several Letters, dated the »Jd of August 1740, N. S. from Spain, their Correspondents in England were informed, That, after infinite Fatigue and Vexation, they had at last obtained their End, without Precedent, having received an Order from the King, and Council of Finances, directing the Administrators of the Rents to return them the Duties for the Wines re-landed, on which they were then putting the finishing Stroke.

Mr. Roberts said. That, on re-landing the Wines which had been shipped,a strict Enquiry was made to find out if they were English Property, and if great Care had not been taken, they would have been confiscated: That the Wines so re-landed, remained as a Deposit for the Duties, and was any Loss to happen to the said Wines, others tnuft be exported, to the Amount of the Duties so returned.

Francis Mannock Esquire, who lately lived in Spain, said. That these Wines are in danger of being seized, if they remain in Spain (supposing the y were not Property!, by an Order of the King of Spain, for the Use of his Fleet, in its present Emergency; and, if so, an Order is given on the Treasury for Payment, which might never be complied with: But thele Wines were aho liable to be (eized by an Information, and the Informer never known, who has f or -f for his Share, and that a strict Enquiry was made at the House where thele Wines were, to find if they were English Property.

He was asked, if any Security was given on re-Janding these W ines for the King’s Duties

He laid, That those Duties being repaid back, on re- landing, is very extraordinary, as it was in this Cafe; but he has ieen an authentick Instrument, in which it is mentioned. That all the Wines re-landed were to remain as a Security for the Duties, which could not be alienated or expended in the Country.

He was asked. Whether the Merchants who sent those Orders, could be ignorant of the Danger and Hazards of them, after the Bill was passed

He said. They must be ignorant of great Part of the Danger, upon Account that the Obstructions to their Orders were pollerior to such Orders, which if the 24th Day of June had not been altered, probably they would have run no Rilque in getting Home their Wines by the Time first limited.

To prove that Orders have been lent to Spain, to ship these Wines for neutral Ports; and that the King of Spain, or his Subjects, cannot now receive any Benefit by the Importation thereof into this Kingdom;

ago, fend a general Order to One of the Houses in Spain (for which he is an Agent), at the Delire of several of the Merchants before particularly mentioned, to ship, by the first Opportunity, all their Wines, for some neutral Ports; and he believes it is too late to countermand the said Order; and therefore no further Benefit can accrue to the King of Spaifrom the Importation thereof into neutral Ports.

.GEORGE R.

It is always with the utmost Reluctance, that his Ma- , jesty alks any extraordinary Supplies of his People; but as hisfaithful Commons have, with the great eft Zealand Unanimity, exp re fled their Concern for the Support of the House of Aujiria, and for restoring the Balance of Power in Europe;and as the Jate Events, in favour of the Queen of Hungary, afford a reasonable Prospect of Suc-eels; his Majesty makes no doubt, but this House will, at this time, readily grant him such a Supply as may enable him to concert proper Measures, and form such Alliances with other Powers, as may be nee elfary for attaining those desirable Ends, which they have in so particular a Manner recommended to him.

Inhabitants of the Town of Kingston oor' upon Hull, in behalf of themselves, and the rest of the Inhabitants, not Freemen, of the said Town, was presented to the House, and read; reciting several Provisions in an Act of Parliament made in the Ninth and Tenth Years of the Reign of his late Majesty King William the Third, intituled, An Act for erecting Workhouses, and Houses of Correction, in the Town of Kingston upon Hull, for the F.mployment and Maintenance of the Poor there: And letting forth, That, in pursuance of the said Act, the Corporation thereby constituted, purchased a large Piece of Ground within the said Town, and built thereon a large Hospital or Workhouse, and House of Correction, and have ever since lodged, and kept to Work, great Numbers of the Poor of the said Town in the said Hospital, or Workhouse; and have therein, or otherwise, maintained all the Poor of the said Town under their Care; and that, by another Act of Parliament made in the Eighth Year of the Reign of her late Majesty Queen Anne, the said Corporation was authorized to make a further, or additional, Assessment, not exceeding One hundred and Thirty Pounds, by the Year, to be employed for the Purposes in the said Fiift Act mentioned; and that a Bill is now depending in this House, for impowering the said Corporation to raise such further or other Sum, or Sums, as shall be necessary for the Maintenance of the Poor of the said Town, to be proportioned, assessed, raised, and levied, by'such Method of Taxation, and subject to, and under such Power and Controul of, the Ma-gistrates of the said Town of Kingston upon , as by the said first-mentioned Act is directed, appointed, and preferred: And representing to the House, That there are great Numbers of Persons inhabiting Kingston upon Hull, who are not Freemen of the said Town, who not only contribute to all Rates and Taxes chargeable upon the Inhabitants, but are also considerably aggrieved with the heavy Burden of paying the Water-Bailiff Dues, which the Petitioners only are subject to, though they are very great Promoters in respect to the Improvement of Trade and Commerce, and the Employment and Support of Numbers of People in the said Town; and that the Mayor and Aldermen of the said Town, and the Officers employed by them, and acting under their Authority, in making the Rates and Assessments for the Relief of the Poor under the Care of the said Corporation, and in the Exercise and Execution of the Power vested in them by the said Acts, have, in a partial Manner, distinguished the Petitioners from the Freemen of the said Town, by charging them with anarbitrary personal Payment of acer-tain Weekly Sum, without any regard to the yearly Rent or Value of their respective Houses, greatly exceeding in

feneral, the Assessments laid upon the other Inhabitants, 'reemen of the said Town, which are regulated and ascertained according to the yearly Rent or Value of the Houses and Tenements occupied by them respectively within the said Town; And further representing, That the Petitioners have not, by virtue of the said Acts of Parliament, any Right of Appeal, except to the Mayor, Aldermen, and Recorder, of the said Town, who have the Power and Direction of the said Rates and Aflelf-mems under which the Petitioners are aggrieved, as aforesaid; and are therefore without Remedy in the Premises, unless they shall be relieved by Authority of Parliament: And therefore praying, That such Pravision may be made for their Relief in the Premises, either by inserting a pro-Voi. 24.

per Clause, or Clauses, in the said Bill now depending for that Purpose, or by such other Ways and Means as to the House shall seem meet.

Mr. John Fletcher, a Lace-Weaver: Who said. That,

of late Years, great Quantities of Tinsel, Copper, and other base compound Metals, have been brought into England, from Nuremburgh, which has been worked up

into Laces, and other Goods which look (o like Gold and Silver, as to deceive the Traders themselves, to the great Discouragement of the Gold and Silver Manufacturers in that Trade:

That the same is brought over chiefly plated upon Quills, and sold at about Si)f Pence per Ounce, which, when worked into Lace, will fell for Two Shillings and Six Pence per Ounce, and looks as well as Gold Lace of Ten Shillings per Ounce, and will wear as long, and as well, if kept dry.

Mr. Euston Scott, a Gold and Silver Wire-drawer, said.

That he has used foreign Plate, made of bale compound Metals, which work as well as Gold or Silver, and, when worked into Lace, look as well:

That the same is brought from Abroad, and fold for about Five Shillings per Pound; and he knows of several Orders sent for Quantities of these fort of Metals, which are expected in a few Days; One particularly for himself: That the same looks so like the real, that he knows Mr. Sharp, a Trader in Gold and Silver Lace, bought some of it for French Plate, and gave Twenty-five Pounds for it; and upon finding the Fraud, he returned it; and he, the Examinant, afterwards bought it for Fifty Shillings :.

That it may be used in Brocades, and not distinguished, and is often used. in Ribbons and Handkerchiefs, and fold in the Country for real, as he has heard by Complaints from Country-Traders, who have given Seven or Eight Shillings per Ounce, for a Metal which he could have fold for Seven or Eight Pence:

That it is the foreign Plate that looks so like, and deceives, and not the English.

Mr. William Dali, a Gold and Silver Lace-Weaver,

laid. That upon the Decay of the Gold and Silver Trade, he took to working bare compound Metals, that come from Abroad, which work in every respect as well as Gold or Silver, and is net to be distinguished when worked into Lace, &c. and that he has worked Two or Three thousand Ounces to go to India.

Mr. James Smith, a Gold and Silver Lace-Weaver, said, That upon the Decay of the Gold and Silver Trade, he began to work base compound Metals, that come from Abroad, which work as well as Gold or Silver, and look as well:

That the Tinsel is frequently worked in Ribbons, and fold in Town and Country for real; and into Buttons, the Price thereof being fallen from 9 j. and ioj. per Dozen, to 2 s.6 d. and 3 s.

The Agent for the Petitioners laid before the Committee, a Report, from the Commissioners of the Customs, to the Lords of the Treasury; by which it appeared to your Committee, That the said Commissioners are of Opinion, that there is room for Frauds to be practised, in exporting Tinsel, Lace, Thread, and Fringe, instead of those of Gold and Silver, and thereby obtain a Bounty, given by Law only upon the latter.

Upon the whole, the Committee came to the following Resolutions:

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Petitioners have fully proved the Allegations of their Petition.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the House be moved, for Leave to bring in a Bill to prevent the Frauds committed by the counterfeiting of Gold and Silver Lace.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill to prevent the Frauds committed by the counterfeiting of Gold and Silver Idee: And that the Lord Mayor of London and Sir John Barnard do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding One hundred Sixty-eight thousand Six hundred and Forty-five Pounds Fifteen Shillings and Seven Pence, be granted to his Majesty, for the Charge of Transports, hired to carry the Forces to America.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum not exceeding One hundred Eleven thousand Nine hundred and Seventeen Pounds Nineteen Shillings and One Peny, be granted to his Majesty, for the Expence of Victuals provided for the Soldiers employed in the Expeditions in America.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, nt>t exceeding Ten thousand Pounds, be granted to his Majesty, upon Account, towards the Support of the Royal Hospital at Greenwich, for the better Maintenance of the Seamen of the said Hospital, worn out, and become decrepit, in the service of their Country.

The laid Resolutions, being severally read a Second time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

Petition of A Petition of William Myddelton Esquire, late High Mr. Myddle- Sheriff of the Shire of Denbigh, was presented to the thar°eHouse, and read; letting forth. That the Petitioner was, ® on the 23d Day of February, ordered by this House to the Custody of the Keeper of his Majesty’s Gaol of Newgate, and did the next Day, in consequence of such Order, surrender himself to the Serjeant at Arms attending this House, and was immediately carried to the said Gaol, where he has remained in close Confinement ever lincc; whereby his Health has been much impaired; and that such Confinement, longer continued, may be the Means of endangering his Life; and that the Petitioner is extremely sorry, and humbly begs Pardon for having given Offence to this House: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration; and that the Petitioner may be discharged out of Custody.

lolchester Mr. Gray reported from the Committee, to whom the ipoor. Petition of the late Mayor, Aldermen, Assistants, and 0 Common Council, and of the free Burgesses and inhabi-VoLi 24.

tants, of the Town of Colchester, in the County of EJJext whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was referred, That the Committeehad examined the Matter of so much of the said Petition, as relates to the Corporation therein mentioned, for the Maintenance and Careo£ the Poor of the said Town; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as follows; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the Petition, the Agents for the Petitioners produced, and laid before the Committee, a Copy of Letters Patent granted by their late Majesties King William and Queen Mary dated the ' 27th of July, in the Fifth Year of their Reign, reciting, That a Charter granted by his late Majesty King Charles« the Second, dated the Third of August, in the Fifteenth Year of his Reign, whereby the Borough of Colchester was incorporated by the Name of the Mayor and Commonalty of the Borough of Colchester, in the County of Essex; and by that Charter it is granted, that there should be within the said Borough, a Mayor, Eleven Aldermen, Eighteen Assistants, Eighteen Common Council, and a Recorder, who should have perpetual Succession:

And also that the Mayor and Recorder for the Time being, and the Alderman who was the last Mayor, and Two other Aldermen, to be chosen annually, should be Justices of the Peace within the said Borough; which Charter was ratified and confirmed by the said Letters Patent granted by their said late Majesties King William and Queen Mary, bearing Date as above-mentioned.

Then the Agents produced an Act of Parliament, made in the 9th and 10th Years of the Reign of his late Majesty King William, for erecting Hospitals and Workhouses within the said Town of Colchester, for the better employing and maintaining the Poor thereof; whereby it is Enacted, That the Mayor and Aldermen for the Time being, and Forty eight Persons, to be chosen in the manner therein mentioned, shall be Guardians of the Poor of the said Town, and a Body Politick and Corporate for the Government and Maintenance of the said Poor; and that Rates and Assessments shall be made by them for and towards the Support of the feme Poor; which Rates shall be certified to the Mayor and Justices of the Peace of and for the said Town, for the Time being; who are, by the said Act, required to issue out their Warrants to authorize and require the Collect ion of such Rates; and divers other necessary and essential Powers were granted to, and veiled in, the Mayor, Aldermen, Recorder, and Justices of the Peace for the said Borough, for the Time being, for putting the said Act in Execution: ,

That some original Records, and examined Copies of other Records, were produced; whereby it appears, that Informations were lately brought in his Majesty’s Court of King’s Bench against Jeremiah Daniel, the last Mayor of that Borough, for usurping that Office; and against him, and also against Matthew Martin Esquire, George Wegg, junior, Esquire, Joseph Duffield, John Blatch, James Boys, John James, Nathanael Lawrence, and Peter Johnson, for their severally usurping the Offices of Aldermen of the said Borough; which Usurpa-tions they severally acknowleged, and disclaimed the said Offices.

Then the Agents for the Petitioners called,

Mr. Samuel Wall: Who being examined, said, That Mr. Serjeant Price, the late Recorder, and also one of the Aldermen of the said Borough, was dead; and that there is not, nor are at this time, any Mayor, Aldermen, Recorder, or Justices of the Peace, of or for the said Borough:

That, for want of such Officers to put the before-mentioned Act of Parliament in Execution, the Poor of the Town have of late been very ill provided for, by reason the Rates made for their Relief cannot be levied; and therefore they are now in great Distress, and must remain so; and unless some speedy Remedy be made by Parliament

in ems. Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred to consider further of Ways and Means for raising the Supply granted to his Majesty, the Proposal of the Governor and Company of the Bank of England, with . the Resolution of the Committee thereupon; both which the Committee had directed him to report to the House; And he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the said Proposal, and the Resolution of the Committee, were read; iand are as followeth; viz.

To the Honourable the Commons of Great Britain in Parliament assembled.

The Governor and Company of the Bank of England, Humbly propose,

That their present Fund of £. 100,000. per Annum,

payable out of the of the yd. per Barrel, Excise, being continued to them unto the ift August 174$* they are contented, after that time, to accept £. 3. per -Cent, per Annum for their present Stock of £. 1,600,000.

- together with £. 4,000.. per Annum towards their Charges of Management, hitherto paid them, out of the said -Fund; after which Payments there being a Remainder of £. 48,000. per Annum on the said Fund, they are ready \xo advance£. 1,600,000. at such Times as shall be agreed ‘ upon, at £. 3. per Cent, per Annum, being allowed a Dif-< count at £. 3. per Cent, per Annum, for such Money, from the respective Times of its Advance, until the said ift 1Augufi 1743.

And they humbly further propose. That they be continued a Corporation, with the foie Power of Banking -with the said Fund reierved entire to them for the Term ' of 21'Years, from the said ift of August 1743, with all the Grants, Privileges, and Immunities, they now enjoy, 22

by virtue or in pursuance of their Charter, or of any Act or Acts of Parliament, redeemable afterwards by Parliament, on a Year’s Notice, and Re-payment of £. 1,600,000. formerly advanced, and likewise of the £. 1,600,000. now proposed to be advanced, and all Ar* rears of the£. 100,000. per Annum, and all the Principal and Interest Money which shall be owing to them upon all such Tallies, Exchequer Orders, or Parliamentary Funds, which they shall have remaining in their Hands, or be entitled to at the time of such Notice to be given as aforesaid; such Funds, for the Redemption whereof, Provision is already made in any Acts of Parliament now in Force, always and only excepted; they continuing a Corporation, with an exclusive Power of Banking, notwithstanding such Notice given, till all the Money due to the Bank, as aforesaid, shall be paid them.

And they humbly hope,- that they shall obtain such further Privileges and Advantages as shall be necessary for their Security, and such as to this Honourable House shall seem reasonable and fit.

Signed by Order of the Court of Directors,

David Le Gross, Secretary.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, Supply-That, towards raising the Supply granted to his Majesty, the Proposal of the Governor and Company of the Bank of England, for advancing the Sum of One Million Six hundred thousand Pounds, upon such’Terms and Conditions as are therein mentioned, be accepted.
