Importation A Petition of the several subscribing Merchants,.

of Spanish Traders, and Importers of Wines, into the antient Town Wines. and port Qf Southampton, in behalf of themselves and* the re ft of the Dealers in Wine, in Great Britain, prese rred to the Ho use, and read; alleging, That as the Legislature, soon after the Commencement of the present War with Spain, thought fit, by Act of Parliament, to prohibit, during the said War, the Importation into Great Britain of Wines, and other Goods, of the Product of any of the Territories of the King of Spain, in Europe, after certain Times by the said Act prescribed, the Petitioners, upon Presumprion of the Continuance of the said Act, and upon Expectation that other Wines would he wanted to supply the Place of Spanish Win§s, have already imported, and have song finee given Qrdfra, for the shipping of much larger Quantities of White ifyr-tugal Wines than usual; anc} that (as the Petitioners foresee if the Bill, now expending in this House, for Mef-; sieurs Nuthall, Fydell, and Mitchell, and certain other Merchants, to import, from neutral Ports, a certain Quantity of Spanish Wines, should pass into a Law, the Petitioners will be great Sufferers by the Markets being Applied with the said Spanish Wines, and their own Portugal Wines left on their Hands unfold), the Petitioners, conceive it will be a great. Hardship upon them, and all other fair Traders in Portugal Wines, a great Discouragement to that valuable Branch of Trade, the Trade tp Portugal, and a great Prejudice to the Navigation of this Kingdom; but that it will be an Advantage to the particular Persons only who own those Wines, which are designed by the said Act to bq imported; and who, for Reasons unknown to the Petitioners, have neglected to make Application for such Liberty of Importation for almost Two Years, and thereby made room for many Frauds and Impositions, which they apprehend cannot be sufficiently guarded against; and thatjthp said Act having been ordered into this House, near Six Months before it became in Force, the Petitioners conceive there can be no room for any Merchants to plead Surprize in point of Time, as to the giving, or forbearing,:Orders for importing Spanish Goods: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into their Consideration* and that the said Bill, calculated for the Benefit of a few Persons only, and tending, as the Petitioners believe, to the Prejudice of all other Traders in Wines, in these Kingdoms, may not pass into a Law, or that the Petitioners may have such other Relief as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of several Freeholders, having a Right of Common in, over, and upon, a certain Common, called Short-Heath, and its Appurtenances, in the Township of Stowerbridge, and of other Freeholders having Right of Common in other common or waste Land in the Parish of Oldfwinford, in the County of Worcester^'vCo its Appurtenances, and also of several Inhabitants of the said Town of Stowerbridge and Parish of Oldjwinford, was presented to the House, and read* representing to the House, That the Petitioners have considered the Bill now depending before this House, for making the Town of Stowerbridge, in the County of Worcester, a separate Parish from the Parish of Oldfwinford, in the said County and for making a Provision for the Minister of the said new Parish and for settling the Right of Presentation to the Church thereof; and the several Clauses of which the same con-fists, with the Amendments from whence only the Petitioners are apprehensive, that, if the same should pass into a Law, all the Petitioners, the Freeholders, will be deprived of their Rights of Common and as well they, as the Petitioners, the Inhabitants, will thereby likewise be burthened with several Rates and Payments, which at present they are not liable to; and that all the Petitioners,

A Petition of Thomas Stevens, Agent for, and in behalf Misappli-of, the People of Georgia in America, was presented to the cation of House, and read representing to the House, That by Money in virtue of Letters Patent, bearing Date the Ninth Day of Georgia, 1 June 1752, a large Tract of waste Land, bounded to the Northward on the River Sevannah, and by the Province of South Carolina, and to the Southward on the River Alatamaha, was granted to certain Persons incorporated by the Name of the Trustees for establishing the Colony of Georgia in America, for the Purposes and Intentions therein mentioned and that, in pursuance thereof, large Sums of Money have been granted by Parliament, several private Donations and Contributions have been made, and Numbers of Gentlemen have adventured on their own Expence, while many industrious poor Persons were font over by the Trustees, to improve and cultivate the Colony on their Scheme* and that the Failure of this Scheme, which has been found to be utterly impracticable, has been properly represented, from time to time, to the Trustees, and necessary Alterations recommended and petitioned for, near Seven Years; and through a Refufel of these Alterations, and Mifepplication of the publick Money, great Delays in discharging the Debts due from the Trustees to the People, and many Abuses in the Civil Power, the Colony is so greatly reduced, both in the Number and Condition of its Inhabitants, as to be incapable of fulfilling his Majesty’s most gracious Designs in establishing it, unlefe such present Red refs be found for the injured People, and such Means procured for their Encouragement, as may concur with the natural Fertility of the Soil, the commodious Situation of the Province, and its excellent Harbours for Trade, to answer the generous Purposes of an effectual Establishment:

And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and grant such Redress as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee of the whole House.

Resolvcdx That this House will, upon this Day Seven-night, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider of the said Petition.

Importation; APetition of the Merchants, whoseNamesaresubscribed, °^Wwes^ ImPorters of Wines into the Port of Exeter, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the House having, so long ago as the Month of December 1739, ordered in a Bill to prohibit Commerce with Spain, which received the Royal Afient on the 29th of April 1740, the Petitioners, at high Freights and Insurances, have imported* and given Orders for, considerable Quantities of Portugal and other Wines, in Confidence that, during the present War, no Spanish Wine could be imported after the 24th June 1740, the Time limited for that Purpose: That a Bill being now depending in the House to enable Messieurs Nut hall, Fydell, and others, to import, from neutral Ports, certain Quantities of Spanish Wines, the Petitioners apprehend, that, if it should pals into a Law, there will be a great Reduction in the Price of white Wines imported from Portugal, and of late from Madeira, Sicily, and other Places, and a collusive Trade may be carried on, to the great Prejudice of the Naviga-. tion and Manufactures of this Kingdom, and to the Loss of the Revenue: And therefore praying, That the said Bill may not pass into a Law, or that the Petitioners.may have such Relief as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

SelcA Parish. Vestries*

The Lord Perceval, according to Order, reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the principal Inhabitants of the several Parishes of St. Martin in the Fields, St. Anne, St. James, St. George Hanover Square, and St. Margaret, within the Liberty of Westminster, in behalf of themselves, and the rest of the Inhabitants of the said respective Parishes, was referred, the Matter of which the Committee had directed him to report to the House, relating to the said Parishes of St. Martin in the Fields and St. Anne; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as follows; viz.

That the Committee, to avoid that Confusion which mud have arisen in a blended Enquiry, as well as to distinguisti those Parishes in which the greatest Errors might be found, from such as might deserve less Censure, determined to consider the Allegations of the Petitioners with respect to each Parish distinctly: Under which Determination of the Committee, the Agents for the Petitioners readily acquiesced; observingonly, that as the several Parishes had united in one Complaint, they did not take upon them to prove the full Allegations of that Complaint separately in each Parish, but in all the Parishes taken^together, which were named in the Petition.

The Committee then proceeded upon the Parish of St. Martin: And Mr, Shute and Mr. Adder ley, Agents for the Petitioners in that Parish, first undertook to prove, that the Vestry assessed and levied the Watch Rate; in Support of which Allegation, they produced the Watch Rate of the Year 1740, signed by several of the Vestry, whose Hands were proved by Mr. Middleton Collector, and Mr. William Godfrey Vestry-Clerk of the said Parish.

The latter of whom being examined concerning the Method of making the Rates, said, that heuiually made out the Rate from that of the former Year, leaving Blanks for the Sums to be charged upon the respective Inhabitants; which Blanks are afterwards filled up by the Vestry: That these Rates were always cast up before the Justices signed them; and that no Alterations were made in them after they are so signed; which was in about a Week after the Rate has been made, as aforesaid.

Whereupon the Agents for the Petitioners produced the Watch Rate for Drury-Lane and Long-Acre Ward, of 1741; in which Books, not a Angle Page was added together; from whence the Managers presumed the Rates may have been left open in former Years, till the Collection was ended.

To this Head, the Petitioners likewise produced the Book of Vestry Orders for the said Parish; wherein it appeared, that a Committee of Vestry was appointed September 21ft, 1725 (a), to examine the Poors Rate, and to make it more equitable, and to rectify it; and that it was there resolved, That Twelve Pence in the Pound must be raised for the Relief of the Poor in that Parish for the Year ensuing: And your Committee desiring to be informed, whether the Practice had been the same in latter times, an Order of Vestry was produced from the same Book, dated April the 7th, 1740 /^,resolv4ng the Rate ior the Poor should be at Eight Pence in the Pound: And it appeared further, that, on the 23d of the same Month (c), the said Resolution was read; and, upon further Consideration, was repealed by the Vestry, and by them increased to Ten Pence.

The Committee then calling for the Rates for the Poor, which were made in consequence of these Orders of the Vefty, it appeared, that the said Rates were entered as if made in a legal Manner, being said to be assessed by the Rector, Churchwardens, and some of the antifent Inhabitants, and signed by Two Justices, according to the Form prescribed by the Act of the 43d of Elizabeth. And,

Mr. William Godfrey, the Vestry Clerk, being called in, was required to inform the Committee, whether a public Notice was always given to the proper Officers and Inha-

bitants to meet for the Making of the Poor’s Rate, as the Law requires i he said, That such Notice was constantly given. Being asked, Whether the Inhabitants did attend by virtue of that Summons ? he laid. They did. But being further questioned, Whether, by Inhabitants, he meant the Inhabitants at large, or only such Inhabitants as were of the feled Vestry? he acknowledged, they were only such as were Members of the Vestry; and that no others attended, as he remembers, except in the Year 1740, when the Disputesat Law arose between the Parish and the Vestry. Being then asked. Why the other Inhabitants did not attend ? he answered, Because the Vestry, being a select Vestry, thought they only were intended by the Word Inhabitants.

He confessed, the Vestry proposed and settled the Poor’s Rate, before it was offered to the Justices to sign. And being asked, If this Rate, when once settled by the Vestry, was ever, in any Instance, altered afterwards by the Juf-rices ? he said, Never, except in one Instance, and that was in the Year 1740, after the Parish had contested their Rights at Law with the Vestry.

Mr. Miller, a Justice of the Peace, being examined, informed the Committee, That he had been frequently at the Vestry, when they made the Poor’s Rate; and he was the only Justice of the Peace present.

Mr. Fabrie being examined, as to the levying the said Rates, said, That he was distrained, by an Order of the select Vestry, for Non-payment of the Watch Rate: That about September or October 1 740, being summoned to attend the Vestry upon this Account, he demanded. Whether they fat there as a Vestry, or as a Petty Sessions ? they answered. As a Vestry. He then complained of the Rate; and they told him, they would distrain him, if he did not pay. He said, that it was an illegal Rate, because there were many Erafements in it, many were over-rated, many under-rated, and many not rated at all. The Vestry then told him. If he would swear that he had been over-rated, they (the Vestry) would reduce him: But he told them, they could not legally alter the Rate, after it had been signed by the Justices. He therefore refused to swear. But that while he was with the Vestry, many other Persons offered their Complaints, and were sworn in his Presence s and that thereupon the Vestry ordered they should be reduced; and that he saw the Vestry-Clerk at that time alter the Rate, in pursuance of the said Orders of the Vestry.

Mr. Phillips, a Grocer, being examined, said. That upon looking into the Rate, observing himself rated more than he ought to have been, he complained, and was told, he should appeal to the Vestry; which he did: That Mr. Turner, the Laceman, and a Vestry-man, treated him at first in an over-bearing Manner; but, after some Discourse, he, the said Turner, ordered the Vestry-Clerk to alter the Rate in his favour; which he did; and he was accordingly reduced from £. 40. to £. 35; and that only one Justice of the Peace (Mr. Frazier) was present at this Meeting of the Vestry.

Mr. Thomas Middleton, the Collector, being examined as to the Method of levying the Watch Rates, acknowledged, that when Persons complained of being over-rated, the Vestry verbally gave him Leave (going with the Churchwarden or the Vestry-Clerk, the former of whom he looks upon as the Umpire of the Vestry) to collect less than the Rate, after it was signed by the Justices; but that he has no written Order for that Purpose. And being asked, what the Abatement might generally be? he said. That, as to the Watch Rate in particular, it amounted to about £. 1,400 per Annum; but that he collect ed not above £. 1,000. Being the ndefired to inform the Committee, in what manner he made those Abatements ? he laid, He did it by a Mark upon a blue Leaf, which was kept in the Book for that Purpose. And being further questioned, to whom he gave in his Accounts, and from whom he received his Acquittal ? he said, He delivered them to the Vestry-Clerk, who cast them up for him; and that he looks upon the Vestry-Clerk’9 Approbation to be his Acquittal: That he is never questioned further: That the

Mr. Godfrey, being again called, was examined* as to the making and levying of Rates, and confdTed, that the Vestry did reduce particular Persons in the Rate,; upon the bare Memorandum of the-Collector on the Blue Leaf t He said, first. That the Justices made a Memorandum likewise, that the Persons so reduced were over-rated; but acknowledged afterwards, that though Two or Three Justices were sometimes present, yet this Business was sometimes transeded only in the Presence of One Justicee of the Peace; and, at last, confefied, That once within these Twelve Months, it had been done by the Vestry, without any One Justice, but said; he Could not recoiled ’ any other Instance.

Where\jpori‘ the Petitioners produced an Order of Vestry, which they called an Order of Petty Sessions, when only One Justice of Peace Waspresent.

Mr. Miiler informed the Committee, as to the levying of the Rates, That, in foroe Cafes*-the Justices have ifeducdd

the Rate upon the Oath of the Party, and in fotne, upon the Credit of the Party, without an Oath: That the Vestry give Notice to the Justices, and Order them to attend when there is to be a Day of Appeal; but that the Vestry attend likewise,- and the Business is done in a Vestry, and the Justices give aSundiontoit, but they are meer Cypl>ers and that the Vestry govern and manage all thote Matters: That there are generally Eight or TeriVeftrymen prefen t, and sometimes Two Justices, sometimes One, and sometimes none at all; and that the Vestry do what they will in every thing.

Beinrgafked, Whether the power of abating legally lay in the Justices or in the Vestry ? He answered, That if the Justices give their Opinion, it just signifies nothing: That if they attempt to controul the Vestry, they overpower and brow beat ’em: And in One Instance, where be desired to look into their Management, Mr. Turner the Laeeman, then in ihe Chair of the Vestry, told him, That if he went on in that manner, he would get him turned out of the Commission of the Peace: Being then questioned as to the Power of the Vestries to relieve upon Oath, after the Rate was legally signed ? He laid, it was the common Custom of a feled Vestry, and he did not care to contend with them in any thing.

Your Committee observed many Erafemenrsin the Rate both in the Sums and in the Names, frequently no less than Three or Four in one Page, particularly in the First Rate to the Watch, for the Year 1736, Fo. 14, where William Meeks, George Errington, a Coach-maker, and Vestry man, and Mary Oltphant, were entered upon an Erafement: In the same Book, and in the same Rate, Fo. 2, Entries of the Names of James Gascoigne and Joseph Crejfwell in like manner: In the same Book, Fo. 4, an Erafement both in the Rate and Money Column, in Fo. 11, Two Erafements; and in Fo. 10, no less than Five in the Money Column only.

Mr. Godfrey, Vestry Clerk, being examined to this Particular, and the Book of the Watch Rate for Spurt-Alley Ward, 1740, being produced, and an Instance shewn of a Name erased in Fo. 8; he answered. That it was erased because it was reported by the Collector to be an empty House; ^fid that there were sometimes Three or Four Tenants in it in One Year, which created Confusion: The Second Rate of the W;atch for the same Year being produced, and a Name appearing to be altered, Fo. 69, he said. He could not tell by whom that Name was altered: Being asked, Whether he had any Authority to make any Alterations after the Rate was signed by the Vestry ? He answered, only to alter Blots; and endeavoured to convince the Committee, that these Erafements

were only oh Account of Blots, df/bti Account of Mif-takes in copying from the former Rates* which he reded before the Rates were signed by the Vestry.

Mr. Miller informed the Committee* That the Rate ought to be fair, without Erafement* when the Justkcs sign it; but that he has never taken much Notice of the Rates, or of Erafements in the Books* before he signed them 5 for that, Seven or Eight Vestrymen make the Rate* and then it is brought to the Justices; and be apprehends it a Matter of Course to sign it; but that once* upon the Book being brought to him far Payment* he observed many Erafements, which he believed to have been made after the Justices had confirmed the Rate; upon which he complained; but was answered* That it had been done by the Vestry; and he was told by the Collector, that after the Justices had signed* the Vestry made the Erafements.

Thomas Middletony the Collector* befog further eft- mined as to an Erafement in the first Wafcch Rate 1738* 'Over-t against the Name of Doctor Ptar.ce, the Re&or, in which he was reduced* answered, That it was altered by Order of the Vestry, after the Rate was signed j and that ' he was reduced again ill the next Half Year, byvan Erafement likewise; because he claimed to be totally excused* but that* upon the late Uneasiness in the Parish on Account of the Conduct of the Vestries, he has since {that Time been raised again.

Dr. Pearce, Vicar of St. Martin's, being examined, said. That he had paid the Watch Rate from the Time of the Commencement of the Ad* which was in the Year 1736: That he was first rated at £40. and that his House was worth as much, but that it was altered afterwards from 40 to £.30. He acknowledged, that this was done without a regular Complaint, the Collector only taking of him at the Rate of £.30. per Annum t That the Gentlemen of the Vestry thought this reasonable, because it was a new Tax; and that his Predecessors had been usually excused all other Parish Taxes, because they never demanded the Burial Fees for the Poor, which Burials might amount to 700 in each Year: He cannot answet by whom his Rate was reduced; but that since that Time, he has consented to be rated at £.40. per Annum.

The Agents conceiving, that they had sufficiently proved, that the Vestry assessed and levied the Watch Rate; and that they assessed that of the Poor, desired that the Acts of Parliament might be read relating to both.

And it appeared by the Watch Ad 1736, That the Vestry, and Two Justices of the Peace of the City and Liberty of Westminster> are impowered to make and confirm the Rate.

Whereupon, the Agents for the Petitioners observed, that the Justices could not controul the Vestry in this Matter.

And that the Vestry taking upon them to make Erased ments, and to alter the Rate after it was signed by the Justices, was in Eflfed the same thing, and the same in its Consequences to the Inhabitants, as if the Justices were not at all concerned in it; so that they humbly apprehend it to be a meerEvafion of the Law.

As to the Poor’s Rate, That the Law requires by the 43d of Eliz. that this Rate shall be made and assessed by the Churchwardens and Overseers of the Poor, with the Consent of Two Justices of the Peace; they therefore conceived, the Vestry, in making the said Rate, have acted contrary to Law; and they took Notice further, from the Evidence that had been given to this Head, That the Forms observed in the Words prefixed to the Rates, were an Imposition on the Publick; for that the Vestry did in Fad appear to make the Rates, though they were, in some Cafes, signed by the Justices, in the manner that the Law directs.

Lastly, That the Assumption of these Powers, contrary to Law, by the Vestry, was of fatal Consequence to the Parish; for that they were thereby obliged to engage in 3 E expend v*

He confessed, that he could not take upon him to lay, that he had done it once.

The Agents for the Petitioners then proceeded to the Article in the Petition relating to the Secreting of Accounts from the Parishioners.

But, as to this Head, they said, That they should not give the Committee much Trouble, the Fast being notorious in the general, and claimed from the Nature of a select Vestry: That they should therefore confine themselves to the Watch Books only; which, by Act of Parliament, they apprehended themselves to be intitled to fee.

And then the Act for regulating the Nightly Watch in this Parish being read, it appeared, that the Parishioners are intitled by that Law to see the Totalsof all Accounts relating to the Watch, whenever they shall so require.

Mr. Fabrie being then called in, and examined, said. That, in the Year 1740, thinking himself aggrieved in the Watch Rate, he applied to the Vestry to see the* Rates, and determined to try the Matter at Law; but being no Vestryman, the Vestry several times refused him the Books, only they produced a Leidgcr, which contained the bare Totals of the Sum collected, which could give no Information; and he was told, this was all he had a Right to fee: That he only asked to look at the Books, and was refused: That he appealed to the Justices at the Quarter-Sessions: That they construed the Law in a different Sense, and gave him an Order to fee all the Books of that Account; but even after this, the Clerk, Churchwardens, and Vestrymen, (huffied him off for some time.: That, after some Interval, they sent to him to let him know, that he might have a Sight of the Books an Hour in a Day: That they allowed him this Liberty the First Day to make Extracts; but Bannifier, the Churchwarden, attending, hindered hinji the next Day, and said. The Justices had no Power to make such an Order; yet at length he was allowed a Copy of them, for which he paid Four Guineas.

Mr. Henry Williams% being examined to the same Particular, said. That, before the Appeal to the Quarter-S^f-(ions in October 1740, he demanded a Sight of the Watch Books, and attended Godfrey, the Vestry^Clerk, two or three times, but could not obtain the Perusal of any of them: TJiat, after the Orderof the Quarter-Sessions before-mentioned, with a View to delay, they interrupted them in their Search, and allowed them but Two Hours in a Day: That Mr. Bannifler, the Churchwarden, interrupted them, and (but up the Books, notwithstanding the Order; and though they attempted no other Use of t hem than to make Extracts; and at last, when they procured the Copies, it was but a few Days before the Trial.

Mr. Miller being examined to this Matter of the Election of Overseers of the Poor, informed the Committee,

Mr. Fabric confirmed this Account of Mr. Miller, and said, That the Vestry continued to ad in this illegal Manner till March 1741; when the Parish having commenced a Suit at Law against the Vestry; out of Ap« prehension, that they should be questioned for this, as well as other Branches of their Conduct, they came into a regular Method, as to the Election of Overseers.

James, and St. George Hanover-Square , they being formerly Members of, and not many Years since erected into distinct Parishes out of St. Martin's, by different Acts of Parliament; which all preferi be, that they should be governed by the Example of their Mother Parish.

Mr. Fabric being examined to this Particular, informed the Committee, That, upon the late Disputes at Law, in which he was concerned, he had Occasion to examine the Constitution of the Vestries, and found several antient Entries, which differed in Practice, but in the general seemed to imply, that the Parish had been governed by a feted Number of the Inhabitants from the Time of Queen Elizabeth: That, in the Time of the great Rebellion, the Constitution seemed to have been altered; but that soon after the Restoration, viz. in 1662, Twenty-three of the Inhabitants applied to the Bishop o»f London for a Faculty to constitute a feted Vestry: Whereupon, an Instrument was granted, appointing 52 Inhabitants to be a feted Vestry, with the Minister and Churchwardens; and Ten*to be a Quorum: That this Quorum being found too large, the major Part of the Vestry applied, by Certificate, a Second time to the Bishop of Londw, in 1673, who granted another Instrument, reducing the Quorum to the Number of 7.

And these Two Instruments being produced to the Committee;

William Godfrey, the Vestry-Clerk, was called in; and being questioned, WhetfTer the Vestry acted under these Faculties ? he said. That he has known the Vestry Nine Years; and that they conformed to the Bishop’s FacuL ties before-mentioned.

Being then asked. Whether the Vestry consisted of 52? he said, That 52 was their Number when complete; but that they may, and do, neglect to fill up Vacancies as long as they please; and that they fill up themselves, and choose their Successors.

Whereupon the Agents for the Petitioners took Nor tice, that they thought themselves, in Decency, obliged to avoid any Reflections, which might naturally result from the Institution of the feied Vestry, as it had been explained to the Committee; for though they should have thought themselves at Liberty to have offered Reasons to prove, that the Bishop of London had no Power to ered a Constitution of such a kind, as being contrary to the common Law of the Land, which avows no Parish Government of such a Nature; and though it was confessed, that the Vestry acted under that Constitution of the Bishop,

And the Committee observed further, That although the Balance of £.282. 11/. 5 d. was not carried to any Account regularly, as it ought to have been; yet Mr. Byron having fairly given Credit for it to the Parish, it does not appear, that this Neglect arose from any Design to defraud ihe Parish.

Hereupon the Petitioners took Notice, That though this Money was fairly accounted for, yet it was not possible, that the Vestry could have examined these Accounts, as they ought to have done, having suffered so great an Irregularity in the Collector’s Account.

By which it appeared, that this Method had been pur-fiied ever since the Year 1722; and that there was a Sum in his Hands in Money, Bonds, and South Sea Annuities, amounting to about £.1,200.which he holds in Trust for the Parish; but that he gives no Security for the faithful ' Execution of his Trust.

Whereupon the Petitioners observed, That this Application of all Surplusses to the Church Account was illegal; for that the Surplusses of every Rate should be kept distinct, and carried on to the same Account, in Ease of the next Year’s Rate: That this Practice was a Contrivance to ease the Church Rate, and to provide a Fund for such Expences, with regard to the Church, as the Parish might not readily acquiesce under, and might not think necessary, if they were particularly rated for such Purposes: That it likewise prevented the Parishioners from judging whether they were rated more than the Service required, or not, and left too great a Power in the Vestry: That, the raising so much more upon particular Rates than was necessary, was very dangerous to the Parish; for that by this means the Parish washable to great Losses by the Deficiencies of Collectors; of which there was an Instance in the Year 1739, when Sanchey, then Churchwarden, died insolvent, with the Sum of £. 129. 8 s. 2\d. which the Parish wholly loft.

The Petitioners then proceeded, inth*e last Place,’to shew the Constitution of the select Vestry in the Parish of St. Anne And they produced an Act of Parliament of the 30th of Charles the Second, by which, the Parish of St. Anne was taken out of the Parish of St. Martin, and made a "distinct Parish:

And also another Act of the First of James the Second, for building a Church in the said Parish; by which Act,

‘ the Bishop of London of that Time, was impowered, within Thirty Days, to appoint, by Iostrument, 30 Persons to be Supervisors till the Church should be built, and, after that, to be Vestrymen, as in other Parishes, and not otherwise; to continue Vestrymen during Life, or Abode in the Parish, unless difpiaced by the Bishop of London for Misdemeanors, and all Vacancies to be supplied by Election; under which general Words,’ Viz. as in other Parishes, and hot otherwise," the Vestry of this Parish have thought themselves intitled to adopt all 'such Habits and Customs as can tend to the Support of their Power, which has no Contrqul but that of their own Discretion, being perpetuated by their Institution *.for Life, and the Choice of their Successors; from whom,

therefore, it can never be expected, that the Government of the Parish should be more juitly conducted hereafter than at present.

A Petition of the Manufacturers and principal Dealers Linen in Linen, within the Town of Paisley, in behalf of them-' Manufacture. selves, and many others, was presented to the House, and read; representing to the House the Progress already made in the Manufacture of Linen in North Britain; which, as the Petitioners allege, would be considerably promoted by discontinuing the Drawbacks on Foreign Linen, carried to our American Settlements, and allowing a Drawback on British Soap, used in whitening of Linen Cloth, Linen-Yarn, and Thread, of our Home Manu-fastnre: And therefore praying the House, to take the Premises into their Consideration, and to give such Encouragement to this Staple, as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom it is referred, to consider of the Petition of the subscribing Merchants of the City of London, and others, Dealers in the Manufactures of Linens made in Great Britain and Ireland, in behalf of themselves, and the Manufacturers of Linens in the said Kingdoms.

- Being then questioned. Whether there-was any. Alteration made in the Rate brought to him, from that which he had first delivered in

He answered, That there was an Alteration with regard to John Laroche Esquire, a Member of this House, who was rated at £. 130. the last Year; in which he, the said Cuflis, was Assessor; and that thinking him over-rated, he had reduced him to/[.i00. in the Assessment which he had delivered in; but that in the Copy of the Assessment, of which he spoke, he found that he had been: reduced to £. 80.

Being then asked. In what Year this Occurrence happened ? and required to consider well before he gave his Answer, he said it was in the Year 1740.

Being further questioned. In what Book he law;Mr. Laroche assessed at £. 130

He said. That, before he was an Assessor, he filw that Sum remarked upon the opposite blue Leaf by the old Assessors.

And, lastly, being required to say. Whether he had ever seen Mr. Laroche's House rated lower than at £.100. before he assessed it at £.100 r he answered. That he could not say he had.

It appears, nevertheless, by the Collecting Book, signed by himself in the Year 1738, That the House of Mr. La) oche was rated no more than £. 92.

Whereupon Mr. Rufiat being called in, and required to give an Account of this Abatement, answered, That \ the House of Mr. Laroche vas reduced from £. 100. to £. 80. upon an Appeal to the Commissioners of the Land Tax in the Year 1737-

The Minute Book of the Commissioners of the Land Tax, from 1731 to 1741> being then produced, it appeared by an Entry, dated October the 7th, 1737, That at a Meeting upon Appeals, at which time many Persons were allowed a Reduction of their Assessments, Mr. Laroche was then reduced from £. 10c. to £. 80.

Upon which Evidence, the Committee observe,

1 ft; That John Cullis having affirmed. That Mr. Laroche had been assessed at £.130. the Year whetl he was last Assessor (nieaning the Year 1738), appears to Have asserted a notorious Falsehood* Mr'. Laroche being proved by the Collecting Book of that Year, signed by the said himself, to have been assessed at no more than £.92. adiy, That the Assertion of the said John Cullis, That he, in his Assessment delivered in, in the Year 1740, had reduced Mr. Laroche from £.130. to £. 100; appears to be another palpable Untruth; the Fact being evident from the Books of the Collectors, that Mr. Laroche was never rated at £.130; and that, in the place of reducing the Rate of Mr. Laroche from £.130. to£. 100. the said John Cullis had raised the Rate of the said Mr. Laroche from £.81. to £* 100.

A Petition of the Manufacturers and principal Dealers Linen in Linen, within the Town of Paisley, in behalf of them-'Manufacture, selves, and many others, was presented to the House, and read; representing to the House the Progress already made in the Manufacture of Linen in North Britain; which, as the Petitioners allege, would be considerably promoted by discontinuing the Drawbacks on Foreign Linen, carried to our American Settlements, and allowing a Drawback on British Soap, used in whitening of Linen Cloth, Linen-Yarn, and Thread, of our Home Manufacture: And therefore praying the House, to take the Premises into their Consideration, and to give such Encouragement to this Staple, as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Confederation of the Committee of the whole House, to whom it is referred, to consider of the Petition of the subscribing Merchants of the City of London, and others, Dealers in the Manufactures of Linens made in Great Britain and Ireland, in behalf of themselves, and the Manufacturers of Linens in the said Kingdoms.

House, by giving false Testimony, at a Committee, relating to a worthy Member; for which Offence the Petitioner is now confined in his Majesty’s Gaol of Newgate; and that the Petitioner is truly sensibleof his Fault, is fin-cerely sorry, and most heartily repents of such his Offence, and humbly begs Pardon of the House, and also of the worthy Member; and that the Petitioner has lately had a violent fit of Illness, is now very weak, and in a bad State of Health, and most humbly assures the House, that if he is confined in Newgate any longer, it will greatly hazard the Petitioner’s Life; which will be an irreparable Loss to his poor Family; And therefore praying the House, to take the Petitioner’s same into Consideration, and give Leave that he may be discharged out of Prison.

A Petition of the several Soap-makers fefiding in and near the City of Exon, whose Names are subscribed, in behalf of themselves, and of all other fair Makers of Soap within this Kingdom, was presented to the House, and read; representing to the House, That, notwithstanding the tare and Vigilance of those employed in securing the Duties on Soap, it is found, by Experience, That the Laws already enacted are not sufficient to prevent great Frauds in the said Revenue, which are daily committed by Soap-makers, especial’y such as live in Villages and Country Places distant from the Residence of an Officer; whereby thfc Crown is deprived of a considerable Part of the said Dut ies, and the fair Trader is greatly injured, and Fraud and Perjury committed with impunity; and that this Evii may be lessened, if not altogether prevented; and proposing, that an Imprtffiort be made with a Stamp upon every Piece of Soap that is weighed, and charged with the Duty; and that those who shall expose any Piece or Cake of Soap to Sale, not having Rich Stamp or Iin-piession thereon, shall forfeit as the Parliament shall think fit: And therefore praying the House, to give such Relief in the Premises, as teethe House shall leem meet. Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of several Merchants of the Town of Great Yarmouth, in the County of Norfolk, and others, Importers of Wine into the said Port, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, in behalf of themselves, and several others, was presented to the House, and read; reciting Part of an Act of Parliament, made in the Thirteenth Year of the Reign of his present Majesty, intituled, An Act for prohibiting Commerce with Spain; and alleging, that several of the Petitioners, and others, upon Pre-fumption of the Continuance of the said Act, and upon Expectation that other Wines would be wanted to {up-ply the Deficiency of Spanish Wines, have imported and given Orders for the shipping of much greater Quantities of Portugal and other W ines than usual; and representing to the House, that the Bill now before this House, for impowering Melfieurs Nut hall, Fydell, and Mitchell, and certain other Merchants, to import from neutral Ports, a certain Quantity of Spanish Wines, may, as the Petitioners apprehend, afford Opportunities for indirect Practices, and render it extremely precarious for Merchants to caiy, on their Trade and Commerce, agreeable to Law, if liable to be defeated, after they have inverted their Effects: And therefore, as the said Bill manifestly tends to the great Prejudice of the Manufactures and Navigation of this Kingdom, and to the Loss of the Revenue, and will greatly affect the Property of the Petitioners; praying the House to take the Premises into Vol. 24.

Consideration; and that the said Bill may notpafs into a Law; or that the Petitioners may have such Relief as to the House may seem meet.

Your Committee now think proper, in order to avoid Repetition, to acquaint the House, that* in pursuance of their Orders, all the Persons examined before the said Committee, were examined in the most solemn manner: And Mr. Michael Gibbons, being examined, said; He was Agent to John Boteler Esquire, who ft bod Candidate at the Election, for a Member of Parliament for t lie Borough of IVendover, in the County of Bucks, in 1735: Thet Mr. Boteler did* the Saturday Night before it came on> advise with the Examinant, what was proper to: be done: That the Examinant told him nothing could be done without 5 or £. 600: That* on this* he believes Mr. Be-teler told him, that he had not so much Money, but he would write a Letter to Mr. Paxton: That the next Morning one Mr. John Jones, who was a Friend of Mr. Boteler's, was sent to London, and returned on the Monday Morning to IVendover\ and on his Return, told the Examinant, that he had delivered a Letter to Mr. Paxton, and Mr. Paxton had given him £. 500. he having, at the same time, in his Hand, great Numbers of Bank Notes, which, he told the Examinant, was the £. 500. in question; and which he immediately carried in to Mr. Boteler, who soon after came out, and informed the Examinant, that the £. 500. was come.

Mr. John Jones, being examined, said. That he had no Interest in the Borough of IVendover, but was employed by Mr. Bottler, as a Friend: That, before the Day of the Election, Mr. Boteler desired the Examinant to go to Town with a Letter, to Mr. Nicholas Paxton, for Money: That he found Mr. Paxton at Fulham, and gave him the Letter; and Mr. Paxton, on reading it, desired the Examinant to meet him the next Day, at Roger IVII-/ww/s Coffee-House: That he did meet him accordingly, and Mr. Paxton gave him a Parcel of Money (of which the greatest Part, if not the Whole, was in Bank Notes,) and told him, oh delivering it. Here is your Answer: The Sum, he believes, might be about £. 500: That he carried it the fime Morning to IVendover, and delivered the fame, or the greatest Part thereof, to Mr. Boteler.

John Boteler Esquire, being examined, said. But your Committee are utterly unable to discover by what Arts and Methods Mr. Paxton could evade passing any Account, during the Time of his being Solicitor to the Treasury, which is upwards of 1 Eleven Years, especially as it appears to your Committee, that it was the Duty of the said Treasury to oblige him to profecnteall such Accomptants as should appear to be in Arrear, by the Certificates of the Auditors of the Imprefts; for your Committee find, from a Eteport of the said Auditors (which is hereunto annexed* by way of Appendix), That, by a Warrant of the T/ealury, dated the 16th of August 1711, and signed Oxford, the Solicitor of the Treasury is directed to take care, that the Process be regularly issued against such Imprest Accomptants, as shall appear to be in Arrear by the Certificates of the Auditors of the Imprefts to the Queen’s Remembrancer; as also against all Persons (landing insuper upon any Imprest, or other Accounts; which Warrant was confirmed in his late Majesty’s Reign, as follows; viz.

And your Committee are at a Loss to determine what Motives could induce the Commissioners of the Treasury to continue the said Mr. Paxton so piany Years in the Office of Solicitor of the Treasury; and to direct, that such large Sums of publick Money should, from time to time, be lodged in his Hands, when they mud have been informed by the Half-yearly Certificates, delivered in to them by the Auditors of the Imprefts, that he had passed no Accounts from the Time of his First Appointment to be Solicitor of the Treasury, which was on the 22d of December 1730.

Your Committee, the better to be enabled to discover by what Services the said Mr. Paxton could deserve such singularand extraordinary Indulgence, did, on Friday {*% direct the Keeper of Newgate to bring him before them; and, upon his being called in, the former Question was again repeated to him; viz.

Did you advance any Money to Mr. John Jones, on the Account of Mr. Boteier, about the Time of the Election at Wendover, in 1735?

Upon which, he desired that his former Answer to the said Question might be read.

Which being read accordingly;

He repeated the very same Words; viz. I will not answer that Question, as it may tend toaccufe myself.

Whereupon he was a(ked, whether the Apprehension that »t might tend to accuse himself was his only Reason for not answering

He said, That is my principal Reason.

Whereupon he was ordered to withdraw.

Gwyn Vaughan Esquire, being examined, he was asked, Jf he knew of any Sum or Sums of Money, paid out of the Salary or Profits of any Place or Office under the Government ? To which he answered;

I do not know of any, at this time.

Being further asked, If he knew of any paid within these Ten Years

Vol. 24.

He desired to know, whether he was to include him- Enquinrinto fdf, or only others. &}*%£*.

He was then informed, That the Question was general, and included all Persons.

Then he said. That he was apprehensive an Answer to that Question might in part affect himself; and therefore desired to be excused answering.

Whereupon he was ordered to withdraw.

And upon his being called in again;

He was acquainted by the Chairman, That the Committee had considered of his Objection to the Question put to him, and would dot press it further at that time.

Your Committee, are.npw proceeding with all possible Dispatch, in prosecuting the Inquiry into the Conduct of the Earl of Oxford, during the l^ft Ten Years of his being First Commissioner of the Treasury, and Chancellor, and Under-Treasurer of his Majesty’s Exchequer; but they cannot conclude this Report without representing to the House the great Difficulty they labour under from this obstinate and contemptuous Behaviour of Mr.iW-ton, who appears to have be^n directly or indirectly concerned in most of the Transactions into which they have hitherto inquired; and when they consider the very large Sums which have been issued to him, during the Time of his beiflgSoiicitor to the Treasury, and that no effectual Methods were ever taken to oblige him to account for any Part thereof (a Circumstance which could not arise from mere Negligence or Inattention), when they consider, that the strong and well-grounded Remarks, made on his Accounts by the Deputy-Auditor of the Imprefts, were in-(lantly followed by a Warrant of the Treasury, directing the Auditor to allow his Accounts; when they consider what strong Suspicions must arise from the foregoing Evidence, that some Part at lead of the Money in his Hands may have been employed in Practices dangerous to the Liberties of this Nation, and destructive of the Independency of Parliament; they cannot help observing, that his Perseverance in refilling to answer, seems to take its Rile from a premeditated Scheme to obstruct and frustrate their Inquiry; and, should it pass unregarded, may probably communicate itself to other Persons, whom they shall have Occasion to call before them, and by that means render it impossible to lay a clear State of Affairs before the House.

Your Committee therefore thought themselves obliged in Duty to report these Matters specially to the House; and do humbly submit the same to their Confederation.

An Order of Vestry was likewise produced, in the Minutes of the Vestry, 20th of December 1723* Folio 26a (g)y requiring the Churchwardens to put out the Balance of the Churchwardens and Overseers Accounts, upon some Security, for the Use of the Parish: Whereupon, the Agents observed, That this Balance amounted to no less than a Sum of £.900; and that the raising of such Sums, above what the Service of the Parish did demand, was a great Burthen to the People, and exposed them to many Inconveniencies.

They then proceeded to shew, That the Vestry assessed unequally and partially; and, in Support of this Allegation, the Overseer’s Book for Marlborough-street Ward, in 1733, was produced; wherein Henry Parsons, a Vestry-man, appeared rated at £.24. for his House in Coventry-street: And Mr. Innefiey, being examined, said, That it was of much greater Value: That this House afterwards came to his Son; and Mr. Vaughan took it at £.80; and that it was rated at £.60, as appeared by the Rate in the Year 1739. x Mr. Richard Bullock informed the Committee, and the

Watch Book 1740 was produced in Confirmation of it, That Mr. Wimberley, a Vestryman, is rated for Two Houses in Ryder-street only at £ 26. per Annum; but that he letts them for £.40. per Annum, and reserves Two Rooms for himself. -,r:

The Agents then informed the Committee, That the Rule of the Vestry in 67. James's Parish is to rate the Parish at Three Quarters of the real Value; but that this is a Rule not generally kfiown to the Parish; by which the Vestry may rate who they please at the full Value; and the Persons so rated do not conceive they are aggrieved, while others are rated One Fourth-part less.

Mr. Whimmes Skinner then informed the Committee, and it was confirmed from the Poor’s Book in Golden-Square Ward, 1739, That his House (which was lett for £.22), was rated at £22; which, according to the Vestry Rule, was £.5. more than he ought to be rated at: And he being asked, Why, he did not appeal ? said, That he did not pay the Taxes himself; and he had not long known the Rule of the Vestry.

Whereupon a Member of this House, and One of the Vestry of this Parish, informed the Committee, That this House was rated to the Land Tax, in the Year 1736, at £.26. per Annum; and t|hat the Vestry made the Poor’s Tax from that of the Land,

The Watch Book for Pall-Mall Ward, 1735, being produced* it. appeared, that pour Houses in the Friery, belonging to Mr. Ludby, a Vestryman, charged to the Land Tax at £.100. per Annum, were affdfed to the Parish Taxes only at the Rate of £.72: And Mrm Bullock bcingexamined, laid. That Mr. Ludby, lately, and now, as be believes, letts these Houses in to Lodgings; and that the Lodgers refuse to pay, because they are Lodgers, and the Landlord, Mr. Ludby, will not pay, because he is Landlord* lu these Circumstances, as they apprehend, the Earish receive no Rates at all for them.

Mr. Rufiat, the Vestry Clerk, being examined to this Matter, acknowleged, That thofeStables and Stable-Yards were never rated to the Parish: And being asked, Whether they were charged to the Land Tax ? he said. They were; but that they paid no Parish Taxes; and that he could not tell the Reason.

Being questioned. Whether the Country Market paid any Parish Taxes ?. he said. That it was never rated.

Being asked. At what Sum it was charged to the Land Tax ? he said, About £.1700.

Being then desired to inform the Committee, To whom that Market belonged ? he said. To Mr. Ludby, a Vestryman, Mr. Bowling, and Mrs. Kilmaine.

Mr. Rufiat being then questioned, Whether Arthur Rawlinfony the High Constable, paid any Parish Pates? he acknowledged, That he paid none s And a Member of this House, and One of the Vestry of this Parish, informed the Committee, That he had issued several Sum-monfes to call the said Arthur RazvHnfott, and the Con-stabks, before him, in order to make him pay; but that he did not care to proceed further to compel him, because he was supported by the Burgesses Court, who said, That he ought not to pay.

The Vestry Minutes, of the 26th of September 1723 (k)y being then produced, the following Entry was read:

Ordered, That all the Clergy and Officers belonging to J " the Church and Vestry be, upon the next Rating of the "Books, excused from paying any Parochial Rate."

The Honourable Member before-mentioned then produced an Order Ten Years antecedent to that last spoken of; viz. in May 1713, "That ali should pay;" but said, this Order was annulled, the Collectors having represented, that the Clergy of St. James would not, because the Clergy of 6/. Martins did not pay; so the Order was repealed, with regard to the Rector; and that the Reafori why the Clergy of St. Martin s did not pay, was, because they claimed this Exemption in lieu of Burial Fees for the Poor, as he apprehended.

Whereupon the Agents for the Petitioners observed. That, as they conceived, the Clergytwere not in titled by Law to any of those Fees; for that the Poor’s Act, of the 43d: of Elizabeth, expressly ordains, That the Clergy shall be charged to the Poor’s Tax in like Manner as the rest of the Parishioners; so that this Exemption was contrary to Act of Parliament.

Mr. Rufiat, the Vestry Clerk, being examined. Whether the Order of Vestry, of 1723, was observed ? said, That it was observed for many Years: And being asked, Whether the Persons excused under that Order do now pay ? he said. That they have paid for some Time. ':

Mr. Seddon, One of the Vestry Clerks, being examined. Whether he paid the Rates ? he said, That he did.

The Committee then called for the Act of the ift of James the Second, by which this Rate was originally imposed; and.it appeared, that the Parish is to be charged to this Kate to far as to raise the Sum of £. 100, and no more, for the Preacher-A Aidant, over and above all Charges and Deduction of the Collection (k).

W hereupon the Agents for the Petitioners took Notice, That the Sum raised for this Purpose was more than double what the Act of Parliament allowed; and that whatever Application might he made of this Surplus, it, was contrary to the Law.

One of the Agents for the Petitioners then produced the Book of Parish Legacies, in order to shew, that a Legacy of £. 150, left to the Poor of the Parish by one Mr. Deferars, having been divided to Twenty Gentlemen of the Vestry, the Distribution of it was not, as he could find, accounted for to the Parish in the same manner that other Legacies have been since that Time.

And the said Book being read, it appeared, that the said Money was ordered to be divided, as above, to the said Twenty Vestrymen; but with this Addition, " To be u by them employed for the Relief of the Poor;" with a Reference to the Minutes of the Vestry of the 25th of April 1716.

Which Minutes of Vestry being produced to the Committee (I), an Entry of that Date appeared in the said Minutes, directing the Sum of £. 133. 12 6d. to be

divided to Nineteen Gentlemen of the Vestry; and among these Dr. Clarke, late Rector of St. James's, and several Persons of Distinction 5 to be by them distributed in small Sums to proper Objects.

(kJ Appendix, N* 13* 0) Appendix, N* 1.

Mali. 1742.

Whereupon some Gentlemen of the Committee taking Offence at the Matter so brought in Evidence by the said Agent, as conceiving it to have been opened unfairly, in the First Instance, by the Agent, who had not mentioned the End for which it was divided to the Vestrymen; (viz. to be distributed to the Poor;) and as it was a Re-fledion upon Gentlemen of great Credit and Worth;

The Agent, tojuftify himself, observed, That he had at first declared, that he asserted nothing positively, but what appeared upon the Books: That, in opening this Matter, he had not thought it necessary to particularize every circumstance of an Entry, the Whole of which was to be read immediately after by the Clerk, and before he could draw any Inference from it 1 and that he could have had no unfair View in what he had said, because he had produced that Order to have it read; and that, when it was read, the latter Part, which he had omitted to mention, must have been read with the former, and could not have been concealed from the Committee: That it was true, that Dr. Clarke, and the other Gentlemen mentioned in the Minutes, as the Persons to whom this Money was divided, were Men of so much Honour, that no Man could suspect their Misapplication of it; nor could he (the Agent) mean it as any Reflection upon them; but that he (till thought this might be properly brought in Evidence under the Head of Misapplication of the Parish Money; because he apprehended, that the Manner in which this was done, might be a Precedent for the like again; and that a Confidence of such a Nature might be hereafter reposed in Persons not of the same Worth: That, for these Reasons, the giving of Money to a/particular Use to any Person, to be distributed, was not a sufficient Account of that Money; and that the Reason for his Mention of it was, because there was no Account afterwards, that he had seen, of the particular Objects who had been relieved by it; which he conceived to be the proper Method that the Vestry should have taken, and which they of later Times had taken, in the Distribution of such Monies: That, therefore, it what he had laid, carried any Reflection, it could not be construed, nor intended, against the Gentlemen who received the Money, but against the Vestry, who, in his Judgment, had applied it irregularly; and that, if he mentioned this by way of Reflection against a former Vestry, even the Vestry of this Time had no Reason to be offended at it; for this was a Transaction which had passed many Years ago; at which Time it is confefied on all hands, that many wrong things were done ;. but that he does not charge thq present Members of the Vestry with what their Predecessors did: He knows many of them to be Men of great Honour; and that they have rectified many Abuses in this Parish: That he has no Charge against the present Vestry; and that it were much to be wished they could transmit their Integrity to their Successors; but that a present good Management is no constitutional Security; which is what they seek by their Petition; and that their Charge is levelled, not at the Persons of the Vestrymen, but at the Constitution of the Vestries; so that they had no Occasion, or Intention, to cast personal Reflections either on the Living or the Dead.

The Agents then produced, to the same Head, the Churchwardens Books of the Year 1723; out of which they extracted the Expences, annexed in the Appendix (m); which, for the greater Part, as they believed, and as far as they were able to judge, were unnecessary and improper Applications of the Parish Money.

The Petitioners then laid before the Committee the Account of Sacrament Wine for the Year 1723, which amounted to £. 77. 14. 7; but they observed. That they had no Vouchers for the Account of this or any other Year, but that of 1730: To which Particular, Mr. Sed-don, the Vestry Clerk, being examined, said. That he never heard that the Churchwardens were obliged to leave their Vouchers with the Vestry; because theij* Vouchers

And the Petitioners conceiving this a larger Sum than was necdftry for that Purpose, Mr. Slephenfony the Sexton, and Mr. Hunty an antient Inhabitant, and formerly Churchwarden of this Parish, were called in to inform the Committee as to the Number of Sacrament Days, and Number of Communicants, in that Parish:

And they both nearly agreed in the following Account: That, as to the Chapels, they could not tell the Number of the Communicants; but that they had a Monthly Sacrament in these Chapels:

That, as to the Church, the Sacrament was administered Monthly; and that, at each Monthly Sacrament in the Summer, the Communicants, as nearly as they could judge, amounted to 2 or 300, and, in the Winter, to never less than or 500: That the Sacrament was like-wife administered upon the Grand Feftivals: That, at Easter and Clirijtmas, they had Two Sacraments; one yearly in the Morning, and the other at Noon: That the Morning Sacrament was attended usually by about 1000, the Noon Sacrament by about 6 or 700 Communicants and that, on Whitsunday, they had about icoo in the Day; but that the Number was diminished of late Years; and that they consumed 38 Bottles of Wine at the Sacrament on the last Easter Day; and that from Easter to Wkitfun-iidey the Sacrament is administered every Sunday.

The Agents then produced the Vouchers for the Year 1730; the only Vouchers which were laid before the Committee, as before observed; the Total of which amounted to £.86. 4s. o\d.y in which Account there were many considerable Articles for Sack and White Wine.

Whereupon a Member of this House, and One of the Vestry of this Parish, informed the Committee, That the Clergy, when they preached, had sometimes White Wine in the Vestry Room:

But he produced an Order of the Vestry, of the 2d of .‘May 1635, fn) directing. That no Wine shall be used in Church or Chapel, unless at the Desire of the Preacher.

Upon which, the Agents for the Petitioners repeated again, what they had before acknowledged, That this and many other good Regulations had been made finee the Year 1735; but said, that it was not the Temporary Management of this Parish against which they complained, lo much as against the Constitution of the Vestries, which, after the Example of former Years, might be abused, if Men of less Worth should have the Management of it; and that the casual Security of the Parish, from the good Government of the present Vestry, was no real or sufficient Security to the Parish, while the Powers of the Vestry continued such as they appeared to be.

They then produced the Legacy Book, wherein it appeared, That, in the Year 1706, one Browne had left a Legacy to the Parish of St. fames of £.42, to be put out to Interest, for the Use of the Poor; and that the said Sum was accordingly put out to one Billingsley at an Interest of £.5. per Centum per Annum.

And it further appeared by the Churchwarden’s Accounts of several Years, That this Sum was regularly carried forward in the Account of the Churchwarden; and that the Interest was likewise accounted for till the Year 1725:

But it appeared in the Churchwarden Milner's Account, in the Year 1725, that though the said Sum ofjf.42. was charged as received by him from Hunt, the Churchwarden of the preceding Year; yet he the said Milner, who died during the time that he was Churchwarden, had not, in his Account, discharged himself thereof.

The Churchwarden’s Accounts of the Year 1726, being then inspected by the Committee, there was, in this

Account, no Entry either of the Interest or Principal of this Sum: c 1

But, in the Account of the Year after that last mentioned, viz. in 1727, your Committee found an Entry, on one Side of the Account, of this Sum said to be paid to Thomas Combes, and there specified to be the Legacy of the said Browne; which Sum is, from that Time, regularly brought to Account for many Years after Whereupon the Petitioners observed, lit. That this wa9 an Irregularity of an extraordinary Kind j since this Sum was, in one Year, only accounted for on one Side of the Account, and, in another Year, not accounted for at all j and that the Interest, as far as they* could find by the Books, was wholly loft to the Parish: But they observed 1 further, That though the Sum of £.42. here spoken of* was, in the third Year* entered and paid over to the next Churchwarden; yet the Money never appears, as they can find, to be received by the former Churchwarden* who has no Article in his Account of it.

Your Committee having spent much time to satisfy themselves about this Account, and not being able to succeed in it, thought it proper to rest it here, without reporting positively with relation to it.

The Agents for the Petitioners then produced again the Churchwarden’s Accounts of the Year 1727; in which* the Balance due to the Parish appears to be £.230.

And the Churchwarden’s Account of the next Year* (1728), being called for by the Committee, the former Balance was found to be carried over, and to Hand, upon an Erafement, only £.200; so that the Balance carried over was less by £.30. than it ought to have been: But the Committee do not determine, that this Money was funk to the Parish, rather taking ir to be an Irregularity in this Account. Mr. Seddony the Vestry Clerk, having informed the Committee, that he believed the Balance was carried short into this Account, because there was an Article which composed the Balance of the former Account, which ought not to have been carried into the Accounts of the Churchwarden, but into those of some other Officers of the Parish.

The Churchwarden’s Book of 1730, being then inspected, the Balance due to the Parish for that Year wafs a Sum of £.21. 9*. 8,

And the Account of the succeeding Year being then laid before the Committee, it appeared, that the Balance was carried over both to the Debts and Credits of thae Account; so that it was, in Effed, no Receipt at all.

Again, in the Account of the Year 1731, the Balance of that Year being £.27. 3. ^\d.

Upon Inspection of the Churchwarden’s Account for the Year 1732, the Balance of the Year 1730, and the Balance of the Year last mentioned, were both brought to the Debts and Credits of that Account, in the like Marnier as before; so that there was, in Effect, no Receipt of Balances for these Two Years.

Your Committee pursued this Account Two Years fur^ ther; and, in that of the Year 1733, these Balances were carried forward in the same Method; but, in the Year 1734, it appeared, that these Sums were entirely dropped, and no Entry made of them in any Shape whatever.

The Petitioners then proceeded to shew. That although the Produce of one Rate ought to be carried to no other Account than that of the same Rate; yet that this was, as far as they could find, the usual Practice in this Parish* and that they believed it to be in 1110ft, if not in every Instance, contrary to Law.

Appendix, N° 13.

" And be it Enacted, by the Authority aforesaid, That the Churchwardens of the said Parish for the Time being, together with Four, Three, or more, substantial Householders thereof, shall, upon the Tuesday in Easier Week next after the End of this Session of Parliament, or at any time within Ten Days after the said Tuesday, and so yearly for ever, proportionably tax, rate, and assess, the yearly Sum of One hundred Pounds upon the Inhabitants and Occupiers of Lands, Houses, Tenements, and Hereditaments, within the said Parish, for the Payment of the Preacher-Assistant, to be nominated and appointed, as aforesaid, which said Assessment shall be confirmed and allowed in such manner as other the Assessments hereby appointed to be made as aforesaid, and be collected, and paid yearly, to the Churchwardens for the Time being, by such Person or Persons as the said Churchwardens shall appoint, at the Four usual Feasts or Times of the Year before-mentioned; the First Payment to begin and be made at the Feast of St. John the Baptist, next after the taxing and assessing thereof; and the said Churchwardens, or either of them, shall pay the said yearly Sum of One hundred Pounds, over and above all Charges and Deductions for collecting the same to the said Preacher-Assistant for the Time being, to be nominated as aforesaid, upon the said Four usual Feasts or Terms in the Year, by even and equal Portions, the First Payment to begin at the said Feast of the Nativity of St. John the Baptist, last mentioned."

Ordered, That no Books of Accounts, or Books of Minutes, or any other Books or Papers relating to Charities, or otherwise belonging to the Parish, be delivered or shewn to any Person, not being a* Member of this Vestry, without a particular Order of Vestry.

!Thursday, the 4th of September, 173$(!)

Ordered, That, for the future, no Copy or Copies of any of the Orders of this Vestry be delivered to, or suffered to be taken by, any Person or Persons whatever, unless to the Churchwardens for the Time being, nor even to the Churchwardens, unless such Orders do concern their Office, without a special Order of this Vestry; and that none of the Vestry Books of Orders be produced and shewn to any Persons, but such as are Members of this Vestry."

In the last Place, the Agents proceeded to shew the Constitution of this Parish:

And John Atkinson, the Vestry Clerk, acknowledged, that the Number of the Vestry is not limited; but that the Vestry fill up Vacancies, and add to their Body, as they fee fit, by Election; in which the Inhabitants at large have no Voices: That the Custom is, for the Churchwarden to nominate at one Meeting, and for the Vestry to confirm such Nomination at the next.

And here the Petitioners rested their Evidence with regard to the Parish of St. Margaret.

The 26th Day of April 1737 (d), w several of the Constables and Beadles of this Parish having acquainted this Board,! hat Thomas Palmer, of James-street, in this Parish, whom they had apprehended for obstructing them in the executing a general Search Warrant, had brought several Actions against them for a Trespass;

Ordered, That Mr. Robert Andrews, Attorney, be employed t(o defend the Constables, fsV. against the said Actions."

20th Day of February, 1738 (e). €t Mr. Andrew's Bill of Law Charges for £.46, was in pursuance of a Minute of the last Vestry, laid before this Board, and examined; and it did appear to be a fair and reasonable Bill:

And it is hereby directed. That some, or One, of the Overseers of the Poor do pay the same forthwith."

Mr. Parry being required to give the Committee an Account of this Affair, said. That 'tis usual for the Justices to issue Search Warrants for Vagrants; in the Execution of One of which Warrants, the said Palmer obstructed, and affaulced, a Constable, who endeavoured to search his, the said Palmer's, House; notwithstanding which, the said House was search ed, and Three or Four Persons taken there; One of whom was committed to Bridewell: That the said Palmer was likewise committed to Prifpn, and, at the next Petty Sessions, bound to Sessions; but compromised the Matter with the Conr liable, whom he had assaulted, and afterwards brought an Action against the rest of the Constables and Beadles, whom he cast; it not appeari ng, that the Con liable, who entered his House, had any legal Authority for so doings having given his Search Warrant to another Constable: That, in confederation of the Inability of the Persons concerned to defray the Expence of the said Law Suit, and that the said Palmer had frequently brought a great Charge upon the Parish by Inmates, the Vestry made the above-recited Order; which they referred to the Justices of the Peace, who postponed the Order Three or Four times, as thinking it illegal; but at last the said Justices allowed it to be paid out of the Poor’s Rate, having no other Fund out of which it could so properly be paid; the Matter having an immediate Relation to the Poor.

Upon which, the Agent for the Petitioners observed. That the Vestry had no Right to make such Allowance to the Rector.

In regard to favouring some Persons in the Rates, an Order of Vestry, of the 14th April 1730 (0), was read, as follows: " Mr. Pordage, the Clerk in Orders, his Affair of paying the Poor Rate was heard;

Ordered, That the Parish Officers excuse him from paying the Rates; it being customary in other Parishes."

Mr. Parry being examined as to this Particular, owned, that Doctor Trebeck, the Rector, has been excused for some time, in consideration of having not taken any Burial Fees for the Poor; but has paid the Rates since the Year 1740: Nor doth it appear, that he was excused by Order of the Vestry.

The Agent for the Petitioners here closed his Evidence, with this Observation, That as this Parish is, by the Act of the Tenth of Queen Anne, under the same Regulations as that of the Parish of St. Martin, he humbly hoped, they shall be intitled to such Relief as the House shall think proper to give to the said Parish of St. Martin.

Upon the Whole, your Committee submit to the House, Whether the Petitioners have made good the Complaints or Allegations, in their Petition, against the select Vestry of this Parish; and whether the said Vestry have conducted the Affairs of the said Parish, under their Direction, to the Benefit and Advantage of the said Parish.

Sir Thomas Hanmer acquainted the Board, That he had received a Letter from Mr. Rowey touching the Disposal of the late General Stewart's Legacy of £. 5,000, Irish Money; which Letter is as follows:

December ift, 1740.

<c Honourable Sir,

Pursuant to the Liberty you was pleased to give me,*I herein fend you an Account of what has been done with regard to the Legacy left by the late General Stewart, for the Benefit of the Parish of St. George Hanover-Square; and what the Executors of the General now propose to do, with the Approbation and Concurrence of 1 he Gentlemen of the Vestry.

In’the Year 1736, it was thought proper by the Gentlemen of the Vestry, and the Executors, to apply to the Master of the Rolls for his Direction to raile £. 5,coo, Irish Money, out of the Estate of General Stewart, to be laid out in building, and endowing, a Charity School, according to the Direction of his Will. Upon hearing the Cause, his Honour was pleased to order Mr. Edwards to compute, and report, what was the Value of £. 5,000 Irish, reduced into English Money; and, at the same time, to state a Plan to the Court for establishing the said Charity.

Pursuant to this Order, Mr. Edwards reported, the £. 5,000 Irish amounted to £.4,484. 6 s. id. English \ and dated a Plan, as diiedted.

Upon further Hearing, his Honour directed, That the £. 4,484. 6s. 1 d. be laid out in Bank Three per Cent. 'Annuities, in the Names of James Stewart, Elizabeth Rowe, and Henry Roive, as Trustees for the said Charity: That a Sum, not exceeding £. 800, should be applied in the purchasing Ground, and eredlinga School and House, and Hirni thing-the fame: That, as soon as the same was finished, Twenty Boys should be admitted, to be taught to read and write, and to be instructd in the Principles of the Christian Religion, and to be cloathed, according to the Estimate, at £.2. 1 os. each: That the Master of the School should be a Clergyman of the Church of England, who had no other Preferment: That he should have £.40 yearly Salary, and also£. 10 yearly for Coals and Candles, and £. 10 yearly more for Books, Pens, Ink, and Paper.

This, Sir, is the Substance of the Master of the Bolls Decree: In Obedience to which, the Executors of General Stewart did vest the Money, as directed; and have used all possible Endeavours to procure a Piece of Freehold Ground in the Parish, but in vain; and now finding themselves utterly incapable of pursuing the said Decree, in that respect, and being great'y desirous to dhpose of the Money, so as to be of a real Advantage to the Parish, and, in some measur, to answer the Intention of the Testator, they beg Leave to propose.

That the Lid Charity Money be, by Direction of Parliament, given towards building, and endowing, an Hospital for deserted and exposed young Children; with this Proviso, That the said Hospital be obliged to take in always Ten Children out of the Parish of St. George Ha-- nover-Square, to be cloathed, entertained, educated, and placed out Apprentices, or otherwise, according to the Establishment of their Charter; and that as Vacancies happen in the said Ten, the Number shall be filled up out of the said Parish.

This, the Executors apprehend, will be a more real Benefit to the Parish, than if the Testator’s Direction, and the Decree, bad been literally pursued; for, according to them, the only Advantage, if it may be called an Advan-3T tage,

Linen

Mr. Hooper, according to Order, reported from the Manufactures Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred to consider further of the Petition of the subscribing Merchants of the City of London, and others, Dealers in the Manufactures of Linens, made in Great Britain and Ireland, in behalf of themselves, and the Manufacturers of Linens in the said Kingdoms; and also of the several other Petitions referred to the Consideration of the said Committee, the Resolutions, which they had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place} and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the ft me were read; and are as follows; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Manufactures of Linens, made in the Kingdoms of Great Britain and Ireland, are greatly improved and increased, whereby the Price of L.inens, as well of Foreign as Home Fabrick, hath been considerably reduced.

Resolved, That it ' is the Opinion of this Committee, That the further Extension of the British and Irish Manufactures of Linens, will be a great Advantage to the said Kingdoms of Great Britain and Ireland.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the granting a Bounty upon the Exportation of all British and Irish Linens from Great Britain, will be a Means of extending the said Manufactures.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That an Allowance of One Penny per Yard upon all British and Irish Linens, of the Value of Twelve Pence per Yard, and under, will be a proper Bounty upon the Exportation thereof.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the said Bounty be paid by an additional Duty to be laid upon foreign Cambricks, to be imported into Great Britain.

The First and Second Resolutions of the said Committee, being severally read a Second time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed to by the House, Nemine contradicenie.

The rest of the Resolutions of the said Committee, being severally read a Second time, were, upon the Question severally; put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

Ordered, That the said Report be referred to the Con-, (ideration of the Committee of the whole House, to

whom it is referred, to consider further of Ways and Means for raising the Supply granted to his Majesty.
