N* 16.

John David Barbutt Esquire, Secretary to the Post-Office, being examined in the most solemn manner, this 28th Day of May 1742, and being asked as to the Dif-position of the Money paid into his Hands, without Account, by a Warrant from the Crown, said. That there is in the Post-House a private Office, for the inspecting foreign Correspondents, and that the greatest Part of that Money is for the defraying the Expence of this Office: That the Accountant-General and Receiver-General, who have inspected the Books, have told him, that the first Traces they find of any Money thus paid by Warrant, was in the Year 1718 c That this Examinant cannot say as to the first Establishment of this Office, having been but Three Years and a Half himself in the Post-Office; but he apprehends there was always an Office of this kind, and that it was defrayed formerly by the Secretaries of State: That he is a Stranger to the Business of the Office, having never been in it; for they pretend to be independent, and to receive their Instructions from the Secretaries of State, and carry their Intelligence to the Secretaries of State, though the Post-Masters have a Right to go into the Office: That the annual Expences of this Office are as follows: To the Chief Decypherer, Mr. Willes, for himself and his Son, £. 1,000: To the Second Decypherer,

Mr. Corbiere, £. Sco: To the Third Decypherer, Mr. Lampe, £. 500: To the Fourth Decypherer, Mr. Zollman, £. 200: To the Chief Clerk, Mr. Le Fevre, £.650: To the Four other Clerks, Messieurs Bode, Thouvcis, Clark, Hemmitt, £. 300 each: To the Comptroller of the foreign Office, Mr. Day, £.60: To the Door-keeper 40 or £. 50. but this Examinant believes £. 50. There are, be-lides, accidental Charges for Seals, &V. an Account of which is brought in by One of the Clerks, which may amount to £. 100. and to Mr. Lavalade, formerly Alphabet-keeper, but now superannuated, £.40. That when these Sums were discharged, the Overplus, which may amount to£: 90. is divided between the Two Post-masters and the Secretary;each Post-master takingThreeSevenths, and the Secretary One Seventh: That Mr. Le Fevre, besides his above-mentioned Salary, is paid something out of Incidents; so that his whole Salary may amount to about, as he believes, £.800. per Annum: That his (Le Fevre's) is a very troublesome Post; it being necessary he should be always present at the going out, and the coming in, of the Mails: That this Examinant docs not know of a Pension of £. 200. per Annum, paid out of this Money; but Mr. Clark, who has formerly attended, and is inca* pacifated at present, has £. 200. paid him out of his Salary of £. 300. and another attends for him.

J. D. Barbutt.

A Motion was made, and the Question being proposed. And then the House adjourned till Tomorrow

That the said Report, with the Appendix, be printed: Morning, Nine of the Clock.

And the previous Question being put, That that Question be now put;

It passed in the Negative.

A Message from his Majesty, by Sir Charles Dalton, Gentleman-U(her of the Black Rod:

Mr. Speaker,

The King commands this Honourable House to attend his Majesty, immediately, in the House of Peers. Accordingly, Mr. Speaker, with the House, went up

to attend his Majesty in the House of Peers; where his Majesty was pleased to give the Royal Afient to the several public and private Bills following; viz.

An Act for granting to his Majesty an additional Duty on foreign Cambricks imported into Great Britain> and for allowing the reout a Bounty upon certain Species of British and Irish Linens exported:

An Act for the more effectual preventing the Counterfeiting of the current Coin of this Kingdom, an<|Uhe Uttering or Paying of false or coqnterfeit Coin:

An Act to impower the Importers, or Proprietors, of Rum or Spirits, of the British Sugar Plantations, to land the same before Payment of the Duties of Excise charged thereon, and to lodge the same in Warehouses, at their own Expence; and for the Relief of Ralph Barrow, in respect to the Duty on some Rock Salt loft by the Overflowing of the Rivers Weaver and Dane.

An Act for the more effectual preventing any Cloth or Woollen Goods remaining upon the Rack or Tenters, or any Woollen Yarn or Wool left out to dry, from being stolen or taken away in the Night-time.

An Act for further regulating the Plantation Trade; and for Relief of Merchants importing Prize Goods from America, and for preventing collusive Captures there; and for obliging the Claimers of Vessels seized for Exportation of Wool, or any unlawful Importation, to give Security for Costs; and for allowing East India Goods to be taken out of Warehouses, in order to be cleaned and refreshed:

An Act to revive several Acts for the Punishment of Persons destroying Turnpikes or Locks, or other Works erected by Authority of Parliament, and for other Pur* pofestherein mentioned; and to continue several Acts relating to Rice; to Frauds in the Customs; to the clan-destineRunning of Goods; and to Copper Ore, of the British Plantations; and for extending’the Liberty given by the Act of the Twelfth Year of the Reign of his present Majesty, for carrying Sugar, of the Growth of the British Sugar Colonies in America, to Ships belonging to any of his Majesty’s Subjects residing in Great Britain, and navigated according to Law; and for the more effectual preventing the Cutting of Star or Bent:

An Act to continue several Laws for the Encouragement of the making of Sail-Cloth in Great Britain, and of the Silk Manufactures of this Kingdom; and for allowing a Drawback on the Exportation of Copper Bars imported; and to explain a Clause of an Act, made in the last Session of Parliament, to prohibit the Exportation of Corn, and other Things therein mentioned; and to give further Time for the Payment of Duties omitted to be paid for the Indentures and Contracts of Clerks and Apprentices:

An Act to explain an Act, made in the Fourteenth Year of the Reign of his present Majesty, intituled, An Act to render the Laws more effectual for preventing the stealing and destroying of Sheep, and other Cattle:

An Act for preventing the Mischiefs which may happen by keeping dangerous Quantities of Gunpowder, in or near the Cities of London and Westminster:

An Act to prevent the Marriage of Lunatics:

An Act for the better enabling the Commissioners for building a Bridge cross the River Thames, from the City of Westminster to the opposite Shore, in the County of Surrey, to finish the said Bridge, and to perform the other Trusts reposed in them; and, for enlarging the Time for exchanging of Tickets unclaimed in the last Lottery for the said Bridge, and to make Provision for Tickets in the said Lottery, loft, burnt, or otherwise destroyed:

An Act for Sale of the Estates late of James Walfing-ham Esquire, deceased, lying in the Counties of Surrey, Essex, Norjolk, and Cambridge, for raising Money to discharge the Incumbrances affecting the fame; and other Purposes therein mentioned:

An Act for Sale of Part of the Estates of Edward Bayn-tun Rolt Esquire, to raise Money for the Payment of Debts affecting the fame, and of Portions for his younger Brothers and Sifter, charged thereon by the Settkment of their

The King’s After which his Majesty was pleased to make a most Speech, gracious Speech to both Houses of Parliament, as followeth; viz. "

My Lords and Gentlemen,

This Session of Parliament has been drawn out into so unusual a Length, and the Season of the Year is so far advanced, that, 1 am persuaded, you are all very desirous of a Recess.

I acquainted you, at the Beginning of the Session, with my Endeavours to bring about an Accommodation between those Princes whose Union was most necessary in this critical Conjuncture: The Treaty lately concluded between the Queen of Hungaty and the King of Prussia, under my Mediation, and so highly to the Honour of Great Britain, mud undoubtedly produce the bed Consequences to the common Cause.

The Successes which have attended the Austrian Arms in Germany, the Conjunction of the King of Sardinia’s Forces with those of the Queen of Hungary, in Italy, the present favourable Disposition of the States-General, and of other great Powers, are, under God, chiefly owing to the generous Aflidance afforded by this Nation to its antient and natural Allies.

These happy Events cannot fail to give Encouragement to our Friends, and to establish the Reputation of our Strength and our jud Influence Abroad.

If, for the further Support and Defence of the Queen of Hungary, and to redore and secure the Balance of Power, so particularly recommended to me by my Parliament, it should become necessary for me to contract new Engagements, or to enter into further Measures, I rely upon your Zeal and Perseverance in so jud a Cause, to enable me to make them good.

In the midd of these extensive TransaClions, I have been, and shall continue to be, attentive to the Prosecution of the War against Spain, with the utmod Vigour; which is of the greated Importance to the Trade and Navigation of my Subjects, the Encouragement and Protection whereof, shall be one of my principal Cares.

Gentlemen of the House of Common^,

The Zeal, Unanimity, and Dispatch, with which you have given such large Supplies, for the Service of the current Year, demand my particular Thanks, and are fresh Proofs of your Duty to me, and of your Concern for the true Intered of your Country: The Success with which these Supplies have been raised, mud convince all the World of the edablithed Credit of this Nation.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

I have the juded Confidence in the Affections of my People; which I shall not fail to cultivate, by a condant Care of their Rights and Liberties, and by promoting their Prosperity and Happiness: Let it be your Endeavour, in your respective Countries, to make these my

good Intentions rightly underdood, to calm and heal all Animosities and Divisions, to support my Authority and Government, and to preserve the Peace and good Order of the Kingdom.

And afterwards, the Lord Chancellor, by his Majesty’s Parliament Command, said, prorogued.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

It is his Majesty’s Royal Will and Pleasure, That this Parliament be prorogued to Thursday the Sixteenth Day of September next, to be then here held: And this Parliament is accordingly prorogued to Thursday the Sixteenth Day of September next.

Jovis, 16° die Septembris;

UfaiJOrders. Resolved, That no Peer of this Realm hath any Right to give his Vote in the Election of any Member to serve in Parliament.

Resolved, That where the House shall judge any Petition, touching Elections, to be frivolous and vexatious, the House will order Satisfaction to be made to the Person petitioned against.

Resolved, That if it shall appear, that any Person hath procured himself to be elected or returned a Member of this House, or endeavoured fj to be, by Bribery, or any other corrupt Practices, this House will proceed with the utmost Severity against such Person,

Resolved, That if it shall appear, that any Person hath been tampering with any With^fs, in respect of his Evidence to be given to this House, or any Committee thereof, or directly or indirectly hath endeavoured to deter or hinder any Person from appearing, or giving Evidence, the same is declared to be a high Crime and Misdemeanour; and this House will proceed with the utmost Severity against such Offender.

Resolved, That if it shall appear, that any Person hath given false Evidence in any same before this House, or any Committee thereof, this House will proceed with the utmost Severity against such Offender.

Resolved, That it is an high Infringement of the Liberties and Privileges of the Commons of Great Britain, for any Lord of Parliament, or any Lord Lieutenant of any County, to concern themselves in the Elections of Members to serve for the Commons in Parliament.

Ordered, That the Serjeant at Arms attending this House do, from time to time, take into his Custody any Stranger or Strangers that he shall see, or be informed of to be, in the House or Gallery, while the House, or any Committee of the whole House, is fitting; and that no Person, so taken into Custody, be discharged out of Custody without the special Order of the House.

Ordered, That the Back-door of the Speaker’s Chamber be locked up every Morning at the Sitting of the House, and the Key delivered to the Clerk, to be locked up by him; and that he do not presume to deliver the same to any Person whatsoever, without Order of the House; and that the Serjeant at Arms attending this House do take care to clear the Speaker’s Chamber every Day before the Door is locked up.

Ordered, That no Member of this House do presume to bring any Stranger or Strangers into the House, or Gallery thereof, while the House is fitting.

Most Gracious Sovereign,

We, your Majesty’s most dutiful and loyal Subjects, the Commons of Great Britain in Parliament assembled, beg Leave to return your Majesty our fine^re Tnanks for your Majesty’s most gracious Speech from the Throne,

It is with the greaicft; atisfaction that we have seen the confta t Attention your Majesty has been graciously pleased to giye to the Advice of your Parliament; and as we think that the Support of the House of Aujiria, and the restoring and securing the Balance of Powerin Europe, are inleparable from the true Interest of these Kingdoms, we desire, in the strongest Manner, to express our grateful Sense of the early Care taken by your Majesty in forming such an Army in the Low Countries, as might be of Service to those great and defuable Ends: And as we are satisfied, that a Force sufficient for that Purpose could not have been so readily assembled, as by your Majesty’s fending a Body of your own Electoral Troops, together with the flejfians, to join the British and Aujirian Forces in thpf$ Parts, we are determined chearfully and effectually to support your Majesty in all such necessary Measures.

We beg Leave to congratulate your Majesty on the happy and unexpected Turn of the Affairs in the North: We assure your Majesty, that we are fully convinced, that it is by the Vigour and Spirit shewn by your Majesty in Pefence of your Allies, that the Queen of Hungary has been principally encouraged to bear up amidst extreme Difficulties, notwithstanding the numerous Armies sent against her: And we are perfuafted, that the same Spirit and Vigour have enabled the King of Sardinia to act a Part so useful to the common Caule, to which the Vigilance and Activity of your Majesty’s Fleet in the Mediterranean have so remarkably contributed.

Your faithful Commons assure your Majesty, that they will, with the greatest Alacrity and Readiness, grant such Supplies as shall be found necessiuy for perfecting tfte great Work in which your Majesty is engaged, for profecu ting with Vigour the just and necessary War with Spain, and for maintaining the Honour and Security of your Majesty, and your Kingdoms.

Your faithful Commons, in all their Deliberations, will endeavour to make manifest to the World, that they have nothing so much at heart as the Honour of your Majesty the Support of ypur Government, and the true Interest of your Majesty’s QrpwnancJ Kingdoms. VOL. 44.

Gentlemen,

I thank you for this dutiful and dfle&ionate Address, and for the great Marks of Confidence you repose in me.

The extraordinary Supplies that I am obliged to alk of my People have become necessary for supporting that Cause, which is inseparable from the true Interest of my Kingdoms.

MR. Comptroller reported to the House, that their Addresses of Thursday last had been presented to VOla. 24.

his Majesty; and that his Majesty had commanded him to acquaint this House, that he will give Directions accordingly.

The House being informed, that Robert Phillipjhill Privilege; attended, according to Order;

He was called in; and the several Letters signed with his Name, and the franked Cover, inclosing them (which were upon Thursday last delivered in at the Table), being shewn to him, he said, that the said Letters, and the Direction on the said Cover, were of his Hand-writhing, but that he received the Frank thereon.from one Stephen Sherlock, from whom also he had received Two more Covers for Letters, franked with the Name of the famfe Member.

And then he was directed to withdraw.

And the House being informed, that the said Stephen Sherlock attended at the Door;

He was called in; and the said counterfeited Frank being shewn to him, he said, that he received it with another Frank (in the Name of the said Member) from Mr. Lloyd, from whom also he had received One or Two more.

And the House being informed, that the said Mr. Lloyd attended at the Door;

He was called in; and the said counterfeited Frank being shewn to him, he denied that he gave that Frank to the said Stephen Sherlock; but he said, that he gave him Two real Franks^ which he had received from the said Member (One of which he produced to the House, the same having been re-delivered to him by the said Robert Phillipjhill, on Saturday last).

And being further examined, he said, that he gave the said Two Franks to the said Stephen Sherlock, about Three Quarters of a Year ago.

Stephen Sherlock being again called in, confessed that he received the said Two Franks at that time, and asserted (what Mr. Lloyddenied) that the said counterfeited Frank was One of the Two which he then received.

And he further said, that he never gave more than these Two Franks to the said Robert Phillipjhill.

And then the said Mr. Lloyd and the said Stephen Sherlock, were directed to withdraw.

The said Robert Phillipjhill was again called in; and examined; and persisted in his Evidence, That he received the said counterfeited Frank from the said Stephen Sherlock. k

And

352

And then he was directed to withdraw*

And it appeared to the House, by Comparishn, that the said counterfeited Frank, and the real Frank (produced by Mr. Lloyd), were of a different Hand-writing.* ..... ..

Resolved, That the said Stephen Sherlock, having counterfeited rhe! Hand-writing of a Member of this House upon a Letter, in order to prevent its being charged with the Duty of Postage, is guilty of a'high Misdemeanor and a notorious Breach of the Privilege of this House.

Ordered, That the said Stephen Sherlock be, for his said Offence, committed Prisoner to his Majesty’s Gaol of Newgate; and that Mr. Speaker do issue his Warrants accordingly.

THE Lord Sidney Beauelerk presented to the House, according to Order, a Bill for confirming Articles of Agreement, and an Award, for Inclosing and Dividing certain common Downs and common Fields within the Manor and Parish of AJliton Tirrold, in the County of Berks: And the feme was received; and read the First time.

Resolved, That the Bill be read a Second time.

An ingossed Bill for naturalizing Daniel Viulars and Peter Thomegay, was read the Third time.

Resolved, That the Bill do pass: And that the Title be. An Act for naturalizing Daniel Vialars and Peter . Thomegay.

Ordered, That Sir Thomas Drury do carry the Bill to the Lords, and desire their Concurrence.

An ingossed Bill for granting, an Aid to his Majesty by a Land Tax, to be raised in Great Britain, for the Service of the Year One thousand Seven hundred and Forty-three, was read the Third time.

Resolved, That the Bill do pass: And that the Title be. An Act for granting an Aid to his Majesty by a Land Tax, to be raised in Great Britain, for the Service of the Year One thousand Seven hundred and Forty-three.

Ordered, That Mr. Francis Fane do carry the Bill to the Lords, and desire their Concurrence.

A Petition of the Prisoners for Debt in the Castle of York, in behalf of themselves, and the Gaols adjacent, was presented to the House, and read; complaining of their Distress: And praying Relief.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Ordered, That a Committee be appointed to consider the Act, made in the Thirteenth Year of his present Majesty’s Reign, intituled, An Act for amending and enforcing the Laws relating to Rogues, Vagabonds, and other idle and disorderly Persons, and for reducing the same into One Act of Parliament; and also for amending the Laws for erecting, providing, and regulating, Houses of Correction; and to report their Opinion to the House, as to what Amendments may be proper to be made thereunto.

And a Committee was appointed of Mr. Carter* Mr. Cdrew, Mr. Hay, Mr. Plumer, Sir John Ramsden, Mr. Gundry, Mr. Bramjldn, Mr. Pryfe, Mr. Selwytt, Lord Dupplin, Mr. Prov)fe, Lord Chetwynd, Sir N. Curzon, Mr. Skuttleworth, Mr. Alderman Marshall, Mr. Speeke, Mr. H, Campbell, Mr. Jolliffe, Mr. Charlton, Lord S. Beauelerk, Sir James Grant, Mr. Bowles, Mr. Smyth, Lord Strange, Sir Charles Mordaunt, Mr. Yorke, Mr. Walpole, Sir C. Cotton, Mr. Alderman Calvert, Mh Alderman Heathcote, Mr. Powney, Mr. Waller, Sir John Aftley, Mr. Lowndes, Mr. Grenville, Mr. Gore, Lord Deerhurst, Mr. Cornwall, Mr. Southwell and all the Gentlemen of the Long-Robe: And they are tb meet this Afternoon at Five of the Clock, in the Speaker’s Chamber: And all that come are to have Voices.

Ordered, That it be an Instruction to the said Committee, That they do consider the Laws relating to the Poor, so far as the same concern the Removal and Relief of poor Persons; and report their Opinion to the House, as to what Amendments may be proper to be made thereunto.

Mr. Francis Fane, according to Order, reported from the Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred to consider further of the Supply granted to his Majesty, the Resolutions, which they had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same were read; and are as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Sum of Five hundred Thirty-four thousand Seven hundred and Sixty-three Pounds and Five Shillings be granted to his Majesty, for defraying the Charge of Sixteen thousand Three hundred and Fifty-nine effective Men (Commission and Non-Commission Officers in* eluded), to be employed in Flanders, for the Year 1743.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Number of Land Forces, for Guards, Garrisons, and other Services (including Two thousand Three hundred and Twenty-two Invalids), amounting to Twenty-three thousand Six-hundred and Ten efteftiveMen(Commission and Non-Commission Officers included), be employed for the Service of the Year 1743.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Surfi, not exceeding Six hundred Forty-seven thousand Eight hundred and Sixty-two Pounds Five Shillings and Ten Pence be granted to his Majesty, for defraying the Charge of the said Twenty-three thousand Six hundred and Ten effective Men, for Guards and Garrisons, and other Services in Great Britain, West Andies, Guernsey, arid Jetfey, for the Year 1743.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Two hundred and Sixty-six thousand Six hundred and Sixteen Pounds Six Shillings and Five Pence Halfpeny, be granted to his Majesty, for maintaining his Majesty’s Forces and Garrisons, in the Plantations, Minorca, and Gibraltar, and for Provisions for the Garrisons of Annapolis Royal, Canso, Placentia, Providence, Gibraltar, and Georgia, for the Year 1743.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That Eleven thousand Five hundred and Fifty Marines (Commission and Non-Commission Officers included), employed for the Year 1742, be continued for the Service of the Year 1743.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Two hundred and Six Thousand Two hundred and Fifty-three Pounds Fifteen Shillings, be granted to his Majesty, for defraying the Charge of the said Eleven thousand Five hundred and Fifty Marines (Commission and Non-Commission Officers included) for the Service of the Year 1743.

The First Resolution of the Committee being read a Second time, was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

The Second Resolution of the Committee being read a Second time;

And a Motion being made, and the Question being put, That the House do agree with the Committee in the said Resolution, that aNumberof Land Forces for Guards, Garrisons, and other Services (including Two thousand Three hundred and Twenty-two Invalids), amounting to Twenty-three thousand Six hundred and Teri effective Men (Commission and Non-Commission Officers ift-eluded), be employed for the Service of the Year 1743 $ The House divided.

The Noes went forth.

The rest of the said Resolutions, being severalfy read a Second time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

And then the House adjourned till To-triorfOW Morning, Nine of the Clock.

HockcEffe, C IR John Cliester reported from the Committee, to lie.Roads. O whom the Petition of the Trustees, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, appointed to put in Execution an Act of Parliament, made in the First Year of the Reign of his present Majesty King George the Second, for the more effectual amending the Highway between Hockliffe and Woburn, in the County of Bedford; and for repairing the Road leading through Woburn to Tick-ford- Bridge, in Newport-Pagnell, in the County of Bucks; was referred, That the Committee had examined" the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of this Petition, the said Act of Parliament, passed in the First: Year of his present Majesty, was produced to the Committee, and Part thereof was read; whereby it appeared, that several Tolls were granted, and made payable, for 21 Years, from the 24th of June 1728.

Then Mr. Thomas Cawne, Clerk to the Trustees, being examined, said. That the Roads mentioned in the Petition are Twelve Miles in Length, and are now in tolerable good Repair, but cannot be kept amended if the Tolls, collected for the future, are only applied towards discharging the Debt due upon the Credit of the present A<fl of Parliament, amounting in the Whole to £.2,001.5J. 4d. Part of which Money carries an Interest off. 5 per Cent; and the other Part, of £. 4 per Cent.

Aftd he produced an Account of the Receipts and Disbursements of the Tolls, collected by virtue of the said Act, from the Commencement thereof, to the 28th

of October 1742. — He further said, That if the Term be continued, the Trustees will be impowered to borrow a Sum of Money, at £. 4. per Cent, sufficient to discharge so much of the present Debt as carries £.5. per Cent. Interest; and will also be enabled to put in Execution such further Trusts as arereposed in them by the former Act,

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill fot enlarging the Term and Powers granted by an Act, passed in the First: Year of the Reign of his present Majesty, fot the rtforeeffectual amending the Highway between Hockliffe and Woburn, in the County of Bedford; and for repairing the Road leading through Woburn to Tickford- Bridge, in Newport-Pagnel, in the County of Bucks: And that Sir John Chefer, Mr. Lowndes, Sir Roger Burgoyne, and Sir Boteler Chernocke, do prepare, arid bring in, the . fatne.

Mr. Comptroller reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Justices of the Peace met at the General Quarter-Sessions of the Peace, held at Thirsk, for the North Riding of the County of York, the 5th Day of October 1742; and also of the Gentlemen, and other Inhabitants, within the said Riding, whose Names are thereunto subscribed; was referred, Tljat the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place ;.and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, the Agent for the Petitioners called,

Willey Reveley Esquire: Who said. That the Road from Borougk-briage to the Town of North Allerton is a Riff Clay, and, in Winter Season, in so ruinous a Condition, as to be dangerous for Persons to travel either on Horse-back or in Coaches: That there is a Causeway for Horse-men, but that not above Three Foot wide, and oftentimes so broken up and ruinous, as even to be dangerous to Passengers on Horseback:

That the Road from the Town of North Allerton to the Passage over the River *7'ees, opposite to the Town of Neefham, is in a more ruinous Condition than the former Road; and that, by the Laws now in Force, neither of the said Roads can be effectually amended, no Materials lying near many Parts thereof.

Mr. Charles Grey, being examined, confirmed the Evidence of Willey Reveley.

Mr. Geo. Lodge, being examined said. That the Road from Borough-bridge to Catherick, and from thence to Piers-bridge, is in a bad and ruinous Condition, as he found, when he travelled the same in October last, after a little Rain, and dangerous for Persons to travel; the Badness thereof being occasioned, as he apprehended, by the Number of Scotch Cattle frequently passing thereon: That he has seen the Inhabitants, at present obliged by Statute to repair the said Road, endeavouring to amend the fame; at which time they have complained to him, that it could not be effectually done without the further Aid of Parliament.

He further said. That many Carriagespafs on that Road with Coals; and, could the feme be effectually repaired, it would be of great Advantage to that Branch of Trade.

Mr. Thomas Thompson, being examined, confirmed the Evidence of Mr. George Lodge.

Sir John Ramsden reported from the Committee, to Rowe* Road, whom the Petition of the Justices of the Peace, Geritle-men, Freeholders, and Inhabitants, in the County of

Westmoreland, and North Riding of the County of York, was referred, That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Witnesses were called; viz.

Mr. Thomas Hutchinson, Mr. James Wharton, and Mr.

William Dent, being severally examined, said. That the Road leading from Bowes, in the North Riding of the County of York, to Brough, in the County of Westmor e-land, about Thirteen Miles in Length, is the Post Road from London to the several Trading Towns mentioned in the Petition; and is the nearest Road to the Western Parts of Scotland; and that the Road is, in many Parts, so very ruinous, that it is dangerous for Coaches and Carriages to travel through the same:

And also they said, That great Part of the Road leads over a Moor, called Stainmore, which is a barren Country, and but few Inhabitants live thereabouts; which Inhabitants are not able to repair the fame, as the Law requires: r

And they added to their Evidence, that the Road cannot be effectually amended, and kept in Repair, unless some further Provision be made by Parliament for that Purpose.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for repairing the High Road leading from Bowes, over Stain-more, in the North Riding of the County of York, to Brough, in the County of Westmor eland: And that Sir John Ramsden, Sir Joseph Pennington, Sir Philip Muf-grave, Mr. Wilson, and Sir James Lowther, do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, the Petitioners called

Thomas Smith Esquire: Who being examined, said, That the several Roads mentioned in the Petition, are Part of the great Road leading from London to Bath, and other considerable Trading Towns in the Western Part of the Kingdom; which, by reason of many heavy Carriages frequently passing through the fame, are become so very ruinous and bad, that Coaches, Waggons, and other Carriages, cannot pass and repass in the Winter Season without great Danger; and that the said Roads cannot, by the ordinary Course and Method appointed by the Laws and Statutes of this Realm, be effectually amended and kept in Repair, unless some Provision be made for railing Money, to be laid out and applied for that Purpose.

And the same Witness further said, That although the Inhabitants of the Parishes of Avebury and Bishops Can-nings, through which the Roads desired to be repaired lead, have constantly done their Statute-work, and raised Nine Pence in the Pound, and laid out the same in repairing and amending the said Roads; yet the same Parishes have been several times indicted on Account of the Bad-ness of their Highways; and that the Parish of Avebury has been fined £. ioo, and the Parish of Bishops Cannings £. 30} both which Sums were laid out in Rqiair of the V01. 24.

A Petition of the Trustees, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, appointed to put in Execution an Act, passed in the Thirteenth Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the First, intituled, An Act for repairing the several Roads leading from the Town of Warminster, in the County of Wiltj, was presented to the House, artd read; setting forth, That, by the said Act, several Tolls were granted and made payable for the Term therein mentioned, for repairing the said several Roads; and the Trustees, impowered to put the said Act in Execution, finding the said Roads in a ruinous Condition, were obliged to borrow a considerable Sum of Money, in order to make the same passable; which Money so borrowed, together with the Tolls collected, hath been duly laid out and applied according to the Directions of the said Act: That the Petitioners find the Money now due and owing on the Credit of the said Act, cannot, during the Continuance thereof, be repaid, and all Parts of the said Road be effectually amended, and kept in good Repair, for the future, unless the Term and Powers granted and given by the said Act be enlarged: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for continuing the Term, and enlarging the Powers, by the before-mentioned Act granted and given, in such Manner as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

A Petition of the Churchwardens, Overseers of the Poor, and other Inhabitants, of the Hamlet of Bethnal Green, in the Parish of Stepney, in the County of Middlesex, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the said Parish of Stepney consists of Five Hamlets, of which the Hamlet of Bethnal Green is One; which Hamlet is a large Part of the said Parish, and contains above Eighteen hundred Houses, wherein are more than Fifteeji thousand Souls, and the most populous Part of the said Hamlet, is distant, at least. Two Miles from the Parish Church of Stepney; which Church is not near large enough to receive the Parishioners of the said Parish, that are desirous to resort thither to hear Divine Service; and that there is no public Chapel, or Place for Divine Worship, according to the Liturgy of the Church of England, within the Hamlet aforesaid; for want of which, the Petitioners conceive, Dissoluteness of Morals, and a Disregard for Religion, have greatly increased; too apparent in great Numbers of the younger and poorer Sort of the Inhabitants of the said Hamlet; which has been the Reason of many of the better Sort of People removing from their Habitations in the said Hamlet, to the great Impoverishment thereof; and that the Commissioners for building of Fifty new Churches in Voi,. 24.

and about the City of London, being sensible of the Inconveniencies aforesaid, did, about Twenty Years since, purchase a Piece of Ground in the said Hamlet, very convenient for building a Parish Church; and also for Burying-ground; but no Church hath been built thereupon, although the Buildings and Inhabitants in the said Hamlet have since been very much increased; and that the Parish Church of Stepney is supplied with Two V icars, called Por-tionifts; the Profits of the Living being divided between them; which Vicars are presented by the Principal, Fellows, and Scholars, of Brazen Nose College, Oxon; and a considerable Part of the Profit, as well of the Rectory, which belongs to the said College, as of the Vicarage of Stepney, arises within the said Hamlet of Bethnal Green in Tythes, and otherwise; and the Petitioners apprehend, that such Part of the Profits of the said Vicarage, as will arise within the said Hamlet, will be sufficient for a yearly Maintenance of a Minister to officiate in the said Church, when built and completed: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for separating the Hamlet of Bethnal Green from the Parish of Stepney; and for making the same a distinct Parish; and for raising

Money for building a Church there, and for making a Provision for Maintenance of a Minister to officiate therein; in such Manner as the House shall think proper.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

A Petition of the Proprietors and Inhabitants of Char- Charter-ter-house-Square, in the County of Middlesex, whose Names j°ll^0ygUare are thereunto subscribed, being the major Part of the Pro- t°v prietors and Inhabitants, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Area of Charter house Square was, in the Year 1717, at the Expence of the Petitioners, and the then Proprietors and Inhabitants, inclosed with Pales, or a Palisade of Wood, in order to preserve the same in a decent Manner; which Palisade, though supported at a great Expence, is decayed: That, if the Palisade should be permitted to be destroyed, the Square will become a Receptacle for Rubbish, Dirt, and Dunghills, and liable to be frequented by common Beggars, Vagabonds, and other disorderly Persons; and will thereby become unfit for the Habitation of Persons of Character;

That the Cleaning, Watching, and Paving, of the said Square has been also greatly neglected, to the Annoyance and Danger of the Inhabitants: And therefore, in order to prevent such Mischiefs, praying, That the House will give Leave, that a Bill may be brought in to enable the prefen't and future Proprietors and Inhabitants of the Houses in Char ter-house Square, in the County of Middlesex, to make a Rate on themselves for raising a sufficient Sum of Money, effectually to inclose, pave, watch, clean, and improve the said Square, and render the same more commodious, and to continue the same in Repair Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House;

Dummer A Petition of Michael Terry Esquire, Lord of the Ma-Inclosure. nor of Dummer, in the Parish of Dummer, in the County of Southampton, and Patron of the Rectory of the said Parish; and of Thomas Stockwell, Rector of the said Pa-rifll Church; and of the several other Persons, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, being Owners and Proprietors of Lands lying in the common Fields and common Pastures of, and belonging to, the Parish of Dummer , aforesaid; was presented to the House, and read; setting forth. That there are several common Fields and common Pastures in the Parish of Dummer aforesaid, wherein the respective Properties of the Petitioners, and other Land-owners, lie dispersed in small Parcels, and thereby are »endei;ed of less Value to the respective Proprietors, and, in their present Situation and Circumstances, are incapable of Improvement; and that the Petitioners are desirous the said common Fields and common Pastures may be inclosed and divided by Commissioners, in that behalf to be appointed; and that the several Shares and Allotments resulting from such Inclosure and Division, may be laid and disposed as commodiously as possible for the Petitioners, and other the said Owners in the said Lands, and may be held in Severalty for such Estates and Interests as they now respectively hold the said Lands in the said common Fields and Pastures; but that the said Inclosure and Division cannot be effectually established, to answer the Intention of the Parties interested in the fame, without the Aid of an Act of Parliament: And therefore praying the House to give Leave, that a Bill may be brought in for the Purposes aforesaid.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill, pursuant to the Prayer of the said Petition: And that the Lord Harry Powlett and Mr. Pilsworth do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

Mile of the said Town of Northampton: That, in order to raise Money to amend all Parts of the said Roads as soon as possible, the Petitioners, the Inhabitants of the said Town, are willing and desirous that the Turnpike, now erected at Harleston, may be removed, and set up nearer than One Mile to the said Town of Northampton; whereby Passengers and Carriages will be prevented from going through other Ways, as they now do, to avoid paying the Tolls laid and made payable by the said Act: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill to explain and amend the Act aforesaid, and for making the same more effectual, in such Manner as to the House shall seem meet.

A Petition of Crayle Crayle Esquire, heretofore called Crayle Bellamy, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth. That Sarah Crayle, of Hatton Garden, in the County of Middlesex, Widow, did, by her last Will and Testament, bearing Date the nth Day of August 1730, give to the Petitioner, her Grandson, the Sum of£.i 5,000 to be paid to him at the Age of Twenty-five Years; and did desire, that the Petitioner should, from and after his Age of One-and-twenty Years (which he hath since attained to,) assume and take on himself the Surname of Crayle instead of the Surname of Bellamy; and from thenceforth call and write himself by the said* Surname of Crayle and not by the Surname of Bellamy; and that the Petitioner is desirous to take upon him the said Surname of Crayle, pursuant to the Directions of the said Will: And therefore praying the House to give Leave, That a Bill may be brought in for the Petitioner to take upon him the Surname of Crayle.

A Petition of the Churchwardens, Overseers of the Poor, Antients, and other Inhabitants, of the Parish of St, Botolph without Aldgate, in the City of London, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, on behalf of themselves, and several other Inhabitants of the said Parish, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the said Parish is a very large Parish, and hath a numerous and burthensome Poor annually to maintain: That, for a great many Years last past, their Poor’s Rates, though very high, and very great Sums of Money have been annually raised thereby, have not been sufficient, in any one Year, for the Maintenance of their Poor; which hath occasioned some Churchwardens and Overseers of the Poor to have Recourse to Borrowing of Money at an Interest of Five Pounds per Centum per Annum, on the Credit of Orders of Vestry 5 and, when that could not be done, hath obliged others to advance out of their own Pockets (as they frequently, and of necessity, have done) several considerable Sums of Money; for some of which the like Interest hath been also paid; which said Interest hath been a great and growing Burthen and Expence to the said Parish, and hath been constantly paid for many Years, till lately; having been defrayed chiefly out of the Fines for Parish Offices, and other small Incomes of the Parish, which now fall considerably short of answering the same y so as there is a great Arrear of such Interest, that, forrthefe Four Years last past, the Poor of the said Parish

have increased to, and now are, double the Number of what they were in former Years; and very large Debts have been necessarily contracted, and are now*due and owing to several Tradesmen, and others, for Provisions and Necessaries supplied by them for such Poor; which the said Parish, under the Circumstances aforesaid, hath not been able to furnish Money for the Payment of: That the said several Debts have been a great many Years contracting, and have been all for the necessary Support and Maintenance of the Poor of the said Parish, and do amount, in the Whole, to between Two and Three thousand Pounds; which the Petitioners are desirous should be discharged; but are advised, that Money for that Purpose cannot be raised upon the Inhabitants of the said Parish by any Laws now in being; nor hath the said Parish any Means of paying the said Debts, without the Assistance of Parliament: Nevertheless, several Suits at Law have already been commenced, and others are threatened to be commenced, for Recovery of the said Debts, to the still greater Burthen, Expence, and Impoverishment of the Petitioners, and the rest of the said Parish: And therefore praying the House to give Leave, that a Bill may be brought in, to enable the said Parishioners to raise such Money upon the Inhabitants of the said Parish, as shall be necessary for the Payment of their Debts, in such Manner as the House shall think reasonable.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House.

And it is referred to Mr. Alderman Calverty Sir W\ W. Wynne, Lord Carpenter, Sir Humph. That loft at Sea. the Petitioner, on or about the 20th Day of August \ 741, shipped at Liverpool, on board the Mary Sloop, Andrew Creash Master, for Account of John Roche, of Limerick, Merchant, 2,500 Bushels of white Salt, in order to be exported to Ireland, and gave Bond to Mr. William Sud-low, his Majesty’s Collector of the Duty on Salt at L2-

Salt i That the said Sloop, in her passage to Ireland, met with a violent Storm at Sea* and was in the greatest Daii* ger of perishing; and had not the Sailors been uncommonly diligent, the said Sloop mu ft have foundered/and funk; (he being several timesuttdbr Wafer, the Sea soak* ing a common Passage over her, and the SeR W a ter wash* ing into the Hold of the said Sloop; 964 Bushels and One Gallon of the said Lad ing of Salt was actually wasted and perished: That the Petitioner duly proved the Truth of the Premises beipre the Quarter-Sessiods; and that 1*535 Bushels and 7 Gallons, Residue of the said Lading of Salt, was landed in Ireland, and the Duties thereon paid \ and as there is a Provision made in the several Statutes relating to the Salt Duty, or some of them, for remitting, Or making SsUisfaction to the Owners or Proprietors for the Duty of such white Salt as should be loft, orperifli at Sea, by the Ship’s foundering, or being taken by the Enemy, the Petitioner applied to the Salt Officers to have a Debenture for the said Salt, which was so exported, and peri (bed at Sea; which they refused to do, alleging that, unless the said Salt had perished by the actual Sinking of the Ship, they could not make out such Debenture; for that though they declared they were fully satisfied that the said 964 Bushels and One Gallon of Salt wasted and perished at Seti, yet as the Ship did not perish, bui was saved, they were not warranted by the Words of the several Statutes to make out such Debenture; That the Petitioner hath applied to the Collector of the Salt Duties atLiverpool, and the Commissioners of the Salt Duties, to have the Bond, so entered into by the Petitioner and his Sureties, and by which the Duties of the said 2,500 Bushels of Salt were secured, to be delivered up, and the Petitioner, and his Sureties, discharged therefrom, and from the Payment of the Duties of the said Salt, who declared it was not in their power to give the Petitioner any Relief; the said Lois not coming within the Letter of the Clauses in the several Statutes for the Relief of Persons wholofe Salt at Sea: That the Petitioner will be forced to pay Duty on the said Salt, so loft and perished at Sea, as aforesaid, to prevent his Bond being sued, if not some Way relieved; and therefore, in regard the Petitioner is advised, and apprehends, that his same is within the Intent and Equity, if not within the Letter, of the said Clauses of the Statutes, fqr remitting or making Satisfaction to the Owners or Proprietors of such white Salt, as should perish at Sea, praying the House to take the Hardships of his same into Confederation, and to give Leave that a Clause may be added to such Bill, and in such manner, as the House shall think fit, for the Petitioner's Relief in the Premises, and the Relief of such Person and Persons who may happen to have any such like Lois or Misfortune hereafter.

Mr. Bathurst reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of several Gentlemen, and other Persons, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, living in and near the Road leading from Cirencester, in the County of Gloucester, through Chesterton, Coates, Kemble, Tarlton, Rod-mar ton, and Charington, to Tethury, in the said County, and from Tethury through Dufton, West on, Byrt, Sher-stone Magna, Dedmarton, Haukjburys, Upton, Horton, Old Sodbury, Little Sodbury, Doddington, Tormarton, Cod-rington, Dirham, and Cold Act on, to the Monument upon Lansdown, in the Parish of Languridge, was referred, That the Committee had examined the Matter o^ the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s 'Fable: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Witnesses were called; viz.

William Dimmock and Brereton Smith: Who, being severally examined, laid, That they know the Road leading through the several Parishes in the Petition mentioned (about 23 Miles in Length), and that, by reason of the Deepness of the Soil thereof, and many heavy Carriages frequently passing through the fame, is become very bad and ruinous; and that many Parts thereof, in the Winter Season, are almost impassable for Travellers.

Vol. 24.

And the same Witnesses being severally asked, whether the Road could be well repaired, and kepe amended, if the Inhabitants of the several Parishes through which the Road leads, performed their Statute-work thereupon, and did what they were required by Law to do ? they severally answered, That if they were to do and perform double the Work thereon, which the Laws-in being require to be done, it would not be sufficient to amend this Road, and keep it in Repair.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for repairing the Road leading from the Town of Cirencester, in the County of Gloucester, to a Place called the Monument, upon Lansdown: And that Mr. Bathurst and Mr.

Nor borne Berkeley do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

Mr. Francis Fane, according to Order, reported from Way* the Committee of the whole House, to whom it was re- *nd Means ferred to consider further of Ways and Aleans for raising the Supply granted to his Majesty, the Resolutions which they had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place, and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same were read; and are as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the Duty of Twenty Shillings Gallon, granted to his Majesty, by an Act of the Ninth Year of his Majesty’s Reign, upon all spirituous Liquors, which any Retailers thereof should bepoirefled of, or interested in, after the 2c>*h Day of September 1736, shall, from and after the 25th Day.of March One thousand Seven hundred and Forty-three, cease, determine, and be no longer paid.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of: this Committee,

That, towards raising the Supply granted to his Majesty, there shall be paid for every Gallon of low Wines or Spirits of the first Extraction, made or drawn from any foreign or imported Materials, or any Mixture therewith, Six Pence over and above all other Duties charged or chargeable thereon^ to be paid by the Distillers or Makers thereof.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That towards raising the Supply granted to his Majesty, there shall be paid for every Gallon of Low Wines or Spirits of the first Extraction, made or drawn only from any Sort of Drink or Wafti, brewed or made from any Sort of /Malt or Corn, other than and except Brewers Walh and Tilts, One Peny over and above all Duties charged or chargeable thereon, to be paid by the Distillers or Makers thereof.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That, towards railing the Supply granted to his Majesty, there shall be paid for every Gallon of low Wines or Spirits of the first Extraction, made or drawn from Brewers Walh or Tilts, or any Mixture therewith. One Peny over and above all other Duties charged or chargeable thereon, to be paid by the Distillers or Makers thereof.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That, towards raising the Supply granted to his Majesty, there shall be paid for every Gallon of low Wines or Spirits of the First Extraction, made or drawn from any other Sort or Kind of English Materials, or any Mixture therewith, Three Half-pence over and above all other Duties 5 E charged

.Goog

}8i

charged, or chargeable thereon, to be paid by the Distillers or* Makers thereof.

Resolved, That it fe the Opinion of this Committee, That, towards railing the Supply granted to his Majesty, there shall be paid for every Gallon of Spirits made in Great Britain, of any Kind of Wine or Cyder imported. Six Pence over arid above all Duties charged, or chargeable thereon, to be paid by the Distillers or Makers thereof.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, Thar, towards railing the Supply granted to his Majesty, there shall be paid for every Gallon of strong Waters, or Aqua Vitse, made for Sale, of any other Materials, Three Pence over and above all other Duties charged, or chargeable thereon, to be paid by the Distillers or Maker* thereof.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, for the Encouragement of the Exportation of Spirits drawn or made from, the Materials aforesaid, a Drawback or Allowance be made of the several and respecti've Duties aforesaid, on the Exportation thereof.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Sum of Fifty Pounds yearly, which by the said Act was granted to his Majesty fora Licence for vending, bartering, or uttering, such spirituous Liquors, shall also, from the 25th Day of March 1743, cease and determine.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, from and after the 25th Day of March 1743, the Sum of Twenty Shillings yearly shall be paid to his Majesty for a Licence, to be taken out yearly by every Person keeping a public Brandy Shop, a public Victualling-house, Coffee-house, or Ale-house, or being an Innholder, who shall vend, barter, or utter, any spirituous liquors.

The First Resolution of the Committee being read a Second time, was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

The Second Resolution of the Committee being read a Second time;

And a Motion being made, and the Question being put, That the said Resolution be re-committed j It passed in the Negative.

Then the said Resolution was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

The subsequent Resolutions of the Committee being severally read a Second time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

Ordered, That a Bill be brought in pursuant to the said Resolutions: And that Mr. Francis Fane, Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer, Mr. Compton, Sir John Rvfhout, Mr. Gybbon, Mr. Attorney-General, Mr. Solicitor-General, Mr. Scrope, and Mr. Jeffreys, do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

A Petition of the Justices of the Peace, Gentlemen, Freeholders, and principal Inhabitants, of the Town of Parjhore, in the County of Wore eft er, and of (Vick near Parjhore, PenJJ am. Great Comber ton, Little Comber ton, Bricklehampton, E m 'ey Castle, Netherton, Over bury, and Conderton, in the said County of Worcester, waspresented to the House, and read; setting forth. That an Act of Parliament was made in the Year 1728, intituled, An Act for repairing and amending several (loads leading to and from the Boroiigh of Evesham, in the County of War-eester; by which a Road leading from the said Borough to the First Chain of Wick Causey, next the Foot of Good ley Hill, next the Bridge at Parjhore, in the said County (being about 400 Yards short of the said Town) is directed to be repaired; and that, in pursuance of such Act, a Turnpike was erected at or near the Foot of the said Goodley Hill; and that the Road leading from the said Turnpike to the Top of the said Goodley Hill, and along the Top thereof to a certain Ground in Wick aforesaid, called the Grove (being in Length about 800 Yards from the said Turnpike, and thedirect Road to Penfham, the Two Combtrtons, and the other Towns and Villages above-mentioned), is, by reason of the Deepness of the Soil, and the many heavy Carriages parting and repafiing from the said Towns and Villages to the said Town of Parjhore and City of Worcester, become very ruinous, and, in the Winter S^afon, almost impartible; and that the Inhabitants of the said respective Towns and Villages, and all Persons travelling to and from thence to the said Town of Parjhore and City of Worcester, are, by the present Act, obliged to pay a Toll at the said Turnpike, although they do not travel One Yard upon the lload by the said Act directed to be repaired; and -that the said lload leading from the said Turnpike to the said Town of Parjhore, is also very ruinous, and out of Repair, and, by reason of the Narrownels and Lowness of the causeys leading to and from the great Bridge over the River Avon there, it is, in Flood-times very difficult, and oftentimes impossible, for Persons travellingon Horseback..lo pass the said causeys, without the greatest Hazard of their Lives, and not without instances of Persons and Cattle having periffied in parting over the said causeys and Water in such Flood-times; and that all Carriages whatsoever are obliged, in Times of Flood (which often continue for a Fortnight or Three Weeks together) to ferry over the said River, by reason of the Lowness and Narrow ness of the said Causey^; which is attended with no small Hazard to the Owners of, and Expence to the Public in ferrying over, such Carriages, which, by the present Act, is directed to be paid out of the Tolls thereby granted: And representing to the House, that these and many other like Difficulties and Inconveniencies might be removed, by rairtng and widening the said causeys; and that the said Turnpike is erected in the most advantageous Place that possibly can be for collecting the Toils by the present Act; yet that there is a common Meadow belonging to the Township of Wick, which adjoins to the Road lying between the said Turnpike and the said Town of Parjhore, through

x7

which, in open Tide, many Persons travelling to and from the many Towns and Villages between Evesham and Par-JJtore can and do pass, without Payment of any Toll, to the great Lefiening thereof; which cannot be remedied by the present Act; and that the carrying on the Roads from the said Turnpike to a Place called the Mill-tail, at or near that End of the said Town of Parjhore, which lies next the said Turnpike; and the erecting a Turnpike at or near the same End of the said Town would remove the above, and many other Inconveniencies the present Act now lies under: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Condderation; and that in case any Bill shall be brought in upon the Petition lately pre-lented to the House, for enlarging the Term and Powers of the said former Act, that proper Clauses may be inferred therein, for repairing and carrying on the said Roads from the Foot of the said Goodly Hill to the said Ground called the Grove; and also from the said Turnpike to the said Mill-tail at the said End of the said Town of Parjhore; and for railing and widening the said causeys (exclusive of the great Stone Bridge over the said River Avon there); and that the Petitioners may have such further Relief as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Con*-sideration of the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Trustees, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, for putting in Execution an Act of Parliament, intituled, An Act for repairing and amending several Roads leading to and from the Borough of Evesham, in the County of Worcester \ and also of several of his Majesty’s Justices of the Peace of and for the said County, and other Gentlemen and principal Inhabitants dwelling and residing in and near the several Parishes wherein the same Roads lie, and many others frequently travelling through the said Roads; as likewise of Hannah Mence, of the City of Worcester, Widow, Relict, and Administratrix, of Samuel Mence Gent deceased, James Smith of Ledbury, in the County of Hereford, Gent, and Hannah Wynn of Bewdley, in the County of Worcester, Spinster, Devisee of Elizabeth Humphreys Widow, deceased, Creditors under the said Act; is referred: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House.

That the Petitioners find a Petition has been presented to this House from several of the Trustees appointed for putting in Execution an Act of Parliament, passed in the First Year of the Reign of his present Majesty, for repairing and amending several Roads leading to and from the Borough of Evesham, in the said County of Worcester; and from several other Persons; praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for enlarging the Term and Powers granted by the said former Act, in order effectually to amend and keep the said Roads in Repair: That the Road aforesaid leading from Evesham, through Wickhamford, to Willerfey, being Five Miles, or thereabouts, joins to the Road directed to be repaired by the Act aforesaid; but the said Road, by reason of the Deepness of the Soil, and of many heavy Carriages frequently passing through the fame, is become so ruinous and bad, especially in the Winter Season, that it cannot, by the ordinary Course appointed by the Laws in being for amending the Highways of this Kingdom, be effectually repaired: And therefore praying, That if a Bill should pass for enlarging the Term and Powers granted by the before-mentioned Act, such Provision may be made therein for repairing the Road leading from Evesham, through Wickhamford, to Willerfey aforesaid, in such Manner as to the House shall seem meet.

Sir Hugh Smithson reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Churchwardens, Overseers of the Poor, and other Inhabitants, of the Hamlet of Bethnal Green, in the Parish of Stepney, in the County of Middle-Jex, whole Names are thereunto subscribed, was referred, That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report m his Place; and afterwards de!ivefed it in at the Clerk’s Table; Where the same was read; and is as follows th; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition,

Mr. Job Lotmon (who had formerly been an Assessor of the Land Tax for that Hamlet) was called; and he gave Evidence, That the Parish of Stepney is composed of Five Hamlets, whereof Bethnal Green is One; and that that Hamlet consists of more than 1,800 Houses; several of which contain more than One Family; so that be believes the Number of the Inhabitants of this Hamlet amounts to between Fifteen or Sixteen thousand.

And the same Witness said, That the mo ft populous Part of the said Hamlet of Bethnal Green lies at the Distance of Two Miles from the Parish Church of Stepney; anfl that there is no other public Chapel or Place of Divine Worship, according to the Liturgy of the Church of England, in or belonging to the said Hamlet, except Stepney Church; which, besides the Dtllance, is much too small to receive so numerous a Congregation as would willingly attend Divine Service there: That the Witness himself, and his Family, have found it impracticable to get Seats there; the Church being always full long before Service begins.

He further informed the Committee, That several Persons of Substance and Reputation have removed from Bethnal Green, to the great Impoverishment of that Ham t; for no other reason (as themselves declared) than the Inconveniencies complained of in the Petition.

To prove what is pledged in the Complaint (which was, that Edward Key hoe* (Viliam Glascock, James Bra-Hard, and Francis Eden, did, upon the nth Day of July last, endeavour to make a forcible Entry into the Hoyfe of Sir Watkyn Williams Wynn Baronet, a Member of this House, in Downing-street, Westminster; and did then and there assault Edward Flemming, Porter to the said Member);

The Counsel for Sir Watkyn Williams Wynn examined the said Edward Flemming \ whose Evidence was, That, on the nth of the said July, in the Forenoon, some Persons knocked at the Door of his Matter’s House in Downing-street; which being opened, Four or Five of those Persons forced in, and asked for Money as a Reward for their having assisted in extinguishing a Fire that had broke out the Evening before at another House in the same Street; and the Witness answering, that his Matter was not in Town, Edward Key hoe. One of those Persons, replied, ‘‘ They would have Money, or " he, Key hoe, would knock the Witness’s Head off;" and at the same time seized him by his Collar: Whereupon the Witness said, he struck Keyhoe:

That William Glascock, another of those Persons, did, at the same time attainted the Witness, place himself between him and the Chimney, where Fire-arms’ were deposited, and prevented the Witness's firing at them; which otherwise he said he should have done, as he was solely intruded with the Care of the House, during his Matter’s llelidence in the Country; and was the only Person in it at that time; and did then, and does now, believe their Intention was to have robbed the House.

Four Persons, whose Names were Edward Key hoe, James Bran an, Francis Eden, and William Glascock, appearing before the Committee, the Witness was directed to view them; and being asked the Question, said, that he could not positively assert that James Branan and Francis Eden were Parties in the Proceeding complained of; but he mentioned some Reasons for the Certainty of his Evidence with regard to Keyhoe an/i Glascock.

And being cross-examined by the Two Persons last-named, he denied that the Door was open, when they and others came for Money; or that he asked them concerning their having Fire-office Tickets; or that, upon their going away, he called or beckoned to them to return; but said, that Keyhoe laid hold of him before he knocked him down with his Staff; and that Glascock placed himself as before described, and swore several Oaths at the same time that Keyhoe assaulted the Witness.

The Persons complained of, in order to disprove the

Evidence given by the said Flemming, called the

following Witnesses:

Christopher Tool; who being examined, said, That he was One who assisted in working an Engine at the Fire before-mentioned; for which a Ticket was delivered him; and the next Day he received Eighteen Pence at the Fire-Office: That he accompanied Keyhoe, Glascock, and others, when they went to several Houses in Down-ing-Jlrcet, to collect Money to drink on that Occasion; and that Glascock was the Person who knocked at Sir Watkyn Williams\ Door, and asked for Money; upon which, the Servant answering, they were no Firemen, Glascock said they had been of Service, and produced a Ticket *, and that the Servant spoke some abusive Words, and then brought out. his Staff, and knocked Keyhoe down, and ftiut the Door.

He said, That the Names of the other Persons in Company, besides himself, Keyhoe, arid Glascock, were one Duncan, Pierfe Carr, and John Deely:

That James Branan was absent at that time; and that the Witness did not fee Francis Eden any time that Day.

Neither did he, as he said, fee any of the other Persons he named, who werepresent at the time he spoke of, eater, into the House; but that Glascock &ood at the Threshold of the Door, when produced the Ticket;

The Committee came to the following Resolutions s Resolved, That it appears to this Committee, That Edward Keyhoe did, upon the nth day of July last, endeavour to make a forcible Entry into the House of Sir Watkyn Williams Wynn Baronet, a Member of this House, in Dozvning-street, Westmiufler, and did then and there assault Edward Flemming, Porter to the said Member.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the said Edward Keyhoe is thereby guilty of a Breach of the Privilege of this House.

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee, That William Glascock did, upon the nth Day of July last, endeavour to make a forcible Entry into the said House of the said Sir Watkyn Williams Wynn, and did then and there assault the said Edward Flemming.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the said William Glascock is thereby guilty of Breach of the Privilege of this House.

Milling A Petition of several Merchants, Maltsters, and Brew-fr°edCorn^" ers’ *n Burgh of Great Yarmouth, in the County of orn‘ Norfolk, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was presented to the House, and read; reciting a Resolution reported from the Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred to consider further of Ways and Means for raising the Supply granted to his Majesty, " That it is the Opinion of the said Committee, That, " towards raising the Supply granted there should " be paid for every Gallon of low Wines or Spirits of " the First Extraction, made or drawn only from any " Sort of Drink or Wash brewed or made from any " Sort of Malt or Corn, other than and except Brewers ts Wash or Tilts, One Peny over and above all Duties " charged or chargeable thereon, to be paid by the Dif-<c tillers or Makers thereof;" and representing to the House, That several Laws were heretofore made, for obliging all Distillers to draw their low Wines, or Spirits of the First Extraction, from clean and wholesome Drink* Vol. 24.

made of malted Corn intirely; and that Spirits drawn from Malt only are more wholesome than such as are-drawn from unmalted Corn mixed with Malt; and that, by the Distillers Use of unmalted C;orn, much less Corn, as well as Malt, is consumed, to the great Disadvantage of his Majesty’s Revenue, and to the Loss of the Manufacture to the Subject, as also to the landed Interest; and is very prejudicial to Trade, as well as Navigation: And therefore, in behalf of themselves, and many others prejudiced by the Use of unmalted Corn, praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and to give Relief therein, that the Distillers may be restrained from the using of unmalted Corn, and the Laws heretofore-made, for the Consumption of malted Corn, be enforced, or revived, or by such other Means as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of the Freeholders, Merchants, and Inha- Boroughbridgi bitants of Tarum, in the North Riding of the County of ^oad*. York, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth,

That the said Town of Yarum is a very antient Market Town, and by its Situation upon the River Tees, which is a navigable River, great Quantities of Lead, Butter, firkins, Corn, Tallow, and ocher Commodities, which ate thete bought, ana shipped for London, and othcJ Places, afe almost daily brought to Yarum aforesaid, by Land-carriage, from the several inland Market Towns of Richmond, Bedall, Middleham, Mafiim, Afkrigg, Reefh, add Rawest and also from divers other Places in she 29 Neighbour-

16 Geo. IL $7° Jamtarii. 395

Neighbourhood of those several Market Towns in the said North-Riding, and likewise great Quantities of Grocery Wares* Flax, Iron, Tar, Timber, Fir Deals, Salt, and other Merchandizes, are sent by Land-carriage from Tarim aforesaid to the above-mentioned Seven several Market-Towns, and other Places thereto respectively adjacent-, and that the Two several Roads, the one leading from Borough-bridge to Cath trick, and from thence to Piers Bridge, on the River Tees 5 and the other leading from Borough-bridge aforesaid to Northallerton, and from thence to a Ford or Passage over the said River Tees, opposite to the Town of Nee/ham (for the Repairing whereof Two several Bills are now depending in the House); both of them lie between Tarum aforesaid, and the said Seven several other Market Towns and Places above-mentioned Ya-rum being situate on the East Side of the said Two Roads, and the said other Market Towns and Places on the West Side thereof; so that all Horses, Carts, and other Carriages, passing and repassing to and from Yarum aforesaid, and the said Seven several other Market Towns and Places are obliged to go cross both the said Roads in several Parts thereof; and representing to the House, that if the said Bills should pass into a Law, and Turnpikes should be fixed upon those Parts of the said Roads where the same must necessarily be crofted by all Horses, Carts, and Carriages, passing and repassing betwixt Yarum aforesaid, and the said Seven several other Market Towns and Places, such Horses, &c. must be subjected to pay the Tolls in the said several Bills mentioned, for and towards the Repair of the said Roads respectively, and would bear the Burthen, and want the Benefit intended thereby; which, in the Judgment of the Petitioners, would be a very great Hardship upon all Persons having Occa-lion to travel cross the said Roads, and tend to ruin the Trade of the said Town of Yarum in particular; for that in the several Places where Travellers cross the said Roads, they, in some Places thereof, only pass a few Yards, and at the most do not travel above a Quarterof a Mile thereon, feve when a Flood (which seldomhappens) renders a Ford or Passage over the River Swale, near Catherick, im-pastable; and in that case they do not travel above a computed Mile upon that Road, which leads from Borough-bridge to Piers Bridge aforesaid: And therefore praying, That these Bills may not pass, without having such Provides, or Clauses of Exception, therein respectively inferred, of aft Horses, Carts, and other Carriages, which make no further or other Use of the said Two several Roads than in crofting thereof, or going so short a Way thereon, as above set forth, as to the House shall seem meet.

Mr. Francis Fane, according ta Order, reported from the Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred to consider further of the Supply granted to his Majesty, the Resolutions, which they had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same were read; and are as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding One hundred Eighty-eight thousand Five hundred Fifty-eight Pounds Thirteen Shillings and Five Pence, be granted to his Majesty, for the Ordinary of the Navy (including Half-pay to Sea Officers), for the Year 1743.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Ten thousand Pounds, be granted to his Majesty, upon Account, towards the Support of the Royal Hospital at Greenwich, for the better Maintenance of the Seamen of the said Hospital, worn out, and become decrepit, in the Service of their Country.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Fifty-eight thousand Eight hundred Sixty-nine Pounds Fifteen Shillings and Seven Pence Three Farthings, be granted to his Majesty, for making good the Deficiency of the General Fund, for the Year ended at Michaelmas 1742.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Three thousand Eight hundred and Nineteen Pounds and Two Pence, be granted to his Majesty, to replace to the Sinking Fund the like Sum paid out of the fame, to make good the Deficiency of the additional Stamp Duties at Christmas 1741.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Forty-two thousand Pounds, be granted to his Majesty, to replace to the Sinking Fund the like Sum paid out of the fame, for One Year’s Interest, due on or before the 5th Day of November 1742, on the principal Sum of One Million Two hundred thousand Pounds, lent on Credit of the Salt Duty, towards the Supply of the Year 1741.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Thirteen thousand Seven hundred Eighty-six Pounds Ten Shillings and Eleven Pence Half-peny be granted to his Majesty, to replace to the Sinking Fund the like Sum paid out of the fame, to make good the Deficiency of the Duty of Twelve Shillings a Barrel on Sweets, or Wines, made from British or foreign Fruit, or Sugar, at Michaelmas 1742.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Four thousand Three hundred Thirty-three Pounds Ten Shillings and One Peny, be granted to his Majesty, to replace to the Sinking Fund the like Sum paid out of the fame, to make good the Deficiency of the Duty upon all Victuallers and Retailers of Beer and Ale, within the Cities of London and Westminster, and the Weekly Bills of Mortality, at Michaelmas 1742.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Ten thousand Pounds be granted to his Majesty, to be applied towards the Maintenance of the British Forts and Settlements, belonging to the Royal African Company of England, on the Coast. of Africa.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Sum of Four thousand Pounds be granted to his Majesty, towards the repairing and finiftring the Collegiate Church of St. Petn, Westminster.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Twenty-five thousand Pounds, be granted to his Majesty, towards enabling the Commissioners for building a Bridge cross the River Thames, from the City of Westminster to the opposite Shore, in the County of Surrey, to finifti the said Bridge, and to perform the other Trustsreposed in them.
