Mr. Carew,.according to Order, reported from the Committee, who were appointed to consider the Act, made in the Thirteenth Year of his present Majesty's Reign, intituled, An Act for amending and enforcing the Laws relating to Rogues, Vagabonds, and other idle and disorderly Persons, and for reducing the same into One Act of Parliament; and alto for amending the Laws for erecting, providing, and regulating, Houses of Correction; and to report their Opinion to the House, as to what Amendments may be proper to be made thereunto; and who were instructed to consider the Laws relating to the Poor, so far as the same concern the Removal* and Relief of poor Persons; and report their Opinion to the House, as to what Amendments may be prbper to be made thereunto; and who were also instruct-cd to consider the Laws relating to the Settlement of poor Persons; and to report their Opinion to the House, as to what Amendments may be proper to be made thereunto; I That the Committee had considered the said Laws accordingly; and had come to several Refblutions; which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read.

Ordered, That the said Report be taken into further Consideration upon Thursday Morning next.

The other Orders of the Day being read 5

Resolved, That this House will, upon Thursday Morning next, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, upon the Bill to explain and amend the Laws touching the Elections of Members to serve in Parliament, for Cities, Boroughs, Towns, Ports, and other Places, within that Part of Great Britain called England, and to restrain the Partiality, and regulate the Conduct, of Returning Officers at such Elections.

Resolved, That this House will, upon Thursday Morning next, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider further of the Bill to explain and amend the Laws touching the Elections of Knights of the Shire, to serve in Parliament for that Part of Great Britain called England, and’ to restrain the Partiality, and regulate the Conduct, of Returning Officers at such Elections.

Ordered, That Mr. Alderman Heathcote have Leave to make a Motion, it being after Two of the Clock:

And he moved the House accordingly; and presented to the House,

A Petition of the Bailiffs, Wardens, Assistants, and Wearing Commonalty, of the Trade, Art, and Mystery of Weavers, G°ld&Lace, London, on behalf of themselves and Trade; which was c* read; setting forth, That the Manufactures of Silk, mixed with Gold and Silver, and of Gold and Silver Lace, in this Kingdom, by the Encouragement they have received from the Crown, and divers Acts of Parliament, are of late Years very much improved, and all Sorts of as rich brocaded Gold and Silver Stuffs, Ribbands, and Gold and Silver Lace, are now made here to as great Perfection as in France, or any other foreign Country; and representing to the House, That, if the Bill now depending in the House, to prohibit the wearing of Gold and Silver Lace,

Thread* or Wire, in Apparel, should pass into a Law, these Branches of the Manufactures will be totally destroyed, and not only great Numbers of the Petitioners, but many Thousand Families, who are intirely dependant thereon, will be deprived of the Means of getting their Bread, and reduced to the greatest Necessity, and must become burthensome to their respective Parishes.: And therefore praying the House so to take the Premises into their Consideration, that these Manufactures.of this Kingdom may not receive such Discouragement as would be the fatal Consequence of this Bill, should the same pass into a Law; and that the Petitioners may be heard by their Counsel against the said Bill.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the said Bill be read a Second time: And that the Petitioners be then heard by their Counsel against the said Bill, if they think fit.

And then the House adjourned till Tomorrow Morning, Nine of the Clock.

Mr. Winford reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Trustees, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, for putting in Execution an Act of Parliament, intituled, An Act for repairing and amending several Roads leading to and from the Borough of Eve-sham, in the County of Worcester; and also of several of his Majesty’s Justices of the Peace of and for the said County, and other Gentlemen and principal Inhabitants dwelling and residing in and near the several Parishes wherein the same Roads lie, and many others frequently travelling through the said Roads; as like wife of Hamah Mence, of the City of Worcester, Widow, llelift, and Aminiftratrix, of Samuel Mence Gentleman, deceased, James Smith, of Ledbury, in the County of Hereford, Gent, and Hannah Wynn of Bewdley in the County of Worcester, Spinster, Devisee of Elizabeth Humphreys Widow, deceased, Creditors under the said Act; and also the Petition of the Justices of the Peace, Gentlemen, Freeholders, and principal Inhabitants, of the Town of Parfhore, in the County of Worcester, and of Wick near Parfhore, Pensham, Great Comberton, Little Comber ton, Bricklehampton, Elmley Castle, Net her ton, Over bury and Conderton, in the said County of Worcester; and also the Petition of several Gentlemen, and other Persons, living near, and frequently travelling through, the Road leading from the Borough of Evesham, in the County of Worcester, through Wick-hamford, to Willerjey, in the County of Gloucester, whose Names are thereunto subscribed; were referred. That the Committee had examined the Matters of the said Petitions; and had directed him to report the fame, as they appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the First Petition,

The Agent for the Petitioners laid before your Committee an Act, passed in the First Year of the Reign of his present Majesty King George the Second, for repairing and amending several Roads leading to and from the Borough of Evesham, in the County of Worcester-, whereby several Tolls were granted and made payable for the Term of Twenty-one Years, from the 30th Day of May 1728; and the Trustees for putting that Act in Execution borrowed of several Persons, upon the Act, £.1*950, in order to repair the Roads; and, for the securing the Repayment of Money so borrowed, several Mortgage Deeds were made to the Persons mentioned in the First Petition; which Mortgages the Agent for the Petitioners laid before the Committee; whereby it appeared, that That Sum was borrowed; but Evidence was given, that the Sum of £.33. 11 s. 4d. was paid in Part of the principal Sum of £. 1,950; so that there is now due, for Principal and Interest, the Sum of £. 1,916. 8r. 8d.

Then Witnesses were called; viz,

Mr. John Bovey and Mr. Samuel Rickards, Treasurers of the several Turnpikes; who laid before the Committee, Accounts of the Money received at the several Turnpike Gates erected upon the said Roads; whereby it appeared, that all the Tolls produce, on an Average, £. 400. per Annum; but subject to the several Expences attending the Receipt thereof, and to the Payment of Incereft of the Money borrowed on the Credit of the Tolls.

And the said Mr. Rickards being examined, said. That the several Roads directed to be repaired by the said Act are, by Computation, Twenty-three Miles; viz, the Road from the Top of Broadway, through the Borough of Eve-sham, to Stone-bow Bridge, isTvvelve Miles, or thereabouts; and the Road from Evesham to the First Chain upon Wick Causeway, next the Foot of Goodley Hilly near the Bridge at Perjhorey Four Miles, or thereabouts $ and so much of the Road to Hinton on the Green, as lies in the County of Worcester, One Mile, or thereabouts; and the Road to the Gate in Offenham Lane, leading to South Littleton, Two Miles, or thereabouts; and the Road to Norton Two Miles, or thereabouts; and the Road toBretfordton Two Miles, or thereabouts: And said further, That un-lel's such Parts of the Roads as have been already amend-

Vol. 24.

ed be constantly taken care of, and repaired, will, by rea-fonof the Deepneis of the Soil, and the heavy Carriages which frequently, pass over the fame, in a short time become bad and ruinous again, and will be almost impass-able: And he added to his Evidence, and said, Tha: several Parts of the Roads are now in a very bad Condition; and the same cannot be repaired, nor can the Money now due and owing to the several Mortgagees, be repaid during the subsisting Term, unless the Term and Powers by the former Act granted be continued and enlarged.

Mr. Thomas Yarnoldy Mr.----- Kettley and Mr.

Richard Horne; who, being examined, confirmed the whole Evidence given by Mr Rickards.

Mr. Nicholas Field being called and examined, laid, That if the Turnpike near the Bridge at Perjhore was removed to a Place called Mill Tail, it would greatly increase the Toll on that Road: And he further Paid, That the Roads cannot be sufficiently amended, and kept in Repair, and Money borrowed on the Credit of the Act repaid, without the Aid of another Act of Parliament.

And to prove the Allegations of the 2d Petition, the Agent for that Petition called

Mr. Samuel Rickards; who being examined, said, That the Road leading from Evesham to the First Chain of the Wick Causeway, next to the Foot of Goodley Hill, near the Bridge at Perjhore (being about 400 Yards short of the Town of Perjhore) is in a very ruinous and dangerous Condition all the Winter Season: That the Statute-work has been constantly done thereupon, which has proved insufficient; and that the Inhabitants of the Parish, in which the Road lies, have expended and laid out £. 200, and upwards, in repairing of that Road; notwithstanding which, the same is almost impastable; and that, by reason of the Narrowness and Lowneis of the Causeways leading to and from the great Bridge over the River Avony where there are Floods, it is very difficult, and many times impossible, for Persons to pals on Horseback: And the said Mr. Rickards further said, That the Floods often continue for a Fortnight or Three Weeks together, when Passengers are obliged to ferry over the River, which is expensive to them; and the Expences by the said Act is paid out of the Tolls thereby granted; but if the Boad was repaired, it would save at least £.10. per Annum, which is paid out of the Tolis for ferrying over: And being asked, Whether the Tolls arising by the Act would be sufficient to repair the Road ? said, that it would; and added, That the Turnpike erected near Per-JJiore Bridge is set up in a Place proper for collecting the Tolls; but as th, ere is a common Meadow belonging to the Township of Wick, lying between that Turnpike and the Town of Perjhorey many , Persons travelling to and from many Towns and Villages bet ween Evesham and Perjhore without paying the Tolls, which very much Jeffens the Toll, and cannot be remedied, as the present Act stands; but this might be prevented, by carrying the Repairs of the Roads from the Turnpike to a Place called Mill Tally at or near the End of the d own of Perjhorey which lies next the Turnpike, and erecting a Turnpike at or near the same End of the Town; thereby the Tolls would be increased.

Thomas Coventry Savage Esquire was called, and being examined, laid. That he knows the Road leading from the Turnpike near Perjhore Bridge to the Top of Goodley Hilly and to the Top thereof to the Ground in Wick, called the Grove; and that the same is about 800 Yards from the Turnpike, and is the direct Road to Pensham, the Two Combertons, and the other Towns and Villages in the Petition mentioned; and that the lame, by the Deep-ness of the Soil, and the many Carriages passing and repassing, is become very ruinous, and unsafe for Travellers; and that the same cannot be repaired by the Statute-work: And said, That the Tolls granted and made payable by the former Act are sufficient to repair as well the last mentioned Road, as the other Roads directed to be repaired and amended by the said Ati.

Diffing A Petition of the several Merchants, Maltsters, and from un- Brewers, in the City of New Sarum, in the County of malted Corn. #7//^ whose Names are thereunto i'ubscribed, was presented to the House, and read; reciting a Resolution reported of the Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred to'considerjfurther of the Ways and Means for raising the Supply granted to his Majesty, " That, towards raising the Supply granted, there should be paid for every Gallon of low Wines, or Spirits of the First c< Extraction, made or drawn only from any Sort of Drink or Wash, brewed or made from any Sort of Malt or Com, other than and except Brewers Wash or Tilts, " One Peny over and above all Duties charged or chargeable thereon, to be paid by the Distillers Or Makers " thereof;" and setting^ forth. That several Laws were heretofore made for obliging all Distillers to draw their low Wines, or Spirits of the First Extraction, from wholesome Drink made of malted Corn intirely: That Spirits drawn from Malt only are more wholesome than such as are drawn from unmalted Corn mixed with Malt; and that by the Distillers Use of unmalted Corn, much less Corn, as well as Malt, by Means thereof, is consumed; which, the Petitioners apprehend, is a great Diladvantage to his Majesty’s Revenue arising by the Duty on Malt, and is a very great Loss of the Manufacture to the Subjects of this Kingdom, and also to the landed Interest, and'is a very great Prejudice both to Trade and Navigation: And therefore praying, as well in behalf of themselves, as of many others employed in the Malting Trade in this Kingdom, prejudiced by the Use of unmaited Corn, that the House will take the Premise^into Consideration, that the Petitioners may be relieved therein; and that the Distillers may be reftrajned from the Using of unmalted Command the Laws heretofore made for the Consumption of malted Corn be enforced, or revived, or by such other Ways or Means as to the House shall leem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table

A Petition of several Yeomen and Farmers in the DistilMlg County of Kent, in behalf of themselves, and all the Farmers of the said County, was presented to the House, or D" and read; setting forth, That the Petitioners have, with great Concern and Surprize, read in the Votes of this House the Contents of a Petition from several Merchants, Maltsters, and Brewers, in the Burgh of Great Yarmouth, in the County of Norfolk; and expressing their Sorrow at the Prospect of impending Ruin, which must inevitably fell upon the Petitioners, if this Doctrine should once prevail, that more Corn would be consumed, by obliging all Distillers to draw their Spirits of the First Extraction from malted Corn intirely; and consequently that the Corn-grower would be a considerable Gainer thereby; whereas in the Opinion of the Petitioners, nothing is more plain

than

Plnltl7pri h" Go

Febrmrii.

A. 1742.

than that the very Reverse is most true: And further setting forth, That the Petitioners have seen a printed Calculation, delivered, as they are informed, to the Members of this House, attempting to prove the abovesaid Proportion: And representing to the'House, Thatalthoughmany things may be true in Figures, and absolutely false in Practice, yet the Petitioners conceive, the Computation pretended to be made upon this proposed Alteration of the Law is not only fallacious in itself, but will, if carried into Execution, prove fatal to the Interest of Landlord and Tenant: That there are every Year, and in the very bed Harveds, considerable Quantities of Corn throughout the Kingdom utterly incapable of being malted; and as this happens even in dry Lands, and early Harveds, the Proportion of such Corn mud be greater in cold wet Lands, and in late Wet Harveds; which great Quantity of Corn is now chiefly used for the Distillation of Spirits; but should a Law pass to confine the Distiller to draw them from malted Corn only, the Petitioners know not any Market which can possibly take such large Quantities of poor Corn off their Hands, which enables the Petitioners at present to pay their Rents: And further representing to the House the great Prejudice, which mud certainly attend the Farmers, with respect to that Part of the Crop . capable of beingmalted; of which at present great Quantities, and that of the very bed Corn, are used dry by the Distillers; and that although the Petitioners allow that more of this Sort of Corn may be consumed, if all was to be malted, and the Malt Duty, as it is urged, would be raised, to the Increase of the Revenue; yet it is as certain, that the Price of Spirits mud be raised by the Distiller, in proportion to the extraordinary Charge this new Method would lay him under, or else he mud abate so much from the Price of the Corn, to the Prejudice of the Farmer; and that the Petitioners are of Opinion, that the Price uponSpirits, which now fell for Three Shillings and Six Pence a Gallon, mud then necessarily be augmented to Six Shillings, or thereabouts j which, considering the present Price of smuggled Brandy, and of that which has paid Duty, will amount to a total Prohibition: That the Distiller therefore, in order to carry on his Trade, indead df raising the Price of his Spirits to this Degree, will naturally, as the Petitioners apprehend, deduct all the additional Charges out of the prime Cod of the Malt y and consequently the Farmer will bear the whole Burden, and be forced to fell so much more Corn, to be made into Malt, for the same Money, besides paying the new iMalt Duty, and the Maltsters Profit: And therefore expressing the Hope of the Petitioners, that no such Alteration may be enacted, as is prayed for in the above-mentioned Petition; but that the late Ad of the Sixth of his present Majesty, and which was made upon mature Deliberation, for the Benefit of the Corn-grower and Land-owner, by opening a Market for the dry Com to the Distiller, will not be infringed upon in this Point, but remain in full Force^and Virtue.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

themselves, and all others concerned in the Woollen Manufacture, ivaspresented to the House, and read; setting forth. That, by an Act made in the Thirteenth Year of his present Majesty’s Reign, to prohibit Commence with Spain, Spanish Oil stands prohibited from being imported into his Majesty’s British Dominions; and representing to the House, Ihat, notwithstanding the wife and good Intention of the Legislature in the Prohibition, the Petitioners conceive the Design of it has been frustrated by the various Turns of Providence, and the many Resolutions in the political Affairs of Europe; and that the Olive Harvell in the Neapolitan Territories have failed; which, with the Motions and Consumptions of the Armies in Italy, have rendered this Commodity scarce and dear, and . advanced it to the Petitioners to above double the Price it was at before; which is owing also in fomemealure, as the Petitioners are informed, to its being monopolized there by particular Persons, who put it upon us at their own Price, knowing we can be supplied from no other Quarter; and that the Price of Oil being advanced at Gallipoli, from whence the Petitioners are chiefly supplied with Italian Oil, the French and Dutch take off the whole Produce of Old Spain; so that the Spaniards are not dif-tressed at all by the Prohibition, but his Majesty’s Subjects only; and that the present Advance of this Commodity /and thereby Soap) is fb great, that it enhances the Price of many Fabricksof our own Woollen Manufactures near Four per Cent.; whereby the French and Dutch obtain a great Advantage over us in foreign Markets; and that a far greater Advance of the Price of Oil is dreaded, and a still greater national Detriment apprehended, if the Petitioners obtain no Relief from the Resolutions of this House; and that the whole Produce of Italy, from the failure of the Crops, and other extraordinary Consumptions, will not be Sufficient to carry on the Manufactures of this Kingdom; and from hence a great Stagnation of Trade, and Confusion, must arise; or at Jeaft, bad, dear, and disgraceful Manufactures, through the Use of improper Oils; and that the Manufacturers, in order to iiipply the Deficiency of Olive Oil, have already had Recourse to Fish Oil; but, to their Cost, and the great Prejudice of their Manufactures, have found it improper for their Use; and that the Regard the Legislature has at all times had for the Woollen Manufactures of this Kingdom, and the kind Indulgcncies they, have been favoured with, shewn particularly by the late free Admis-fion of Cochineal and Indigo, though enumerated Commodities, and the important Consequences of the present high Price of Oil, have emboldened the Petitioners to request, that the Prohibition of Spanish Oil may be taken off; or that they may have such other Relief in the Premises, as to the House shall seem meet.

A Petition of the Mayor, Burgesses, and principal Inhabitants, of the Borough and Town of Marlborough, in the County of Wills, was presented to the House, and readj letting forth. That the Petitioners observe by the Votes of this House, that a Bill has been brought in for repairing the Roads leading from Marlborough, through West Kennet, to Shepherds Shord, and from the Hare and Hounds in Beckhampton, to the Top of Cheril Hilly and from the Town of Avebury to the Ciofs-way at Beckhampton, in the County of Wilts; and that several of the present Petitioners did petition for the Bill for amending the Roads lead i ng from Marlborough, t h rough West Kennety to Beckhampton and Shepherds Shord; but have since better considered of the Premises, and viewed the Hoads leading from Marlborough, not only through West Kennet to the Cross-way at Beckhampton, called the lower Road, but also the Roads leading from Marlborough, over Marlborough Common, through Manton Inclosures, leaving Wroughlon Coppice on the Left Hand, through Avebury, to the said Cross-way, called the upper Road; and beg Leave to lay before the House their maturerThoughts, that, in order to complete a Turnpike Road from Marlborough, through West Kennet, to the said Cross-way (it being great Part of it a deep hollow Way, and confiding of but a tingle Track for Wheel-carriages; it being lb very narrow in most Places, that Carriages cannot pass by each other; and Brcakings-out being but few; and, as the Bill now stands, neither Stones nor Soil being to betaken from the Estates lying on that Road, nor Landscobe purchased, by virtue of this Bill, without Consent of the Owners), the Petitioners conceive, that the making this Road a good Turnpike Road will cost a great Sum of Money, and cannot be completed in many Years, by the Tolls to be collcded by virtue of this Bill; becaulc it is to bepre-fumed, that the other Part of the Roads leading from the said Cross-way to Shepherds Shordy having never been repaired since the Memory of Man, and though lying on the open Downs, being become very ruinQus, by being lately inclosed by Ditches, will, as the^Petitioners apprehend, in common Prudence, be mended first; and that to guard against the Inconveniencies above-mentioned, and for the Satisfaction of this House, the Petitioners have caused the lower and upper Roads, leading from Marlborough to the said Cross-way, to bemeasured with a Chain in the Common Track, where Coaches and Waggons pass; and upon this Measure they find, that the lower Road is Six Miles Three Quarters and Eight Pole; the upper, Seven Miles One Quarter and Eleven Pole; and that there is no more than Half a Mile and Three Pole difference between the one and the other; and that the upper Road lies in an open champ Country, and that Materials may be had for the repairing it, without injuring the Lands; which cannot be said of the lower Road; and that the Petitioners conceive that it may be amended, and made very good, for a Fifth of what mull necessa-rily be expended on the lower Road: And further repre-fenting to the House, That the lower Road is at this time a good champ Road for Waggons and Horsemen, and may be easily kept so by Half a Day’s Statute-labour yearly, according to the Laws now in being for the Amendment of the Highways in this Kingdom: That these several Particulars the Petitioners are able to shew to be true; and pray to be heard as to the Matter and Things before-men-

Vol. 24,

tioned: And therefore praying, That the House will please to admit of a Clause to be inserted in the said Bill, for the Amendment of the upper Road from Marlborough Town’s End, through Avebury, to the Cross-way at Beckhampton, instead of the lower Road, or otherwise as to the House shall seem meet: And further observing, that, as the Bill now stands, the upper Road is to be amended above a Mile and a Half to Avebury; so that there will be but about Six Miles to be amended.

A Petition of the Merchants of London, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, in behalf of themselves, and others, trading to Italy, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth. That the Trade from these Kingdoms to Italy hath long been, and still is, very large and beneficial, in taking off great Quantities of the Woollen Manufactures, FiHi, Lead, Tin; Leather, and other Goods; and that such Trade hath been carried on, since the present War, by large Ships of Force, with great Numbers of Seamen, and without Convoys, at a very great Expence to the Petitioners, and with Safety to the Mariners, that iife-ful Part of the People; and that, ih order to the (peedy Return of such large Ships, the Petitioners have been, and are, obi iged to provide great Quantities of Italian Oil in Readinefe, as Foundations for reloading them homewards; and considerable Quantities of such Oil are lately arrived, and at Market; not less than a Thousand Tons more are now on the Way hither, and Orders are already gone for further great Quantities, which the Petitioners have engaged in, under the Security of the Law, that Spa-nish Oil could not, during the War, be imported; and that the Spanish Court, since the War, hath rigorously and repeatedly prohibited the Introduction of British Woollen and other Manufactures, even by the Way of neutral Ports; and that although Olive Oil was lately at a Price higher than ufua), the same didjiot, as the Petitioners apprehend, arise from the Cause assigned by the Petition of the Clothiers of Stroudwater, and Places adjacent, in the County of Gloucester, presented to this House; but from a Short ness in the Growth thereof in the Years 1740 and 1741; neither was the Excess of Price so great as represented; and that the Quantity used by the Petitioners, the Clothiers, is so small, that the high Price, if it had continued, would not prove such a very great Burthen and Inconvenience on the Woollen Manufacture, as alleged; and which, if it had, the Petitioners, who export and vend laige Quantities thereof, must themselves have felt; but that the introducing Spanish Gil during the War, which must be paid for in Money, and exported from thence in neutral Ships, however it may be of present Advantage to a very few j N particular

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, towards raising the Supply granted to his Majesty, the Sum of One Million be raised by Annuities, at Three Pounds per Cent, per Annum and the Sum of Eight hundred thousand Pounds by Way of a Lottery, to be attended wit}\Annuities, after the Rate of Three Pounds per Cent. per Annum \ which said several Annuities . shall be transferrable at the Bank of England, and charged on the several Duties on spirituous Liquors granted to his Majesty this Session of Parliament.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, in lieu of the said Rates and Duties now charged with the Payment of the principal Sum of Four hundred Eighty-one thousand Four hundred Pounds in Exchequer Bills, the said Sum remaining unsatisfied in Exchequer Bills, together with the Interest thereupon, and Charges of circulating the fame, shall, from and after the 25th Day of March 1743, together with the Sum herein after granted to his Majesty, be charged on the Duties granted to his Majesty this Session of Parliament, for Licences to sell spirituous Liquors, or strong Waters, by Retail, fub-ject to the same Rules and Methods as were prescribed concerning the circulating and paying off the same Exchequer Bills, in and by the Act passed in the Twelfth Year of the Reign of King George the First, for laying a Duty upon all Victuallers, and Retailers of Beer and Ale, within the Weekly Bills of Mortality.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, towards raising the Supply granted to his Majesty, his Majesty be enabled to borrow by Loans, or Exchequer Bills, any Sum or Sums of Money, not exceeding in the Whole the Sum of Five hundred and Eighteen thousand Six hundred Pounds j which said Sum of Five hundred and Eighteen thousand Six hundred Pounds, together with

Importation A Petition of the Mailer, Wardens, Assistants, and

Olive Oi?1 Commonalty, of the Society of Merchants Adventurers within the City of Bristolunder their common Seal, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth. That the Petitioners observe, by the Votes of this House, that feme Clothiers of Stroudwater, and Places adjacent, in the County of Gloucester, have represented, by their Petition, the great Burthen and Inconvenience they lie under by the high Price of Olive Oil, occasioned, as they fugged, from the Prohibition thereof from Spain, during the present War, to the Prejudice of the Woollen Manufactory; and representing to the House, That the Trade from Great Britain to Italy, so beneficial by the Exportation of our Woollen Manufactures, Fish, and other Commodities (the Product of these Kingdoms, and our Plantations), has been carried on, since the War, by Ships of Force, at a very great Expence to the Proprietors; who are obliged to provide a great Quantity of Italian Oil for their Return home; and that the High Price of Oliye Oil, as the Petitioners conceive, was occasioned chiefly from the Failure of the Recultas in Italy and Portugal, in the Years 1740 and 1741; and that the Quantities ordered, under the SanClion of the British Laws, and shortly expected, will, in all Probability, reduce the Price considerably, without the Admission of Spanish^ Oils; for which, Money must be paid, at the same titne that Spain wiHnot admit any of the British Manufactures; and that the Crown of Spain has frequently, on the Failure of the Olives, prohibited the Exportation of Oil; so that, at this time of actual War, instead of distressing its Subjects as much as possible, the taking off the Prohibition would assist them with ready Money for a Commodity, which must otherwise lie on their Hands: And therefore praying the House to be heard, by their Counsel herein, against the said other Petition.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom it is referred to consider of the Petition of the Clothiers of Stroudwater, and Places adjacent, in the County of Gloucester: And that these Petitioners be heard, by their Counsel, before the said Committee, upon their said Petition, if they think fit.

Jamaica Currency, for £. 100. Jamaica Currency, for every £. too. Sterling; the said Paymaster-General therefore prays their Lordships Directions, whether he shall fend Instructions to his Deputy to continue to take up such Sums of Money as the Service of the Troops shall require, from the Agents to the Contractors, upon the Terms of their Contract, or whether he shall be directed to take up what Sums of Money the Service shall, from time to time, require, at the bed Rate of Exchange he can obtain, to draw Bills upon the Paymaster for the fame, and keep a distinct Account in Writing of the Difference arising by Exchange, subject to future Directions.

The Lords having taken into their Consideration a Report, dated this Day, and made to them by the Right Honourable Henry Pelham Esquire, Paymaster-Genera] of his Majesty’s Guards, Garrisons, and Land Forces, concerning Remittances: Which Report is as follows.

N. B. The Copy of the Report being made, and delivered in to the House, is omitted here----- The Copy

is marked (B).

Their Lordships, on mature Deliberation, as well for the Reasons stated in the said Report, as from the allowed Abilities of the Remitters Correspondents in Holland, and the Contract for the Remittances being for a Time certain, and the Experience they have had of the punctual and effectual manner in which they have been hitherto carried on, and from the great and irretrievable Detriment it would be to the public Service, if any Interruption should happen in the Payment of the Forces, by making any Alteration in the Contract at this time, are of Opinion it will be for the Interest of the Public to accept the Proposals therein mentioned, of Messieurs Gore, Gulf on, and Poyntz.

In obedience to your Lordships Order of Reference; bearing Date the 5th of this instant January 1742-3, inclosing the Memorial of Messieurs Henry Muilman and Pinckney Wilkinson, offering to make Proposals for remitting the Money necessary for the Payment of the Forces in Flanders, and defining me to inquire into the Matter* and to give my Opinion thereupon:

I have talked with the said Messieurs Muilnian and Wilkinson, and have received their Proposals, whereby they offer to remit all such. Sums as may become necefl&ry for the Service of the Troops abroad, at the Rate of 10 Guilders 16 Stivers, current Money of Amsterdam, for every Pound Sterling: " That as the Exchange between " England and Holland is now at 34*. which* with the Agio, is upwards of 10 Guilders 17 Stivers per " Pound Sterling: The Profit on this Proposal to the " Remitters will be better than Half per Cent, they acknowlege there are some Expences attending this Affair*

" but that as they now deal in Affairs of this kind, with " other People, and find some Profit thereby, they imagine " they shall find a still better Account by supplying,-at " the First hand: They tell me they negociate their Affairs in Holland with Messieurs Muibnan and Sons, and " Messieurs Clifford and Sons, who, as they allege, are " at least equally sufficient with Messieurs Pells and Sons,

" and that they are very certain they can establish a Gre-"dit so as to keep up the Exchange, and carry oh this " Transaction for a Continuance at 10 Guilders 16 Sti-t( vers per Pound Sterling; but this they did agree must

" be supported chiefly by the Means of exporting foreign " Gold, or Specie, to keep up the Course of Exchange,

" as it hath been for above Two Years, last past, but " they intend to remit as much by Bills of Exchange on " Amsterdam, and other Places, to be negociated there, as " the Nature of the Affair will permit.

" That the Government shall be always well furnished " with Money; but if hereafter the Exchange should " alter much to their Disadvantage, upon proper Notice,

>" they hope to be permitted to make other Proposals, as " they are informed hath been the Cale of other Remits u ters.

" That they will answer for their Correspondents supplying, the Public with any large Sums, upion any " Emergency, as securely and efJe&ually as hath betfn " done by the present Remitters; and if the Treasury will " be pleased to make a Trial for One, Two, or Three " Remittances, a Profit will arise to the Public from " thence, worth attending to; but if any other Persons " make Proposals fora fixed time, they are ready todofo " too, but at a different Rate of Exchange from what they " now propose :’’ And being asked, at what Rate? They answered, " They were not at present prepared to say."

I have likewise talked with Mr. Gore, the present Remitter; and, for your Lordships more certain Information, beg Leave to annex hereunto a Paper, delivered by him, signed by himself, Mr. Poyntz, and Mr. GuIston, justifying their Proposals lately laid before your Lordships:

For my better Information I have also consulted with some Gentlemen of undoubted Credit and Reputation, One of which has been formerly greatly experienced in these Affairs, and at present no ways concerned in public Bu-finess, nor desires so to be, and of consequence not at all interested in the present Question: And I find it to be the Opinion of these Gentlemen, That the Proposals of Mr. Gore, Mr. GuIston, and Mr. Poyntz, at the Rate of 10 Guilders 13 Stivers current Money of Holland, considering the great Sums that will be probably remitted this Year, are rather a bold Undertaking than otherwise, and what, in their Opinion, if accepted, will tend to the -Service of the Public.

Having offered thus much to explain the Equitable-ness of the Proposal submitted to the Lords of the Treasury, the Contractors hope they may be allowed, without Vanity, to value themselves upon the Experience which the Lords of the Treasury have had of their Diligence and Punctuality in the Discharge of this great Trust j as also to observe, that the only Houses they make use of at Amsterdam, are those of Messieurs Andrev) Pells and Sons, and Messieurs George Clifford and Sons, Names of the, mod known and established Credit in the mercantile World; and as our Dependence on them, and the Assurances they have sent us of their Readiness and Zeal to give this Service the Preference to any other that can be offered them, has been our chief Inducement to undertake this important Affair; so we beg Leave to assure you. Sir, that they have let us know their good Opinion of us is so reciprocal, that they will not engage in the Credits necessary to carry on this Service with any other Persons but curselves.

We have only to add, that, having consulted with Persons best versed in the Exchanges, and particularly in that of Holland, they are unanimously of Opinion, that our Proposals are at as high a Rate as can be offered, with any Prospect of Safety to ourselves and the Public. All which is most humbly submitted by,

Sir, your most humble and obedient Servants,

John Gore,

(as thereinafter-mentioned) was prefen ted to the House, and read; representing to the House, That, at the same time that the Petitioners are burthened with a heavy Land Tax, and many other Taxes, they lie under very great and particular Dilfcouragements besides, from the low Price of Wool, and the precarious Stale of feeding Stock, now for many Yfears past, occasioned chiefty, as the Petitioners apprehend, by an Act of Charles the Second; prohibiting the Importation of Irish Cattle, which, as Sir William Temple then foretold it would, has, as the Petitioners conceive, since been the Cause of turning a considerable Part of the Trade of Ireland into a wrong Channel, to the further Detriment of Englatidin its Produce and Trade, not only in’ the Articles of Hides, Leather, Tallow, Butter, &c. but the total Loss of our Beef-trade abroad, and (which is still worse), by occasioning a vast Increase of the Breed of Shebp in that'Kingdom, has greatly contributed to the Increase of that'pernicious Practice of running Wool from therice to France, and other foreign Parts, to the inexpressiblb Damage of the Petitioners and of the whole Kingdom: And therefore pitying, by way of Remedy and Prevention for the future, tjiat a Bill may pass to permit the Importation of Irish Cattle, upon Conditions of Advantage and Security to the Wool-Vol-. 24.

Bethnal A Petition of the several Persons, who fe Names are

Green thereunto subscribed, being Freeholders, Leaseholders, and

Parife, Occupiers of Land, in the Hamlet of Bethnal Green, in the

Parish of St. Dunstan, Stepney, in the County of Middle-Jexy and of several other Persons, Inhabitants of the said Hamlet, was presented to the House, and read; representing to the House, That the Bill, now depending in the House, to make the Hamlet of Bethnal Green, in the Parish of St. Dunjtatty Stepney, in the County of Middlesex, a separate and distinct Parish, and for erecting a Parish-Church therein, will (as the Petitioners apprehend) prove extremely burthensome to the Petitioners, by laying upon them such weighty Taxes as will be unable to be paid, or borne by the Petitioners, should the same pass into a Law; and setting forth, That the Inhabitants of the said Hamlet consist chiefly of Journeymen Weavers, and other inferior Artificers, belonging to the Weaving Trade, who, by hard Labour and Industry can scarcely, in the moll frugal Way of Life, maintain themselves and Families; and as such Journeymen Weavers, and other Artificers, and their Families, are extremely numerous, so a great Number of the Inhabitants of the said Hamlet, consist likewise of Bakers, Butchers, Victuallers, Chandlers, and such-like Trades and Occupations, whorefide in the said Hamlet, and who, by their industrious Way of Life in their respective Trades and Callings, maintain themselves and Families, in supplying such Journeymen Weavers, and other Artificers, and their Families, and Dependants, with the Necessaries of Life, and that by far the greatest Part of the Houses in the said Hamlet are lett at Ten Pounds per Annum, and under; and are mostly lett out by the Owners of such Houses, in Two or Three distinct Parts or Tenements, by reason of the great Poverty of the Inhabitants, who are unable to take a whole House upon themselves, and the chief Part of the parochial Taxes for such Houses is now paid or allowed by the Landlords thereof, otherwise few Tenants could be found to inhabit therein, which is a sensible Hardship to such Landlords; and that several of the Petitioners, who are Artificers in Building, have very lately taken long Leases of a great Number of Houses within the said Hamlet, at certain yearly Rents, and have laid out upon such Houses, very large Sums of Money, in order to make the same tenantable; so that the Taxes and Assessments intended to be made payable by the said Bill, will prove extremely burthensome to, and fall wholly upon, such of the Petitioners; and that the Petitioners would be very glad that the want of a Place for the public Worshipof Alfiiighty God, within the said Hamlet, could be supplied, Was the said Hamlet capable of bearing the Taxes and Assessments intended for the Supply of such Want; but, to the Peti-. tioners great Concern, the said Hamlet is incapable of bearing such Taxes and* Assessments, as they hope to make appear, to the Satisfaction of the House: And therefore praying the House, that they may be heard by themselves, or Counsel, against the said Bill.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the said Bill be read the Third time: And that the Petitioners be then heard by their Counsel against the said Bill, if they think fit.

Ordered, That Counsel be admitted to be heard at the same time, in favour of the said Bill, against the said Petition.

Resolved, 3. That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That a Sum, not exceeding Forty-one thousand Four hundred Thirty-five Pounds Eighteen Shillings and Eight Pence Halfpeny, be granted to his Majesty, for defraying extraordinary Expences and Services of his Majesty’s Land Forces, incurred Anno 1742, and not provided for by Parliament.

Resolved\ 4. That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That a Sum, not exceeding One hundred Thirty-three Thousand Eight hundred Seventy-one Pounds Eight Shillings and Eleven Pence, be granted to his Majesty, for the Freight of Transports, between 1 ^January 1741, and 31st December 1742.

Resolved, 5. That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That a Sum, not exceeding Thirty-five thousand and Seventy-five Pounds Nine Shillings and One Peny, be granted to his Majesty, for the Expence of Victuals provided for his Majesty’s Land Forces, between the ift Day of January 1741, and the 31st of December 1742.

Resolved, 6. That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That a Sum, not exceeding Twelve thousand Pounds, be granted to his Majesty, for the further settling and improving the Colony of Georgia in America.

feme of the Gentlemen of the Bank being of Opinion, that it would be of Service to the Public, and an Eate to the Bank, if they had the Remitting of the next £.300,000 for the Service of the Troops in Flanders, his Lordship desired to speak with them together, to fee how that Matter could be best accommodated. Sir lays, He

believes, if the Bank would please to make their Propofi-tion, it might be so turned as to answer their Intent, without being any Prejudice to his Affair of Remittance. Mr. Eyles fays, the Bank do propose to give Bills fer £.300,000, payable at Amsterdam, for the Service of the Troops in Flanders, at 3? Ufance, and 4$, in equal Proportions, at the Rate of 9 Guilders 16 Stivers, Bank Money, for a Pound Sterling; and to receive their Payments in Exchequer Bills. Sir Henry thinks the Rate not unrea-fbnable; and fays he is willing to give them the like Ease and Accommodation in this Proposition, as he did in March 170J-, by taking the Bills they shall draw on Amsterdam for the said £.309,000; which will be the same Service to the Bank as if they remitted, and prevent the Inconveniencies that might happen to the Public, if the Remittances for the Army were in several Hands. My Lord approves of what is so offered.

20th December 1709.

Mr. Brydges and Sir Henry Furnefe called in fays, Mr. Brydges makes Difficulty to take his Bill at 10 Gs. 3 St. in lieu ofthofe agreed by the Bank to be given at io Gs. 6 St. He fays, the Reason he gives his Bills for.no more i$, that they are payable at 10 and 15 Days Sight, the Bank’s at 4 (Jfonce; and besides, his Bills are upon Account. My Lord orders Mr. Brydges to take the Bills drawn in that Manner from Sir Henry; and at the same time directs, that Mr. Brydges should examine the several Accounts of the Bills given by Sir Henry since he has been Paymaster, and lay a State thereof before his Lordship, as soon as conveniently he can.

A Proposal of Sir Henry Furnefe for 6,000 Moidores to be sent up the Straights, for the Service of the Troops in Spain, is read, and agreed to; and is in the Words following:

To the most Honourable the Lord High Treasurer of Great Britain.

My Lord,

My Correspondents at Lisbon having shipped on board her Majesty’s Men of War, bound for Barcelona, 6,000 Moidores of Gold; viz.

3.000 on Board the Banelagh, Captain Falkner,

1.000 D° per the Hampton Court, Captain

1.000 D* per the Dartmouth, Captain Charles Stewart,

1.000 D* per the Elizabeth, Captain Under down.

6.000 Moidores, making 38,400'Crowns; which I humbly propose to make over for her Majesty’s Account and Risque, clear of all Charges, at 55!^. per Crown; which will amount to £.8,880 Sterling.

Signed, H. F.

10 November 1710.

Sir Henry Furnefe called in His Proposal for furnish* ing£.100,000at Lifben, is read, in these Words:

To the Right Honourable the Lords Commissioners of her Majesty’s Treasury.

My Lords,

This being the Time of the Year wherein Provision is made for the Supply of her Majesty’s Forces in Spain, by way of Portugal; and the present Situation of Affairs not allowing of Remittances to be made from hence as usual; 1 humbly propose to your Lordships, for the Accommodation of the public Service, to furnish Mr. Morris at Lisbon with the Value of £.100,000. in Gold, upon

his Bills at 30 Days Date; the Price of Exchange to be adjusted between Mr. Morris and my Correspondents; the great Disproportion of the Exchange between Lisbon and London, at this time, making it impracticable to fix a Price. If this Gold is not made use of for the Service of Spain, it may be imported into England; which will be a great Benefit to the Nation, and Support of the public Credit.

Signed,

London, 15th November 1710. Henry Furnefe.

My Lords approve these Proportions, with these Explanations, that this Money shall be furnished to Mr.

Morricewithin Six Weeks, or sooner, after the Advice

arrives: The Bills are to be satisfied by Land Tax Tallies of 17x1, in a Course not exceeding £.1,410,000; but no Interest is to be demanded on the Bills, if they should be due before the Course on the Tax arises to that Height; and if the Bills do not arrive time enough, so as to be satisfied in the said Course, then the Tallies are to be struck without Interest, and to be indorsed ut Jupra.

A PETITION of the Aldermen, Justices, Common Rerifferm;

Chuncil, and other Burgesses, Manufacturers, and of Wool. Inhabitants, of the Borough of Grantham, in the County of Lincoln, who are greatly mterelted and concerned in the several Articles of Wool, Hides, Leather, (Ac. as therein

6 A after-

458 8* Ma. . 1742*

after-mentioned, on behalf of themselves, and many others, was presented to the House, and read; repre-fenting to the House, That, at the-lame time that the Petitioners are burthened with a heavy Land Tax, and many other Taxes, they lie under very great and particular Dif-couragements besides, from the low Price of Wool, and the precarious State of feeding Stock now for many Years past, occasioned chiefly, as the Petitioners apprehend, by an Act of Charles the Second, prohibiting the Importation of Irish Cattle; which, as Sir Temple then

foretold it would, has, as the Petitioners conceive, since been the Cause of turning a considerable Part of the Trade of 7 'relandinto a wrong Channel, to the further Detriment of England in its Produce and Trade, not only in the Articles of Hides, Leather, Tallow, Butter, but the total Loss of our Beef-trade abroad, and (which is still worse) by occasioning a vast Increase of the Breed of Sheep in that Kingdom, has greatly contributed to the Increase of that pernicious P raft ice of running Wool from thence to France and other foreign Parts, to the inexpressible Damage of the Petitioners, and the whole Kingdom: And therefore praying, by way of Remedy and Prevention, a Bill to permit the Importation of Irish Cattle, upon Conditions of Advantage and Security to the Woollen Trade of Great Britain, or such other Relief as to the House shall seem meet: And further representing to the House, That it is at present doubtful (considering the present State of our Trade, Agriculture, and other Manufactures) what further Measures would prove most salutary to our Woollen Trade, by reason of the Uncertainty of the Proportion of the Quantity of our own Wool to the Number of our Hands, proper for manufacturing the fame, together with Irish, and

Woolalfo; and that if the former should exceed the latter to any great Degree (the illicit Exportation of Wool bfing stopt, as in all reason it ouajit to be) the Grower, already depressed for many Years, would, in that case, be hurt beyond all Conception: And therefore further praying, as one sure Point to proceed upon, and to the end this great Affair may the sooner receive due Regulation, a Bill for registering, from the Grower and the Feltmonger, the whole Crop of Wool in Great Britain, or in England and W only, for One Year, or such other Relief, as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Mr. Secretary at War, according to Order, reported from the Committee of the whole House, to whom the

Bill for the more effectually preventing the Importation Foreign and Wear of Gold or Silver Thread, Lace, Fringe, or Gold or other Work, made of Gold or Silver Wire, manufactured in foreign Parts, was committed, the Amendments, *c' which the Committee had made to the Bill; and which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered the Bill, with the Amendments, in at the Clerk’s Table:

Where the Amendments were once read throughout; and then a Second time, one by one; and, upon the Question severally put thereupon, with Amendments to some of them, were agreed to by the House.

A Clause was offered to be added to the Bill; which was read with Blanks; and is as followeth;

Provided also, and be it further Enacted, That it shall and may be lawful for any Person, being a Subject of Great Britain, at his Arrival from foreign Parts, to import, for his own proper Use and Wear only, complete Suits, and no more, of Apparel, confiding of, or wrought or made up with, Gold or Silver Wire, Plate, Thread, Fringe, Buttons, Tissue, Embroidery, Brocade, or other Work or Ornaments, of Gold or Silver, wrought, fabricated, or manufactured in foreign Parts; which said Suits

shall be entered at the Custom-house of the Port where they shall be imported; and, upon such Entry, the Person so importing the same shall make Oath before the Collator, Customer, Comptroller, or other chief Officer, of the Customs of such Port, that the said Suits are for his own proper Use and Wear only, and for no other Person whatsoever:

And if any Person, summonedas the Wearer of such Apparel, by Justices of the Peace, according to the Directions of this Act, shall make Oath before such Justices, that the Appirel, for

which he is so charged as the Wearer, was imported by himself at his Arrival from foreign Parts, and was Part of Suits only by him then imported, and

entered upon Oath, as aforesaid, every such Person shall, from thenceforth, be from all further

Prosecution, and from all the of this Act, in

respect of the said Offence; any thing in this Act to the contrary notwithstanding.

The said Clause being read a Second time;

An Amendment was proposed to be made thereto, by inserting after the Word " his," and before the Word " Arrival," the Words " or her:"

And the Question being put, That those Words be there inserted;

The House divided.

The Yeas went forth.

Reasons to be offered at a Conference with the Lords, upon the Subject-matter of the Amendments, made by their Lordships to the Bill, intituled, An Act to amend the Laws relating to Rogues, Vagabonds,

and other idle and disorderly Perfofts; and to Houses of Correction.

The Commons agree to all the Amendments, made "’by your Lordships to the Bill, intituled, An Act to amend and nuke more effectual the Laws relating to Rogues, Vagabonds, and other idle and disorderly Persons; and to Houses of Correction; except to the Amendment in Prds 12, Line the last, and the Amendment in Press 19, Line 2C.

To'the Amendment in Press 12. Line the last, of the said Bill, the Commons disagree,

Vol. 24.

> — 150 Aprilis. 477

Because the Allowance for passing and conveying Rogues, Vagabonds, and incorrigible Rogues, is, by the said Amendment, limited to be according to the Rates and Allowances appointed at the General or Quarter Sessions of the Peace, as is by the Bill after directed: For, though the Clause to which this Amendment refers, directs the Justices of the Peace, at their General or Quarter Sessions, to appoint such Rates and Allowances, and requires all Justices of the Peace to observe and fub-mit to such Rates and Allowances so appointed; yet, since the Bill, as to the Pafling and Conveying of Rogues, Vagabonds, and incorrigible Rogues, will commence before such Rates and Allowances can possibly be appointed at the General or Quarter Sessions, the Commons conceive, that, in the mean time, the Allowance for passing and conveying mud of Necessity be ascertained by the Discretion of the justice or Justices of the Peace, who shall make the Pass; and that, consequently, before such Rates and Allowances shall be appointed at the General or Quarter Sessions of the Peace, the Limitation, proposed by your Lordships in this Amendment, will be improper,-and, after such Appointment, unnecessary.

The Commons also disagree to the Amendment, made by your Lordships in Press 19. Line 20. of the said Bill (which Amendment directs the Treasury of the County to pay to the Governor of the House of Correction the Rates ascertained in the Certificate by him delivered, and directs such Payment to be allowed in the said Treasurer’s Account);

Because such Payment and Allowance are sufficiently provided for by the Bill; and the Commons observe, that the unnecessary Specification of particular Rules doth, in some Cafes, Weaken the Force of general Directions.

The Commons decline, at this time, offering any other Reasons for disagreeing to the said Amendments, made by your Lordships; apprehending that the Reasons already given will induce your Lordships not to infill upon the said Amendments, that so necessary a Bill may not be loft.

The said Report being read a Second time;

An Amendment was proposed to be made thereto, by leaving out the Words " that so necessary a Bill may " not be loft

And the same was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

Then the said Report, so amended, was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

The Zeal, Prudence, and Dispatch, with which you have carried on the public Business, during the Course of this Session, give me the greatest Satisfaction.

That this Nation, and the common Cause may reap the most beneficial Fruits of your vigorous Resolutions, I have, at the Requisition of the Queen ordered

my Army, in conjunction with the Troops, to

pass the Rhine, as Auxiliaries to her Hungarian Majesty; and for her Support and Assistance; and to oppose any dangerous Measures that might assess the Balance and Liberties of Europe, or hinder the lle-estab'ishment of the public Tranquillity upon just and solid Foundations, I have continued a strong Squadron in the Mediterranean, and another in the West Indies, in order to carry on the great Work ofdiftreffingourEnemics the Spaniards, and reducing them to safe and honourable Terms of Peace, as well as of maintaining the Rights of Navigation and , . Commerce belonging to my Subjects; and, from the former of thele Squadrons, my Allies in have found, and still continue to receive, a most useful and advantageous Supporc.

Gentlemen of the House of Commons,

I return you my Thanks for the ample Supplies which you have granted for the Service of the current Year; and which, you may be allured, shall be applied to those great Ends for which they were given.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

I have a firm Confidence in your good Affcftions; and it is the fixed Purpose of my Heart to promote the true interest and Happiness of my Kingdoms: In Return for this, I expect, on your Part, that you will exert your best Endeavours, in your respective Stations, 10 render my Government eaiy, and to preserv the Peace and Quiet of the Nation.

And afterwards, the Lord Chancellor, by his Majesty’s Command, faic|.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

It is his Majesty’s Royal Will and Pleasure, that this PsrNrfnt Parliament be prorogued to Tuesdaythe Seventh Day of P‘cro.-ud-June next, to be then here held: And this Parliament is accordingly prorogued to Tuesday the Seventh Day of June next.

That the House had attended Speech re- his Majesty in the House of Peers: Where his Majesty ported* Was pleased to make a most gracious Speech from the Tljrone, to both Houses of Parliament^ of which Mr. 'Speaker laid, he had, to prevent Mistakes, obtained a Copy: Which he read to the House j and is as followeth; viz.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

SINCE your last Meeting, I have, pursuant to your Advice, and in consequence of your Support, exerted my Endeavours for the Preservation of the House of Au-Jlria, and the Maintenance of the Balance and Liberties of Europe. It has pleased God to give Success to our Arms, in Conjunction with those of the Queen of Hungary, and as her Auxiliaries. The Dominions of that Princess have been intirely evacuated by her Enemies; and the powerful Armies, which had marched to their Af-‘fiftance, have been obliged to retire out of the Empire. In this Conjuncture, it is a great Satisfaction to me to acquaint you, that I have been joined by a Body of Troops of my good Friends and Allies the States General.

In further Prosecution of these Measures, the Definitive Treaty between me, the Queen of Hungary, and the King of Sardinia, has been happily concluded; which shall be laid before you. The Advantages which cannot fail to result from this Alliance to the common Cause are apparent; and it will be particularly conducive to the Interests of my Kingdoms, by difuppointing the ambitious Views of the Crown of Spain, with which we are engaged in (0 just and necessary a War. As I make no doubt but you will proceed upon these Foundations with Firmness and Constancy, we may reasonably hope to see the public Tranquillity re-established, and a general and honourable 23

Peace obtained. These are my View?, to which my utmost Attention and Resolution shall not be wanting: But, in order to bring about thele great Ends, Measures of Vigour are necessary; and, to enable me to concert anfd carry on such Measures, I do, with a just Confidence, rely on your zealous, chearful, and effectual Support.

The Marriage 01 my youngest Daughter with the Prince Royal of Denmark, cannot but give Satisfaction to all my good Subjects, as it tends to cement and strengthen the Pnotcftao): Interest in Europe.

Resolved, That no Peer of this Realm hath any Right to give his Vote in the Elettion of any Member to serve in Parliament.

Resolved, That where the House shall judge any Petition touching F.le&ions, to be frivolous and vexatious, the House will order Satisfaction to be made to the Person petitioned against.

Resolved, That if it shall appear, that any Person hath procured himself to be elected or returned a Member of this House, or endeavoured lo to be, by Bribery, or any other corrupt Practices, this House will proceed with the utmost Severity against such Person.

Resolved, That if it shall appear, that any Person hath been tampering with any Witness, in respect. of his Evidence to be given to this House, or any Committee thereof; or, directly or indire6Uy, hath endeavoured to deter or hinder any Person from appearing, or giving Evidence; the same is declared to be a high Crime and Misdemeanor; and this House will proceed with the ut-raoft Severity against such Offender.

Resolved, That if it shall appear, that any Person hath given false Evidence in any same before this Housei or any Committee thereof, this House will proceed with the utmost Severity against such Offender.

Resolved, That it is an high Infringement of the Liberties and Privileges of the Commons of Great Britain, for any Lord of Parliament, or any Lord Lieutenant of any County, to concern themselves in the Elections of Members to serve for the Commons in Parliament.

Ordered, That the Constables, and other Officers of Middlesex and Westminster, do take care, that, from Eleven of the Clock in the Morning, to One in the Afternoon, and from Four till Six in the Afternoon, during the Session of Parliament, the Passages through the Streets between 'Temple-bar and Westminster-hall shall be kept free and open; and that no Obstructions be made by CaH, Drays, Carts, or otherwise, to hinder the Patfage of the Members to and from this House: And that the Serjeant at Arms attending this House do give Notice of this Order to the Officers aforesaid.

Ordered, That the Constables in Waiting do take care that there be no Gaming, or other Disorders, in ffeft-minster-hally or the Passages leading to the House, during the Sitting of Parliament; and that there be no Annoyance by Chairmen, Footmen, or otherwise, therein, or thereabouts.

Ordered, That the said Orders be sent to the High Bailiff of Westminster; and that he do fee the same put in Execution.

Ordered, That no Footman be permitted to be within the Lobby of the House, or upon the Stairs leading thereto.

Ordered, That the Serjeant at Arms attending this House do take care, that there be no Gaming, or other Disorders, in the Room appointed for the Footmen attending the Members of this House, to wait in.

Ordered, That the Serjeant at Arms attending this House do take into his Custody such Footmen as shall presume to disobey the Orders of the House; and that no such Footmen be discharged out of Custody, but by the Special Order of the House.

Ordered, That, to prevent the Intercepting or Losing of Letters directed to Members of this House, the Person appointed to bring Letters from the General Post-Office to this House, or some other Person to be appointed by the Postmaster General, do, for the future, every Day, during the Session of Parliament, Sundays excepted, constantly attend, from Ten of the Clock in the Morning, till One in the Afternoon* and for Two Hours at the lead immediately after the Rising of the House; and also on every Monday, fVedne/day, and Friday, from Five of the Clock in the Afternoon till Seven, at the Place appointed for the Delivery of the said Letters; and take care, during his Stay there, to deliver the same to the several Members, to whom they shall be directed, or to theii known Servant or Servants, or others bringing Notes under the Hands of the Members fending for the fame.

Ordered, That the said Officer do, upon his going away, lock up such Letters as shall remain undelivered; and that no Letter be delivered but within the Hours aforesaid.

Ordered, That the said Orders be sent to the Postmaftet General.

Ordered, That the Serjeant at Arms attending this House do, from time to time, take into his Custody any Stranger or Strangers, that he shall see, or be informed of to be, in the House or Gallery, while the House, or any Committee of the whole House, is fitting; and that no Person, so taken into Custody, be discharged out of Custody, without the Special Order of the House.

Ordered, That the Back-door of the Speaker’s Chamber be locked up every Morning, at the Sitting of the House, and the Key delivered to the Clerk, to be locked up by him: And that he do not presume to deliver the same to any Person whatsoever, without Order of the House: And that the Serjeant at Arms attending this House do take care to clear the Speaker’s Chamber every Day, before the Door is locked up.

Ordered, That no Member of this House do presume to bring any Stranger or Strangers into the House, or Gallery thereof, while the House is fitting.

Ordered, That when any Letter, or Packet, directed to this House, shall come to Mr. Speaker, he do open the fame, and acquaint the House, at their next Sitting, with the Contents thereof, if proper to be communicated to this House.

Ordered, That the Serjeant at Arms attending this House do, from time to time, when the House is going to Prayers, give Notice thereof to all Committees; and that all Proceedings of Committees in a Morning, after such Notice, be declared to be null and void.

Ordered, That the Votes of this House be printed, being first perused by Mr. Speaker; and that he do appoint the Printing thereof: And that no Person but such as he shall appoint do presume to print the fame.

Resolved, That this House will receive no Petition for Private Bills, private Bills after the First Day of February next.

Most Gracious Sovereign,

We, your Majesty’s most dutiful and loyal Subject?, the Commons of Great Britain, in Parliament assembled, beg Leave to return our humble Thanks for veur Majesty’s most gracious Speech from the Throne.

We beg Leave to congratulate your Majesty on your safe and happy Return into this Kingdom; and, with Hearts full of Gratitude, we acknowledge the Goodness of Divine Providence to this Nation, in protecting your Majesty’s Sacred Person amidst the imminent Dangers to which your invaluable Life has been exposed, in Defence of the common Cause, and of the Liberties of Europe. Your Majesty’s Regard and Attention to the Advice of your Parliament, in exerting your Endeavours for the Preservation of the House of Austria, require our warmed Acknowledgments; and it is with the highest Satisfaction we reflect on the Succels of your Majesty’s Arms, in the Prosecution of this great and necessary Work, with so much Glory to your Majesty, and Honour to this Nation.

As the Interests of this Kingdom and those of the United Provinces are inseparable, nothing could be more welcome to your Majesty’s faithful Commons, than your Majesty’s having been joined by a Body of the Troops of \ the States General.

We beg Leave to declare our Satisfaction in your Mar jesty’s having concluded a Definitive Treaty between your Majesty, the Queen of Hungary., and the King of Sar- diniay an Alliance, which must naturally contribute to the Advantage of the common Cause, and to the disappoint* ing and distressing the Crown of Spain, with which this Nation is engaged in fojuft and necessary a War.

It is with the sincerest Joy that we congratulate your Majesty on the happy Marriage of the Princess Louisa with the Prince Royal of Denmark, which tends to unite and strengthen the Protestant Interest in Europe.

We likewise beg Leave to congratulate your Majesty on the Increase of your Royal Family, by the Birth of a Prince; as it is an additional Pledge and Security for the Continuance of the Protestant Succession in your Royal House.

Your faithful Commons beg Leave to allure your Majesty, that they will, with the greatest Zeal, Unanimity, and Dispatch, grant to your Majesty such effectual Supplies as shall be found requisite for the Honour and Security of this Nation, and as may enable your Majesty to concei t

A Petition of the Trustees, whose Names are thereunto Chatham subscribed, appointed to put in Execution an Act of Par- Hoad, liament, made in the Third Year of the Reign of his present Majesty King George the Second, intituled, An Act for repairing and widening the Road from that Part of Chatham, which lies next to the City of Rochester, to St.

Dunstan s Cross, near the City of Canterbury, in the County of Kent; and for repealing so much of a former Act, as appropriates Part of the Money arising by the Tolls or Duties therein mentioned, towards repairing the Road be^ tween the Town of Chatham and iHoughton under the Bleane, in the said County of Kent', was presented to the House, and read; letting forth, That, by the said Act, several Tolls were granted and made payable for the Term of Twenty-one Years, from the Twenty-fourth Day of June 1730, for repairing the said Roads, containing in Length about Twenty-five Miles; and that the Trustees appointed by the said Act, finding the same Roads in a very ruinous Condition, and the annual Income not being sufficient, they were obliged to borrow a considerable Sum of Money, in order to put and keep the same in Repair; which Money so borrowed, together with the Tolls col-leded by virtue of the said Act, has been duly laid out and applied according to the Directions thereby given; and that the Sum of One thousand Pounds remains still unpaid; and that the Petitioners find the Money now due on the Credit of the said Act cannot be repaid, nor can the Roads, during the Residue of the said Term now subsisting, be effectually amended and kept in Repair for the future, unless the Term and Powers thereby granted be continued and enlarged: And therefore praying, That the House will be pleased to give Leave to bring in a Bill for continuing and enlarging the Term and Powers by the said former Act granted, for such Time, and in such Manner, as to the House shall seem meet.

Vol. 24.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, the Act of Parliament afcrcfeUfwas hiid before the Committee, and read; whereby it appeared, that several Tolls were granted and made payable? for 21 Years, for repairing the said Roads, which are about 23 Miles in Length.

And it appeared to the Committee, by the Testimqny of several Persons, that, at the Time of passing thaa\$ft, the said Roads, iri many Parts thereof, by reason ftf the Beepness of the Soil, and the heavy Carriages frequently faffing through the fame, were io bad in the Winter Season, that many Parts were impassable for Waggons and^Carriages, and also f6r Horses laden; and other Part* were dangerous for Travellers.

It likewise further appeared to your Committee, that the Trustees for putting the said Act in Execution, finding the said Roads (which lie in the Vale of Evcfham) to be so very ruinous, and the yearly Income arising from the Tolls not sufficient so amend the fame, borrowed a considerable Sum of Money upon the Credit of the said Act.

Then Mr. Bright, Agent for the Mortgagees, laid before the Committee the several Mortgage Deeds of the Toll; whereby it appeared, that the Trustees had borrowed, on the Credit of the Ad, several Sums of Money, amounting in the Whole to the Sum off. 1,950.

And Mr. Bright gave Evidence, That in the Year 1738, One of the Mortgagees exhibited his Bill in the Court of Chancery against the Trustees, in order to fore-close the Equity c>f Redemption of the Tolls' so mortgaged to him; and, on the 10th Day of July 174b he, in pursuance of an Order of that Court, took Possession of One of the Turnpikes; and, after discharging all Expences, between that Time and the 3d of November last, the net Money received by such Mortgagee amounted to £.188. 17s. id.; which being deducted from f. 1,950, first borrowed, there remains the Sum of f. 1,761. 2J. 10d. H ill due and owing on the Credit of the said Act.

Then there was produced, and laid before the Committee, an Account of all the Money coileded at the several Toll-gates erected on the Roads; by which it appeared, that about f. 400 per Annum had been collected.

That, after deduding the yearly Expences of the Gates, and paying the necessary Officers employed from the before-mentioned Sum, the Income arising by the Tolls will not, during the remaining Part of the Term, be sufficient to discharge the said Debt of f. 1,761. is. 10d. and the Interest thereof; so the Roads (which were proved to be very bad) will loon become again ruinous and impassable, unless some further Provision be made by Parliament for raising Money for amending and keeping them in Repair.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for continuing the Term and Powers granted by an Ad, passed in the First Year of the Reign of his present Majesty, intituled, An Act for repairing and amending several Roads leading to and from the Borough of Evesham, in the County of Worcester, and for making the same more effectual: And that the Lord Deerhurst and Sir John Rufhout do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

Ordered, Nemine contradicente. That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for the more speedy and.effectual Manning of his Majesty’s Fleet: And that Vice Admiral Vernon, Sir John Philipps, and Mr. Sydenham, do prepare, and bring in, the fame.
