The said Copy is bound up with the other Papers of this Session; and the Translation thereof is as fol* loweth; viz.

after which, the rest of Italy would no longer be able to resist them, and all the Coasts of the Mediterranean Sea would be under Subjection to one and the same Family.

To obviate as much as in them lies such imminent Evils, and an Enterprize whole Consequences would be so fatal to all the Princes and States of Italy, to their Liberty and Commerce, and to that of the Maritime Powere in the Mediterranean Sza, the most Serene and most Potent Prince, George the Second, King of Great Britain, Elector of Brunswick Lunenburg, &c. the most Serene and most Potent Princess Maria Therejia Queen of Hungary and Bohemia, Archduchess of Austria, &c. and the most Serene and most Potent Prince Charles Emanuel King of Sardinia, Duke of Savoy, &c. having such an essential Interest in the Preservation of a just Balance in Europe, on which depends the Liberty of Europe, and in the Maintenance of the Liberty and Security of Italy in particular; on which depends that of its Commerce, and of the Commerce of the Mediterranean; have resolved to enter into a closer and more inseparable Union, in this fixed Intention, and to perfeyere inviolably in joining their Forces and Councils, in order to obtaining the Effect defued therefrom 5 and more especially for the fake of repelling with one Accord the unjust Invasion made by the Kings of Spain and Naples, and for securing Italy, if possible, for the future, from all Attempts of the same Kind.

In this View, and in order to prevent the said Invasion without Lo£> of Time, his Majesty the King of Sardinia did enter, from the ill Day c f February 1742, into a provisional Convention with her Majesty the Queen of Hungary; the Tenor whereof is as follows:

As it is sufficiently evident, that the Motions of the Spanish Troops, which, having landed in the States of the Prajidii, are advancing in the Dominions of the Pope, in order to join those of Naples, and from thence to pursue their March as far as Imola, are bent, according to certain Intelligence, towards Lombardy, and must necessarily very much affect his Majesty the King of Sardinia, as well as her Majesty the Queen of Hungary and Bohemia; their Majesties have thought, by the Means of the Marquis d'Ormea, and of the Count de Schulenbourg (they being respectively provided with the necessary full Powers) of concerting and agreeing upon the following Articles, under the Hopes of their being ratified and accepted.

Translation of his Majesty’s Ratification of the Treaty concluded at Worms the ^th September 1743.

GEORGE the Second, by the Grace of God, King of Great Britain, France and Ireland, Defender of the Faith, Duke of Brunswick and Lunenburg, Arch-Treasurer and Prince Elector of the Holy Roman Empire, To all and singular to whom these Presents shall come, Greeting. Whereas the Ministers Plenipotentiary, as well on our Part as on the Part of our good Brother the King of Sardinia, &c. and of our good Sifter the Queen of Hungary and Bohemia, &c. being assembled at Worms, and sufficiently authorized thereto, did conclude and sign a certain Treaty of mutual Friendship and perpetual Alliance, on the Day of the present Month of September, in the Form and Words following:

In the Name of the most Holy Trinity;

Be it known to all and every one, to whom it appertains, or may appertain, in any Manner whatsoever.

Forasmuch as the Disturbances which, upon the Decease of the Emperor Charles the Sixth, of glorious Memory, without Male issue, arose in Germany, notwithstanding the express Tenor of the mostfolemn and recent Treadies of Peace and Alliance, corroborated by the authentic Guaranty of the Body of the Empire, which do allure to his eldest Daughter, and to her Posterity, the intire and indivisible Succession to his hereditary Dominions, do manifestly tend to the Overthrow of all Balance in Europe, and do expose its Liberty, and that of its Commerce, to the most evident Danger; which Danger is still increased by the Conquest which the Kings of Spain and Naples have openly undertaken to make of the Dominions possessed by the most Serene House of Austria in Italy, contrary to the Faith of their own Engagements;

*3

Article ift.

The Forces of her Majesty the Queen of Hungary alone, which are now in Italy, appearing sufficient to make head against the Aggressors, they shall be brought together, in order to march towards them, and to give an immediate Check to their Progress; and particularly, in order to cover the States of Modena and Mirandola, which are, as it were, a Bulwark to the Dominions of the Queen of Hungary in Italy.

Article 2d.

The said King of Sardinia shall, in the mean while, have a considerable Body of his Troops upon the Frontiers of his Dominions, towards the Borders of the Milaneje, and of the Duchy of Placentia; which shall be disposed in such a manner as that they may be brought together in a short time; and, in case the Forces of the Aggfessors should come to be augmented, and that there should be Cause to fear anew Invasion on any other Side, as is probable, according to the Advices that have been received, that a Second Convoy of Spanish Troops has already set Sail at Barcelona; and that they are to land in the Harbour of La Spezia, his Majesty shall then co-operate with ail his Forces, for preventing the Body of Austrian Troops, which shall have marched forward, from being either taken in Flank, or intercepted, by that new Reinforcement of Spanish Troops; and, to this End, all the Passages in the States above-mentioned, and principally the Places of Parma, Placentia, and Pavia, shall remain free and open to the King’s Troops, for their Convenience and Security.

Article 3d.

As to what relates to further Motions, and such other military Operations as might be afterwards undertaken, as

they

X

i*7 Geo. II. 90 Ja\

they must depend upon the Circutnstances which fall out from Day to Day, it is necessary to refer them to the Concert which shall be entered into, in proportion to the Circumstances which shall happen; and, for this Purpose, his Majesty the King of Sardinia shall fend One of his General Officers to the Army of her Majesty the Queen of Hungary, ancf her Majesty the Queen of Hungary shall lend One of hers likewise to reside with his Majesty the King of Sardinia; to which General Officers shall be reciprocally communicated all the Advices that shall be received about the Enemy; and all the Resolutions which shall be taken on either Side shall be concerted with them.

Article 4th.

Nothing being so necessary towards obtaining the End desired on each Side, as the reciprocal Security of the respective Possessions and Rights, and a Confidence in the good Faith of the Parties who are to co-operate towards the same End, his Majesty the King of Sardinia promises, upon the Faith and Word of a Prince, to her Majesty the Queen of Hungary, ift, That, for as long time as the present provisional Agreement shall last, he will not avail himself of his pretended Rights to the State of Milan, which are not entered into in this provisional Convention; forasmuch as the Queen of Hungary cannot admit them, and the King of Sardinia, on the contrary, thinks them founded; and, 2dly, That, if it should be necessary that his said Majesty should enter with his Forces into any one of the States above-mentioned, he will not exercise in the same any Act of Sovereignty, and will not in any-wile hinder the Queen of Hungary from continuing to exercise them in the manner that That Princeis has done it hitherto; neither will his Majesty exact any Contribution, and will content himself, in the said Gale, with being fiir-niffied with such Things as are indispensably requisite to an Army: As for Instance, Forage, Wood, Quarters, Carts, Beds, Caferns, and Straw; the Rations whereof shall be regulated upon the Foot on which they are usually allowed to his Troops; as also, Horses, Mules, and Oxen, for the Use of the Artillery; and Victuals.

Article 5.

On the other hand, her Majesty the Queen of Hungary declares in the like solemn Manner, that it is not her Meaning, that the abovelaid Promises of his Majesty the King of Sardinia, nor the Execution of them, should Prejudice the Rights by him pretended to the State of Milan, nor ever to avail herself of them, so as to infer from thence, that the said Rights were no longer subsisting; the Intention of the Two high contrafting Parties being to preserve to each of them their respective Rights in their full Force, in such manner as they may appertain to them, independently of the present Convention.

Article 6.

And it is likewise in this View, that his Majesty the King of Sardinia reserves to himself expressly the intire Liberty of availing himself of his said Rights at whatever Time, and by whatever Means, either by himself singly, or by such Alliance as he shall judge to be most for his Convenience.

Article 7.

But as his Majesty does not mean to acquire any Advantage by the said Reservation, and defigqs to proceed with all the good Faith which is natural to him, he promises and engages, in the same above-mentioned, not to ad himself, nor to permit any Prince with whom he might be allied, to ad (which his Majesty will take care to fti-pulate as a principal Condition in any Treaty whatsoever which he might conclude), sooner than after the Space of One Month from the Time that he shall have caused Notice to be given by the Means of the General Officer which he shall have at the Queen of Hungary's Army; to the end that the Commanding Officer of the Austrian Troops, being thus put upon his Guard, may take such Measures and Resolutions as he shall judge most for his Advantage.

Article 8.

Moreover, the King of Sardinia promises, in that Cafe, to make his Troops evacuate all the Dominions of the . Vql. 24.

mm. 499

Queen of Hungary, and all the Places and Pods which Treaty he should have taken Possession of during the present provisional Agreement, without carrying any thing off; to iLmpe*' the end that the Troops of the abovesaid Queen* may, during the said Month, retake freely, and without any Hindrance, the Pods which they shall think proper.

Article 9.

The present Convention shall be ratified by the King of Sardinia and by the Queen of Hungary, and the Acts of Ratification shall be exchanged within the Term of Twenty Days.

Article 10.

During the said Term, the King of Sardinia shall not understand himself to be obliged to cause his Troops to enter into the States possessed by the Queen of Hungary; and if, after the Expiration of the said Term, the Queen should not have sent her Ratification, so that, for want of it, the present Convention should remain without Effect; nevertheless, the King shall not, in that Cafe, cause his Troops to enter into the above-mentioned States during the Term of other Ten Days; neither, during that Term, shall he give any Hindrance to the irse Return of the Austrian Troops into the feme States, and inj^uch Pods, as the Queen of Hungary's Ger^r^ffjudge to be most convenient.

In Witness whereof, we the under-written Plenipotentiaries have signed the present Convention, (Ac. at Turin, the id February 1742.

In consequence of this Convention, his Majesty the King of Sardinia did immediately join a considerable Body of his Troops to those of the said Queen; his Majesty the King of Great Britain having sent a strong Squadron, to co-operate for the Maintenance of the Liberties of Italy,

In order not to leave fruitless so great Expences, and to secure still farther, and to accelerate for the present, the intire Execution of so necessary and just a Kef Jution, and in order likewise to perpetuate the Effect of it for the Times to come, their said Majesties have authorized, and do authorize, their Ministers Plenipotentiary to make an immediate Regulation of the Particulars, and of the Conditions; viz. His Majesty the King of Great Britain, his Privy Councellor John Lord Carteret, Baron of Hawnes,

One of his Principal Secretaries of State, &c. his Majesty the King of Sardinia, the Chevalier OJforio, Chevalier Grande Croix, and Grand Conservator of the Religious and Military Orders of the Saints Maurice and Lazarus,

Envoy Extraordinary and Minister Plenipotentiary of his said Majesty to his Majesty the King of Great Britain; and her Majesty the Queen of Hungary and Bohemia, the Sieur Ignatius John de IFafner, her Minister Plenipotentiary to his said Britannic Majesty; who, after having communicated to each other their respective full Powers, and having maturely conferred together, have agreed upon the following Articles:

Article 1.

There shall be from the present Time, and for all Times to come, between his Majesty the King of Great Britain, her Majesty the Queen of Hungary and Bohemia, and his Majesty the King of Sardinia, a close Friendship, and sincere, perpetual, and inviolable Alliance; by virtue of which, they shall be obliged to support, defend, and succour each other reciprocally, and constantly to be attentive to the Security each of the other, as to their own, to procure all Advantages, and to keep off all Damage and Prejudice from one another, to the utmost of their Power.

Article 2.

To this end, the Allies engage themselves afresh to a most express Guaranty of all the Kingdoms, States, Countries and Dominions, which they are now in P ffeftion of, or ought to possess, by virtue of the Treaty of Alliance, made at Turin in *703, of the Treaties of Peace of Utrecht and Baden, of the Treaty of Peace and Alliance commonly called the Quadruple Alliance, of the Treaty of Pacification and Alliance concluded a: Vienna, the 16 March 173.1, of the Act of Guaranty given in

consequence

500

9° Januarii. A. 1743.

Treaty with the Eaiprefi, Arc

consequence thereof, and passed into a Law of the Empire, the nth of January 1732, of the Act of Accef- fion signed likewise in consequence of the said Treaty at the Hague, the 20th of February 1732, of the Treaty of Peace signed at Vienna, the 18th of November 17 28, and of the Accession thereto, done and signed at Versailles, the 3d of February 1739; all which Treaties are fully recalled and confirmed here; forasmuch as they may concern the Allies, and as far as they have not derogated from them by the present Treaty.

Article 3.

In conformity to the Guaranty contained in the foregoing Article, and to the end that no Subject of Dispute may remain between the Two most Serene Houses of A/</?ria and Savoy, his Majesty the King of Sardinia, forhimself, his Heirs, and Successors, renouncesby Name, and forever, but solely in favour of her Majesty the Queen of Hungary and Bohemia, and of her Heirs and Successors, to his pretended Rights upon the State of Milan; which Rights, though never admitted on the Part of the Queen, he had reserved to himself, by the provisional Convention, the Liberty of availing himself of; and besides, his Majesty the King of Sardinia engages himself formally and specially to the Guaranty of the Order of Succession established in the said most Serene House by the Pragmatic Sanction, in the same manner as it is set forth in the Treaty of Pacification and Alliance, made at Vienna the 16th of March 1731; excepting, however, that his said Majesty shall never be obliged to fend Succours out of Italy.

Article 4.

For this Purpose, his Majesty the King of Sardinia, who has already joined his Troops to those of the Queen of Hungary, and who has already considerably augmented them, shall continue to concert and execute, jointly with her and her Generals, all the Measures and Operations which shall be judged the most effectual for keeping off and repelling the Invasion now made, or to be hereafter made, against the Dominions of the said Queen, and for securing them from all Danger, present and future, as much as possible.

Article 5.

In order to attain this End, and as long as the present War shall last, her Majesty the Queen of Hungary engages not only to keep in Italy the Number of Troops which she has there now, but to augment them to the Number of 30,000 effective Men, as soon as the Situation of Affairs in Germany will permit it; and his Majesty the King of Sardinia engages to keep and employ the Number of 40,000 Foot, and 5,000 Horse; comprehending in it what will be necessary for the Garrisons, and Defence of his own Dominions.

Article 6.

His Majesty the King of Sardinia shall have the supreme Command of the Allied Army, when he shall be there in Person; and he shall regulate the military Motions and Operations of it in concert with her Majesty the Queen of Hungary, according as the common Interest and Occasions shall require.

Article 7.

As long as it shall be necessary towards favouring and fcconding those Operations, and as long as the Danger of the Allies and of Italy shall demand it, his Majesty the King of Great Britain engages to keep in the Mediterranean Sea a strong Squadron of Ships of War, and Bomb Vessels, and Fire Ships; the Admiral and Commanders whereof shall have Orders to concert constantly and regularly with his Majesty the King of Sardinia, or with his Generals, and with those of he Majesty the Queen of Hungary, who shall be nearest at hand, the most proper Measures for the Service of the common Cause.

Article 8

Moreover, and in order to aftift n* Gearing the extraordinary Expence which his Majesty the King of Sardinia is and will be obliged to support, for raising, and causing to act, a much greater Number of Troops than his own Revenues can maintain, his Majesty the King of Great Britain engages to furnish to him, for as long as the War, and 23

the Occasion for it, shall continue, a Subsidy of Two hundred thousand Pounds Sterling per Annum, to be paid every Three Months, and to commence from the iflof February 1742, New Stile, being the Day upon which the provisional Convention was signed between the said King and her Majesty the Queen of Hungary; and the said Subsidy shall be punctually paid, from Three Months to Three Months, in Advance; provided, however, that what shall have been advanced to his Majesty the King of Sardinia, before the Signature of the present Treaty, shall be reckoned into it.

Article 9.

In consideration of the Zeal and Generosity with which his Sardinian Majesty has been willing to expose his Person and his Dominions for the public Cause, and for that of her Majesty the Queen of Hungary and Bohemia, and of the most Serene House of Austria in particular, and of the effectual Succours which the said Cause has already received from him; in consideration also of the burthensome Engagements of Assistance, and of the perpetual Tye of Guaranty, which he contracts with her by the present Alliance, her said Majesty the Queen of Hungary and Bohemia, for herself, her Heirs, and Successors, yields and transfers, from this present time, and for ever, to his said Majesty the King of Sardinia, his Heirs and Succefe fors, to be united to his other Dominions, the Distri&of Vigevano, called the Vigevanafco, the Part of the Duchy of Pavia which is between the Po and the Thejin; fothat the Thefin shall for the future, by the Middle of its Stream, from the Separation and Limit between the respective Dominions from the Lago Maggiore, or greater Lake, to the Place where it falls into the Po; excepting only the Island formed by the Canal over-against the City of Pavia; which Island shall be reserved to her Majesty the Queen, upon these Conditions, that the King shall have, nevertheless, the free Communication of the River 'Thejin, for the Passage of Barks, without their being either stopt, visited, or subjected to the Payment of any Duty; and that the said Canal shall never be filled up, and shall serve in this Place for a Limit. Moreover, that other Part of the Duchy of Pavia, called the Paveje, beyond the Po, Bobbie, and its Territory, being reckoned into it, the City of Plaisance, with that Part of the Duchy of Placentia which is between the Pavefan and as far as the Bed of the River Nura, from its Source quite to the Po, in such manner that the Middle as well of the Nura as of the Po do. make, in this Part, the Limit of the Two States; and, consequently, that which has hitherto belonged to the Duchy of Placentia, on the other Side of the Po, do remain separated from it.

Lastly, That Part of the County of Anghiera, or of the State of Milan, whatsoever particular Name may be given to it, which borders upon the Novarefe, the Valley of Sejia, the Great Alps, and the Country of Vallais, extending to the Swiss Prefectures of Val Maggia and Locarno, and along the Banks of and in the Lago Maggiore to the Middle of the said Lake, in such manner that, for the future the Confines between the Dominions of his Majesty the King of Sardinia and those of her Majesty the Queen of Hungary, shall be continually fixed by a Line drawn from the Borders of the Swiss, in the Middle and all along the Lago Maggiore, to the Mouth of the Thejin; which Line shall go from thence along the Middle of the Stream of that River to the Place of its falling into the Po, excepting the Front of the above-mentioned Island before Pavia; and from thence goon along the Middle of the Course of the Po to the Place where the Nura falls into the Po, and go up by the Middle of the Bed of the Nura, quite to its Source, which is opposite to the Country of Genoa.

The abovesaid Division of the Course of the Rivers shall not prevent the Navigation remaining free, as it is to remain to the Subjects of the Two Sovereigns in the whole Breadth of the said Rivers, with Liberty to pass upon the Banks on cither Side, for the Towing of Boats which go up Stream; the said Banks being nevertheless to appertain, as well with regard to the Property, as in

To enjoy the same in full Property and Sovereignty, a9 her Majesty the Queen and her Predecessors have enjoyed them hitherto. Which Countries her Majesty the Queen difmembers forever from her Hereditary Dominions, and from the State of Milan; derogating for that Purpose* as far as there can be Occasion for it, from every thing that might in any manner be contrary thereto; laving always the direct Jurisdiction of the Empire.

Article io.

Besides, as it is of Importance to the public Cause, that his Majesty the King of Sardinia should have an immediate Communication of his Dominions with the Sea, and with the Maritime Powers, her Majesty the Queen of Hungary and Bohemia yields to him all the Rights which Ihe may have in any Manner, and upon any Title whatsoever, to the Town and Marquisate of Final; which Rights (he yields and transfers, without any Restriction, to the said King, in the same manner as (lie does the Countries described in the foregoing Article* in the just Expectation that the Republic of Genoa will facilitate, as far as shall be necessary, a Disposition so indispen&bly re-quisite for the Liberty and Security of Italy, in consideration of the Sum which shall be found to be due to the said Republic, without his Majesty the King of Sardinia, nor her Majesty the Queen of Hungary, being obliged to contribute to the Payment of the said Sum: Provided always, that the Town of Final be, and remain for ever, a free Port, as is Leghorn; and that it shall be allowable for his Majesty the King of Sardinia to re-establish there the Forts which have been demoliftied, or to cause others to be built* according as he (had judge convenient.

Article n.

His Majesty the King of Great Britain, her Majesty the Queen of Hungary and Bohemia, and his Majesty the King of Sardinia, engage themselves not to make either Peace or Truce, without comprchending therein, in express Words, all the above-mentioned Cfcflions, and without stipulating also full Restitution to the King oi Sardinia, of every Part of his other Dv)minions, which may have been seized or occupied in Hatred of his Union with the Allies; provided, that the King of Sardinia shall hold himself to be, from tins present lime, indemnified for the Revenue which might be so with-held from him, by that of the Countries,) ielded aful transferred to him by the present Treaty.

Article 12.

In Return, his Majesty the King of Sardinia shall remain firmly and inseparably united and attached so the Interests and to the Cause of the Allies, not only for as long as the War may Jail in Italy, but to the Conclusion of the Peace in Germany, and of the Peace between Great Britain and Spain; and this is the principal Condition, and Sine qua non, of the Cessions made to him above by the 9th and 10th Articles of this Treaty; which Cessions shall not receive their full and irrevocable Force, but from its intire Accomplishment; after which, the Countries yielded to the said King shall be deemed guarantied to him by the Aliies for ever, as his other Dominions are.

Article ij.

And as soon as Italy shall be delivered from Enemies, and out of all apparent Danger of being afrelh invaded,-her Majesty the Queen of Hungary shall not only be at

Liberty to withdraw Part of het* Troops, but, if (he fc- Treaty v.*!rh quires ir, his Majesty the King of Sardinia shall furnish the E^press, her some of his own Troops, to be employed for the Security of her Majesty’s Dominions in Lombardy; that so (he may be able to make use of a greater Number of her own in Germany, in like manners as, at the Requisition of the King of Sardinia, the Queen of Hungary should cause some of her Troops to pass into the Dominions of the faici King, if it were necessary, for defending the Pat sages thereof, which an Enemy’s Army should undertake to force; and for delivering from Enemies all the Do* minions of his Majesty the King of Sardinia, and freeing them from any Danger of a freth Invasion.

Article 14.

In any Cafe, the Allies shall not make either Peace or Truce, or Accommodation whatsoever, with the common Enemy, but in concert, and with the Participation and Advice, one of the other; nor without the Guaranty of such Powers as should have aShare in the Pacification, for the Possessions and Acquisitions of the Allies, as let forth in this Treaty; and, after the Conclusion of the Peace, the present Alliance'shall equally and unalterably subsist, as well for the Security of its Execution, as, in general, for the mutual and constant Security of the Allies.

Article 15.

His Majesty the King of Sardinia, and her Majesty the Queen of Hungary and Bohemia, in Gratitude for the generous Concern of his Britannic Majesty for the public Security, and for theirs, and for that of Italy in particular, do not only confirm to the British Subjects the Advantages of Commerce and Navigation which they enjoy in their respective Dominions, but promise to fecufe them still further to them, and, as far as it shall be found reasonable and practicable, by a specific Treaty of Commerce and Navigation, whenever his Britannic Majesty shall require it of them.

Article 16.

The Lords the States General of the United Provinces, being already under the same Engagements towards the -moil Serene House of Austria, and having the same Id- -

terest with his Britannic Majesty in all the Objects of the present Treaty, the Allies will jointly invite them to enter into this Alliance, as a principal contracting Party.

Article 17.

The other Princes and States who have at Heart the Peace, the Liberty, and the Security, of Europe, of the Empire, and of Italy, and who will be willing t6 enter into the present Alliance, shall be admitted info it.

Article itt.

This Treaty of Alliance shall be ratified by all the Allies; and the Ratifications of it shall be exchanged with^-in the Space of Six Week?, orfooner, if possible.

New Malton A Petition of the Borough Bailiff and Inhabitants of Butter Mar- the Borough of New Malton, in the North Riding of the ket, &c. County of York, and of several other Persons, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, living in or near to the said Borough, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth. That Butter is One of the chief Commodities of the ProduCl of several Parts of the County of York, near to the said Borough; and great Quantities thereof are brought into the said Borough of New Malton; through which runs a navigable River, whereby the said Butter, and other Commodities, are from thence sent to the City of London> and otherwise disposed of; and that

there hath. Time out of mind, been within the said Borough a free Market for Butter; but there is not, as in some other adjacent Markets for Butter, any particular Place for keeping such Market; nor are the Farmers of Dairies, and Owners of Butter brought to the said Market, obliged to have their Butter searched, weighed, or sealed there; by reason whereof, several Trader* in the said Commodity have been greatly deceived in the Weight, Goodness, and Soundness, of the said Commodity; and such Butter, so bought at the said Borough, for want of a proper Weigher, is reduced in its Credit, and made to bear a less Price than at other Markets where a proper Place and Person are appointed for felling, searching, weighing, and lealing, the fame; and representing to the House, That if a particular Place was to be appointed within the said Borough for keeping the said Market, and all the Butter brought in Firkins, Half Firkins, Tubs, or other Vessels, to such Market, was to be weighed, (earched, and sealed, it would effectually prevent the Frauds and Abuses in the salt’e Weighing and Packing of Butter brought to such Market; but that the same cannot be done without the Aid of an Act of Parliament: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for appointing a particular Place within the said Borough for keeping the said Market, and for viewing, searching, weighing, and sealing, all the Butter brought in Firkins, Half Firkins, Tubs, or other Vessels, to the said Market; and that such other Provision may be made for preventing the Frauds and Abuses by the Faultinest, false Weight, and Packing, of the Butter brought to the said Market, as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideratioa of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the fame, with their Opinion thereupon, to the House:

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Sum of Six hundred Thirty-four thousand Three hundred and Forty-four Pounds Eleven Shillings and Four Pence be granted to his Majesty, for defraying the Charge of Twenty-one thousand Three hundred and Fifty- eight effective Men (Commission and Non-commission Officers included), to be employed in Flanders, for the Year 1744.

Colonel Mofiyn reported from the Committee, to whom New Milton the Petition of the Borough Bailiff and Inhabitants of the But, Cf Borough of New Mallon, in the North Riding of the County of York, and of several other Persons, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, living in or near to the said Borough, was referred, That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, together with the Resolutions of the Committee thereupon, to the House 5 and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, the Agent for the Petitioners called the following Witnesses; viz.

Mr. Thomas Belch; who, being examined, said. That Butter is One of the chief Commodities of the Product of several Parts of the County of York, particularly near to the Borough of Neiv Malton; and great Quantities thereof are brought to the said Borough; through which runs a navigable River, whereby Butter and other Commodities are conveyed from thence to the City of London and other Parts: That there hath been, Time out of mind, within that Borough a free'Market for Butter, but no particular Place appointed for keeping such Market; nor are the Farmers of Dairies, and Owners of Butter, obliged to have their Butter searched, weighed, or sealed there; which is a great Diladvantage to those who make it, and a Discouragement to the Dealers therein, who have been frequently deceived in the Weight and Goodness of such Butter; whereby the Credit thereof hath been reduced, and the Value lessened.

Mr. Abraham Dehorn, being examined, confirmed that Part of the Evidence given by Mr. Belch, of the Dealers having been frequently deceived in the Weight and Good- , ness of Butter.

And both the Witnesses further said, that if a particular Place was appointed within the said Borough for keeping such a Market, and the Butter brought in Firkins, Half Firkins, Tubs, or other Vessels, was to be weighed, searched, and sealed, it would effectually prevent the Frauds and Abuses in thefalfe Weighing and Packing of Butter brought to that Market, and be a general Good to the Town and Country.

Upon the whole Matter, the Committee came to the following Resolutions; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the Petitioners have fully proved the Allegations of their Petition.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the House be moved, that Leave be given to bring in a Bill to prevent the committing of Abuses in Weighing and Packing of Butter in the Town and Borough of New Malt on, in the County of York.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill to prevent the committing of Abuses in the Weighing and Packing of Butter in the Town and Borough of New Mal~ ton, in the County of York: And that Colonel Mostyn,

Mr. Cholmley Turner, Major General IVentworth, and Mr.

Henry Finch, do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

Were severally presented to the House, and read; representing to the House, That the Office of Coroner is one of the most antient Offices belonging to the Crown, and was formerly executed by Persons of high Rank, and considerable Estates; and that no Fee or Reward was ever allowed for the Execution of such Office, save in Cafes of Murder, where they are intitled to Thirteen Shillings and Four Pence of the Goods of the Murderer; and that, of late Years, only Persons of small Fortunes or Estates have been chose into the said Office; several of whom are often obliged to travel Fifty or Sixty Miles from their own Habitations, at great Expences, and spend several Days in taking Inquisitions, examining Witnesses, &c. to the great Neglect of their private Affairs, and Detriment of their Families; and that they the said Coroners are oftentimes prosecuted, and run to great Expences, at Sessions and Assizes, for accepting of any Pay, or voluntary Gift, from any of his Majesty’s Subjects, for their Trouble, and Expences in their Journies, to take inquisitions; and that the said Coroners, finding themselves unable to attend the Duty of their Office for nothing, and to avoid such Trouble and Prosecutions, and that the Deaths of his Majesty’s Subjects may be inquired into, and Murder may not be concealed, and that his Majesty, and Lords of Liberties and Franchises, tnay not be defrauded of their Deodands, fsV. have found it necessary to apply to this House for Relief: And therefore praying, That the Limits, Power, and Nature of the Office of Coroner, may be ascertained, with such Fees annexed, as to the House shall seem right.

The Lord Advocate of Scotland reported from the Scotch Committee, to whom the Petition of Robert Wallace and George Wijhart, Commissioners for and on the behalf of

the Ministers of the Church of Scotland, and of the Universities of St. Andrews, Glasgow and Edinburgh, was referred. That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, several Members of the House informed your Committee, that there was no legal Fund for Maintenance of the Widows and Children of the Ministers of the Church, or Matters in the Universities, in that Part of Great Britain called Scotland *, who are frequently left in indigent Circumstances, without any Provision for their Subsistence or Education, save only small Allowances made by feme Synods and Presbyteries, which are voluntary and uncertain, and amount in the Whole to a very inconsiderable Sum.

Then the Reverend Mr. Wallace, Moderator of the Commission of the late General Assembly of the Church of Scotland, produced to the Committee an Extra# of an A# of the said General Assembly, extracted from their Records, and signed by William , Clerk to the said Assembly; which Act bears Date the 23d Day of 1743: Upon the Reading of which, it appeared to your Committee, that the said General Assembly, having taken-into their Consideration the deplorable same of the said Widows and Children, and having consulted with all the Ministers of the said Church, did approve of a Scheme or Plan for providing for the said Widows and Children, by an annual Rate payable by the Ministers of the Church out of their Stipends; viz the annual Rate ofjf. 2. tar. 6d.

or of £. 3. i$j. 9</. or of £. 5. 5*. c or of 1 u. lawful Money of Great Britain, in the Option of the said Ministers, to be applied to the Payment of proportionable Life-rent Annuities to their respective Widows* of £. 10, £. 15, £. 20, or £.25; and to the Payment of proportional Provisions to the Children of the said Ministers, of £. 100, £. 150, £. 200, or £. 250, lawful Money of Great Britain.

Note. — No distinct Account can be given of what has been annually paid into the Exchequer upon this Duty; because the Payments into the Exchequer thereon are made promiscuously with what arisesfrom the other Commodities charged by the Malt Act, being applicable to the same Uses; and also, because the Charges of Management of this Branch of the Malt Act are blended with the other Branches thereof.

And we beg Leave further to observe,

That when the 4 s.Duty is charged on the First Buyer, it cannot then be determined whether such Cyder or Perry is for the First Buyer’s own Use only; because the 6 s.id Duty is not chargeable till such Cyder or 1‘erry is sold by Retail; which is frequently Six or Twelve Months after, or more; and therefore it is impracticable to distinguish what is annually paid by the First Buyer for his own Use only.

Excise-Office, London, 24th January 1743.

ing of the County of York; but that the Proprietors and Fanners of the said Navigation have ever since refused to

Then the Agent for the Petitioners called Mr. Robert Barber: Who said. That the Trustees appointed to put the aforesaid Act in Execution were obliged to borrow upwards of 1,000, to put the said Roads in Repair; which Sum was duly laid out in amending thereof; £.200 of which Sum is now owing; and, without a further Continuance of the said Act, the said Sum cannot be paid off, and the Roads kept in Repair; many heavy Carriages passing thereon to the several Towns thereabouts:

That the Road from the lower End of the County of Stafford, through Woore, in the County of Salop, and Nantwich, to the City of Chester, is in a very bad and ruinous Condition, and dangerous to Travellers in the Winter Season; many Hollows being the rein, particularly the Hollow at Woore, where, in a fnotvy Season, Carriages cannot pal's; and, was the said Road repaired, many more Carriages would pass that Way to London from Chester; it being the Post Road, and esteemed the nearest Way, and the other being liable to Floods:

That the Statute-work has been duly laid out on the said Roads; and ’tis apprehended, that if One of the Gates erected by the aforesaid Act was to be removed nearer to the Town of Namptwich, the said Road might be effectually repaired, and the Roads, in the said Act directed to be repaired, kept in Repair.

Mr. Thomas Williams laid. That the Road from the lower End of the County of Stafford to the City of Chester, is in a very ruinous Condition, and frequently, in inowy Sealbns, Woolt Hollow is so deep, that Carriages have been stopt for several Days, notwithstanding the Statute-work has been duly performed on the said Road and a Contribution of several Parishes laid out thereon:

That the said Road is the Post Road, and the nearest Way from Chester to London; and, was it repaired, would be more frequented, the other being liable, from its Situation, to Floods.

Mr. Crowle reported from the Committee; to whom Kingston the Petition of the Mayor arid Burgesses of the Town "P®*1 Hull of Kingston upon Hull, under their Common Seal *, and also 03 the Petition of the Mayor, Aldermen, and Burgesses, of the Town of Beverley, in the East Riding of the County of York, who have thereunto affixed their Common Seal; were referred, That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petitions; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petitions,

Mr. Richard Bell was called, who laid. That he was well acquainted with the Road leading from Kingston upon Hull to Beverley, and that the same lies in a Tow, flat; miry Country, and near to the Wolds, or Range of Hills, running through the East Riding of the County of York; and that from thence great Quantities of Water, in rainy Sealbns, defeend, and frequently overflow great Part of the before-mentioned Road, by reason whereof, and the Deepness of the Soil in most Places, the said Road is become so ruinous, that it is, in the Winter, and frequently in the Summer Season, impaflabie for Wheel-carriages, and dangerous for Travellers on Horleback to pals through the fame.

Mr. Geo. Hopfon confirmed the Evidence before given by Mr. Richard Bell; and said further, That the Inhabitants of the Villages and Hamlets, lying contiguous to the said Road, have been assessed Sixpence in the Pound towards the Repairs thereof, besides performing their Statute-work, which has all been found inefficient to put and keep the said Road in tolerable Repair; and the same Witness added to his Evidence, That the Road cannot be effectually amended, and kept in good Repair, without the Aid of an Act: of Parliament.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for repairing the Road between the Town of Kingston upon Hull, and the Town of Beverley, in the East Riding of the County of York: And that Mr. , Mr. Charlton, Mr. Carter, Mr. Strickland, and Mr. Charles Pelham, do prepare, and bring in, the lame.

A Petition of the Dean and Chapter of the Collegiate Church of St. Peter, Westminster, being offered to be presented to the House;

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer, by his Majesty’s Command, acquainted the House, That his Majesty, having been informed of the Contents of the said Petition, recommends it to their Consideration.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read; fitting forth, That the said Collegiate Church came into the Hands of the First Dean and Chapter unfinished, and by Length of Time, and Badness of Materials, became so decayed and ruinous, that, in the Eighth and Ninth of William the Third (in regard to its being of antient and royal Foundation), an annual Sum, for a certain Term of Years, was granted, by Parliament, towards repairing the fame, under the Direction of the Chancellor of the Exchequer, the Lord Chief Justice of the King's Bench, and the Dean of Westminster, who were appointed Commissioners for that Purpose; and that by an Act, passed in the Ninth of Queen Anne, the Sum of Four thousand Pounds per Annum, for a certain Term of Years, was granted to the said Commissioners towards repairing and tinithing the Collegiate Church of St. Peter, Westminster, and the Chapels of the lame; and in order to the finishing thereof, as directed by Parliament, Sir Christopher Wren, the then Surveyor, formed a Ddign of ereifting a

VOL. 24.

Spire on the middle Tower, a Model of which he therr prepared, and a Draught of which, with the rest of the intended Building, has been laid before this House; and that by several Acts, passed in the Reign of his present Majesty, several Sums of Four thousand Pounds have been issued and applied towards carrying on the said Work, and a considerable Progress has been made therein, and an Account, how the Money has been expended, has been annually laid before this House; and that* to facilitate the said Repairs, Two of the prebend^! Houses, and Three Leasehold Tenements, lately (landing in St. Margaret's Church Yard, have been taken down; and thereby the whole North Side of the Church, from the North to the West Gate, has been laid open; but that the Monies already granted being near expended, the said Works will soon be at a (land; and submitting the same to the Consideration of the House, acknowledging the Favours already conferred on the said Collegiate Church, as well by the present, as by former Parliaments: And praying for the Continuance of them.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom it is referred to consider further of the Supply granted co his Majesty.

The House being informed. That one of the Sheriffs of the City of London attended at the Door, he was called *in; and, at the Bar, presented to the House a Petition of the Lord Mayor, Aldermen, and Commons, of the City of London, in Common Council assembled:

And then he withdrew.

Then the said Petition was read; setting forth, That by an. Act of Parliament, made in the Ninth Year of the Reign of his present Majesty, intituled, An Act for the better Enlightening of the Streets of the City of London, several Provisions are made for the better enlightening the said City, and for collecting the Money necessary for /that Purpose; but that the fame, as the Petitioners conceive, have not fully answered the good Ends and Purposes intended by the said Act: That the Rates by the present Act, being chargeable only on Houses from Ten Pounds to Forty Pounds per Annum, inclusive, hath, by Experience, proved a heavy Burthen on the middling and inferior Inhabitants, which might be remedied, if Power was given to charge Houses of a superior Rent in a proportionable Manner: That the Time of Appealing, ap-.pointed by the said Act, is so short, that in many Instances, it hath, and in future may prove, an absolute Exclusion to Persons appealing, who may think themselves aggrieved by any Rate or AHeffment: That the Time for chusing the Collectors, and Time of their accounting, is incon-fiftent with each other; and that there are many other Inconveniences in the said Act: And therefore praying the House to take the said Act into Consideration; and to explain and amend the same in such manner as to the -House shall seem meet and reasonable.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House.

And it is referred to Mr. Alderman Calvert, Mr. Al-dermatr Heathcote, Mr, Onslow, Mr. Hay, Mr

Road from the Watch-house in Edmonton to the Marketplace in Enfield; was presented to the House, and read; setting forth. That, by the said Act, several Tolls and Powers were granted and continued for the Terms therein mentioned, for repairing the Roads aforesaid (in Length Thirteen Miles, or thereabouts), and for other Purposes therein expressed; and that the Inhabitants of the Parish of Hackney (through which the before-mentioned Road leads) are, by the said Act, passed in the Twelfth Year of the Reign of her said late Majesty, Charged with, and made liable to pay, the Sum of One hundred Pounds yearly, in lieu of such Statute-work as they were obliged to do on the Turnpike Road within the said Parish; which said Sum is directed to be assessed, raised, and paid, in such Manner as in the said Act is prescribed; but that some Doubts having arisen lately touching the affef-sing, railing, and paying, the said yearly Sum of One hundred Pounds, the Petitioners have not received the same for above Three Years past; and that the Petitioners are under some Difficulties how to enforce the Payment of what is now due, and shall grow due from the said Parish for the future; and that great Progress hath been made in repairing the said Road; but that the Petitioners find that all Parts thereof cannot be effectually amended and kept in good Repair, unless the Powers given by the before-mentioned Acts be enlarged: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for explaining, amending, and making more effectual, the before-mentioned Acts, in such manner as to the House shall seem meet.

A Petition of the several Persons, being Fishermen, Whose Names are thereunto subscribed, on behalf of themselves, and a great Number of other Fishermen, using the Craft of Fishing in the River of Thames, and Places adjacent, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth. That the Company of Free Fishermen of the River of Thames were, by his late Majesty King James the Second, by his Royal Charter, made in the Third Year of his Reign (upon the Resignation of a former Charter, made to them by King Charles the First) in-corporated by the Name of the Mailer, Wardens, Assist-ahts, and Commonalty, of the Art and Mystery of Fishermen of the River of Thames, with Powers to make Laws and Ordinances, with Penalties, for the reforming and preventing Abuses and Inconveniencies in the Fishery, for the Preservation of the Spawn and Fry of Fish, for the public Good and Government of the said Company, for the better Discovery of Goods imported or exported, the Customs not being paid, and for other the good Purposes therein mentioned: That, by an Act of Parliament, passed in the Ninth Year of her late Majesty Queen Anne, intituled, An Act for the better Preservation and Improvement of the Fishery within the River of and for regulating and governing the Company of Fishermen of the said River, One Matter, Six Wardens, and Thirty Assistants, were to be chosen yearly by the next Court of the Lx>rd Mayor and Aldermen of the City of London, to be held after the Tenth Day of June, in every Year (out of Nominations to be made for that Purpose by the Court of Assistants of the said Company)} who are thereby constituted the Court of Assistants of the said Company, for the Time being, for regulating and reforming Abuses in the said Fishery, and for the due Ordering and Government of the said Company; witji Powers for their calling before them all common Fishermen, using to fish within the Limits of the said Fishery; for registering such Persons, and their Apprentices, for the Supply of Seamen for the public Service j and for other the Purposes in the said Act mentioned: That the said Company continued, not without several Intervals and Interiniffions, from the time of making the said Act till the Year 1727; since which Year,

no Nomination of a Mailer, Wardens, and Assistants (by the Court of Assistants), of the said Company, and consequently no Choice by the said Court of the Lord Mayor and Aldermen, has been made, pursuant to the said Act; but the said Company has, ever since, been totally discontinued; lo that it doth not now any longer subsist: That the Body of Fishermen are now under no Government or Regulation, the Times and Seasons of Fishing are constantly broken info, new Methods of unlawful Fishing are daily deviled and practised, the Encouragement for the Sale and Destruction of the young Fry is increased, and the present legal Means for apprehending Offenders are, by their Combinations, become greatly deficient; in consequence of all which, the Fry and Spawn of Fish arc dellroyed, the Price of many Sorts of Fish is become excessive, the Fishermen are greatly impoverished, the public Utility, intended to be provided for by the said Charter and Act of Parliament, is intirely frustrated and loll, and Offenders herein escape unpunished, notwithstanding the most vigorous Methods allowed by the Law have been exerted for bringing them to Justice: That the said Company, being so discontinued, cannot now be re-established or subsist, nor the said Abuses be prevented or redressed, without the Aid of Parliament, by reason of many Defects in the said Act, and for want of other sufficient Powers and Provisions: And therefore praying the House, That they will please to give Leave, That a Bill may be brought in for the re-establishing and continuing the said Company, and for the better preventing the Destruction of the Fry and Spawn of Fish, and for apprehending and bringingOffenders to Justice; or that the House will please to make such other Provision in the Premises, as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof j and report the fame, with their Opinion thereupon, to the House.

A Petition of the Rector, Churchwardens,.and Inhabitants, of the Parish of St. John the Evangelist, in minster, being offered to be presented to the House;

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer, by his Majesty’s Command, acquainted the House, That his Majesty, having been informed of the Contents of the said Petition, recommends it to the House, to do therein as they shall think proper:

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read; letting forth, That the Parish Church of St. John the Evan-getift was One of the Fifty new Churches built pursuant to Twofeveral Acts of Parliament, the one made in the Ninth, the other in the Tenth, Year of the lteign of her late Majesty Queen Anne; and was endowed by virtue of an Act of Parliament, passed the First Year of the Reign of his present Majesty; and, in consequence thereof, was consecrated on the 20th Day of June, in the Year 1728; and that the said Church, from the Time of its Consecration, was constantly made use of for Divine Service, until the 26th of September 1742; on which Day a Fire unhappily broke out in the Chimney of the Vestry-room of the said Church, occasioned (as it appeared to several experienced Workmen who were appointed to inquire into the Cause of the said Fire) by the Mismanagement of the Builders in laying the Ends of the Beams into the Funnel of the Chimney, by which means, the whole Roof, the Galleries, Pulpit, Reading-desk, and Altar, were, in a very ftiort Time, entirely consumed, and very little of the Pewing was saved; inso much, that upon a Computation, made bylkilful Surveyors, the Charge of repairing the said Church will amount to near Four thousand Pounds; and that, notwithstanding the Parishes of St. Margaret and St. John the EvangelTft are equally liable to the Repair of the said Church, yet the said Parishes are so burthened with a numerous Poor, and are so frequently obliged to make Re-assessments on account of the Land Tax, that they are in no Condition to pay the Rates, which must necessarily be made, for the Repairs of the said Church; and that, until the said Church shall be repaired, the Parish of St. John alone is obliged to pay One hundred and Twenty-five Pounds a Year for the Maintenance of their Minister, which was in a great m&fure paid by the Monies arising from the Pews of the said Church, before this Accident happened, but is now entirely raised by a Pound-rate on the Inhabitants; and that many of the Inhabitants of the said Parish, who are only Tenants at Will, having already declared their Intention of quitting their Houses upon the Account of the high Rates and Taxes, and for want of a Church, it is to be feared the said District will soon become in a manner uninhabited, unless the said Church be repaired: And therefore praying, That the House will be pleased to give them such Assistance to enable them to repair their said Parish Church, as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom it is referred to consider further of the Supply granted to his Majesty.

A Petition of the Royal African Company of England . being offered to be presented to the House;

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer, by his Majesty’s Command, acquainted the House, That his Majesty, hav-

ing been informed of the Contents of the said Petition, recommends it to the House, to do therein as they shall think fit:

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read; letting forth, That it having appeared to this House, upon full Examination and Consideration of the State of the Trade to Africa, that the British Forts and Settlements, belonging to the Petitioners there, cannot be supported, and the Trade preserved, without the Aid of Parliament, and the House having thereupon been pleased, for several Sessions of Parliament last past, to grant the Sum of Ten thousand Pounds annually towards the Maintenance of the said Forts and Settlements, the said several Sums have been applied accordingly; and ferther setting forth. That the Petitioners have found, by Experience, that the said annual Sum of Ten thousand Pounds has been so far From answering and defraying the necessary Charges and Exigences of the said Forts and Settlements, that the Petitioners have totally exhausted even the trading Stock which they were possessed of when the said annual Allowance was first granted; so that they are now absolutely disabled from maintaining and supporting the said Forts and Settlements any longer with the said annual Allowance of Ten thousand Pounds only; and submitting to the Consideration of the House to make such an additional Allowance as may enable the Petitioners effectually to maintain and support the said Forts and Settlementsin Africa, in such manner as they ought to be, for the Protection and Benefit of all his Majesty’s Subjects trading to the Coast of Africa, or interested in the Preservation of that most essential Branch of our foreign Trade; or to put the said Forts and Settlements under such other Care and Management; and to make the Petitioners such a reasonable and just Satisfaction for their Property and Interest therein, as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine, and state to the House, the Matter of Fast contained in the said Petition:

And it is referred to Sir Nathanael Curzon, General Oglethorpe, Mr. Alderman Heathcote, Mr. Hay, Admiral Vernon, "Lord Baltimore, Mr. Mr. Win-

nington. Lord Perceval, Mr. Secretary at War, Mr. Brooksbank, Mr. Laroche, Lord Dupplin, Mr. Gybbon, Mr Newnham, Mr. Kent, Mr. Scot, Mr. Yorke, Captain Gough, Mr. Sydenham, Mr. Lifter, Mr. Pratt, Mr. Wynn, Mr. Alderman Lambert; and all the Members who serve for the Sea Ports; and all the Merchants of the House: And they are to meet this Afternoon at Five of the Clock, in the Speaker’s Chamber: And have Power to fend for Persons, Papers, and Records: And all who come to the Committee are to have Voices.

And then the House adjourned till Tomorrow Morning, Nine of the Clock.

A Petition of the Gentlemen, Farmers, and other Inhabitants, of the Towns and Parishes of , Kigh-

Bridge to Inghay Bridge-, and that such Navigation, when completed, would be highly advantageous, not only to the Inhabitants of the Towns, Parishes, and Places, aforesaid, but to all the neighbouring Towns and Places, and to the Public in general, from the more easy Conveyance, and cheaper Sale, of Coal, Lime, Wood, and several other Sorts of Goods, Merchandizes, and Commodities; the Prices whereof, by the heavy Charge of Land Carriage, occasioned by the Badness and Unevenness of the Roads, are very much enhanced, to the great Discouragement of Husbandry, and other Employments: And therefore praying the House, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for making navigable the said River Aire, from Cottingley Bridge, to Inghay Bridge, aforesaid, by such Means, and in such Manner, as to the House shall seem meet.

and that many of the Offences are committed at or near the Town of Qravefend, in the County of Kent; but the Justices of Peace of that Corporation have not Power given them to hear and determine the Offences against the Slid Act; low Wines or Spirits, from Drink brewed from malted Com, or Cyder, subject to the Duties and Penalties therein mentioned; notwithstanding an Act of the Fifth Year of the Reign of Qeen Elizabeth, which debarred »ny Person using an Occupation, not having served as an Apprentice thereto for Seven Years; and that, the Trade being opened, many Persons, not bred up in the Business, for Gain, without Regard to Reputation, encouraged excessive Drinking, which occasioned many Vices and Irregularities } to restrain which, the Legislature passed an Act, in the Ninth Year of the Reign of his present Majesty, prohibiting all Persons selling spirituous Liquors in less Quantity than Two Gallons, which was the Ruin of many Persons bred up in the Business, while others, the Intruders, sold by Retail, in open Defiance of the Law; and that, the said Act not having the defned Effect, an Act was passed, in the last Session of Parliament, laying double the Duties before laid on spirituous Liquors, and a Liberty of retailing them was granted to those Persons only, who keep Taverns, Victualling-houses, Inns, Coffee-house, or Alehouses, first taking out a Licence, as the said Act directs; and that, the Trade being thus opened again, many Victuallers and Alehouse-keepers have laid Part of their Houses into Brandy Shops, and others, not contented to enjoy Part of the Pet i t ioners Bufi ness, have erected Stills to become Distillers; by which Means 'the Petitioners apprehend the Trade is put into the Hands of the meaner Sort of People, and excessive Drinking noways restrained; and the Petitioners, many of whom had considerable Sums of Money given with them when put to Apprenticeship, who have laid out their Fortunes in the Business, and whose whole Dependence, for the Support and Maintenance of themselves and Families, is thereon, aredeprived of the Benefit of retailing, in a reputable Manner, their own Goods, and are in Danger of having their Trade taken entirely from them: And therefore praying. That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill to impower Dif-. tillers to fell their own Goods in any Quantity; and to prevent Persons from becoming Distillers for the future, not having served an Apprenticeship thereto; or to grant them such other Relief, as to the House shall feetn meet.

That the remaining Commissioners, named in the said Act for each respective County, omitted, from time to time, to nominate and appoint other Persons to be Commissioners, as Deaths, Avoidances, or other Incapacities, happened amongst them; so that there are no such Commissioners now in being for any of the said Counties: And therefore praying. That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for the Revival of so much of the said Act as concerns the Nomination, and perpetual Succession, of Commissioners for each of the respective Counties of Norfolk, Suffolk, Cambridge, Huntingdon, Northampton, Lincoln, and for the Isle of Ely, by appointing new Commissioners for the said respective Counties and Isle, to be inverted with such Powers, and for such Intents and Purposes, only, as are specified in the same Act.

Kingston A Petition of the Inhabitants of Beverley, and the upon Hull Owners and Occupiers of Lands in the Villages and Ham-iUad. Jets contiguous to the Road leading from Kingston upon Hull to the said Town of in the East Riding of

the County of York, was presented to the House, and read; representing to the House, That whereas the Corporations of the said Towns of Kingston upon H#//and Beverley have severally applied to their respective Representatives in this present Parliament, for the obtaining an Act for repairing and amending the above-mentioned Road; and that whereas the said Road, in the Summer Seasons, is generally very good, and passable for all Chaises, Carts, and Carriages.whatsoever; and never, in Winter Seasons, dangerous orimpaflable for Travellers on Horseback, by reason of a very good Causey running along moll Part of the fame; and that, to render a Communication more advantageous, a navigable River, for Ships of considerable Burthen, runs betwixt the said Towns, at a small Distance from the said Road, which, by proper Sluices and Clows, of late Years made and erected, takes off the Waters defeendingfrom the Wolds, or Range of Hills, running through the said East Riding; and that the said Road is thereby made more dry, firm, and good, than ever before in the Memory of Man: And that also, along the said River, Two Wherry-boats pass, twice every Week, betwixt the said Towns, with Passengers, and all kinds of heavy Goods and Merchandize; and that, notwithstanding the Petitioners have been at a very great Expence in meliorating the Road as aforesaid, they Hill continue yearly to raise the fame, in the lowelt Places in the Carriage-road, with Stones and Gravel; and that the Petitioners, having Occasion several times weekly to frequent the Markets of the said Towns, must be at asur-tnei unnecessary and unreasonable Expence, should a Bill, for the Purposes aforesaid, pass into a Law, without any other visible Advantage than what the Petitioners already enjoy: And therefore refuelling, That any Bill for repairing and amending the said Road, or converting the same rinto a Tunpike, may not pass into a Law.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Bill for repairing the Road between the Town of Kingston upon Hull and the Town of Beverley, in the East Riding of the County of York, be read a Second time.

Mr. Walter reported from the Committee, to whom Cun tot the Petition of several Justices of the Peace, Gentlemen, and other Persons, living in, near, and usually travelling through, the Road leading from the Bound Stone, in the Great Western Road, is the Parish of Cantt, in the County of Dorset, through the Town of Shafton, otherwise Skaf-te/bury, to Bow Bridge, in the Road to Sherborn, in the same County, was referred, That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, the Agent for the Petitioners called Mr. Samuel Foot; who informed your Committee, That he is perfectly well acquainted with the Road mentioned in the Petition, which is the common Pod Road from London to the western Parts of the Kingdom; and is about Ten Miles long: That many Parts thereof are in a very ruinous Condition; and that the Materials, proper for repairing the fame, lying Two Miles distant from several Parts of the said Road, the Expence of the Carriage of such Materials makes it impracticable to amend the said Road by the ordinary Course of Law.

Mr. Henry Glover confirmed the aforesaid Evidence:

And further said. That he had examined the Hates of the several Parishes, who by Law, are appointed to repair the said Roads; and finds, That they have paid the full Rate of Six Pence in the Pound for that Purpose, bc-fides performing their Statute-work.

Sir John Rnjhout reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Trustees, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, appointed to put in Execution an Act of Parliament, palfed in the Fourth Year of the Reign of his present Majesty, for repairing the Road leading from Chappel on the Heath, in the County of Oxon, to the Quarry above Bourton on the Hill, in the County of Gloucester, was referred. That the Committee ha<J examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, an Act, passed in the Fourth Year of the Reign of his present Majesty, for repairing the Road leading from Chappel on the Heath, in the County of Oxon, to the Quarry above Bourton on the Hill, in the County of Gloucester, was read; by which it appeared several Tolls and Duties were granted and made payable for 21 Years:

Then the Agent for the Petitioners called Mr. John George; who said. That he had travelled the said Road Thirty Years; and before the A ft passed for the repairing of it, it was in a very bad and ruinous Condition; and Carriages were obliged to go by Stozv, Two or Three Miles out of the Way: That the Road is now repaired; but, if the Turnpike is not continued, it would be as ruinous as ever, many heavy Carriages frequently passing thereon.

Mr. Thomas Cooke and Mr. Robert Bright severally confirmed the Evidence of Mr. John George.

It also appeared to your Committee, That there is now owing, on the Credit of the said Tolls, about £.800; which Sum cannot be paid off, and the Road kept in Repair/ without a further Continuance of the said Act; and the annual Income being only about £.120, and the annual Expence about £. 80, exclusiveof Materials and Workmen’s Wages, to repair the lame.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for enlarging the Term and Powers granted by an Act, passed in the Fourth Year of the Reign of his present Majesty, for repairing the Road leading from Chappel on the Heath, in the County of Oxon, to the Quarry above Bourton on the Hill, in the County of Gloucester: And that Sir John RuJhout, Mr. Gybbon, the Lord Deerhttrft, Sir Francis Dashwood, Mr. Nor borne Berkley, and Mr. Pytts, do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

Being crois-examined, he said. That the Turf was cut on the East Side of the HiM: That 'Thomas Griffiths and Griffith Evans have Freehold Lands lying to the West and to the North: That he has heard Mr. Pryfe has likewise an Estate there, valued at about Three Pounds per Annum; but on Which Side the Hill it lies, he cannot lay: That the Top of the Hill is called the Common,' and which it is impossible to plow or fow.

Being asked, If Roderick Richards gave him Power to take Possession of any other Land but Waste or Common > he said, He called it a Common; and that when his Father directed him to give Possession, no mention was made of entering upon Mr. Pryfe's Land: but the Direction was, to go into what was called the Common; and the Witness laid, he believed the said Richards went with no other View but to give Possession of the Common.

Being asked the Question, he said, Roderick Richards is, as he believes, about Eighteen or Nineteen Years of Age, not Twenty; and that the Witness does not imagine Richards would have given him Possession as he did, had he been aware that the Ground belonged to Mr. Pryfe.

Being further examined, he said, that the said Roderick Richards, when he went with the Witness, parted from him for a little time; saying, his Father directed him to call upon one of his Tenants to shew the Ground; and then returned, accompanied with others; and that many Persons accompanied them of their own accord.

And being asked the Question, he said, they reputed the Ground to be Common; but that the Witness did not understand it so, because Mr. Pryfe laid Claim to it; and, as he had been informed, Mr. Pryfe and Mr. Griffith claim a Right to turn Sheep upon it; and the Witness has also heard Griffith Evans say, that he had a Right to Part of Daran Hill.

To prove that the Ground, upon which the Entry was fnade, was Part of Mr. Pryfe'% Estate, his Counsel offered to examine the said Griffith Evans; which was objected to by the Counsel who appeared for the Defendant; alleging* that the Dispute being, whether Daran Hill was the Waste of the Lord of the Manor, or whether particular Persons had a Property therein, in Right of their Freeholds, for which they paid Quit Rents to the Lord ? and as the said Evans claimed a Property in Part of the Hill, in Right of his Freehold, he ought not to be allowed to give Evidence, tending to eft%blish another Person’s Claim of the same Nature.

On the contrary, it was inlisted by the Counsel for Mr. Pryfe, that the general Property of the Hill was not in Question, but only the Property of a particular Tenement, which was Part of it; in which Evans was noway9 interested.

And it being determined by the Committee, that Griffith Evans should be examined to this Point, he said, That the Tenement called Penydatren-vach is Part of Mr. Pryfe's Estate; to which appertains some small Matter of an undivided Land belonging to him and Mr, Griffith, exclusive of any other: That the Witness was shewn, by David Hadley, the Two Pits said to be dug by Mr. Roderick Richards and William Paul; one of which is upon the undivided Land, the other near upon the Mear which separates the Bounds of Mr. Griffith's n$J>d Mr. Pryfe's Estates.

:' Being cross-examined, he said, that Penydafren-varh lies near to the Top of the Hill, and is uninclosed: That Mr. pryfe's and Mr. Griffith's Tenants turn their Cattle upon this undivided Land; which Land, he said, he never knew to be ploughed: That, Four Years ago, lie was upon a Jury for dividing certain Lands th^re; who made a Presentment, in which there is a Saving of Right of Common upon the Mountain; But that the Witness never knew this Ground reputed to be Common; nor is there any Common within a Mile of the Place: And he said, that though he has a Right to a Freehold on the North Side of the Hill, he never turned his Cattle upon this Piece of Ground.

Tire Coulife 1 for the Defendant Roderick Richards alleged, that his-Client not having had Time to prepare lor his Defence, he had no Witnesses to examine, and had but a little while before received his lnftrudions.

SI R John Chester reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Trustees, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, appointed to put in Execution an Act of Parliament, passed in the Sixteenth Year of the Reign of his present Majesty, for continuing an Act, made in the Thirteenth Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the First, intituled, An Act for amending and repairing the Roads from Luton, in the County of Bedford, to Westibood Gate, in the said County; and for repairing the Roads from Luton to St. Albans, in the County of Hertford; was referred, That ^he Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the lame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table; Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, the said Act, passed in the 16th Year of his present Majesty, was laid before the Committee, and Part thereof read; whereby it is Enacted, " That no Person shall be capable of " acting as a Trustee for executing the Powers contained " in the former and the last mentioned Act, unless such " Person be possessed of a beneficial Lease or Term, ori-c< ginally created for 99 Years, taxed at £.50 per An-€t num, or more, above the reserved Rent upon such " Lease; or is seised or possessed, for his Life, or some greater Estate, to his own Use, of Lands, Tenements,

" or Hereditaments, which were taxed at £. 50 per Annum, or more, in the Counties of Bedford and Hert-Vol. 24.

Februani. 557

"ford, towards railing the Land Tax for the Year 1742, " ot which shall be so taxed as aforesaid, for any Year or " Years in which such Person shall, as aforesaid, aft as a <c Trustee for putting the said former and the last mentioned Act in Execution, except the Mayor and Three " senior Aldermen of the Town of Bedford, for the Time " being, and the Mayor and Three senior Aldermen of " the Town of St. Albans, in the said County of Hertford, for the time being."

Then Mr. Thomas Cazvne was called: Who said, that the greatest Part? of the Trustees apprehend themselves incapable to act as the Law now Hands, unless they are possessed of such beneficial Lease, or seised or possessed of an Estate taxed at £.50 a Year in both the said Counties of Bedford and Hertford; for which reason, they have refused to act, in order to execute the Powers by the last Act given.

That the Road directed to be repaired by the Act of the 13th Year of his late Majesty, lies only in the County of Bedford, and through Part of the Town of Bedford; but is enlarged by the Act of the 16th Year of his present Majesty, and leads through Part of the County of Hertford; as also through Part of the Liberty and Town of St. Albans, in the said County of Hertford:

But there is no Power given by either of the said Acts, for the Justices of the Peaceof the said County of Hertford, Town of Bedford, or Liberty and Town of St. Albans, to act within the respective County, Towns, or Liberty:

That, the said Mr. Cazvne said, the said Acts are likewise defective in several other Respects j that is to say, there being no Power given to the Justices of the Peace for Hertfordshire, and the Town of St. Albans, to oblige the Parishioners in the several Parishes, through which the Roads in Hertfordshire and the Town of St. Albans do lead, to do their Statute-work in Hertfordshire and the Town of St. Albans; nor are the Surveyors of the Parishes through which the Roads lie in Hertfordshire, and the Town of St. Albans and Bedford, compelled to give in Lists of the Personsobliged to do Statute-work; nor 'are the Surveyors impowered to dig Gravel, remove Annoyances, or make causeways or Bridges; nor are the Owners or Occupiers of Watercourses or Ditches compellable to cleanse the fame, in the said County of Hertford, and the said Towns of Bedford and St. Albans; nor are Persons going to, or returning from, Elections for Knights of the Shire for the said County of Hertford, exempted from paying Toll:

That the Justices of the Peace for the County of Hertford are not impowered to appoint Persons to view the Roads which lie in Hertfordshire and the Town of St. Albans; and the Trustees appointed to put the Acts in Execution have no Power to cleft new ones in Hertford-shire, in the room of those who shall die, remove, or refuse to act; the said former Act confining the ! ruftees to elect new ones living in the County of Bedford only; nor are the said Trustees restrained from accepting Offices and Places of Profit relating to the said Toll, in the said County of Hertford, or Towns of St. Albans and Bedford:

That there is no Provision in the said last mentioned Act to restrain Persons from permitting Persons passing through private Grounds, in order to avoid the Payment of the Tolls in the County of Hertford.

The same Witness also informed The Committee, that the Tolls granted by the late Act are insufficient to answer the Expence of amending the Road, and other Purposes for which the same were granted; there being only one Toll paid between St. Albans and Bedford, which is Thirty Miles in Length.
