A Petition of the Justices of the Peace, Gentlemen, Freeholders, and principal Inhabitants, of the Town of Par/Jiore, in the County of Worcester, and of Wick near Parjhore, and several other Villages lying near the said Town, and other Persons travelling on the Road between the Town of Parjhore and Borough of Evesham, in the said County, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That an Act of Parliament was made in the Year 1728, intituled, An Act for repairing and amending several Roads leading to and from the Borough of Evesham, in the County of Worcester; by which, a Road leading from the said Borough to the First Chain of Wick causey, next the Foot of Goodley Hilly next the Bridge at Parjhore, in the said County, being about Four hundred Yards short of the said Town, is directed to be repaired; and that, in pursuance of such Act, a Turnpike was erected at or near the Foot of the said Goodley HUT, and that the Road leading from the said Turnpike to a Place called the Mill 'Tail, at or near the lower End of the said Town of Parjhore, which lieth next the said Turnpike, by reason of the Deepness of the Soil, and the many heavy Carriages passing and repassing to and from the said Town, is become very ruinous, and, in the Winter Season, very dangerous, and almost impassable; and cannot be repaired by the Statute-work now appointed by Law; and that the Inhabitants of the Parish of St. Andrew, in the said Town of Parjhore, in which the said Road doth in Part lie (who are but Part of the Inhabitants of the said Town), have not only done their full Statute-work on the said Road, but have also this Year expended near Thirty Pounds, towards repairing the fame; but, by reason of the heavy Taxes, and the great Burthen they lie under in maintaining a very numerous Poor, are not able wholly to repair the said Road, without the Aid of Parliament -, and that the said Road, when effectually repaired, will be so raised as to lave the Expence, and prevent the great Danger, of ferrying over in Flood-times; and representing to the House, That as the Turnpike is now erected near the Foot of the said Goodley Hill, a considerable Distance from the said Town, and their being Two Common Meadows belonging to the Township of Wick, which adjoin to, and lie on, each Side the Road between the said Turnpike and the said Town of Parjhore (which Meadows are common at lead One Half-part of the Year); through which, in open Tide-time, many Perron'S travelling to and from the many Towns and Vib

lages between Evesham and Parjhore, qin and do pals, and thereby evade the said Turnpike, without Payment of any Toll thereat, to the great Lessening of the said Toll; which cannot be remedied by the present Act; the removing the said Turnpike to or near the Place called the Mill Tail, at the lower End of the said Town of Par-Shore, would prevent the above and many other Inconveniencies the present Act now lieth under: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration; and that in the Bill now brought into the House, for enlarging the Term and Powers of the said former Act, such proper Clauses may be inserted for repairing and amending the said Road, from the said Turnpike at the Foot of the said Goodley Hill, to the said Mill Tail at the lower End of the said Town of Parjrfore (exclusive of the Bridge over the River Avon there), and for removing the said Turnpike to or near the Place aforesaid, as the House shall think most meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof: and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

And it is referred to Lord Deerhurji, Sir John Rushout, Mr. Watson, Sir James Grant, Mr. Sydenham, Sir Nathanael Curzon, Mr. West, Lord Barrimore, Lord Middlesex, Mr. Pitt, Lord Guernsey, Sir Roger New digate. Lord Dupplin, Mr. Douglass, Lord Barrington, Sir Wm. Courtenay, Mr. Yorke, Mr. Cor new all, Mr. Hob/yn, Mr. Neal, Mr. Strickland, Mr. Popham, Mr. Abercrombie, Mr. Gray, Sir Philip Musgrave, Sir Robert Grosvenor, Mr. Mount agu, Mr. Cartwright, Mr. Liddell, Mr. Sel-wyn\ and all the Members who serve for the Counties of Worcester, Gloucester, Hereford, Salop, and Ox on: And they are to meet this Afternoon at Five of the Clock, in the Speaker’s Chamber: And have Power to fend for Persons, Papers, and Records.

Sir Hugh Smithson reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Trustees, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, appointed to pur in Execution an Act of Parliament, passed in the Twelfth Year of the Reign of her late Majesty Queen Anne, for repairing the Highways from Shoreditch to the furthermost Part of the Northern Road in the Parish of Enfield, in the County of Middlesex; and Two other Acts, one of the First Year of his late Majesty, and the other of the Second Year of his present Majesty, for continuing and making the first-mentioned Act more effectual, and for amending the Road from the Watch-house in Edmonton to the Marketplace in Enfield; was referred. That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, the said Act of the 12th Year of Queen Anne was produced, and read; by which it appeared, several Tolls were granted for repairing the Road from Shoreditch to Enfield, which were to commence from the 24th of June 1713, and to continue for Thirteen Years; and all Persons by Law chargeable towards repairing the said Road, were by the said Act still chargeable, and were directed to do their respect ive Statute-work in the fame, as they used to do, or ought to have done, except the Inhabitants of the Parish of Hackney, who were discharged therefrom, and, in lieu thereof, were to pay yearly One hundred Pounds; which Sum was vested in the Trustees for putting the said Act in Execution, and was to be assessed, by Agreement of the Parishioners of Hackney, within themselves, or, in default thereof, by the Churchwardens and petty Constables of the same Parish, or the major Parc of them; or, in default of their Agreement, by the Order of such Justice or Justices of the Peace as should dwell in the said Parish, or, if none be there dwelling, in the Parts next adjoining; and the said Sum, so to be assessed and paid, was to be collected by the Churchwardens and petty Constables, z or

Shoreditth

Roads.

or some of them, and to be paid by them to the Collectors or Receivers of the said Tolls, for the Purposes aforesaid, from time to time, as the same should be collected; and the Churchwardens and petty Constables were impowered to levy any Portion of Money, so assessed, by Distress and Sale of the Goods and Chattels of any Person refuting or neglecting to pay the same; rendering to the Party the Overplus raised upon such Sale; and any Churchwarden or petty Constable, or his Executors or Administrators, failing to make Payment thereof in manner directed by the Act, was to forfeit the Sum of Fifty Pounds, to be levied by Warrant of Two or more Justices of the Peace residing in the said Parish, or any Two or more Justices residing in the Parts next adjoining.

By another Act , made in the First Year of his late Majesty’s Reign, and produced to the Committee, the before-mentioned Act was continued for the further Term of Eleven Years: and several additional Powers and Provisions were made and granted.

Both which Acts were further continued by an Act, made in the Second Year of his present Majesty’s Reign, for the further Term of One-and-twenty Years; and several other Powers were granted; and there was like-wife Provision made therein for amending the Road from the Watch-house in Edmonton, to the Market-place in Enfield.

Then Mr. Samuel Sadler, Vestry Clerk of the Parish of Hackney, and Clerk to the Justices of Peace within that Division, said, That he is present at the making of all Assessments in the said Parish: That, in the Year 1740, the Inhabitants of the said Parish agreed to raise £. 100 in lieu of their Statute-work for that Year; and that £.50, in Part thereof, was accordingly collected, and paid to the Treasurer of the Turnpike: That the Method fixed upon for making this Rate, was to charge every Inhabitant of that Parish to the Amount of One Fourth-part of what he paid to the Poor’s Rate; but as several Perl’ons, by such Proportion, were liable to pay a greater Sum than what their Proportion of the Statute-work would have amounted to, several refuted to pay this Rate; and, upon a Debate had thereupon at the Parish Meeting, it was the Opinion of those then present, that the Act gave no Power to distrain:

That, in the Year 1741, there was another Parish Meeting, in order to raise the £. 100 due for that Year; but it being doubtful whether any Person was liable to pay more than what his Proportion of Statute-work amounted to, or whether the Proportions of the Poor’s Rate was to be the Rule for the Collection, they came to no Resolution; and the Churchwardens did nothing thereupon:

That the Justices, upon the Application of the T ruftees, made an Order for the Payment of the £. 100 for the said Year 1741; but, as to the Arrear of /.50, it was not in their Power to do any thing in that Matter; and, upon Application to the Court of King’s Bench, the Court issued a Mandamus, requiring the said Justices to make a Rate for raising the said £. 100, and also the said £. 50 in Arrear; but the Justices made a Return, that they had no Power to raise the said £. 50;.and the Court allowed the Return to be sufficient:

That, for the Year 1742, a Rate was made upon the Inhabitants in proportion to One-third of what each Person was to pay in lieu of their Statute-work; and £. 100 was raised upon that Rate:

That, at a late Meeting of the said Parish, it was the Opinion of those present, that the bsft Method to raise the Arrears was by a Pound Rate:

That a Rate has been made for the Year 1743, which would have been collected, had there not been a Difficulty which of the Two Methods was to be followed, that of the Poor’s Rate, or in proportion to One-third of the Statute-work.

Alexander Spur liner and Joseph Bar severally said, They had been employed by the Trustees to collect the said Rates (the First Witness for the Year 1741 and 1742); and the Answer given on behalf of the Parish was, that

Vol, 24.

they did not refuse to pay, but could not ascertain the Method of collecting the m.

With regard to the Condition of the said Road, the said Spurling laid, that the said Road, notwithstanding the Expence bestowed thereupon, is in a ruinous Condition; which is, in a great measure, owing to the Scarcity of good Materials to be had fit for such Repairs.

William Evans spoke to the same Effect, with regard to the Condition of the Road; and said, that within Jess Compass then Four Miles, there had been laid upon it 3,630 Load of Gravel.

John Smart produced the Books of the Receipt and Disbursements of the Tolls collected on the said Roads; whereby it appeared, that, in 1742, there was a Debt of £. 2,080. 19 s. 3d. due; and that the Expence annually amounted to more than the Income of the Tolls.

And the said Spurling being again examined, laid. That, without an Increase of some of the Tolls, and a further Continuance of the Term, and some additional Powers, the said Road cannot be amended, or the Debt paid off.

Mr. Robert Henjhaw being examined, said, That the Rates that are now made are not sufficient to answer the good Ends and Purposes intended; for only Houses from Ten to Forty Pounds per Annum, are chargeable towards the Payment thereof; which, by Experience, hath proved a heavy Burthen on the middling and inferior Inhabitants; whereby the Collectors frequently crave an Allowance for Deficiencies on their Collections.

Mr. Alderman Ladbroke being examined, said, That the Collectors in the Ward where he presides, have frequently come to him for Certificates to be signed for Deficiencies on the Rates in such Ward; the People not being able to pay: That he has signed such Certificates; which are allowed by the Chamberlain to the Collectors in their Accounts, as Cash paid.

Mr. Child being examined, said. That he lives in the Ward of Farringdon Without, and greater Deficiencies happen in that Ward, which is the largest Ward in the City: That there are great Numbers of Persons who pay low Rents; therefore greater Deficiencies happen: That the Collectors are charged with the whole Rate; but are obliged to pray for an Allowance for the Deficiencies occasioned by the Poverty of many Persons assessed: That there are so many poor Inhabitants in that Ward not able to pay the Rate, that, if they were not supported by others, the Ward must, in a great measure, remain unlighted.

Mr. Henjhaw further said, That the Time of Appealing, appointed by the said Act, is so short (only Twenty Days being allowed after the Rate is made), that, in many Instances, it hath, and in future may prove, an absolute Exclusion to Persons appealing, who may think themselves aggrieved by any such Rate or Assessment.

And he further said, That the Time of chusing the Collectors is on the 21st of December, who continue till that time Twelve Months, and the Rates are made from Christmas to Christmas; so that the Collectors are, by that Act, to account for the last Quarter, which is not due till Four Days after they are out of their Office; and that there are many other Inconveniencies in the said Act.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill to explain and amend an Act, passed in the Ninth Year of the Reign of his present Majesty, intituled, An Act for the better Enlightening of the Streets of the City of London: And that Mr. Alderman Calvert, Mr. Onslow, Sir John Barnard, Mr. Alderman Iieathcote, and Mr. Alderman Lambert, do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

Mr. John Platt, being examined, laid. That the Body of Fishermen have not, since the Year 1727, been under any Government or Regulation; by reason whereof the Times and Seasons of Fishing are constantly broken into, and new Methods of unlawful Fishing are daily practised, whereby the Fry and Spawn of Fish are destroyed.

Roger Griffiths Esquire, being examined, confirmed the Evidence given by Mr. Platt.

And Mr. Platt further said, That he has seen several Bushels of young Fry landed, and the Scales taken off, and the Fry buried in the Ground; and that it is the common Practice to fell the Scales to Bead-makers By reason of such Abuses, the Price of many Sorts of Fish is greatly increased, and the Fishermen impoverished.

Ananias Hungerford, being examined, confirmed the Evidence of the said Mr. Platt.

Upon the whole Matter, the Committee came to the following Resolutions;

; Spawn of Fish.

j awful Fishing being devised and practised.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, the Act of Parliament before mentioned was laid before the Committee; and Part thereof read; Whereby it appeared.

That several Tolls and Duties were granted and made payable, for the Term of Twenty-one Years, for repairing and amending the said Roads.

TWfen the following Witnesses were called; viz.

Mr. John Heath and Mr. Francis Hiccombottom; who, being severally examined, ft.id. That, at the Time of passing the said Act, the Commissioners appointed to put the same in Execution, finding many Parts of those Roads (which are about Forty-one computed Miles) in a ruinous Condition, borrowed, of several Persons, the Sum of

£.$,ioo on the Credit of the Tolls, in order to put the said Roads into Repair.

Then they produced to the Committee an Account of the annual Income received at the several Toll-gates erected on the said Roads, and of the annual Out-goings; which was read: Whereby it appeared. That the annual Income of the Tolls amounts to .£.521. 14/. and the annual Expence of the several Gates and Interest amount to £. 450. 1o s.;so that there only remains the Sum of 71. 4J. to be applied towards the Repair of the said Roads.

And they severally said. That the Tolls collected, together with the Money so borrowed, had been duly laid out in repairing the said Roads, and paying Interest on the said Debt: That about Twenty Milts of the Roads have been repaired; but the several Tolls granted by that Act being fixed at low Rates, considering the Extent of the Roads, and the annual Produce but small: That the same will not be near sufficient to pay off the said Debt, with Interest, and the remaining Part of the Roads be repaired, and the whole kept in Repair, for the future, unless the Tolls be increased, and the fir id Act further continued.

GEORGE R.

His Majesty having received undoubted Intelligence,

That the eldest Son of the Pretender to his Crown is arrived in France; and that Preparations are making the re to invade this Kingdom, in concert with disaffected Persons here; and that such Invasion is to be supported by the Squadron of French Men of War, which has been entiling several Days in the British Channel; his Majesty has judged it proper to acquaint the House of Commons with an Intelligence of such high Importance to his Crown, and to the Peace and Security of these Kingdoms; and his Majesty doubts not, from the experienced Zeal,

Duty, and Affection, of his faithful Commons, that they will strengthen his Hands, and concur in all such Measures as shall be necessary, for disappointing and defeating lb dangerous an Attempt; and for the Security of his Person and Government; and the Religion, Laws, and Liberties, of these Kingdoms.

Then the Address, lent from the Lords, was read; and is as followeth; viz.

JMbfi:Gracious Sovereign,

We, your Majesty’s most dutiful and loyal Subjects, the Lords Spiritual and Temporal,

in Parliament assembled, return your Majesty our humble Thanks for having been graciously pleased to acquaint us, that you have received undoubted Intelligence of the Pretender's el deft Son being arrived in , and of

the Preparations which are making the re to invade this Kingdom, in concert with difafle<51ed Persons here.

As this Mark of your Majesty’s just Confidence in us demands our most grateful Acknowledgments, lb we cannot but look upon such a Design with the utmost Indignation and Abhorrence.

Loyalty, Duty, and Afledtion, to your Majesty, Concern for ourselves and our Posterity, every Intceft, and every Motive, that can warm or engage the Hearts of Britons and Protestants, call upon us, on this important Occasion, to exert our utmost Endeavour?, that, by the Ble/Iing of God, your Enemies may be put to Confusion; and we do, with the greatest Sincerity and Firmnels, give your Majesty the strongest Assurances, that we will, with the warmest Zeal and Unanimitytake the most effectual

Measures to enable your Majesty to friistrate and defeat so desperate and infoJent an Attempt, and to secure and

preserve your Royal Person and Government, and the Religion, Laws, and Liberties, of these Kingdoms.

And we beg Leave to declare to your Majesty, and to the whole World, that it is the fixed Resolution and Purpose of our Hearts, at the Hazard of our Lives and Fortunes, to support and defend your Majesty, and your undoubted Right and Title to the Crown of these Realms, and the Protestant Succession in your Royal House, in Opposition to, and Defiance of, the Pretender and his Adherents, and all other your Majesty’s Enemies.

The said Address being read a Second time;

Resolved, Nemine contradicente , That this House doth agree with the Lords in the said Address to be presented to his Majesty,

And the Blank therein was filled up with the Words " and Commons.’*

Ordered, That the Lord Marquis of Harrington do carry the said Address to the Lords, and acquaint them, that this House hath agreed to the fame.

The House being informed, that Mr. Parsons, Comptroller General of the Customs, attended at the Door;

He was called in; and, at the Bar, presented to the House, pursuant to their Address to his Majesty, an Account of the gross Produce of the Duties of Four and a Half per Cent, payable upon Sugars in his Majesty’s Plantations in America, from Chr *732, to

1742; distinguishing each Year; together with a Return of the Commissioners of the Customs.

And then he withdrew.

And the said Return, and a Memorial contained therein of the Comptroller General of the Customs to the said Commissioners, were read.

The laid Return and Memorial, and also the said Account, are as followeth; viz.

To the Honourable the Commons of Great Britain, Parliament assembled.

tn

In Return to your Minute of this Date, founded on an Address of the House of Commons to his Majesty, I lay before you an Account of the grols Produce of the Duties of Four and a Half per Cent, upon Sugars in his Majesty’s Plantations in America, from Christmas 1732, to Christmas 1742.

And 1 beg Leave to represent, that I cannot, from the Journals of the Collectors, or any other Materials in my Office, render the Account in the Terms required by the Order; for, in the First place, the said Collector’s Accounts of this Duty are kept in Specie (or Kind), and not in Money; nor are the Values of the Sugars collected any where, in their said Accounts ascertained, in Money; and, for this Reason, J could not give the Account of the gross Produce in Money, having neither Authority, nor any Rule whereby to afee tain the Values of the Sugars; and as they bear different Prices in different Islands, and are variable in each Island at different Seasons, no exact Rate can be fixed here, to reduce the said gross Produce in Kind, to Money; and, in the next place, it is impossible for me, from the said Journals of the Collectors, or other

Materials in my Office, to make out the net Produce of the said Duty of Four and a Half per Cent, on Sugars;

Having received the Commands of the Lords of the because they are promifcuoully, with other Commodities, Treasury, pursuant to your Address of the 7th Instant liable to the said Duty made use of for Payment of the to his Majesty, that we should cause the following Ac- Charges of Management in the Islands. count to be made out, and laid before you; viz.

An Account of the gross and net Produce of the Du-

ties of Four and a Half per Cent, payable upon Sugars in I74»*

his' Majesty’s Plantations 'in America, from Christmat 1732, to Christmas 1742; distinguishing each Year.

Preventing Frauds by Goldfmhh's Workmen.

Ordered, That the said Account do lie upon the ’fable, to be perused by the Members of the House.

A Petition of the several Goldsmiths, Jewellers, and Watchmakers, whole Names are thereunto subscribed, in behalf of themselves, and others exercising the same Trades, was presented to the House, and read; letting forth, That the Petitioners, by the nature of th’eir Business, cannot make any Vessels or Pieces of wrought Gold and Silver Plate, Watches, Rings, Trinkets, and other Jewellers Work, without fending the Materials of which they are made through a Variety of Hands, who perform several different Operations thereupon before the same can be finfthed, fit to be exposed to Sale; and that it is impossible for the Petitioners to keep within their ownHouses all the Sorts of Artificers and Workmen that must necessarily be employed in working and finishing the several Sorts of Wares and Manufactures aforesaid, by reason that the most (kilful Artificers and Workmen in those several Trades generally take in Work from a great Number of VoL. 24.

different Matter Workmen, as their Occasions require; and many such Artificers and Workmen being drunken, loose, and evil-minded Persons, frequently fell, pawn, embezzle, or otherwise make away-with, the Petitioners Gold, Silver and other Materials, so intruded with them to manufacture, to the great Damage and Loss of their Employers; and such Persons having so done, generally shift their Lodgings, and otten remove into some other Part of the Kingdom, to conceal themselves. from the Persons they have (o defrauded 5 by which means, the Petitioners Gold and Silver, and other unfinished Materials, though (bme-times not pawned for half the Value, cannot be found out, so as to be redeemed again by the Petitioners, for want of knowing where the same are left 5 and if by Chance a Discovery can be made where such Goods are pawned, the Pawnbrokers, who have taken them in, will frequently refuse to acknowledge whether they have iji their Custody such Goods, or to search their Books for the fame, till a Sum of Money be first deposited in their Hands, sufficient to answer the Money lent, and the usual extortionable Interest taken by Pawnbrokers; and if the Petitioners can by any means find out the Persons who have thus pawned or embezzled the Materials intruded with them, 'the Petitioners can proceed no otherwise against them than by Action at Law; which can afford no Satisfaction for the Petitioners Lofifes, after the Money raised by Sale or Pawning of such Goods is spent and wasted by the Offenders: And therefore, in consideration of the great Damages sustained by the Petitioners, and other fair Traders, by means of such evil Practices, and that the Laws in being are defective for the due Punishment of such Offences, and as there is a Bill now depending before this House, for preventing Draymen, Brewers Servants, and others, from felling, pawning, and making away-with, Barrels, Calks, Butts, and other Vef* fels, intruded with them, respectively, without the Content of the Owners or Proprietors thereof, which is a same similar to the Grievances hereby complained of, praying. That a Clause or Clauses may be admitted into the said Bill for their Relief; or that they may have such other Assistance and Relief in the Premises, as to the House (Kail seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Whitehall, February 3d, 174!.

Sir,

His Majesty having received Advice, that the Pretender’s elded Son set out from Rome on the 27 th or 28th of December, O. S. for France; and that he actually arrived at Antibes on the 17th past; it is his Majesty’s Pleasure that you'should immediately go to Monsieur Amelot, and let him know, that his Majesty, considering the Engagements his most Christian Majedv, is under by Treaties, with regard to the Pretender and his Descendants, had commanded you to acquaint him with the Informations the King had received 5 and that his Majesty

,20

did not'doubt, but that if those Accounts were founded, his most Christian Majesty would, pursuant to the Treaties, give effectual Orders that the said Perfcm may be obliged forthwith to quit the French King’s Dominions, if he should be still there; and that he may net be countenanced or protested by any of his most Christian Majesty’s Officers or Subjects.

You will transmit to me the Answer that Monsieur Amelot shall give you from his most Christian Majesty, that I may acquaint the King with it.

I am, tec*

Mr. Thompson. Holies, Newcastle.

Extract of a Letter from Mr. Thompson to the Duke of Newcastle.

Paris, February T7Tth 1741.

I received this Morning the Honour of your Grace's Dispatch of the jd Instant, O. S. by Hammond the Messenger, just as I was going to Monsieur Amelot's; lb that no Time was loft in executing the Commands year Grace was pleased to fend me from his Majesty. 1 had very little Talk with iMonlieur Amelot upon this Subject:

I told him, that the News which had been public here for this Week pad, had like wile reached Louden, where I heard that People were greatly scandalized at it; that I had now Orders from the King to tell him (Monsieur Amelot) what his Majesty had heard of this Matterand to represent to him, that, considering the Engagements his most Christian Majesty was-under to the King* with respect to the Pretender and his Defendants, by virtue of the most solemn Treaties, his Majesty did not doubt, but, upon the Representations I was now ordered to make, this Person would not only be obliged to retire out of France, if he was actually in it, but that his most Christian Majesty would also fulfill; in all Respects;. the Engagements he was under to the King, on Account of the Pretender, his Defendants, and Adherents; In a Word, I told him, that, not to go beyond or fall Abort of what I was directed to say to him, nor to make a Mi flake of any kind, I would, if he pleased, read to him your Grace’s Letter to me; which he desired I would. When I had done, Monsieur Amelot told me,- now that I spoke to him by Order, he mull likewise receive the Freitch King’s Commands. He promised he would speak to the King the very first Opportunity; and would acquaint me immediately with his most Christian Majesty’s Pleasure.

The Information, upon Oath, of Captain Alexander Ridley, Matter of one of his Majesty’s Packet Boats at Dover:

Who faith, that he failed from Dover on Tuesday the 14th instant, and arrived the same Day at Calais. Upon his Arrival there, he was ordered to hawl his Vessel into a Place called Paradise, where seized and condemned Vessels usually lie: That several English Merchant Ships were the same Day ordered into the same Place: That* on Friday the 17th, the English Mail from Paris arrived at Calais; upon which, this Informant applied, to the Pott-master of Calais, to know Whether he might proceed with it to England; who told him, he would ask the Governor; and soon after acquainted him he mutt not go to England; That, on the same Day, Hammond the Meflen-ger arrived from Paris with Dispatches from Mr. Thompson, and went to the Governor, to know whether he might proceed to England; which he was not permitted to do: That, on Saturday the 18th, the said MefTcnger delivered, in a private Manner, to this Informant, Mr. Thomp~ fons Dispatches, which he immediately concealed in a very private Place on board his Vessel. That, on Monday or Tuesday last, another English Mail arrived at Calais; upon which, the Post-master came to this Informant, and asked him whether he would fail with the Mails for England-y which, he said, he was ready to do; but the Mails Were not delivered to him till the next Day; viz. IVed-\iefday: That, on the same Day, between Two and Three o’Clock in the Afternoon, a File of Mufqueteers, with some Officers, came on board, and searched his Vessel very strictly; and particularly asked him whether he had not the English Messenger’s Dispatches for the Duke of Newcastle on board ? which he denied: That this Informant asked the Commandant, whether the Messenger might not proceed to England f which the Commandant said he might do. Upon which, this Informant sent his Mate to acquaint the Messenger with it, and to desire him to come on board; but as the Messenger was preparing to come on board, he was stopt on the Quay by the Commandant, and others, who asked him for his Dispatches; but he told them he had no Dispatches, only a few private Letters, which he shewed them: That, upon this, the Mate returned on board, and having acquainted this Informant, that the Messenger was detained, he immediately put to Sea, and arrived the same Night, past 12 o'Clock, at Dover; from whence he immediately lent his Vessel, with*his Mate, to Sir John Norris in the Downs, to acquaint him with what he had observed and heard at Calais

This Informant further faith, that he heard, whilst he was at Calais, that there were between 20 and 30 Transports in Dunkirk Road: That Seven or Eight final 1 Men of \yar were also there, and 16 more Men of War expected: That there were several Dunkirk Pilots still at Gz-lais, and several Captains of French Merchant Men taken up to serve as Pilots on board the Fleet: That it was <he common Talk at Calais, that Fifteen thousand Men were to be embarked on board the Transports, in order to make a Descent upon some Part of his Majesty's Dominions; and that Part of the said Troops were already embarked, and the rest embarking: That Four Battalions of French Foot marched on Monday last from Calais to Dunkirk, in order, as was said publicly at Calais, to be embarked at Dunkirk: That, amongst the Troops

Vol. 24.

S87

embarking, and to be embarked, there were some Dragoons, who carried their Bridles and Saddles with them, but not their Horses: That some said, the Landing was to be in Kent, others in Scotland: That Count Saxe arrived at Calais on Tuesday the 14th instant (on which Day the Embargo was laid at Calais^ Boulogne, and Dunkirk), and went to Dunkirk, as thisInformant was told, the Saturday following, in order to take upon him the Command of the Troops designed for the Invasion: That there werefeve-ral Irish Officers, and others, in Company with Count Saxe-, amongst which there was a person, whom this Informant; saw upon the Quay, and who was said by the French there to be the Pretender’s eldest Son, and whom they called publicly the Chevalier, and seemed to pay him a great* deal of Respect: That the said Person is a tall slim young Man, of about 24 Years of Age-: That the Examinant could not fee his Face distinctly; and that there was another young Man in Company with him, who was said to be his Brother.

This Informant further faith, that he was told, the Transports at Dunkirk were not victualled for more than Four or Five Days: That there was a Ship loading at Calais with Provisions for the Fleet: That they had heard1 of the Embargo laid upon Provision in Ireland, at which they expressed great Concern and Resentment: That it was the common Report at Calais, that there had been an Action in the Mediterranean between Admiral Mathezvs's Squadron and the French and Spanish Squadrons: That this Informant heard a Letter read, but docs not remember the Date of Time or Place, which was written to a French Officer by his Brother, who, as this Informant heard, lives near Toulon; in which he fays, that he saw several French Ships without Masts.

This Informant further faith, that, on Friday or Satur* day last, an Englishmen was brought from Dunkirk to Ca*> lais, where he is confined; the Occasion of his Imprisonment is said to be his having hired a French Vessel to bring Dispatches to England: That this Person is supposed to be Mr. Laye, his Majesty’s Agent at Dunkirk.

Anno 170 Georgii IP1 Regis, 1743. Prayers.

MR. Comptroller reported to the House, That their Address of Yesterday (That his Majesty would be graciously pleased, in this dangerous and critical Con-jun&ureof Affairs, when this Nation is threatened with an Invasion by a French Power, in favour of a Popish Pretender to his Crown, to Augment his Forces by Sea and Land, in such Manner as he shall think proper and necessary; and to assure his Majesty, that this House will make good all such Expences as his Majesty shall be at, for the Defence of his sacred Person, and for the Security of these Kingdoms), had been presented to his Majesty; and that his Majesty was pleased to give this most gracious Answer:

His Majesty thanks his faithful Commons for their dutiful and affectionate Address. The best Return he can make them for the Confidence they repole in him, is to assure them, that no further Expence shall be brought upon his People, on this Occasion, than what shall be found absolutely necessary for the Defence and Security of these Kingdoms, and for the Preservation of our happy Constitution.

Levant A Petition of the Governor and Company of Mer-

Trade. chants of England trading into the Levant Seas, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That his late Majesty King James\he First, by his Letters Patent, hearing Date the 14th Day of December, in the Third Year of his Reign (reciting as therein is mentioned), did grant to several Persons therein named, and to their Sons, atad all other Merchants as should then after, from time tio time, be admitted, or made free of the said Company, that they should be One Fellow ship, and One Body Corporate and Politic, by the Name of the Governor and Company of Merchants of England trad i ng i nto the Levant Se ts, and by that Name should have perpetual Succession 5 and that there should be a Governor of the said Company, Deputy Governor, and Eighteen Af&stants, who are to be elected annually, and sworn to the due Discharge of their said Offices; and are to settle and manage all things concerning the good Rule, State, and Government, of the said Company, who were to receive into their Freedom all Persons, Subjects of the Realm, being Merchants, and under the Age of Twenty six Years, or not out of their Apprenticeship, on their requiring the same within the Time therein limited, and paying to the Company, at their Admittance, Twenty-five Pounds; and all Subjects, being Merchants, and above Twenty^six Years of Age, who should, at any time after the Time limited by the Charter, demand the fame, on paying Fifty Pounds; and all the Sons of such Freemen, and all their Apprentices, were to be admitted to the Freedom of the said Company on Payment of Twenty Shillings only; and several Privileges are granted, by the said Letters Patent, to the said Company; and that his late Majesty King Charles the Second, by his Letters Patent, bearing Date the 2d Day of April. in the Thirteenth Year of his Reign, after reciting the said Letters Patent of King James the First, was graciously pleased to ratify and confirm the and did further direct, that no Person, residing within Twenty Miles of London (except Noblemen, and Gentlemen of Quality), should be admitted into the Freedom of the said Company, or have any Benefit of the Privileges thereof, unless they be made Free of the City of London: And further setting forth, That the said Company, confiding in the said Royal Charters, and in their Enjoyment of the Liberties and Privileges thereby granted to them, have ever fitice carried on a very confix derable Trade to the Levant Seas, in the Course of which they have yearly exported to Turkey very large Quantities of the Woollen and other Manufactures of Great Britain, and brought back, in Return, large Quantities of Raw Silk, Mohair, Yarn, and other unmanufactured Cortimo-. Vojl. 24.

dities, to be wrought up and manufactured here, to the great Benefit and Advantage of this Nation; and have likewise been at a very great and considerable Expence, both annually and otherwise, in supporting the Charge of an Ambassador at Constantinople, and of Consuls in Turkey:'

That they have also been at a very large Expence in obtaining and renewing the necessary Capitulations with the Ottoman Porte, for the Establishment and Security of the said Trade; and have been at a very great Charge in making considerable Settlements at Constantinople, Aleppo, and Smyrna, in erecting and purchasing Houses, as welt for the Use of the Ambassador and Consuls, as of the several Houses of Business they are under a Necessity of having the re, for the better carrying on and managing the said Trade, and in supporting Agents and Factors, and many other Charges depending thereon; and have likewise a great Property now lying in Turkey: And repre-fenting to the House, That the Petitioners apprehend* that the Bill now depending in this House, for enlarging and regulating the Trade to the Levant Seas, will, if the same should pass into a Law, deprive the Petitioners of the Liberties and Privileges granted by the said Royal Charters, greatly affect the Petitioners in their Properties, and very much distress (if not occasion the total Loss to this Nation of) the Turkey Trade, to the great Prejudice of tjiofe Two most valuable Branches of the British Commerce,* the Woollen and Silk, as well as other, Manufactures; and also of the general Trade and Navigation of the Kingdom: And therefore praying the House, That they may be heard by their Counsel against the said Bill; and that the same may not be patted into a Law.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the said Bill be read a Second time; and that the Petitioners be then heard by their Counsel against the said Bill, if they think fit.

Ordered, That Counsel be admitted to be heard, at the same time, in favour of the said Bill, against the said.

Petition.

Ordered, That the said Bill be read a Second time, upon Thursday Sevennight.

in the said Act are mentioned; arid certain Lands,-Marshes, Salt-grass, and other Lands, in the said Act mentioned, were thereupon vested in the said Under-, takers, to and for their proper Use, under the Provisoes and Conditions in the said Act mentioned, as in and by the said Act of Parliament will more fully appear: That the said Undertakers, in pursuance of the Powers and Authorities granted by the said recited Act, cut a new Channel, for the said River Dee, through the adjacent Marshes, several Miles in Length, and made a Dam, and set Sluices, aerpfs the old Channel, and turned the said River into the said.nevyfChannel, Jthrough which the said Navigation hath since been carried on; in doing which, the Undertakers expended great Sums of Money; and the said Undertakers have, from the 25th of March 1740, received and collected the Rates of Tonnage granted by the said Act: That by a subsequent Act of Parliament, made in the Fourteenth Year of his present Majesty’s Reign, intituled, An Act for incorporating the Undertakers of the Navigation of the River Dec> the said Undertakers were incorporated, and had fevqral Powers given them for the better managing the said Undertaking: That the Petitioners having found by Experience, that the Rates of Tonnage, granted to the said Undertakers by the first-mentioned Act, are too high, and; a Discouragement to the Trade of the said City; the Petitioners therefore requested the said Undertakers, that the same may, by Authority of Parliament, be repealed; and that, inlieu thereof;Other.anddelsTonnage or Keelage-rates may be granted to the said Undertakers; to winch the said Undertakers have assented: That the Petitioners apprehend it will be for the common Good, and an Encouragement to the said Undertaking: That the said recited Acts of Parliament, of the Sixth and Fourteenth.

Years of his. To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, an Act, made in the 3th Year of the Reign of his present Majesty, for the better Regulation and- Government- of Pilots licensed by the Cprporation of Trinity House of Deptford Strond, in the County of Kent", and to pteverU Mischiefs and Annoyances upon the River of Thames, below London Bridge, was produced; whereby it is enacted, That if any Person shall take upon himself the Charge of any Ship or Vessel, as Pilot, within the Limits described in the Bill, other than such Persons as shall be licensed to act as Pilots by the Corporation of Trinity House; every Person being thereof lawfully convicted before any Two or more Justices of the Peace for the City of London, or the Counties of Middlefez, Efex, Kent, or Surrey, within their respective Juiiidiftions, in the Manner prescribed in the Act, shall forfeit £. 20. (the Matters or Owners of Ships in the Coal Trade and qthejr Coasting Trade^excepfed)kj and1 Liberty is given* fof Petfoqs, who think themselves aggrieved by such JudgpVent, to ^ppeal to the Justices at the next Quarts Sessions for the County, City, or Place, wherein, such Offence shall be committed, who are to hear and determine the same; andhhe said Act di-rests, that all pecuniary Penalties and Forfeitures, incurred as aforesaid, shall be applied for the Benefit of the Poor of the Corporation of Trinity House.

Mr. William Bedford, Attorney at Law, being examined, said. That he had been concerned for the licensed Pilots in the Prosecution of several Persons for Offences contrary to the said Act; but the Persons convicted, upon their Appeal to the Quarter Sessions, not being obliged to give Security for Payment of the Penalty, in case the Judgment appealed from should be affirmed; and also, by reason of Expence in carrying on Prosecutions to obtain final Judgments, the Act is by those Means evaded;

Vol. 24.

and that, in Three Instances, where Appeals had beet! brought in the County of Middlesex, the Pilots recovered only one Fine: ,

That Endeavours have been used to prosecute Persons for the same Offences committed in the Town of Gravesend\ but the Justices of the Peace of that Corporation having, by the Act, no Jurisdiction in this Cafe, and it being difficult to get Two Justices for the County of Kent to convict Offenders there, by reason of the Distance of their Residence from the said Town, and from each other, Offenders frequently escape without Punishr ment. J \

Francis Lilly, licensed Pilot, said, that there are about 80^or 90 licensed Pilots employed beyond Gravesend.:

That Foreigners, particularly Danes, have refused to take the Witness as a Pilot; and that they frequently pilot their own Ships (but not any others) up and down 0 the River.

Mr. John Whormby, Secretary to the Corporation of Trinity House, being examined,; confirmed what Mr.

Bedford said, with regard to the Acts being evaded, by reason of the Manner in which an Appeal is granted.

AS to their Proceedings in carrying on the Building *.

In Queen Mary’s Court,

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr. Thomas Shirley was called: Who said. That he was well acquainted with the Roads between Buckingham and Warmington, which are in a very bad Condition: That it is a Road of great Resort, many Carriages, as well as Passengers on Horseback, passing through the fame.

Edinburgh The House proceeded to the further Hearing of the Election. Matter of the Petition complaining of an undue Election and Return for the Shire of Edinburgh.

And the Counsel were called in.

And the Counsel for the Petitioners examined a Witness, in order to prove, that the Roll of Freeholders, called over before the Election of Praefes and Clerk to the Meeting, on the 13th Day of January last, for chusing a Representative to Parliament for the Shire of,

agrees with the Roll of Freeholders made up in 1742:

He was also examined, in order to prove, that several Gentlemen are complained of, in the Two Petitions pre-lented to the Lords of Council and Session in Scotland, whole Names are not inserted in any Roll other than that of 1742:

He was also examined, in order to prove, that the Inrollment of Sir James Stewart is not complained of in either of the said Petitions:

He was also examined, as to the usual Method of enrolling Heirs Apparent, after the Death of their Ancestors.

And an Extract of the Minutes of Election of a Representative to Parliament for the Shire of Edinburgh, 21 May 1734, being produced j

And the Name of Sir James , of Goodtrees,

not appearing in the Roll of Freeholders made up after that Election;

The Counsel for the Petitioners proposed to examine a Witness, in order to prove (which the Counsel for the Sitting Member admitted), that the Death of Sir James Stewart, Father of the present Sir James , was

the Reason of that Omission:

And Part of the Minutes of the said Meeting, on the Vol. 24.

13th Day of January last, was read, in order to prove, that the Prtefes of the said Meeting refilled to call over the Name of Sir James Stewart: '

And Part of the said Minutes was also read, in order to prove, that the Name of Mr. Falconer, of Monketon, was then called over:

And Part of the said Minutes was also read. In Order to prove, that the Name of Sir Stewart', of Good-trees, is not inserted in the Roll made up after the said Election; and that the Names of the said Mr.

and of Mr. Wauchop, are inserted in the said Roll:

And Part of the said Minutes was also read, in order to prove, that the Clerk of the said Meeting did nbt take the Oath prescribed by an Act of the last Session of Parliament, immediately after his Election.

And a Witness was examined, and Evidence was produced, in order to prove, that the Minutes of the Election of Prafes and Clerk to the said Meeting were not ligned and delivered to the Clerk, elected pursuant to the Directions of the said Act:

And a Witness was examined, and Evidence was produced, in order to prove, that neither the Roll of Electors, nor the Minutes of the Election, were produced by the said Clerk, to the Sheriff, before the Return of the Representative to Parliament, pursuant to the Directions of the said Act.

Then the Counsel for the Petitioners summed up their Evidence.

And the Counsel for the Sitting Member were heard; and examined a Witness, in order to prove, that many the Freeholders inserted in the Roll, which was called over at the said Election, were then dead:

He was also examined, as to the Manner of signing the Minutes then taken, and the Agreement of the Freeholders then present, concerning the said Minutes.

Then the Counsel for the Sitting Member offered to prove (which the Counsel for the Petitioners admitted), that Sir James Stewart, the Son, had never voted at former Elections.

And the Counsel for the Sitting Member having offered to prove, that the said Sir James Stewart has not been inrolled as a Freeholder in any Books of Inrollment;

The Counsel for the Petitioners admitted, that he does not appear to be inrolled otherwise than in the Roll before-mentioned of 1742.

And a Witness was examined, in order to prove, for what Reason the Name of Sir James Stewart was not mentioned in either of the Petitionsprefepted to the Lords of Council and Session in Scotland.

And the Counsel for the Sitting Member having gone through their Evidence;

And the Counsel for the Petitioners having been heard by way of Reply;

The Counsel on both Sides were directed to withdraw. A Motion being made, that Sir Charles Gilmour Baronet is duly elected a Commissioner to serve in this present Parliament for the Shire of Edinburgh;

Sir Charles Gilmour was heard in his Place:

And then he withdrew.

Resolved, That Sir Charles Gilmour Baronet is duly elected a Commissioner to serve in this present Parliament for the Shire of Edinburgh. '

Ordered, That the Order of the Day, for taking into Consideration the Report from the Committee, to whom the Bill for remedying feme Defeats in the Ad, made in the 43d Year of the Heign of Queen Elizabeth, intituled, An Act for the Relief of the Poor, was committed, be now read.

And the said Order being read accordingly;

Ordered, That the said Report be taken into Consideration Tomorrow Morning.

Ordered, That the Order of the Day, for the House to resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, upon the Bill for the more easy taking the Poll at Elections of Knights of the Shire to serve in Parliament for that Part of Great Britain called England, and to restrain the Partiality, and regulate the Conduct, of Returning Officers at such Elections, be now read.

And the said Order being read accordingly;

Resolved, That this House will, upon Thursday Morning next, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, upon the said Bill.

The other Order of the Day being read, for the House to resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider of the State of the Linen Manufactures of Great Britain and Ireland;

Ordered, That the Account of the Total Amounts of the Value of all Exports and Imports to and from England and Germany, for Fifteen Years, ending at Christmas 1742; distinguishing each Year j be referred to the said Committee*

Ordered, That the Account of the Quantity of Flax imported into that Part of Great Britain called England, for Seven Years, ending at Christmas 1742; distinguisti-ing each Year; be referred to the said Committee.

Ordered, That the Account of the Quantities of Linen imported from Holland into that Part of Great Britain Called England, under the Denominations of broad and narrow' Germany, for Seven Year-, ending at Christmas 1742; distinguishing each Year; be referred to the said Committee.

Ordered, That the Account of the Quantity of Linens imported into England from foreign Parts, from Christmas 1740, tb Christmas 1743, inclusive; distinguishing each Year; be referred to the said Committee

Then the House resolved itself into the said Committee.

Mr. Speaker left the Chair.

Mr. Francis Fane took the Chair of the Committee.

Mr. Speaker resumed the Chair.

Mr. Francis Fane reported from the Committee, That they had made some Progress in the Matter to them re-, ferred; and that he was directed by the Committee to move, that they may have Leave to fit again.

Resolved, That this House will, upon Lhurfday Morning next, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider further of the State of the Linen Manufactures of Great Britain and Ireland.

And then the House adjourned till Tomorrow Morning, Nine of the Clock.

and public Notice was given, that all Merchants and others, who had any Claims to be laid before the said Commissaries, might forthwith bring them to the Office of the Lords Commissioners for Trade and Plantations, with such Proofs and Vouchers of their several Losses, authenticated in such manner as the Claimants should judge most convenient: That the Petitioners, according to these Directions, did deliver to the said Lords Commissioners their Proofs and Vouchers; but as yet they have not received any Satisfaction: That, in January 1738 — 9, a Convention was agreed between the Crown of Great Britain and that of Spain, and Plenipotentiaries were appointed by both Crowns, in order to settle and adjust all Differences which had been raised on account of visiting, searching, and taking, of Vessels, &V.; and it was agreed, that the King of Spain should cause to be paid to his Britannic Majesty the Sum of Ninety-five thousand Pounds, for a Balance which had been admitted as due to sche Crown and Subjects of Great Britain, after Deduction made of the Demands of the Crown and Subjects of Spain; to the End, that the above-mentioned Sum, together with the Amount of what has been acknowledged, on the Part of Great Britain, to be due to Spain on her Demands, may be employed by the King of Great Britain, for the Satisfaction, Discharge, and Payment, of the Demands of the English Subjects upon the Crown of Spain; A Petition of the Woollen Manufacturers, and other principal Inhabitants, of the City of New Sarum was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioners perceive, by the Votes of this House, that a Committee is appointed to consider of the State of the Linen Manufactures of Great Britain and Ireland; and further setting forth. That the Vent in foreign Markets of great Quantities of the Manufactures, wherein the

Petitioners, and vast Numbets of other Persons in this - Kingdom, are employed, depends in great measure on the

Intercourse of Trade between those Countries and this Kingdom, and the taking of Linen Goods from thence, in Part of Payment; notwithstanding which, the Balance remains in favour of this Kingdom, as the Petitioners have great Reason to believe; and representing to the House, That the Petitioners are apprehensive there may '* be some Design to lay an additional Load or Burthen upon foreign Linens imported hither; in which Cafe, the Petitioners have too much Reason to fear the Loss of the valuable Exports of the Manufactures they are employed in, whereby the Petitioners, and many Thousands of other British Subjects at present employed in the Woollen. Manufacture, will be brought to the greatest Poverty and Distress: And therefore praying the Consideration of the House; and that they may have Liberty to be heard by themselves, or their Counsel, before the House shall please to come to any Resolution to increase the Burthen at present lying upon foreign Linens.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Prayers.

Linen Ma- A Petition of the several Persons, whose names arc nuUdiurcsfc thereunto subscribed, in behalf of themselves, and great Numbers of others concerned and employed in the Woollen Manufactures in and about the Town of Leeds, in the County of York, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That, by the Votes of this House, the Petitioners perceive a Committee is appointed to consider of the State of the Linen Manufactures of Great Britain and Ireland; and representing to the House, That the vending in foreign Markets, of great Quantities of the Manufactures, In which the Petitioners, and Numbers of others in this Kingdom, are employed, in great measure depends upon the Intercourse of Trade between this Kingdom and the Places abroad, where such Manufactures are vended, and the taking of Linen Goods from rhence in Part of Payment; notwithstanding which, the Balance remains in favour of this Kingdom, and very greatly in respect to the Manufactures of the Neighbourhood of the said Town; and that the Petitioners are apprehensive there may be some Design to lay an additional Duty or Burthen upon foreign Linens imported into this Kingdom, which the Petitioners have great reason to fear will be a means to prevent the Exportation of very large Quantities of Woollen Manufactures, and tend to the great Prejudice of the Petitioners, and Thousands of other British Subjects employed therein: And therefore praying, That the House will take their same into Consideration; and that they may be at Liberty to be heard by themselves, or their Counsel, before the House will please to come to any Resolution to increase the Duty or Burthen upon foreign Linens.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Artillery.

The Pensionary and Monsieur Opdam have been already spoke to, to get some from this Country.

It was thought more proper, that the Duke cTArem* berg should make a Demand of the fame, r. ther than myself; but afterwards wc discovered, that Monsieur Fenelon told the Pensionary Yesterday, that the English could undertake nothing for want of Artillery.

We have considered what there was in the Low Countries: There is enough, if the Carriages were good; some Money would be wanting to put it all in Motion. On -the other hand, our Sea Carriages will be sufficient.. In Matters of War, nothing ought to be i’pared.

As we are in want of Hussars, the Two Marshals think it would be very useful to augment the free Companies in the Low Countries, and to mount them forthwith.-Money will be necessary for this Purpose, and fora groat many other Uses; and the Marllials will take care that it will be well employed.

Time is short; every thing must be forced with Money; and, with that, it appears that one might answer for every thing.

- As Things shall appear to be wanting, Notice will be given thereof immediately.

It the mean time, it seems necessary to specify what is above-mentioned, and to fend an Express without Lois of Time.

A Petition of the Mayor, Aldermen, and Bufgeffes, Linen of the Borough and Town of Taunton, in the County of Mawfaaurtrt-Somerset, and of the Woollen Manufacturers in the said Town, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioners observe from the Votes of this House, that a Committee is appointed to consider of the State of the Linen Manufa#uresof Great Britain and Ireland; and further setting forth, That the Exports of the Woollen Goods of the Manufactory of thV laid Town, and of great Part of this Kingdom, is greatly encouraged By taking foreign Linens in Part of Payment, though vastly inferior to the Balance in Trade in favour of the Petitioners, and other Woollen Manufa#urers in this Kingdom; and representing to the House, that the Petitioners are apprehensive, that any additional Burthen or Duty on foreign Linens imported, will be prejudicial to the Woollen Manufactory of this Kingdom in general; whereby the Petitioners are liable, with all other his Majesty’s Subjects in the Staple Trade of this Nation, to be great Sufferers, and may be reduced to the utmost Poverty: And therefore praying the Confederation of the House* and expressing their Hope, that the House will not increase the Burthen on foreign Linens, by laying any additional Duty thereon.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of the Woollen Manufacturers, and the Ditto* Merchants and Traders dealing the rein, in and about the Town of Rochdale, in the County of Lancaster, and other Inhabitants in or about the said Town, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth. That very large Quantities of Woollen Goods, of various Kinds, are ma-nufadured at the said Town, and in a very populous Country around it, and exported to Germany, and other Places abroad; whence Linens are imported in Part of Payment thereof* and representing to the House, that the Petitioners areadvised, that it is the Intention of Parliament to lay an additional Duty on such imported Linens; which, if carried into Execution, the Petitioners apprehend, will be a very great Discouragement to the Exporting of the Manufactures in which the Petitioners, and many Thousand others, are employed, and, in some Markets, may put a Stop to the Sale thereof: And therefore requesting, that no additional Duty may be laid on any foreign Linens imported into this Kingdom.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

The King’s Mr. Speaker also reported, That his Majesty was after-Speech; wards pleased to make a most gracious Speech from the FiSace!1 Throne, to both Houses of Parliament; of which Mr.

Speaker said, he had, to prevent Mistakes, obtained a Copy: Which he read to the House; and is as followed; viz.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

The Preparations which were so long carried on in France, to invade this Kingdom in favour of a Popish Pretender, have at last been followed with a-r Declaration of War by that Crown against me. The Duty, Affection, and Zeal, for me and my Family, which have been so fulJy’and cordially expressed in the unanimous Resolutions of both Houses of Parliament, and in the loyal and feasonable Addresses of all my goofl Subjects, ought to have convinced our Enemies how ill-grounded any Hopes of Success were, with which they might have vainly flattered themselves in such an Attempt. Tome it is the truest Satisfaction, and must be the greatest Security to my Government, that, just at the time of entering into this War, I have had such solemn Assurances and Pledges of the Fidelity and good Affections of my People.

Whatever Colours may be endeavoured to be put on these injurious Proceedings of the Court of FrancCy I can appeal to the whole World for the Rectitude and Equity of my Conduct, always steadily directed to the Defence of the antient Allies of my Crown, conformably to Treaties, to the Preservation of the Balance and Liberties of Europe, and the Maintenance of the Commerce and essential Interests of my Kingdoms, pursuant to the Advice of my Parliament, without invading the Rights of any other Power.

Under these Circumstances, I have declared War, on my Part, against the French King; and have made the proper Requisitions to my Allies, particularly the States General of the United Provinces (whole firm Friendship I have so lately experienced) to join with me, and perform their Engagements on this important Occasion.

(Senr'emen of the House of Commons,

I take this Opportunity to thank you for the Readiness and Dispatch with which you have already granted me

Vol. 24.

639

such large Supplies; and That on Terms so advantageous to the Public, although we were then actually menaced with an Invasion. It would give me the utmost Concern, to fee our Expences increased by this new Event; but if you shall find any thing further necessary for the Support of the Honour of my Crown, and your own Security, in the present Conjuncture, I depend on your wonted Zeal to provide for it.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

In so just a Cause, I rely on the Divine Protection, and on your vigorous and effectual Support and Assistance. Let the Enemies of our Peace, who have long aspired at the universal Monarchy of Europe, and envied the Liberty and flourishing Condition of my Kingdoms in particular, fee that Great Britain, in conjunction with her Allies, is able to withstand and defeat their destructive Projects. I will do my Part I have no Interest at Heart but yours; and in that common Interest let us all unite.

Resolved, Nemine contradrcente, That an humble Address be presented to his Majesty, to return his Majesty the Thanks of this House for his most gracious Speech from the Throne; and to express our utmost Indignation and Resentment, £hat, after an Attempt the most perfidious to surprise his Majesty’s Kingdoms by a sudden Invasion, in favour of the Pretender, the French King should publish a Declaration of War, couched in Terms injurious to the Honour and Dignity of his Majesty’s Crown, Person, and Government, and avowedly founded upon his Majesty’s having supported, pursuant to his Engagements, an Ally oppressed by the French King, contrary to his Faith, solemnly pledged and dearly bought; to congratulate his Majesty on the ready Assistance he has lately received from the States General; to return his Majesty the Thanks of this House, for asserting the Honour of this Nation, in declaring War against the French King* and for having, on this important Occasion, made the proper Requisitions to his Majesty’s Allies, and particularly to the States General, united in one common and invariable Interest with this Nation; not doubting but that, by his Majesty’s steadily pursuing the said Instances, they will, from their known Regard to Treaties, and their just Sense of the impending Danger, co-operate with his Majesty in the most vigorous and effectual Measures for checking the ambitious Views of France, and preferring the Liberties and Balance of Europe; to allure his Majesty, that, in the Prosecution of this unavoidable War, whatever further Expences shall be found necessary for the Support of the Honour of his Majesty’s Crown, and our own Security, his Majesty may depend upon a ready and effectual Assistance from this House, such as becomes a free and grateful People, in Defence of their Liberties against that Power which has long aspired at the universal Monarchy of Europe, and whose ambitious Views and destructive Projects have hitherto been defeated by the Blessing of God on the Arms of Great Britain, and her Allies.

Ordered, That a Committee be appointed to draw up an Address to be presented to his Majesty, upon the said Resolution:

A Petition of the Woollen Manufacturers of the City and County of Norwich, was printed to the House, and read; setting forth. That the Petitioners perceiving,«by the Votes of this House, that a Committee has been appointed, and are now proceeding, to take irito Coti-sideration the State of the Linen flfonufactures of Great Britain and Ireland; with a View* as they apprehend, and have been informed, to lay an additional Duty upon Linens imported from foreign Parts,; beg Leave to represent to this House, tthat the Support of the;Woollen Manufacture of that City greatly depends upon the Intercourse of Trade between this Kingdom anchthofe-foreign Countries, from whence Linens -are imported: That an additional Duty upon foreign Linens here may produce the like upon our Woollen Manufactures in foreign Parts, in Return: That foreign Countries, finding by such Duties less Demands for their Li nens,;and consequently less Employment for their Poor, may be,4nduced to encourage the Increase of their own Woollen Manufactures, which they daily improve: That the Petitioners.cannot but -be greatly alarmed even at the mostdistant; Hazard oflofing To beneficial a Branch of their Trade as that to foreign Parts, from whence Linens areiimporteti, which employs many Thousandsof their Mamjfacturers; much more are their Fears awakened at the Pfospect of any Success attending the Designof the present Inquiry: And pray trig, That, before any additional duty be laid upon Linens imported from foreign Parts, it hey may be heard, by themselves, or their Counsel, before this House.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

the King’s Yesterday to diaw up an Address to be presented to his Speech. Majesty, That the Committee had drawn up an Address accordingly i which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the same in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

VOL. 24.

Most gracious Sovereign,

We, your Majesty’s most dutiful and loyal Subjects, the Commons of Great Britain, in Parliament assembled, beg Leave to return your Majesty our mofl hearty Thanks for your Majesty’s gracious Speech from the Throne; and to express our utmost Indignation and Resentment, that after an Attempt the most perfidious to surprise your Majesty’s Kingdoms by a sudden Invasion, in favour of the Pretender, the French King should publish a Declaration of War, couched in Terms injurious to the Honour and Dignity of your Majesty’s Crown, Person, and Government, and avowedly founded upon your Majesty’s having supported, pursuant to your Engagements, an Ally opprested by the French King, contrary to his Faith, iolemnly pledged and dearly bought.

We congratulate your Majesty on the ready Assistance your Majesty has lately received from the States General.

We beg Leave also to return your Majesty our sincere Thanks for having alFerted the Honour of this Nation, in declaring War against the French King; and for having, on this important Occasion, been graciously pleased to make the proper Requisitions to your Majesty’s Allies, and particularly the States General, united in one common and invariable Interest with this Nation; and we cannot doubt but that, by your Majesty’s steadily pursuing the said Instances, they will, from their known Regard to Treaties, and their just Sense of the impending Danger, co-operate with your Majesty in the most vigorous and effectual Measures for checking the ambitious Views of France, and preserving the Liberties and Balance of Europe.

Your faithful Commons do humbly assure your Majesty, that, in the Prosecution of this unavoidable War, whatever further Expences shall be found necessary for the Support of the Honour of your Majesty’s Crown, and the Security of this Nation, your Majesty may depend upon their most ready and effectual Assistance, such as they think becomes a free and grateful People^ in Defence of their Liberties, against that Power which has longafpired at the universal Monarchy of Europe, and whole ambitious Views and destrudive Projcds have hitherto been defeated, by the BlefTing of God on the Arms of Great Britain, and her Allies.

The said Address being read a Second time, was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House,

Nemine contradicente.

Resolved, That the said Address be presented to his Majesty by the whole House.

A Petition from the Manufacturers of British Sailcloth Linen Maim* at Warrington, in Lancashire, was p re fen ted to the House, failures, and read; representing to the House, That the Petitioners apprehend that a further Duty on foreign Linens will not only be of great Benefit to the Linen Manufactures of Great Britain and Ireland, but also a great Encouragement to the British Sailcloth Manufacture, as also to the Revenue, here being great Quantities of brown Linen Cloth imported from Germany, entered as narrow Germany, which are used in making and mending of Sails* and that large Quantities thereof are also exported to the Plantations for the same Uses, and draw back almost the whole Duty, contrary to an Act of Parliament of the Ninth of his present Majesty, for encouraging the Mahu-fasture of Sailcloth in Great Britain; which enacts, That all foreign Cloth, used for Sails, shall pay a Duty of Two Pence Half-penny per Eil inwards, and have no Part thereof drawn back when exported: And therefore praying, That the Importers of the said Linens may be obliged to conform to the said Act of Parliament, and pay Duty as Sailcloth; and also representing to the House, That as there is an Act in being, that the Sailmaker, or any other Person, who shall make any foreign Canvas un-stampt into Sails, shall, on Information, forfeit the Penalty of Twenty Pounds, the Petitioners presume, that* was that Penalty.made One hundred Pounds, it would put a Stop to the Importation of all Ticklingburghs whatever, of which Species probably many Thousand Ells are exported annually.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committeeof the whole House, to whom it is referred to consider further of the State of the Linei\, Manufactures of Great Britain and Ireland.

A Petition of the underwritten Merchants trading to Sicily, in behalf of themselves, and others, being offered to be prefen ted to the House;

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer, by his Majesty’s Command, acquainted the House, That his Majesty had been informed of the Contents of the said Petition; and recommends it to the Consideration of the House.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read; setting forth, That upon the Defeat of the Spanish Fleet off Sicily, in the Year 1718, the English Merchants residing at MeJJina were imprisoned, their Ships, Goods, and Effects, seized and fold, by Order of the Marquis De Lede, then General of the Spanish Forces in Sicily, whereby the Petitioners!!]stained very great LofiTes, which were claimed and let forth, before a Committee of the whole House, in the Year 17:£, and the Estimates of the said Losses then delivered in, and ordered to lie upon the Table; but that as yet no Restitution hath been made, notwithstanding it was expressly agreed in the Treaty of Peace made with Spain in the Year 1721, that the Goods, Merchandize, Monies, Ships, and other Effects, that were seized or taken before War was declared between the Two Crowns, or since, should be restored in the Species they were seized or taken, or else should be paid the just and true Value they were worth at the Time of their being seized or taken; and therefore submit ting the same of the Petitioners to the Consideration of the House: And praying the y may have the same Relief, as shall be granted to the Petitioners the Portugal, Spanish, and Italian Traders.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee, to whom the Petition of several Merchants of London, who’ trade to Portugal, Spain, and Italy, whole Hands are thereunto subscribed, is referred: And that they do examine, and state to the House. the Matter of Fast contained in this Petition.

A Petition of the Clothiers and Woollen Manufactn* rers in and about the populous Town, extensive Parish and Neighbourhood, of Halifax, in the West Riding of the County of York, in behalf of themselves, and many Thousand others concerned and employed in this particular Branch of Trade, on which depends their principal, nay almost intire. Support and Livelihood, was presented to the House, and read3 representing to *the House, That the Consumption of great Quantities of the Petitioners Manufactures abroad very much depends on the Vent and Intercourse of Trade between those Countries and the trading Parts aforesaid; and that, by Exchange of their Goods or Commodities for ours, not only a much greater Return and Demand is made of ours, but other innumerable Benefits and Advantages flow to the Petitioners; and that a considerable Balance remains thereby to this Kingdom, as the Petitioners have great Ileafon to believe; and that an additional Duty or Burthen on foreign Linens, imported into this Kingdom, will greatly embarrass that foreign Trade, and not only lessen the Petitioners Correspondence and Dealings abroad, but prove destruftrve of that most beneficial Branch of Trade, their Woollen Manufacture at home, to the Ruin and Distressof many Thousands of Families in those Parts: And therefore praying the Consideration of the House; and that the Petitioners may beat Liberty to be heard by themselves, or their Counsel, before the House will please to come to any Resolution to increase the Burthen at present lying upon foreign Linens.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom it is referred to consider further of the State of the Linen Manufactures of Great Britain and Ireland.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, towards raising the Supply granted to his Majesty, there be issued and applied the Sum of One Million, out of such Monies as have arisen, or shall or may arise, of the Surpluses, Excesses, or Overplus Monies, commonly called the Sinking Fund.

Re/ohedy That ir is the Opinion of this Committee, That all Borax and Camphire, which shall be refined in Great Britain, be intitled to the same Drawbacks on Exportation, as are now by Law on a like quantity of unrefined Borax, or unrefined Camphire, exported.
