Mr. Henry Archer reported from the Committee, who ^ere appointed to inquire what Laws are expired, or near expiring, and to report their opinion to the House which of them are fit.to be revived or continued, That the Committee had inquired accordingly, and had come to several Resolutions; which they had directed him to report ro the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the Resolutions of the Committee were read, and are as followed); viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That an Act, made in the Thirteenth and Fourteenth Years of the Reign of King Charles the Second, intituled, An Act for preventing of Theft and Rapine upon the Northern Borders of England; which, by several Acts, hath, froth time to time, been continued; and, by an Act made in the Sixth Year of the Reign of his present Majesty, for making perpetual several Acts, and for other Purposes therein mentioned, was further continued until the First Day of September 1744, and from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament; is near expiring, and fit to be continued.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the several Clauses, Powers, and Authorities, in the afore-mentioned Act, made in the Sixth Year of the Reign of his present Majesty, for the more effectual preventing of Theft and Rapine upon the Northern Borders of England, and which, by the said Act, were to continue in Force until the First Day of September 1744, and from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament; are near expiring, and fit to be continued.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That an Act, made in the Ninth Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the First, intituled, An Act for the more effectual punishing wicked and evil-disposed Persons going armed in Disguise, and d ing Injuries and Violences to the Persons and Properties of his Majesty s Subjects; and for the more speedy bringing the Offenders to Justice} which was to continue in Force from the Firil Day of June 1723, for Three Years, and from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament; and which, by an Act made in the Twelfth Year of the Reign of his said late Majesty, was continued, from the Expiration thereof, for Five Years, and from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament; and which, by another Act, made in the Sixth Year of the Reign of his present Majesty, for making perpetual several Acts; and for other Purposes therein mentioned; was further continued until the First Day of September 1736, and from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament; and which, by another Act, made in the Tenth Year of the Reign of his present Majesty, was further continued, from the Expiration thereof, until the First Day of September 1744, and from thence to the End of the then

next Session of Parliament; is near expiring, and fit to be continued.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Clause in an Act, made in the Sixth Year of the Reign of his present Majesty > for making perpetual several Acts; and for other Purposes therein mentioned; to prevent the cutting or breaking down the Bank of any River, or Sea Bank; which was to continue in force during the continuance of the afore-mentioned Act, made in the Ninth Year of the Reign of his said late Majesty; tand which, by another Act, made in the Tenth Year of the Reign of his present Majesty, was further continued, during the continuance of the afore-mentioned Act, made in the Ninth Year of the Reign of his said! late Majesty; is neat expiring, and fit to be continued. V

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Clause in the said Act, made in the Sixth Year of the Reign of his present Majesty, for making perpetual several Acts; and for other Purposes therein mentioned; to prevent the malicious cutting of Hop-binds growing on Poles in any Plantation of Hops; which was to continue: m force during the Continuance of the afore-mentioned Act, made in the Ninth Year of the Reign of his said late

Majesty; and which, by another Act, made in the Tenth Year of the Reign of his present Majesty, was further continued during the continuance of the afore-mentioned* Act, made in the Ninth Year of the Reign of his said late Majesty; is near expiring, and fit to be continued.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Clause in an Act, made in the Tenth Year of the Reign of his present Majesty, for continuing an Act for the more effectual punishing wicked and evil-disposed Persons going armed in Disguise, and doing Injuries and Violences to the Persons and Properties of his Majesty's Subjects; and for tire more speedy bringing the Offenders to Justice; and for ocher Purposes therein mentioned; to extend, during the Continuance of the said Act, all the Provisions therein contained, for the more speedy and easy bringing the Offenders against the said Act to Justice, and the Persons who shall conceal, aid, abet, or succour, such Offenders; and for making Satisfaction and Amends to all and every the Person ana Persons, their Executors and Administrators, for the Damages they shall have fuP tained or suffered by any Offender or Offenders against the said Act; and for the Encouragement of Persons to apprehend and secure such Offender and Offenders; and for the better and more impartial Trial of any Indictment or Information which shall be found, commenced, or prosecuted, for any of the Offences committed against the said Act; together with all Restrictions, Limitations, and Mitigations, by the said Act: directed; to all Cafes of Offences committed by unlawfully and maliciously breaking down, or cutting down, the Bank or Banks of any River, or any Sea Bank, thereby any Lands shall be overflowed or damaged; or by unlawfully and maliciously cutting any Hop-binds growing on Poles in any Plantation of Hops; or by wilfully and maliciously setting on Fire, or causing to be set on Fire, any Mine, Pir, or Dclph, of Coal or Cannel Coal; is near expiring, and fit to be continued.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That several Clauses in the said Act, made in the Tenth Year of the Reign of his present Majesty, for the more effectual Punishment of Persons maliciously fecting on Fire any Mine, Pit, or Delph, of Coal or Cannel Coal; or unlawfully hunting or caking any red or fallow Deer in Forests or Chaces, or beating or wounding the Keepers, or other Officers, in Forests, Chaces, or Parks; which were to continue in Force during the Continuance of the aforementioned Act, made in the Ninth Year of the Reign of his said late Majesty; are near expiring, and fit to be continued.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That an Act, made in the Twelfth Year of the Reign of his present Majesty, intituled, An Act for granting a Liberty to carry Sugars of the Growth, Produce, or Manufacture, of any of his Majesty’s Sugar Colonies in AmericOy from the said Colonies directly to foreign Parts, in Ships built in Great Britain, and navigated according to Law; which was to continue in Force for Five Years, from the 29th Day of September 1739, anc* ^rom thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament; is near expiring, and fit to be continued.

The said Resolutions, being severally read a Second time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

A Petition offeveral Traders, in behalf of themselves, American and others concerned in the Provinces of America, was Paper El,ls presented to the House, and read; reprefehting to the 0 Crcdlt’ House, That on Application to the last Parliament, setting forth the evil Consequences of railing the nominal Value of Silver a^nd Gold in the several Provinces in America, the then House of Commons came to several Resolutions, condemning the mischievous Practice of altering., the Rates of Silver and Gold, by issuing Bills of Credit as Money; and likewise by several Addresses to his Majesty, humbly desired him to command the respective Governors of the Colonies effectually to observe his Majesty’s Instructions relating thereto; and that, in pursuance of the said Resolutions and Addresses, his Majesty has, from time to time, given Orders to the respective Governors* punctually to execute the Laws now subsisting, and likewise restrained them from giving their Aflcnc to any Act for further Emissions; but that as all the Provinces have not been observant of the present Laws, although recommended and enforced by his Majesty’s Royal Orders and Instructions, large Emissions of Bills of Credit have lately been made, and, as the Petitioners are informed, more are intended, whereby all Estates in those Provinces, where such Bills of Credit obtain Currency, will be depreciated, and the Petitioners, among others, greatly injured; and representing to the House, That the Petitioners apprehend this Mischief cannot be remedied, and the like prevented for the future, without the Inter-pofuion of the British Legislature: And therefore praying the House to take this Matter into their Confide ration; and give such relief, as the House shall think fit.

The House was moved, that the Journal of the House, of the 25th and 28th Days of April 1740, in relation to the said Resolutions and Addresses, and his Majesty’s Answer to the said Addresses, might be read.

And the same being read accordingly;

fie said, that the said Sum was by him cotleded with great Pains and Care from a very large Number of the Company’s Books and Papers, chiefly from those kept by the Company’s Agents abroad, and by them transmitted home to the Company, and partly from the Company’s Books kept in London, and from the Vouchers from which the said Books, as well those from abroad as those at home, were collected and composed.

He said, that, by Books, he meant Journals, Ledgers, Cash Books, and Invoice Books: That, by Papers, he meant Invoices, Bills of Lading, Day Books, and other small Books, kept at Out-fadories, Lists of Living and Dead, Lists of Castle Slaves, and Canoe Men, inventories, Receipts, and all other Vouchers:

That the Vouchers for every thing paid in England were common Receipts, Invoices, and Bills of Lading; all which had undergone the Inspection and Examination of the Court of Assistants themselves, or some Committee thereof, as well as of this Examinant.

As to the Vouchers for all Payments and Disbursements made abroad, he said, That, by the established Rules of the Company, every Person in their Service, in what Station soever, who is intrusted with any of their Effects, whether the Value be much or little, is obliged to keep a true Account of all Receipts, and Dispofds thereof, in Writing, and, at the End of every Two Months, at farthest, to render to the Council which resides at the principal Fort, Two Originals, signed by the said Person so intrusted, and attested to be true by some other of the Company’s Servants, who has been privy to his Transactions: That then the Accountant refidingat the principal Fort, examines, and makes his Remarks upon, the Accounts so rendered, and requires Vouchers in Writing for such Transactions as are therein mentioned to have been had with Europeans (it being impradicable to have written Vouchers for Dealings with the Natives): That the said Accountant lays all Accounts so rendered, with his Remarks thereon, before the said Council; which examines, allows, or disallows, such Accounts, and makes such Deductions or Abatements therein as they fee causet That, afterwards, every such Account is returned to such Accountant, as one of the Vouchers from whence he is to compose the General Books to be sent home to the Company: That, by General Books, is meant Journals and Ledgers: That such Journals and Ledgers are Col-ledions arising from such Vouchers as before-mentioned, reduced into Order and Method: That the Councils abrqad have not Power to pais or allow any Account or Voucher finally, every thing being subject to the Company’s future Examination and Approbation in England: That each Journal and Ledger comprises the Accounts for Six Months; and, after having been duty stated and balanced abroad, they are sent home to the Company by the first safe Conveyance, together with all the original Vouchers from which they are composed: That, upon their Arrival in England, the said Journals and Ledgers are compared by this Examinant with the Vouchers; and the said Vouchers themselves are examined: That Objections and Deductions are thereupon made by the Company

The said Examinant being asked, Whether he could make Oath to the Truth of the Five total Sums last above-mentioned?

He answered, That he could not; for that whereas, in the Accounts of the first Seven Years, Recourse was had to every original Voucher, and every particular Item examined, compared, and written out; which was a very laborious Work, each Year’s Account being sufficient to employ a good Clerk for a whole Year’s Time; in the Accounts for the last Five Years, he had been obliged, for want of Time, to trust, in some Degree, to the Collections made and entered in the original Books from abroad, by the Accountants there: That, however, he is very certain, the total Sums for the last Five Year^ are less than the same will be found to be upon a minute and more careful Examination; because he had left every Charge out, of which he had not Time to be fully satisfied.

Your Committee having gone through all the Articles of the Account delivered to the House, and referred to the Committee, it was found, That the Royal African Company have paid for maintaining their Forts and Settlements upon the Coast of Africa, in Twelve Years, from December 31st, 1729,10 December 31st, 1741, the Sum of £. 203,433. 5. 10; which, when taken on an Average, comes to the Sum of £.16,952. 15. 5, for each Year: That there is the further Sum of £. 280. 7, paid each Year for Fees at the Exchequer; which being added to the said Sum of £. 16,952. 15. 5, makes the said annual Charge to be£. 17,233. 2. 5.

Then the Committee proceeded to examine into the Trading Stock of the Company, in order to fee how far the same was exhausted:

And the Company’s said Accountant offered to the Committee a Paper, containing a State of the Trading Stock and Debts of the said Company, as the same flood on the 31st Day of December 1729; and also a State of the like Debts and Trading Stock, as the same flood on the 31 ft Day of December 1743; propoling thereby to shew to the Committee how much the said Company were impaired in their Circumstances, by the Increase of their Debt, in 14 Years.

But the Committee requiring to be informed by what Gradations the said Debts had increased upon the Company, ordered the said Accountant to lay before them several States thereof, ending at different Periods within the said Fourteen Years; and accordingly he laid before the Committee a Paper, intituled, Four General States of the Debts and Trading Stock of the Royal African Company of England, as the same flood on December 31st, 1729;

December 31 ft, 1743:

By which it appeared, that the Company’s Debts, on the 31 It Day of December 1729, exceeded their Trading Stock by the Sum of £. 13,005; and, on the 31 ft of December 1733, the said Debts exceeded their Trading Stock by the Sum of £. 13*535; and, on the 31st of December 1737, ^a,c^ Debts exceeded their Trading

Stock by the Sum of £. 33,314; and, on the 31st of December 1743, the said Debts exceeded their Trading Stock by the Sum of £. 72,640.

And the said Accountant being examined thereupon, and asked, Why the Excess of the Company’s Debts above their Trading Stock had increased in the full Four Years no more than from £. 13,005 to £. 13,535 ? he said,

That the Company had raised the Sum of £.25,895. 16. 6, very soon after the said December 31st, 1729, by the Sale of African Stock belonging to the Company in their Corporate Capacity; all which was applied to the Payment of the Debts that were due December 31st, 1729; and thereby not only discharged the Sum of £. 13,005 (the Sum by which the said Company’s Debts exceeded their Trading Stock, December jifl, 1729), but also a further Sum of their Debts then due, to the Amount of £. 12,891; without which the Sum of £. 13>535» at the End of the Year 1733, would have been increased by the said Sum of £. 12,891, and the Company’s Debts would have exceeded their Trading Stock on the said December 31st, 1733, by £. 26,426, instead of £. 13,535, as it now {lands in the Paper so presented.

The said Examinant being asked, How the Excess of the Company’s Debts, in 1743* came to exceed the Excess in 1719, by no more than about £. 60,000, when the Charges of maintaining the Forces did exceed the Allowance by Parliament by a much greater Sum ? he said,

That the Company had raised £. 25,895. 16. 6, as before-mentioned; and, besides, the Profits in Trade had 20

been very considerable, or otherwise the said Debts mud at this time have been increased further, by means of the Charge of maintaining the Forts; and also by the whole Charges on Trade, the whole Charges of Management at hortie, and by all bad Debts and Losses which have accrued in the 14 Years.

And being asked, Whether by Trading Stock was meant and intended the Company’s whole Stock, or all which they reckoned themselves possessed of? and he having informed the Committee, that the Trading Stock was by no means the Whole of the Company’s Stock, he was required by the Committee to explain and distinguisti the fame, by making such Additions, as should be proper, to the Paper last presented.

This being done, and laid before your Committee, it appeared thereby, that, by the said Trading Stock, is meant. Gold, Goods, Merchandize, Negroes, and other Commodities for Barter or Sale: That the said Trading Stock is exclusive of all permanent or fixed Stock, comj moniy called Dead Stock; which, besides Castle Slaves, Canoe Men, Ordnance, Ammunition, Stores, Tools, Materials, and Furniture, confills principally in the Company’s Property in Ten several Forts or Castles: And, in the said Addition to the said Paper, the Value of 592 Castle Slaves, 71 Canoe Men, 307 Pieces of Ordnance, and Ammunition, Stores, Tools, Materials* and Furniture, according to the last Accounts and In* ventories received from the Coast of Africa, is set down to be £. 38,697 Sterling:

Also the Names of the Company’s Forts or Castles, with their Number of Guns, arc set down in the said Addition; but the Value of the Forts themselves is not fixed, otherwise than by certain Considerations offered to the Committee, in the following Words:

" As to the Value of the said Ten Forts or Castles, if " the same were to be fixed according to their Usefulness and Importance to the Trade and Navigation of €€ this Kingdom, depending thereon, it must be an im-" mense Sum of Money; or if valued according to " what they have cost the Company, in upwards of 70 " Years pall, exclusive of all Monies received from the " Public, or otherwise, such Value would amount to €( above One million of Money:

" But if valued according to what other neighbouring " Nations might afford, and would probably give for " them, they may, at a moderate Rate, be valued at " £ 500,000,

" Which Valuation must appear moderate to every of one who considers of what Importance the Trade to " Africa would be to any Nation possessing the fame; " and the said Valuation is likewise verified from ihefollowing Instances of the like Nature:

<c In the Year 1713, the Lords Commissioners of Trade and Plantations had an Offer from the King of " Prussia to fell to this Nation One Fort at Cape Three " Points, and Two other Out-works belonging to the " fame, for the Sum of £. 200,000 Crowns, amounting " t6 about £. 50,000 Sterling; and, according to that " Estimation, the African Company’s Forts and Castles " cannot be valued at so little as £. 500,000.

" And, in the Year 1718, the French Senegal Com-0 pany, who were possessed of only one small Fort in the " River Senegal, and another in the Island of Goree, near " the other, fold them to the new Company, then lately " established at Paris, for 1,600,000 Livres, or about " £. 80,000 Sterling; and, according to that Proportion, the Value of the Royal African Company’s Forts " and Settlements would amount to above £. 800,000.’’ With regard to the Letters from Four Captains of Four Men of War, to the Secretary of the Admiralty, which were referred to the Committee, concerning the State of the said Company’s Forts and Settlements at different times.

the Committee, on behalf of the said Company* that, although the said Company have exported from England Supplies of Merchandize, Stores, and Recruits, to their Forts and Castles, in 14 Years past, to the Amount of £. 160,000 Sterling, and have procured further Supplies of Merchandize there in Barter for such Commodities, as incourse of Trade ought to have been returned to England, to the Amount of a Very large Sum more; yet they have not of late Years been enabled to repair, fortify, and supply, their several Forts and Castles upon the Coast of Africa, in a sufficient Manner to secure the said Forts, and the Possession of the Trade on that Coast; (b that they are now become very much out of Repair, and not in a proper defensible Condition against any Enemy that may attempt to attack them; but with regard to what is further alleged in the said Letters, in relation to the Com* pany s not having sent any Supplies to several of their Forts, during certain Periods of Time, and the Numbers of white Men employed at the said Forts at the respective Times when the said Captains were on that Coast; it was observed* that, as those were Matters which could not come within the particular Knowledge and Observation of the Captains, they might be misinformed in relation to them; and, to prove this, the following Evidence was given: And, First,

As to the Supplies,

That Supplies of Goods, Stores, and Recruits, were sent by the Company, and delivered at Gambia; viz.

Captain Gregory, in his Letter [o Mr.

Corbett, dated June nth 1743, writes, "That the Storehouse of Dixcove was quite empty, having had no " Supply ffbm Cape Coast, or from the Royal African Company, for Three Years, as the Chief told him." The kid Accountant informed your Committee, That they never fend Supplies to Dixcove, or any other Out-fprt, directly from England: That Dixcove is a Place of more Use for supplying all other Forts with Timber, Vot. £4.

than for Trade t That Captain Gregbry Wds upon the Gold Coast about the Months of August and September, 1742: That the Company have not received their Accounts from the Gold Coast for all the Time of the Three Years mentioned in Captain Gregory's Letter j but the said Company’s Accountant proved, by the original Accounts and Books, signed by the several Chiefs of Dixcovt Fort, (which he presented to the Committee)* that Supplies had been sent to, and received at; that Fort by the said Chiefs in 2} Years, preceding December 31st, 1741, to the Amount of ^.983. 7s. j J. at prime Cost in England; all which, together with the Profits made by the Disposal thereof, had been applied to the Maintenance of that Fort in that time.

Captain Gregory, in the same Letter, fays the same of Gommenda as he does of Dixcove; in Answer to which* the said Company’s Accountant proved, by the original Accounts and Books signed by the several Chiefs at Commenda Fort (which he presented to the Committee', that Supplies had been sent to, and received at, that Fort by the said Chiefs, in 2\ Years preceding December 31st, 1741, to the Amount of £. 2,614. 13/. lid. at prime Cost in England.

Captain Gregory further writes, 44 That the People at, Cape Coast Castle complain of the Company’s not fend-1 u ing out any Goods or Provisions, as they promised; which occasioned them to be in a starving Condition;

" except only a Ship from Bristol, with £. 280 worth of Provisions for them and the Out-Forts:" To which the said Accountant, on behalf of the Company, said. That Captain Gregory must needs have been misinformed concerning the £. 280 worth of Provisions from Bristol, as they did not send out any such Parcel: That, provided Cape Coast Castle, and the other Forts, had been well furnished with good Cargoes of Merchandize, there would have been no absolute Necessity for fending out Provisions: That the Provisions which did arrive at Cape Coast Castle, during the time Captain Gregory was there, cost the Company the Sum of £. 719. 5. 8, Sterling before mentioned: That it is true, the Company’s Forts have n 4 been sufficiently supplied with Goods, but not true that the Company have sent no Goods, as appears by what was proved in Answer to the Complaint contained in Captain Wyndham s Letter: Also, the said Accountant proved, by Two Bills of Lading (which he presented), that a Cargo was sent to Cape Coast Castle in May last, amounting to £. 3,906. 14. 1.

As to the Number of white People mentioned to be employed in the Company’s Service* according to the Four Letters from the Four Captains of the Men of War;

The said Accountant admitted, on behalf of the Company, that the Number which they have had in their Service for some Years, have been by no means sufficient: That, nevertheless, the said Captains have been misinformed in that Matter: To prove which, the said Accountant presented to the Committee Four Lifts, drawn up by him, setting forth the Number, Names, and Employments, of the Persons who were living at each Place upon the Coast of Africa, at the respective Times, answering to the Times when the said Ships of War were there; alloan Abstract of the said Four Lifts; likewise Five original Lifts ot Living and Dead, received from the proper Officers abroad, as Vouchers to the Truth of the Lifts by him drawn up.

From whence it appeared, that the Number of white Persons flood as followeth:

By Captain Strange's Letter, 84. By the Company's Lift, 135.

By Captain Wyndham's Letter, 64. By the Company's Lift, 109.

By Captain Gregory's Letter, 52. By the Coiffpany’s Lift, 107.

By Captain Frogmore's Letter, 65. By the Company’* Lift, 101.

A Petition of the subscribing Merchants and Traders of the City of London, in behalf of themselves, and the Trade of these Kingdoms, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That, in the late War with France, upwards of Eleven hundred Sail of Ships and Vessels were taken by that Nation, from the Commencement of the War in 1702, to the Year 1707; when the Merchants of the said City, applying to Parliament for Protection, were relieved by an Act of Parliament* intituled, An Act for the better securing the Trade of these Kingdoms, by Cruizers arid Convoys; and rhat, in consequence of the said Act, the Cruizers and Convoys, appointed for the Defence and Safety of Trade, were immediately put under such proper Regulations, as, in a most effectual manner, answered the Ends proposed, to the great Emolument and Security of the trading Subject, and the Increase of the public Revenue; and representing to the House, That the melancholy Consideration of such heavy Losses, sustained within the first Five Years of the late War with France, and what they have suffered from the present War with Spain, have filled the Petitioners with the utmost Apprehensions from the formidable Inion of those Two Powers against thele Kingdoms; and that the Petitioners do not intend hereby to complain of any Loss through Neglects or Misconduct; but, in this their early Application for the Aid of this House, are finely prompted by a just and natural Desire to hav their Safety and Pro-tedlion established, by the Revival of a Law heretofore experienced to have been effectual: And therefore, as the Trade of this Nation is the only Source of its Treasure, and Support of its naval Strength, and as, consequfcntly, the Welfare and very Being of these Kingdoms, in the present Corijunfture, are closely connected with that Pro-tedlion and Security, which are the Objects of the Petitioners Application, praying, That the House will be pleased to take the Premises into their Consideration, and cause the Act of the Sixth of Queen Anne, intituled, An Act for the better securing the Trade of these Kingdoms, by Cruizers and Convoys, to be revived, or make such other Provision, by a Law, for the Protection of the Trade and Navigation of these Kingdoms, as the House shall think fit.

Ordered, Nemine contradicente, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for the better Securing of the Trade of these Kingdoms, by Cruizers and Convoys: And that Mr. Alderman Meathcote, Sir Daniel Lambert, the Lord Strange, Mr. Curzon, Sir John Philipps, Mr. Dodington, Sir John Bamards Adriniral Vernon, Mr. Bance, Mr. Southivell, and Mr. Hoblyn, do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

An ingrossed Bill for repealing the present Duties payable upon Glass Beads, and for granting to his Majesty other Duties in lieu thereof; and for allowing the same Drawbacks on the Exportation of all refined Borax and Camphire, as are allowed on unrefined Borax and Cam-phire exported; was read the Third time.

Resolved, That the Bill do pass: And that the Title be. An Act for repealing the Duties payable upon Glass Beads, and for granting other Duties in lieu thereof; and for allowing the same Drawbacks on the Exportation of refined Borax and Camphire, which are allowed on the Exportation of unrefined Borax and Camphire 1 and for preventing the fraudulent Exportation of British and Irish Linens, for the lake of the Bounty allowed by an Act, made in the Fifteenth and Sixteenth Year of his present Majesty’s Reign; and for explaining and amending the said Act, as to the Persons who are to receive the said Bounty.

Ordered, That Mr. Francis Fane do carry the Bill to the Lords, and desire their Concurrence.

A Motion being made, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for the better Encouragement of Seamen in his Majesty’s Service, and Privateers, to annoy the Enemy;

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer informed the House, that his Majesty had commanded him to acquaint the House, that, in case the House shall enter upon this Affair, his Majesty recommends it to their Consideration.

That on the 13th of June 1721, N. S. a Treaty of Peace was concluded at Madrid, between Great Britain and Spain; wherein it was expressly agreed, That all Goods, Merchandizes, Monies, Ships, and other Effects, which were seized or taken before War was declared between the Two Crowns, or since, should be immediately restored in the Species as they were seized or taken, or elle there should be paid the just and true Value they were worth at the Time they were seized or taken.

'Your Committee find, that, pursuanc to the said Treaty, the King of Spain wrote a Letter, by the Marquis de Cajlilar, to the Intendants of the Provinces of

and the Illes of the Canaries and Mallorca, dated the 16th of August 1721, wherein he referred to the said Treaty, and ordered them to restore, or pay the Value of, the Seizures or Captures which were made by virtue of an Order in the Month of September 1718, before the Time that the War was declared between the Two Crowns, or since; and ordered the same should be every where put in execution, and performed with all the Punctuality therein exprefifed, without any Exception:

That, on the 13th of March 1728, a Petition of divers Merchants, and others, trading to Portugal, Spain, and Italy, was presented to the House, and read; complaining of great Losses by their Ships and Effects being seized in the Ports or Harbours belonging to the King of Spain, and taken at Sea by the Men of War and Privateers belonging to the Crown, which was referred to a Committee of the whole House; and the Petitioners were heard before that Committee; and proved many Particulars in so plain and full a manner, that the House, on the 3d of April, agreed with the Committee in their Resolution;

" That several Ships, Merchandizes, and Effects, belonging to the Merchants of this Kingdom trading ro " Spain, Portugal, and Italy, have been taken and seized " by the Spaniards in manifest Violation of the Treaties " subsisting between the Two Crowns, for which no Restitution has yet been made; and that the Matters " and Crews of several of the said Ships have been barbarously and inhumanly treated."

And the same Day the House resolved, " That an " humble Address be presented to his Majesty, That he " will be graciously pleased to use his belt Endeavours to VOL. 24.

That, on the 9th of April, Mr. Treasurer reported his Majesty’s Answer in the following Words:

" That his Majesty is always extremely concerned " when he hears of the Losses and Sufferings of his Subjects, and will continue to use his best Endeavours, as he hath hitherto done, upon all Occasions, to obtain " for them just and reasonable Satisfaction."

A-Petition of the subscribing Merchants and Traders of the City of London, was prd’ented to the House, and read; setting forth, That many Privateers of great Force are now fitting out; and that the Merchants who trade inro foreign Parts, and in Goods of great Value, for the Security of their Ships and Cargoes, are obliged to take a greater Number of Men on board than is usual in Times of Peace; and represenring to the House, that, among such Numbers of Men, there is great Danger of Mutiny and Desertion, and many other Irregularities: And therefore praying. That a Clause may be inserted in the Bill, now depending in the House, for the better Encouragement of Seamen in his Majesty’s Service, and Privateers, to annoy the Enemy; whereby the Commanders of such private Men of W ar, or Merchant Ships having Letters of Marque, may be impowered to use such Discipline, for the Preservatkm of their Ships, and the better to annoy the Enemy, as may keep their respective Crews within the Bounds of their Duty and Obedience to the lawful Commands of the Captains and Commanders of the said private Ships of War, or Merchantmen, who shall take out Letters of Marque; which Request being for the general Good of the Trade of this Kingdom, the Petitioners submit to the Consideration of the House, to do therein as they shall think fit.

A Clause was offered to be added to the said Bill, pursuant to the Prayer of the said Petition:

And the same was twice read with a Blank, which was filled up; and the said Clause was amended.

Then the said Clause was, upon the Question pot thereupon, agreed to by the House to be made part of the Bill.

Ordered, That the Bill, with the Amendments, be ingrossed.

Pr. 3. L. 8. " After" High Treason," insert Clauses A. and B.

Clause A.

And be it further enacted, by the Authority a fore said,*

That if the eldest or any other Son or Sons of the said Pretender shall, after the said First Day of land, or attempt to land, or shall be found, in Great Britain or Ireland, or any of the Dominions or Territories belonging to the Crown of Great Britain, or shall be found on board any Ship, Vessel, or Boat, being so on board with Intent to land in Great Britain or Ireland, or any of the Dominions or Territories aforesaid, he and they, respectively, shall, by virtue of this Act, (land and be adjudged attainted of High Treason, to all Intents and Purposes whatsoever, and shall suffer and forfeit as Persons attainted of High Treafop by the Laws of the Land ought to suffer and forfeit.

Clause B.

And whereas in and by the said recited Act, of the Seventh Year of the Reign of her late Majesty Queen Anne, it is provided and enacted, That, after the Decease of the Person who pretended to be Prince of Wales, during the Life of the late King James, and since pretends to be King of Great Britain; and, at the End of the Term of Three Years after the immediate Succession to the Crown, upon the Demise of her said late Majesty, should take Effect, no Attainder for Treason should extend to the Difinhe-riting of any Heir, nor to the Prejudice of the Righc or Title of any Person or Persons, other than the Right or Title of the Offender or Offenders, during his, her, or their, natural Lives only; and that k should and might be lawful to every Person or Persons, to whom the Right or Interest of any Lands, Tenements, or Hereditaments, after the Death of any such Offender or Offenders, should or might have appertained, if no such Offender had been to enter into the fame; be it further enacted, by the Authority aforesaid, That the said Provision, so made by the said last recited Clause, shall not take place, nor have any Operation, Force, or Effect, whatsoever,

17 Geo. II. 3° — 4*

soever, until after the Deceases not only of the said Pretender, but also of his eldest and all and every other Son and Sons.

To the Title of the Bill add, "and for attainting " them of High Treason, in case they shall land, orattempt to land, in Great Britain, or any of the Dominions " thereunto belonging; and for suspending the Operation and Effect of a Clause in the Act of the Seventh " Year of the late Queen Anne, for improving the Union " of the Two Kingdoms, relating to the Forfeitures for " High Treason, until after the Decease of the Sons of " the said Petender."

Clause A, the First of the said Amendments, was read a Second time; and, being an ingrossed Clause, was read the Third time} and, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That no private Business be entered upon any Day, in the House, after One a Clock.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That no new Motion be made after Two of the Clock, unless the same relates to Business which has been entered upon before that Hour, and entertained by the House till, the Time of making such Motion.

The King’s After which, his Majesty was pleased to make am oft Speech, gracious Speech to bothHouses of Parliament, as*fpI]ow; eth; viz:

My Lords and Gentlemen,

I cannot put an End to this Session, without returning you my hearty Thanks for the many Demonstrations you have given me, during the Course of it, of your good Affedjons, and of your Zeal for the Support of my Government.

The great Preparations made by France on the Side of the Aufiridn Netherlands, mu ft convince all Europe of the ambitious and destrudive Views of that Crown in beginning the present War. It shall be my Care, in conjunct idn with my Allies, to pursue the most proper Measures to disappoint them, and to prosecute the War in such a manner as may be most effectual for procuring a safe and honourable Peace. My good Friends the States Genetal have already, in pursuance of my Requisition, agreed tofurnifli the Succours Stipulated by our Treaties; and 1 have received the strongest Assurancesof their just Sense not only of the common Danger, but also of the irriiparable Conned ion of their Interests with those of this Kingdom; which I shall not fail.to improve for the general Good of the common Cause.

Gentlemen of the House of Commons,

The great Readiness and Regard to the public Service, which you have shewn in granting the Supplies for the current Year, are highly acceptable to me: You may depend upon it, that they shall be strictly applied to the Ends for which they were given, and in such manner as may be most for the Honour and Advantage of Great Britain.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

' Let me earnestly recommend to you, in your several Stations, to be vigilant in preserving the Peace and good Order of the Kingdom. I promise myself, you will fe-riously confide r* that, in the present Conjundure, you are particularly called upon, by all the Motives of Duty and Interest, to stir up and cultivate in the Minds of my People, an hearty and more than ordinary Zeal for the Maintenance and Defence of our holy Religion, and excellent Constitut ion, against the malicious Designs of our Enemies.

And afterwards, the Lord Chancellor, by his Majesty’s Command, said,

My Lords and Gentlemen,

Pa^l am nt It is his Majesty’s Royal Will and Pleasure, that this prorogued. Parliament be prorogued to Thursday the Twenty-first Day of June next, to be then here held: And this Parliament is accordingly prorogued to Thursday the Twenty-first Day of June next.

The King’s Mr. Speaker reported, That the House attended his Speech Majesty in the House of Peers; where his Majesty was reported, pleated to make a most gracious Speech from the Throne, to both Houses of Parliament; of which Mr. Speaker said, he had, to prevent Mistakes, obtained a Copy; Which he read to the House; and is as followeth; viz.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

It is always a great Satisfaction to me to meet you in Parliament, and it is particularly so in this Conjuncture, as the present Posture of Affairs abroad requires your most serious Consideration. The Events of the last Summer have been so various, and some things have fallen out during the Course of it so much to the Disadvantage of the common Cause, the Consequences whereof remain still undecided, that great Attention must be given to them, and proper Measures taken for preventing or removing the ill Effects of them.

I have, in pursuance of your repeated Advice, exerted my Endeavours for the Support of the House of Austria, and in the Prosecution of the just and necessary War in which we are engaged. The Queen of Hungary, though attacked and invaded by Powers from whom she had the lead Reason to expect such a Conduct, has shewn the greatest Constancy and Resolution; and the King ofPa-land, pursuant to his Engagements with her, hath sent a very considerable Force to her Assistance. The King of Sardinia, with a Magnanimity and Firmness superior to the greatest Difficulties, has, with the Assistance of my Fleet, relifted the combined Forces of France and Spain sent against him; and, at last, happily defeated an En-terprize formed for his Destruction, and for the Reduction of Italy, as well as most of the Ports in the Mediterranean, under the Power of the House of Bourbon. Though our Success has not been answerable to our Willies, yet the vast Expeditions and Deligns of our Enemies, built upon new Intrigues and Alliances, and an additional Strength, have not hitherto taken place $ Vol. 24.

and will, I hope, by the Blessing of God, and the mutual united Vigour of Great Britain, and her Allies, be dilap-pointed. In conjunction with them, and with their effectual Assistance, and your Support, I am determined to carry on the War in such a manner as may be most conducive to that important End, which is my foie Aim, a lafe and honourable Peace; it being my firm Resolution never to abandon my Allies, and to procure the utmost Security to the Religion, Liberties, and Commerce, of my Kingdoms.

For this Purpose, I have always infilled, and am still endeavouring, with my Allies, particularly my good Friends the States General of the United Provinces, to fix the certain Proportions of Forces and Expence to be furnillied by each of the Confederates in the Prosecution of this just and necessary War.

Gentlemen of the House of Commons,

I have ordered the Estimates, for the Service of the ensuing Year, to be prepared, and laid before you; and desire you to grant me such Supplies, as shall be requisite for the Security and Welfare of the Nation, and for carrying on such Measures, as it shall be necessary for Great Britain to pursue in the present extraordinary Crilis. I am deeply fenlible of, and concerned for, the Burthens which lie upon my good Subjects; and you maybe assured, that no Endeavours shall be wanting on my Part to ease them in every Instance where the Consequences of doing so may not endanger their own true Interests.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

I have laid before you my Views and Intentions: Your Concurrence with me in a steady Pursuit of them, will bell manifest your Zeal for the common Cause, lay the surest Foundation for the real Support of our Allies, and for the Security and Prosperity of your Country; and nothing can add so much to the Weight and Efficacy of your Resolutions, as Unanimity and Dispatch.

Resolved, Nemine contradicente. That an humble Address be presented to his Majesty, to return his Majesty the Thanks of this House for his most gracious Speech from the Throne, to express our great Concern at what has happened, during the last Summer, to the Disadvantage of the common Cause; and to assure his Majesty, that, as we are very apprehensive of the Consequences of these Events, we will not only give great Attention to them, but do all that is in our Power to prevent or remove the ill Effects of them: That we cannot sufficiently applaud the Constancy and Resolution of the Queen of Hungary, nor can we less admire the Magnanimity and Firmncls of the King of Sardinia, who, with the Assistance of his Majesty, has been able to obstrud the ambitious Deligns of the House of Bourbon, in Italy; to return his Majesty our Thanks for his prudent and tender Regard to the Condition of his Subjects, and for his Endeavours to concert and stipulate with his Allies, particu-8 N larJy

Resolved, That if it shall appear, that any Person hath procured himself to be elected or returned a Member of this House, or endeavoured so to be, by Bribery, or any other corrupt Practices, this House will proceed with the utmost Severity against such Person.

Resolved, That if it shall appear, that any Person hath been tampering with any Witness, in respect of his Evidence to be given to this House, or any Committee thereof; or, directly or indirectly, hath endeavoured to deter or hinder any Person from appearing, or giving Evidence; the same is declared to be a high Crime and Misdemeanor; and this House will proceed with the utmost Severity against such Offender.

Refohedy That if it shall appear, that any Person hath given false Evidence in any same before this House, or any Committee thereof, this House will proceed with the utmost Severity against such Offender.

Refohedy That it is an high Infringement of the Liberties and Privileges of the Commons of Great Britain, for any Lord of Parliament, or any Lord Lieutenant of any County, to concern themselves in the Elections of Members to serve for the Commons in Parliament.

Address on Mr. York reported from the Committee, appointed Socttl? Yesterday to draw up an Address to be presented to his Majesty, That the Committee had drawn up an Address accordingly; which he read in his Place 5 and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

Most gracious Sovereign,

We your Majesty’s most dutiful and loyal Subjects, the Commons of Great Britain in Parliament assembled, beg Leave to return your Majesty our unfeigned Thanks for your Majesty’s most gracious Speech from the Throne.

It is with the deepest Concern we reflect upon what has l^appened, during the last Summer, to the Disadvantage of the Common Cause; and, as we cannot but be extremely apprehensive of the Consequences of these Events, we assure your Majesty, that we will not only give the greatest Attention to them, but exert our utmost Endeavours to prevent or remove the ill Effects of them.

We cannot sufficiently applaud the Constancy and Resolution of the Queen of Hungary under so many severe Trials; nor can we less admire the Magnanimity and Firmness of the King of Sardinia, whose excellent Con-dud, supported by your Majesty’s Assistance, has obstruded and defeated the ambitious Designs of the House of Bourbon, in Italy.

Your faithful Commons, with Hearts full of Duty and Gratitude, acknowledge your Majesty’s prudent and tender Regard to the Condition of your Subjects, as well as your continued Endeavours to concert and stipulate with your Allies, particularly the States General, whose Interests are inseparably connected with those of Great Britain, the Proportion of Forces and Expence to be borne by the respective Confederates in this War; and we beg Leave to assure your Majesty, that we will, to the utmost of our Power, assist and support your Majesty in carrying on this just and necessary War against the Enemies of these Kingdoms, and the Disturbers of Europe, till a safe and honourable Peace shall be obtained.

And, as your Majesty has been graciously pleased to lay before your Parliament your Royal Views and Intentions, your Majesty may depend upon your faithful Commons for their ready and chearful Assistance to maintain the Honour and Dignity of your Crown, effectually to support your Allies, and to contribute whatever shall be found necessary or expedient to bring about, with Honour, a just and reasonable Settlement of the present embroiled State of Europe.

The said Address, being read a Second time, was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House, Nemine contradicente.

Ordered, That the said Address be presented to his Majesty by the whole House.

Ordered, That such Members of this House as are of his Majesty’s most honourable Privy Council do humbly know his Majesty’s Pleasure when he will be attended by this House.

Gentlemen,

I thank you for this loyal and affectionate Address.

Your Unanimity, on this Occasion, cannot fail of having great Weight both at home and abroad: You may be allured whatever Supplies you shall find necessary to grant, shall be managed with the utmost (Economy, and applied to the Support of my Allies, and of the true Interests of my People.

A Petition of Henry Conyngham Esquire, was presented Great M«v to the House, and read; setting forth, That at the last low Election. Election of a Member to serve in this present Parliament for the Borough of Great Marlow, in the County of Bucks, in the room of Sir Thomas Hoby Baronet, deceased, the Petitioner and William Ockenden Esquire, were Candidates, and Thomas Harris and John Gibbons, Constables of the said Borough, presided as Returning Officer: That the Petitioner was duly elected by a Majority of legal Votes; but the said Constables acted in a very partial Manner, and admitted several Persons to vote for the said William Ockendeny who had no Right, apd refilled other? who had a legal Right, to vote; and were ready, and offered, to poll for the Petitioner: That feme of the Persons who had no Right, and were admitted to vote for the said William Ockenden, were objected to at the Time . of Polling, but were polled with Queries; it being proposed by the Agents of the said William Ockendeny and consented to by rum and the Petitioner, that the Legality of such Votes should be inquired into upon a Scrutiny, which was then agreed to be had; notwithstanding which, the said Constables very arbitrarily closed the Poll, by de<-daring the said William Ockenden duly elected by a Majority of Two Votes, without mentioning the Number? entered on the Poll; and absolutely refused going into a Scrutiny, though the Petitioner infilled upon their granting one, in pursuance of the aforesaid Agreement: That there was a great Mob collected, who were very outrageous, and intimidated and prevented several Persons from coming to poll foj* the Petitioner; whereby, and by many illegal and unwarrantable Practices, the said William Ockenden has been returned, in manifest Prejudice of the Per titioner, and in open Defiance of the Laws for securing the Freedom of Elections of Members to serve in Parliament; and that the Petitioner apprehends the said William Ockenden was not, at the Time of the said Election and Return, seised of, or intitled to, such an Estate as is required by Law to qualify him to beeleded, and serve as a Member in Parliament for the said Borough: And therefore praying the House to take the Premii.es into Consideration; and to grant the Petitioner such Relief, as to the House shall seem meet.

MR. Crow/e reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Mayor and Burgesses of the Town of Kingston upon Hull, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth j viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition,

Mr. William Mantley, being examined, said, That the Road leading from the Town of Kingston upon Hull, to and through Anlaby, is Part of the common Post Road from thence to Ixndon, and is also Pan of the public Road leading from Hull to Leeds, Wakefield, Halifax, and other trading towns in the West Riding of the County of York> through which Road many Persons go and return, in order to carry on their Trade and Traffic.

And the same Witness further said, That the Road lies in a low, flat, miry Country; and chat the Rains fall upon the same from the neighbouring Hills; and, for want of a proper Current to carry such Waters off, they settle on great Part of the Road, which is frequently under Water; and that by reason thereof, and of the Deepness of the Soil, and many heavy Carriages patting through the Road, the same is become so ruinous and bad in many Places, that, in the W inter Season, the same is dangerous to Travellers.

Mr. George Hopfon confirmed the Evidence of Mr. Mantley, and added, That, by reason of the Road being often under Water, Carriages and Travellers were obliged, for a great Part of the Year, to go another Way; which is not so near, by Three or Four Miles, as the other Road is.

And the same Evidence also said, That although the Statute-work has been constantly performed upon the Road, yet the same is far from being sufficient to repair 8 P the

As to their Proceedings in carrying on the Building:

In Queen Marys Court,

The Plinths of the Columns are cut down level with the Paving in the intended Kitchen; the digging and making Drains there, and carrying out Rubbish; the fitting up Four Cabins in the North West Corner Room in the Ground Floor of the South Building, including Bedsteads, Chests, Stools, Fire-grate, Fender, Tongs, Shotfel, and Poker; the Paving in the great Kitchen, an J at the Entrance from the intended Dining Hall to the said Kitchen, the Frames, Salhes, and Glass, in Five Windows in the East Front of the Kitchen, and the rough Pur beck Paving on the ‘South Side of the Sooth Building; are all finished and brought to Account; which amount to the Sum of One hundred Eighty-four Pounds Fifteen Shillings and Nine Pence -

The ordinary Works done this Year amount to the Sum of One thousand One hundred Twenty-three Pounds Thirteen Shillings and Eleven Pence -

Mr. Crowle reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Mayor, Bailiffs, and Burgesses, of the Town of Hedon in the County of York; and also the Petition of the Mayor and Burgesses of the Town of Kingston upon Hull; were referred. That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petitions; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To £rove the Allegations of the said Petition, the following Witnesses were called:

John Find, George Hopton, and Rickard James: Who being severally examined, said, That they know the Road leading from a Gate next the Township of Thorngtimbald in Holderness, in the East Riding of the County of York, called Sacred Gate, being the Extent of the Liberty of Hedon, on the South East Side of the said Town; and through the said Town of Hedon to the Bridge over the River Hull, called Hull North Bridge; which is the great Road from the East End and other Parts of Holderness ta the Town of Kingston upon Hull: That the same is, in many Parts thereof (except through the Streets of Hedon), through the Nature of the Soil, which is a deep Clay, and, by reason of the many heavy Carriages frequently passing through the fame, become so deep and ruinous, that, in the Winter Season, Travellers cannot pass and repass through the fame, without great Danger:

And further said, That if the said Road, which is about Eight computed Miles in Length, was amended, and kept in good Repair, the same would be of great Advantage to that Part of the Country, and to the Public in general.

And they also said, That although it is visible the Inhabitants of the several Parishes and Towniliips, rhrough which the said Road leads, have been at considerable Expences, over and above their Statute-work, in amending that Road; yet the same hath proved ineffectual, and cannot, by the ordinary Course provided by the Laws for repairing the Highways of this Kingdom, be effectually amended, and kept in good Repair, for the Accommodation of Travellers, unless some further Provision be made by Parliament for that Purpose.

A Petition of the Justices of the Peace, Gentlemen, Glergy, and Freeholders, inhabiting in Holderness, and 20

other Parts of the East Riding of the County of York, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth. That the Road leading from a Gate next the Township of Yhorngiimbald in Holderness, in the East Riding of the Countv of York, called Sacred Gate, being the Extent of the Liberty of the Town of Hedon, in the said Riding, on the South East Side of the said Town of Hedon, and, through the same Town, to the Bridge over the River Hull, commonly called Hull North Bridge, is Part of the great Highway from the East End and other Parts of Holderness aforesaid to the Town of Kingston upon Hull: That the said Road, in most Parts thereof, except through the Streets of Hedon aforesaid, is, through the nature of the Soil, and by reason of the many heavy Carriages passing through the fame, become so deep and ruinous, that, in Winter*time, Travellers cannot pass thereon, without great Danger; and that the Amending thereof would be of great Convenience and Benefit to the Public; and that although the Inhabitants of the said several Parishes and Town mips, through which the said Road lies, have been yearly act'efied, and paid several considerable Sums of Money for the repairing thereof, besides having done their common Day-woiks therein; yet it hath been found by Experience, that it cannot, by the ordinary Course provided by the Laws for repairing the Highways of this Kingdom, be effectually amended, and kept in good Repair, unless some further Provision be made for raising Money, to be applied for that Purpose: And therefore praying. That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for repairing and amending the said Road, except through the Streets of Hedon aforesaid.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for repairing the Road leading from a Gate, commonly called Sacred Gate, on the South East Side of the Town of Hedon, through the said Town, in the East Riding of the County of York, to Hull North Bridge: And that Mr, Crowle, Mr. OJbaldeston, Mr. Berkeley, and Major General Pulteney, do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

Ordered, That Mr. Lumley be added to the Committee, to whom the Petition of the several Inhabitants within the Counties of York and Durham, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, is referred.

CreatMarlow The House proceeded to the further Hearing of the Election. Matter of the Petition of Henry Esquire, complaining of an undue Election and Return for the Borough of Great Marlow, in the County of Bucks. 1

And the Counsel were called in.

And the Counsel for the Petitioner having proposed to prove by whom, since the Death of John Simes, whose Will was Yesterday by them produced, the Rents of Part of the Estate claimed by the Sitting Member, Mr. Ocken-den, and mentioned in the Particular, or Rental, by him delivered, have been received;

The Counsel for the Sitting Member acquainted the House, that as they doubted not to prove the Sitting Member to be legally qualified by the Addition of the Estates claimed by him, and mentioned in the Second Part of the Particular, or Rental, by him delivered, they did not intend to trouble the House with entering into the Title, Amount, or Value, of any of the Estates comprised in the Wills of John and Elias Simes, which were objected to by the Counsel for the Petitioner; but that they would rely upon the Value of such Part of the Estate comprised in the said Wills, and claimed by the said Sitting Member, and mentioned in the First Part of the Particular, or Rental, by him delivered, as is admitted by the Counsel for the Petitioner to belong to the said Sitting Member.

Then the Counsel for the Petitioner examined several Witnesses, and produced Evidence, in order to reduce the Value of another Part of the Estate claimed by the said Sitting Member, and mentioned in the Secofid Part of the Rental, or Particular, by him delivered.

They also examined several Witnesses, in order to prove that great Violences were committed by a Mob in the Streets of the said Borough at the time of the Election; and that the Tythingmen, appointed by the Returning Officers to guard the Door of the Place where the Poll was taken, denied Access to several Persons who claimed a Right to vote at the said Election.

Vex 24.

J. Clevland, Witt. Corbett, Alex. Geddes, J. Compton.

They also examined a Witness, in order to prove that One of the Returning Officers, who chiefly acted in taking the Poll at the said Election, was guilty of Patriality; that the Poll was hastily closed, and a Scrutiny denied, in Breach of an Agreement entered into during the time of the Election.

They also examined several Witnesses, and produced Evidence, in order to disqualify several Persons who voted for the Sitting Member, some as not having been rated, One as not having paid the Rates, and some as having received Alms.

And they having proposed to disqualify another Person who voted for the said Sitting Member, as having been induced to give his Vote both ,by Threats and Promises:

And they having proposed to prove that Fact by Evidence of the Confdfion of the said Person;

The Counsel for the Sitting Member objected to the Admission of that kind of Evidence.

And the Counfei for the Petitioner having been heard in Answer to that Objection:

And the Counsel for the Sitting Member having been heard by way of Reply;

The Counsel on both Sides were directed to withdraw.

The Counsel on both Sides were again called in; and the Counsel for the Petitioner were directed to proceed in their Evidence.

Then they examined a Witness, in order to prove what the said Person had confefied concerning his Inducement to vote for the Sitting Member.

Then the Counsel for the Petitioner examined several Witnesses, and produced Evidence, in order to add to the Poll of the Petitioner several Persons who tendered their Votes for him at the said Election, and were re-jedted.

And the Counsel for the Petitioner having finrlhed their Evidence:

And the Counsel on both Sides being directed to withdraw;

Ordered, That the further Hearing of the Matter of the Petition of Henry Conyngham Esquire, complaining of an undue Election and Return for the Borough of Great Marlow, in the County of Bucks, be adjourned till Tuef-day Morning next.

And then the House adjourned till Tuesday Morning next, Nine of the Clock.

Mr. Carew reported from the Committee, appointed to consider of the Laws in being relating to the Office of Coroner; and to report their Opinion to the House what further Provisions or Alterations may be proper to be made therein; That the Committee had considered the said Laws, accordingly; and had come to several Resolutions; which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and the Resolutions of the Committee are as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Office of Coroner is an antient Office at Common Law.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the said Office ought to be executed by Persons sufficient, having Lands of Freehold within the County wherein they execute such Office.

Vol. 24.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That such Coroners ought to have reasonable Satisfaction for executing their said Office.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That such Satisfaction ought to be paid to the said Coroners by the Treasurers of each respective County, to be repaid to the said Treasurers out of the County Stock.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the Election of such Coroners ought to be by Freeholders having Lands of Forty Shillings per Annum, as in the same of Election of Knights of the Shire.

Ordered, That the said Report be taken into further Consideration upon Thursday Morning next.

Mr. James Allen, being examined, said, That the Road from Borough-bridge through Northallerton, in the County of York, and through Darlington, in the County of Durham, to the City of Durham, is in a very ruinous Condition: That many Parts thereof are, in the Winter Season, byreason of the Depth of the Soil, very dangerous; and that several Accidents have happened to Travellers] and the Wheels of Carriages been frequently broke, in attempting to pass through the said Road:

That if the Inhabitants, besides their Statute-work* which they have constantly performed, were to beaffdTed at-Six Pence in the Pound yearly, to be applied towards amending the said Road, it would not be sufficient to keep the same in Repair.

Mr. John Parker, being examined, said, That he ha$ often known the Road from Borough-bridge to the River Tees impassable; and that the Road from the River Tees to Durham islikewife in a very bad Condition.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for repairing the High Road leading from Borortgk-bridge, in the County of York, through Northallerton, in the same County, to Croft Bridge on the River Tees, and from thence through Darlington, in the County of Durham, to the City of Durham: And that Mr. Hedworth, Mr. Bowest Sir Myles Stapylton, Mr. Turner, and Mr.- Van:, do prepare, and bring in, - the fame.

A Petition of the Commissioners appointed by virtue ft ye

of the Acts of Parliament for restoring the Harbour of Htrbo®r, Rye, in the County of Sussex, to its anticht Goodness* being offered to be presented to the House;

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer, by his Majest/s Command, acquainted the House, that his Majesty, having been informed of the Contents of the said Petition, recommends it to their Consideration.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read; setting forth, That the Port of Rye lies very convenient for Ships, which pass up and down the Channel, to favtf themselves in Strels of Weather, and from Enemies in Time of War: That it having been judged necessary by the Legislature, that the Harbour should be preserved; for the Benefit of Trade and Navigation; and that it might be rendered more commodious and useful, by making a new Cut from the Winchelsea Channel right out to Sea, the Commissioners appointed to execute the Powers given by the Acts of Parliament for that Purpose, have proceeded, with the utmost Integrity and Diligence, to perfect so desirable a Work, as fast as the Income of the Fund granted, and the Money which could be borrowed thereon, would allow: That the most difficult and expen-five Part of the Works are done, and the Whole might be completed within Two Years at furthest, for a small Sum of Money; but the annual Produce of the Fund, after the Interest due to the Creditors is paid, is now so low, that the Commissioners cannot proceed further till the present Debt is discharged; whereby the Public must, for many Years, be deprived of the Benefit of a Harbour so commodiously situated for the Safety of Navigation, and which, in Tufte of War, might preserve the Lives and Effects of very great Numbers of his Majesty’s trading Subjects; and from whence his Enemies might be greatly annoyed: And therefore pray this House to take the Premises into Consideration, and to do therein what to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Resolved, That an humble Address be presented to his Ditto. Majesty, That he will be graciously pleased to direct, that the Import of the Officers of the Navy, and Elder Brothers of Trinity-house, relating to the Harbour of Rye, taken by Order of their Excellencies the late Lords Justices, be laid before this House.

Ordered, That the said Address be presented to his Majesty, by such Members of this House as are of his Majesty’s most Honourable Privy Council.

Art. 1.

Whereas, from the dangerous Situation of Affairs in Europe, there is an atjfolute and prefiing Necessity for his most Serene Ele&oral Highness to make such an Augmentation of his Troops, as may enable him to garrison his Towns, and to cover his own Frontiers, as well as those of the Allies of his Britannic Majesty, and the Frontiers of their High Mightinesse, he obliges himself to proceed to such an Augmentation immediately; but his Subjects not being in a Condition of themselves to provide for this extraordinary Expence, his Britannic Majesty, having weighed the Advantage that must result therefrom to the common Cause, and in order to enable him accordingly, does grant and promise to his most Serene Electoral Highness an annual Subsidy of Two hundred and Sixty thousand Dutch Florins, for the Term of Four Years to come; and their High Mightinesse do grant and promise to his most Serene Electoral Highness the like Sum of Two hundred and Sixty thousand Dutch Florins, for the likcATcrm of Four Years, to commence from the Day of flgning this present Treaty; which said Subsidy shall be regularly paid by Quarterly Payments, as the same shall become due.

Art. 2.

In consequence of this Subsidy, his most Serene Electoral Highness promises and engages to keep and main-tab, during the Term of Four Years, a Body of Nine thousand Foot and One thousand Horse, Troops of Mun* Jler, in good Condition, and in Readiness to serve either in Camp and in garrisoning such Places of his Dominions, as shall be judged most necessary, as well for their Security as for that of the neighbouring Jetties of his Britannic Majesty, atfd for the‘Safety1 or the States of their High Mightinesse,

...: . ;Art- 3*

And if it is found indispensably necessary by the high

contracting Parties, that a further Augmentation of the Troops of his most Serene Ele&oral Highness should be made, in order to join the Forces of his Britannic Majesty, or those of the States and their Allies, they shall be raised in consequence of a further Subsidy, in that same to be agreed upon, and the Manner settled according to which the said Corps is to be employed.

'Art. 4;

For a further Proof of the Uprightness of his Intentions, his most Serene Electoral Highness obliges himself torejett constantly all such Propositions of Engagements, from what Quarter soever they may come, as ball appear to his Britannic Majesty and their High Mightinesse inconsistent with the Good of the common Cause. . , Art. 5.,

' The present Treaty of Alliance shall be ratified by the high contracting Parties, and the Ratifications shall be exchanged here at thtHague within the Space of a Month, or sooner, if possible.

Translation of a Treaty concluded the 1 ith August 1744, at London, with the Queen of Hungary.

Her Majesty the Queen of Hungary and Bohemia having caused to be represented to his Majesty the King of Great Britain, with as much Instance as Regret at being any longer a Burthen to him for her own Support, and for that of the common Cause, that her Finances arein-tirely exhausted, and the Subudy granted by his Britannic Majesty for this present Year actually consumed by the extraordinary Efforts that she has made, and by the vast Number of Troops which file has kept in the Field, amounting to upwards of One hundred and Seventy thousand Men, for making head in all Parts, jointly with her faithful Allies, against the common Enemies, and particularly- for putting a Stop to their Progress in the Low Countries, by a powerful Diversion upon the Rhine: For effecting winch, her Majesty has spared nothing, and which has effectually obliged France to fend thither from Flanders a great Body of her Forces; so that, without a fneeciy Succour of an additional Subsidy, her Majesty the Queen will be under an absolute Impossibility even to continue tile Pay to the Troops that she has on Foot; far from being able to make a farther Levy, and support the other Mea lures and Expences which are indispensably necessary towards enabling her to resist effectually the ifew Invasion formed by the King of Prussia against her h.reditary Dominions, and to repel it speedily; to the end that France may not again turn her whole Force against the Allies of the Queen:

Vol, 24,

after having provided for the Safety of *her hereditary Dominions; and she. shall cause to be exhibited to his Britannic Majesty the effective Muster Rolls within the Space of Three Months at the farthest.

So done, settled, and agreed, between the under-written Ministers of his Majesty the King of Great Britain* and of her Majesty the Queen of Hungary and Bohemia, under the reciprocal Assurance, that their Majesties will ratify it, and cause the Ratifications to be exchanged as soon as possible. London, the Eleventh Day of the Month of Augiiji 1744.

(L. S.) Hardwicke, C. (L. S.) Harrington, P. (L. S.) Holies Newcastle. (L. S.) Carteret.

(L. S.) H. Pelham.

frtcan ' A Petition of the Royal African Company of England, fort* Icc. being offered to be presented to the House;

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer, by his Majesty’s Command, acquainted the House, That his Majesty, having been informed of the Contents of the said Petition, recommends it to their Consideration.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read; setting forth. That the Trade to Africa is of the greatest Importance^ not only as it takes off great Quantities of Home Manufactures, which are paid for in Gpld, Gums, Dyeing Woods, Ivory, Bees. Wax, and other valuable Commodities; but likewise as it furnishes the Colonies arid Plantations in America with Negro Servants; upon v/hofe Labour the said Colonies and Plantations, and the Trade and Navigation arising the reby, do principally depend: That it hath always been the Sense of this House, that Forts and Castles are necessary for carrying on and prefetving the Trade to Africa to this Nation: That it hath appeared to this House, upon full Examiriation.and Consideration of the State of the Trade to Africa that the British Forts and Settlements, belonging to the Petitioners there, cannot be supported, and the Trade preserved, without the Aid of Parliament: That the said Company did, for many Years, bear the whole Burthen of preserving to this Nation that inestimable Trade, to their own irreparable Loss and Damage; and that it hath been made appear to this House, that, in the Fourteen Years preceding the 31 ^.December 1743, the Petitioners had expended above One hundred thousand Pounds, on the Support of Maintenance of their said Forts and Settlements, more than had been granted by Parliament for that Service; whereby the Petitioners have incurred a large Debt: That, in case this House shall think fit to make effectual Provision for repairing and keeping the said Forts and Settlements 1 in a sufficient defensible Condition, for the Protest ion and Benefit of all his Majesty’s Subjects trading to those Parts, and for the Support and Preservation of his Majesty^ Colonies and Plantations in America, depending upon that Trade, and to ease the Petitioners of the heavy Burthens which have so long laid upon them, the said Petitioners do apprehend, that they shall be well able not only effectually to protect and support the British Interest in Africa, but also to put an intire Stop to the last great Encroachments of other Nations there, and likewise to make such Improvements, and to procure to this Nation such farther Benefits and Advantages, as the said most va-luableTrade is capable of affording: That the Petitioners did present to this House, last Session, the most moderate Estimates they could make, as well for putting their Forts and Settlements into good Repair, as for supporting and maintaining them afterwards in a defensible Condition; whereupon the Sum of Twenty thousand Pounds only, was granted for the Year 1744: That although the Petitioners well know, that the said Sum of Twenty thousand Pounds, being much less than their Estimates, would fall far short of what was necessary for any one Year, and more especially in this Time of War with France, of late. Years grown to be our most formidable Rival in this fundamental Branch of Trade; and although the Sum of One hundred thousand Pounds, by them expended as before-

mentioned, was not then taken into Consideration, yet the Petitioners were ind uced to accept of the said Sum of Twenty thousand Pounds, in firm Reliance and Hope of being fully and justly considered during this present Session: That the Petitioners have accordingly received from the Lords of the Treasury the said Sum of Twenty thousand Pounds, parfuant to the Resolutions of this House the last Session; and have thereupon fitted out sundry Ships of their own, to assist in repairing, and to attend the other Services of the said Forts and Settlements; and, for the more Expedition, have taken up another large Ship upon Freight; and, by them, have sent out as many Recruits of Soldiers and Artificers as they could procure in Time, and as the said Ships could carry; and likewise such Supplies of Stores, Arms, Ammunition, Goods, and other Necessaries, for the Repairs, Defence, and Subsistence, of the said several Forts and Settlements, as amount, in the Whole, to upwards of Twenty thousand Pounds; a par- , ticular Account whereof the Petitioners are ready to lay before this House, when they shall be pleased to require the fame: That the Petitioners, therefore, apprehend it to be their Duty to lay the Premises before this House, and to submit it to their Consideration to grant the Petitioners such Relief, and to make such effectual Provision for repairing, supporting, and maintaining,'their said Forts and Settlements in a proper Condition, for the most valuable Ends herein before set forth; or otherwise to put the said Forts and Settlements under such other Care and Management, and to make the Petitioners such a reasonable and just Satisfaction for their Property and Interest therein, as to this House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Ordered, That the Royal African Company of England Africa* do lay before this House, an Account of what Supplies Forts»*c-they have sent out for the Repairs, Defence, and Subsistence, of their Forts andj Settlements in Africa, for the Year 1744; distinguishing the Species, Numbers, Quantities, and Amounts, of all the Particulars whereof the said Supplies have consisted, and the Places they were sent to.
