A Petition of the Mayor, Aldermen, and Burgesses, of Beverley the Town of Beverley, in the East Riding of the County of York, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That by an Act, passed in the Thirteenth Year of the Reign of King George the First, intituled, An Act for cleansing, deepening, and widening, a Creek, called Beverley Beck, running into the River Hull; and for repairing the Staiths near the said Beck; and for amending the Roads leading from the said River to the Town of Beverley, in the East Riding of the County of York; several small Tolls and Duties on divers Goods, Wares, and Merchandizes, in the said Act mentioned, laden, or unladen, in any Part of the said Beck, or at any of the said public Staiths, or other Places therein mentioned, were granted and made payable to the Mayor, Alderfcen, and Capital Burgesses, of the said Town of Beverley, for the Time being, for the cleansing, deepening, widening, and preserving, the said Beck, and amending and maintaining the said Staiths, Roads, and Ways: That the said Beck,

Staiths, and Roads, being in a very ruinous Condition at the time of passing the said Act, the said Mayor, Aldermen, and Capital Burgesses, were obliged to borrow} a considerable Sum of Money, to put the same into tolerable Condition; which Money so borrowed, together with the Tolls collected by virtue of the said Act, have been duly laid out and applied according to the Directions thereby given; but that the Petitioners find, that the Money arising from the said Tolls and Duties will never be sufficient to discharge the said Debt, and answer the Purposes of the said Act; and that the said Beck is now in very great Danger of being warped and choaked up by the Sludge and Soil brought in by the Tides, and by the Earth falling in from the Banks of the said Beck; which, in many Places on both Sides thereof, are Ihot in, and will require to be supported by Piles and Jetty-work: That the Tolls and Duties, granted by the said Act, are not duly proportioned to the Values of the Goods on which they are laid; so that the same fall heavy on some Tradesmen, whilst: others pay little or nothing; and many of the said Tolls and Duties are loft, for want of proper Powers to examine into the several Sorts of Goods chargeable therewith, and the Weights and Measures thereof: That it hath been found by Experience, that the Carriage of Goods to and from the said Beck, and lliver Hull, in Carriages having narrow Wheels, (hod with Iron, hath greatly contributed to the Destruction of the several Ways, Banks, Roads, and Pavements, leading from the said Town to the said Beck and River: That keeping open the said Beck, and having good Roads thereto, and to the said River Hull, have been found very beneficial to the Inhabitants and Traders of the said Town, and Country about the same: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a

A Petition of the Surgeons of London, whose Names 9f Surgeons. arc t^crcunt^ subscribed, on behalf of themselves, and other the Surgeons in the City and Suburbs of London, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth,

' That, by an Act of Parliament, made in the 3 2d Year of the late King Henry the Eighth, afeer reciting, That, within the City of London, there were Two several and distinct Companies of Surgeons, occupying the Science and Faculty of Surgery; the one called the Barbers of London, and the other the Surgeons of London; and that the Company of Barbers were incorporated in the Reign of King Edward the Fourth; and that the other Company, called the Surgeons, had not any Manner of Corporation; and that it was necessary, for the Purposes in the said Act mentioned, that the said Two distin<5l Companies should be united, it was thereby enabled, " That the said Two several and distintft Companies of Surgeons, that is to, say, both the Barbers and the Surgeons, should be united, and made one Body Corporate, by the Name of Masters or Governors of the Mystery and Commonalty of Barbers and Surgeons of London; and that they should, by the same Name, possess and enjoy, to them and their Successors, all inch Lands, Tenements, and other Hereditaments, which the Company of Barbers then had and enjoyed, and all Liberties, Privileges, and Franchises, and other Things, at any time given or granted to the said Companies of Barbers or Surgeons by Act of Parliament, Letters Patents, or otherwise;" and it was there by.enabled,

" That no Person within the City and Suburbs of London, and One Mile Compass of the said City, using any Barbery or Shaving, should pratftife any Surgery, except Drawing of Teeth only; and that no Person, practising Surgery within the Circuit aforesaid, should use or exercise Barbery or ShavingThat King Charles the First, by Letters Patents under the Great Seal, in the Fifth Year of his Reign, confirmed the Possessions and Privileges granted to, and vested in, the said united Company by the said former Act of Parliament, and other Royal Grants therein mentioned, and referred to; and gave Power to the said Company to make By-laws, for the Government of the said Society, and to cleft Masters or Governors, and to constitute Ten Persons to be Examiners of the Surgeons of London, during their Lives; and it was thereby farther granted, that no Person, whether "Freeman, Foreigner, Native of England, or Alien, should praftifr Surgery in London or Westminster, or within Seven Miles of the City of London, unless previously examined, allowed, and admitted, by the Company, in manner therein mentioned; and that the Surgeons, so examined, might practise Surgery in any £art of England; and that the Vol. 2<j.

and Practice therepf of great and public Benefit and Utility to this Kingdom; and that the Barbers, belonging to the said Corporation, are now, and have been many Years, employed in a Business foreign to, and independent of, the Practice of Surgery; and that the Surgeons, belonging to the same Corporation, being now become a numerous and considerable Body, and finding their Union with the Barbers inconvenient in many Respects, and in no degree conducive to the Progress or Improvement of the Art of Surgery, arc therefore desirous that the Surgeons, being Freemen of the said Company, may be made a Corporation separate and distinct from, and independent of, the Barbers of, and belonging to, the said Company:

And therefore praying the House to give Leave, that i Bill may be brought in for dissolving and vacating the Union and Incorporation of the Barbers and Surgeons, made by the said former Act; and for making the Surgeons of the said Company a separate and distinct Corporation; and for making a Partition and Division of the real and personal Estate and Effects of, and belonging to, the said united Companies, unco, and for the separate Benefit of, the said Two Companies, so proposed to be separated, as to this House shall seem meet and reasonable.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the fame, with their Opinion thereupon, to the House:

A Petition of several Persons, under the Denomination Regular; of Pawnbrokers, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, in behalf of themselves, and several others, within the Ci-bruri ties of London and Westminster, and the Bills of Mortality, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth,

That the Petitioners have, for many Years, carried on the Business of lending (mail Sums of Money upon Pledges; great Numbers of whom have regularly served Seven Years Apprenticeship, and many Years Journeymen; and have, for a long time, been settled as Mailers in the Business; and have large Families depending on them for their Support; and, by long Experience, find, that a Business of this Nature is absolutely necessary in Places where Trade and Commerce floorish: That the Petitioners have long laboured under the public Reproach and Infamy of being Extortioners, and great Encouragers of Thieves; which, they apprehend, is owing to Misreprescntations of the Nature and Profit of their Business; for they are so far from being Encouragers of Thieves, that they very frequently detest them, and could oftener do so, if authorized to (lop suspected Persons; which chey many times dare not do, left, by miflaking Persons, they should subject themselves to vexatious and expensive Law Suits: That the Petitioners apprehend, their being deemed Extortioners arises from comparing their reputed or seeming Profit with the legal Interest of Money, without considering the great Expence and Labour attending the Business; for the Petitioners hope to make appear, to the Satisfaction of this House, that it cannot be carried on at a lower Rate, unless a certain Time was lectled and limited for tfv Redemption of Pledges, and the Petitioners not obliged to keep great and perishing Stocks by them; in which Cafe, they could afford, and would supply, the honed and industrious Poor at a cheaper Rate than they at present do:

That the Petitioners, not being legally justified in taking more than after the Rate of Five Pounds for the Loanot One hundred Pounds for One Year; and not being authorized to fell the Goods pledged with them, though of ever so peri(liable a Nature, many vexatious and expenfiveLaw Suits are daily commenced and carried on against the Petitioners, in respect thereof: That if the Business was regulated, and only such as should appear to be honed and reputable Persons were licensed by proper Authority to follow the fame, it WQuld not only be of much greater

Service

18 Geo. II.

I6 Februarii. , 733

Service to the honest and industrious Poor, but of public Benefit, by hindering Persons of ill Fame and Reputation from acting the rein; which, at present, is too much prac-tiled; and, from whose ill Conduct, the public Odium, conceived against the Business, has arisen: That the Petitioners, beinff conscious of their Innocence, are very desirous of having their Business and PraClices examined into; and are ready to do every thing in their Power to give Light into the same; not in the lead doubting but, upon the strictest Enquiry, they shall be so happy as not only to wipe off the unmerited Calumny they have so long groaned under, but that they shall be so regulated by this House, as to be able to carry on their Business, for the future, with Credit and Reputation: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Confutation, and grant such Relief therein as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Navy Ofti- A Petition of the several Persons, whose Names are

cers Widow* thereunto subscribed, distretted Widows of Commission

Pensions. ani Warrant Officers of his MajestyVRoyal Navy, in behalf of themselves, and many Hundred others under the like Circumstances (together with a Copy of the Letters Patent herein after-mentioned), was presented to the House} and the said Petition was read } reciting his present Majesty’s Letters Patent, under his Privy Seal, dated the 50th Day of August 1732, granting and appointing Three Pence in the Pound from thenceforth to be deduced out of the Pay and Half-pay of all Officers of his Majesty's Navy, to be applied for the Support of the Widows of all Officers dying after that time; and also reciting, That his Majesty did thereby appoint a certain Number of Persons, confuting of the then Lords of the Admiralty, all the Flag Officers of the Navy, divers Captains, Lieutenants, Matters, Boatswains, Gunners, Carpenters, Pursers, and Surgeons, therein named, to be Commissioners or Governors, for the Management of such Charity; and to be under the Direction of a President, who is always to be the Lord High Admiral, or First Commissioner of the Admiralty, for the Time being, Two Vice Presidents, to be annually chosen, and a Treasurer, who is to be always the Treasurer of the Navy for the Time being; who were impowered to receive as well the said Three Pence in the Pound, as also all Pensions granted upon the ordinary Estimate of the Navy, and all Gifts and Benevolences which might thereafter be given towards the Support of such Widows; and that / whereas several of the Commissioners therein named could not conveniently meet, in order to carry on his Majesty’s Royal Intentions, by reason whereof, many Inconveniences might ensue, Fifteen of the said Commissioners are thereby appointed to be a Court of Assistants of the said Charity; who are to be chosen annually at a General Court, and then to elect Two new Vice Presidents; and they are required to meet once a Month, or oftener, to the Number of Five or more, of which One of the Vice Presidents, or the Treasurer of the Navy, to be always One; and, upon the Death of a Vice President, or One of the Court of Assistants, a Court to be called, toconfift of Seven at the least, to fill up such Vacancy; and such Court

j. 1744.

of Assistants are to have the whose Management of the said Charity, and to examine, upon Oath, all Claims relating thereto, and propose, from time to time, such regular Methods to his Majesty as shall be necessary for the due Execution of this Trust; and setting forth, That, in the Year 1733, his Majesty, by his Sign Manual, established certain Orders for the Government of the Corporation of this Charity; whereby the Widow of a Captain, not possessed of Forty-five Pounds fer Annum, the Widow of a Lieurenanc or Master, not possessed of Thirty Pounds fer Annuirn> and the Widows of all inferior Officers, not pof- fefied of Twenty Pounds fer Annum, are intituled to a Distribution of this Charity; the Quantum to be settled by the Court of Assistants, who are impowered to lay out the Surplus in Government Securities, for raising a capital Stock for the Benefit of the Charity; and each Widow is to make Oath every Year, that (he is not possessed of an Income to the Value above prescribed, before (he can receive any Part of this Charity; as also, that (he is not married again j and it is especially directed, that no Officer or Servant, employed in this Chariry, shall receive any Salary or Gratuity, but that the whole shall be transacted gratis; and further setting forth. That, in the Year 1735* the Pay and Victualling of a fictitious Man in every Hundred Seamen borne on the Books of his Majesty’s Navy, was granted by Parliament as a Provision for all Sea Officers Widows in general, as well such whose Husbands died before as since the Date of his Majesty's Letters Patent; which is also under the Government and Direction of the Corporation and Court of Assistants thereby efla-blittied; and representing to the House, Thar, notwithstanding his Majesty’s wife and charitable Provision foe a just and proper Management of this Charity, the Petitioners have been very great Sufferers by the Dilute off holding such regular Monthly Meetings of the Court of Assistants, as directed by his Majesty 5 the said Court confiding principally of Persons in great Stations and Employments; their necessary Attention to more public and weighty Affairs have not offered them Ldfare to giirc such constant Attendance as the Nature of this Trust requires by which Means, the Business thereof hath beer* chiefly transaded by Clerks, who have been frequently imposed upon by artful and designing Women, to admit them into a Participation of this Charity, who were nowise intitled thereto; and that particularly some Women have been admitted, whose Circumstances exceeded his Majesty^ Limitation j some who have been married again, and others, whose Husbands had not been dead above Three or Four Months, have received an equal Share with those whose Husbands had been dead several Years; ail which Abuses could not have happened, if their Claims had been publicly entered before a Court of Assistants; to which the Petitioners might have had Rc-course, to disprove the same; and that, notwithstanding his Majesty’s express Command to the contrary, considerable Sums have been deducted for Salaries, and Fees for making up and passing Accounts, and other incident Charges; and further letting forth. That the Money arising by the Hundredth Man, and the Deduction of Three Pence in the Pound out of the Officers Pay, amounted to upwards of Nine thousand Pounds one Year with another, when no more than Ten thousand Men were borne upon the Books of his Majesty’s Navy; and that as Forty thousand have been allowed for Four Years past, the Petitioners did expect the Funds would of cotirfe have produced Four times the Money that arose from only Ten thousand; but no more than Fifteen thousand Seven hundred Eighty-four Pounds Nine Shillings and Eight Pence was distributed in the Year 1742; and*no more than Sixteen thousand Fifty-one Pounds Seven Shillings and One Penny, in the Year 1743; which fell far short of the respective Sums allowed by his Majesty; and the Petitioners are now near Twenty Months in Arrear; to wit, from the First Day of June 1743; and most of them having no Subsistence but what arises from this Charity, are driven to inexprtffible Want and Misery; for the

reduced, so as to be unable to provide for their numerous Poor, without the Assistance and Support of the Surgeons: That as the Surgeons have thought proper, for above Two hundred Years, to acquiesce under the Union of the Two Companies, whilst it was advantageous to them, they ought, in Justice and Gratitude, to submit to it, when become beneficial to the Barbers: That, nevertheless, the Petitioners find, by the printed Votes of this House, that forne of the Surgeons have, without the Concurrence of the Petitioners, presented a Petition for Leave that a Bill may be brought in to dissolve the said Union, and to make a Partition of the real and personal Estates of the united Company: That the Petitioners are satisfied, this House will not, without the most evident and abiblute Necessity, agree to the Repeal of an Act of / Parliament, in which the Petitioners Rights and Properties are so deeply concerned: That the Petitioners are not conscious that the said Union is, in any respect, inconvenient to the Practice of Surgery, or to the Progress or Improvement of that Science, or in the lead detrimental to the public Good; nor is the Business of Barbery or Shaving become more foreign to, or independent of, the Practice of Surgery than it was by the Legislature understood and declared to be at the time the said Union was established: That the Petitioners hope, if they may have an Opportunity cf being heard, to make it appear, that the Diflblution and Division prayed by the Surgeons will be a manifest Prejudice and lnjustice to the Petitioners; and that the Allegations of the said Petition have no manner of Foundation, nor are sufficient to induce a Repeal of the Act in Question: And therefore praying the House to take the Calc of the Petitioners into Consideration; and that they may have Leave to be heard, by their Counid, in what they have to offer against the Allegations and Prayer of the said Petition, at such Times, and in such Manner, as the House shall please to order; or that the Petitioners may have such other Relief in the Premises, as to the House shall seem meet.

A Petition of several Yeomen, Farmers, and Graziers, in the Counties of Middlesex, Surrey, and Kent, whole Names are thereunto subscribed, in behalf of themselves, and many others, concerned in the Growth of Corn, and Vol. 24.

the Breeding and Fatting of Cattle, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That, by an Act, made in the Second Year of the Reign of King William and Queen Mary, for encouraging the Distilling of Brandy and Spirits from Corn,*which recites, That, by an Act, made in the Parliament held in the First Year of their* Majesties Reign, intituled, An Act for prohibiting all Trade and Commerce with Francey all Brandies, Aqua Vita, and Spirits, were prohibited to be imported into this Kingdom; and that good and wholesome Brandies, Aqua Vnaj, and Spirits, might be made and drawn from malted Corn; for the Encouragement, therefore,^of Making of Brandies, strong Waters and Spirits, from malted Corn, and for the greater Consumption of Corn, and the Advantage of Tillage in this Kingdom, a Duty of One Peny only was imposed on every Gallon of low Wines of the First Extraction, drawn and made from Drink brewed and made of any Sort of malted Corn; and the several Duties of Eight Pence, Twelve Pence, and Three Pence, were imposed on every Gallon of such low Wines made or drawn from the several other Materials therein mentioned; and several Provisions were thereby made, for obliging all Distillers to draw their low Wines, or Spirits of the First Extraction, from clean and wholesome Drink, made of malted Corn intirely, without any Mixture with any Melasses, Walh, or Tilts, or other Materials whatever; and, for the further Encouragement of Distillers, and others, to draw and make Spirits of Brandies from malted Corn, and to export the fame, a Drawback, upon Exportation, was allowed, of Three Pence for every Gallon of Brandy or Spirits made and drawn from Drink brewed from malted Corn, without any Mixture with any other Materials; and further setting forth, That the several Du ties were continued, and the said Provisions, with the Allowance of the said Drawback, were re-enacted by an Act, made in the 7th and 8rh Year of the Reign of King William the Third; and that by an Act, made in the 12th and 13th Year of the Reign of King William the 3d, which imposed several new Duties on low Wines or Spirits of the First Extraction, the like Drawback is allowed upon Exportation, of Spirits or Brandy made from malted Corn only, as aforesaid; but that, notwithstanding these and other Acts made to encourage the Consumption of malted Corn, Distillers and others, in preparing Spirits and other Liquors, use considerable Quantities of unmalted Corn, of Corn not sufficiently malted the said Distillers pretending that they are licensed so to do by an Act, made in the Sixth Year of his present Majesty’s Reign; whereby, for the Encouragement of Spirits drawn from Corn in Great Britain, a Drawback, upon Exportation, is allowed of £.4. 18s. for every Ton of such Spirits; and, for every Ton of Spirits drawn from Barley, Malt, or other Corn, the Bounty of£. 1. 10s. is also directed to be paid to the Exporter of the fame, when Barley is at Twenty-four Shillings per Quarter, or under; which Act, nevertheless, doth not, as the Petitioners apprehend, repeal any of the Provisions made by the Acts before-recited, for obliging all Distillers to draw their low Wines, or Spirits of the First Extraction, from clean and wholesomeDrink, made of malted Corn intirely; and further setting forth, That, by such Use of unmalted Corn, much less Corn, as well as Malt, is consumed; and that, with the Grains of unmalted Corn now used in Brewing, and preparing spirituous, and other Liquors, Distillers, and others, dofeed and fit a great Number of Hogs, which would otherwise be better fed and fatted in the Country by Farmers and Graziers, or would necessarily consumeagreat Quantity of Pease and Beans, and coarse Corn mixed with Grains, if the said Distillers, and others, were obliged to use malted Corn only: And therefore praying, in behalf of themselves, and many others, thus prejudiced by the Use of unmalted Corn, which alfe tends so much to the Diminution of the public Revenue, Jeffening the Consumption of Corn, also the Breeding and Fatting of Cattle, That the House will take the Premises into Consideration, and give Relief to the Petitioners, by enforcing the said Laws heretofore made for the Consumption

Sir Miles Stapylton reported from the Committee, to Beck Credc w^om the Petition of the Mayor, Aldermen, and Bur-Can. -geffes, of the Town of Beverley, in the East Riding of the County of York, was referred, That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had jdirected him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards d.eliyeredit in at the Clerk’s Table,: 'Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the^aid Petition,

An Act, made in the 13th Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George, intituled, An Act for cleansing, deepening, and widening, a Creek, called Beverley Beck, running into the River Hull; and for repairing the Staiths near the said Beck; and for amending the Roads leading from the said River to the Town of Beverley, in the East Riding of the County of York, was produced, and Part thereof read; whereby it appeared, that several Duties were granted to the Mayor, Aldermen, and Burgesses, of Beverley, for the Time being, upon all Goods laden or unladen in any Part of the said Beck, or upon the River Hull, within the Precincts of the said Town, for cleansing, deepening, widening, and preserving the said Beck; and for repairing the Staiths adjoining the re; and for amending the Roads leading from the said Town to the said River.

Then Mr. William Nelf on junior, being examined, said, That, in order effectually to carry on the said Works, the said Mayor, Aldermen, and Burgesses, borrowed the Sum of £.1,050; which, as well as the Tolls collected, was applied according to the Directions of the said Act: That lS

the greatest Part of the said Sum still remains unpaid; and that the present Duties will not be sufficient to discharge the fame, and repair and maintain the said Works, Being examined as t<* the Condition of the said Beck, he said, ThaFthefame is in Danger of being choaked up with Mud Spil brought into it by the Tide: That the Banks are fallen in, in several Places, and will require to be supported by Piles and Jetty-work; and that, upon a moderate Computation, the Charge of cleansing the said r ! BecK, and making the Works necessary for preserving she fame, will amount to 3 or £. 400. '

Being further examined> he laid. That many of the Duties imposed by the said Act are loft; because it is apprehended, that the Collectors have not Power to examine into the several Species of Goods chargeable therewith; and he instanced in Salt, for Three Hogslieads of which (each Hogshead containing 14 or 15 Hundred Weight), being packed as Sugar or other Goods; only 4^.'is paid; whereas the Duty payable for Salt is 4^. a Ton:

That the Tolls laid by the said Act, are, in many Cafes, unequal to the Value of the Goods; the same Duty being paid for 1,000 Bricks as is paid for 3 Hogsheads of Sugar.

11 Being further examined, he said, That the Carriage of Goods to and from the said Beck and River Hull, in Carriages having narrow Wheels (hod with Iron, has been very detrimental to the Roads and Pavement; but that the same would be prevented, were the Carriages obliged to have broad Wheels unihod.

And he added. That the keeping open of the said Beck, and preserving of the Roads leading thereto, will be of great Benefit to the Inhabitants of the said Town, and the Country adjacent.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for explaining, amending, and making more effectual, an Act, passed in the Thirteenth Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the First, intituled, An Act for cleansing, deepening, and widening, a Creek, called Beverley Beck, running into the River Hull; and for repairing the Staiths near the said Beck; and for amending the Roads leading from the said River to the Town of Sever-leyiin the East Riding of the County of York; and for cleansing the Streets of the said Town; and for regulating the Carriages to and from the said Beck and River Hull: And that Sir Miles Stapylton, Mr. Vane, and Mr.. Charles Pelham, do prepare, and bring in, the fame,

Borough- A PETITION of the Gentlemen, Freeholders, Far-brid^e Road. Lx. mers, and Inhabitants, of- and in the Liberty or Wapentake o\ Langbaurgh, called Cleveland, in the North Riding of the County of York, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, on behalf of themselves, and all other the Freeholders and Inhabitants of and in the said Liberty, was presented to the House, and read 5 fettingibrth, That the said Liberty, or Wapentake, commonly called Cleveland, is of a very large Extent 5 the farpe confiding of Four several Market Towns, and near-Eighty other fe--veral Townships or Constableries: That a great Part of the Grounds therein, are proper for Tillage, and used as such; for the._manuring and improving whereof, the Owners and Occupiers thereof are obliged yearly to fetch very great Quantities of Lime out Of the County of Durham-, from whence the most Part of the Inhabitants of Cleveland aforesaid are also supplied with Lime for building, and other Uses, and likewise with Coals for their Fires; all which they fetch with Hdrfes, Carts, and other Carriages, at a very great Expaice; a great Part of Cleveland aforesaid lying about Twenty-five Miles didarit from the Coal Pits, and Twenty Miles didant from the Lime Kilns: That the said Coal Pits, and the most of the Lime Kilns, from whence die Petitioners are supplied with Lime and Coal, as above let forth, are respectively situate on the Wed Side of the Road leading from Croft Bridge oh the River Tees, through Darlington, in the County of Durham, to the City of Durham; for the repairing of which laid Road, a Bill is now depending in this House; and that Cleveland aforesaid being situate on the contrary Vol. 24.

Side of the said Road, all Horses, Caris, and other Carriage*; passing and repairing from thence to and from the said Coal Pics and Lime Kilns, are obliged td cross the said Road in several Parts thereof; and, in some Parts where they cross the said Road; must necessarily travel a fllort Sjjace there-

oil; that; should the said Bill pass into a Law, and Toll-, gates or Turnpikes be erected or placed on such Parts of the said Roads, as the Petitioners Horses, Carts; or other Carriages; must necessarily cross or travel upon, in fetch- ing of Coal or Linle, and the Petitioners be thereoy sub- jested to the Payment of the Toils Or Duties intended to be laid by the said Bill, the Petitioners apprehend the same would be a very great Hard ship, and very much hinder the Improvement of their Lands: And therefore praying, That the said Bill may not pass into a Law, without Provisoes or Clauses therein for exempting of all such.

Horles, Carts, or other Carriages, from the Payment of any Toll; which do not otherwise use the said Road thari in passing and repairing to and from the said Coal Pits and Lime Kilns above-mentioned, in the fetchingoTCoal and Lime from thence; and that the Petitioners may be relieved in the Premises, as to Justice shall seem meet.

A Petition of several Aldermen of the City of London, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, on behalf of themselves, and others, was presented to the House* and read; setting forth, That, in an Act, made in the Eleventh Year of the Reign of King George the First, intituled, An Act for regulating Elections within the City of London, and for preserving the Peace, good Order, and Government, of the said City, is contained the following Clause; viz. " And, to the Intent that a final End may <c be put to all Disputes between the Mayor and Aldermen and the Commons of the Common Council of the c< said City, touching the Making or Palling of Acts, " Orders, or Ordinances, in Common Council; and " that no Ad, Order, or Ordinance, may, for the future, " be made or passed in Common Council, without the <c full Consent of the Representative Body of the said " City, according to the antient Constitution of the same; <c be it enacted, by the Authority aforesaid, That no Ad,

'<c Order, or Ordinance whatsoever, at any time, from and " after the said First Day of June 1725, shall be made cc or passed in the Common Council of the said City, " without the Assent of the Mayor and Aldermen present at such Common Council, or the major Part of " them, nor without the Assent of the Commons present

at such Common Council, or the major Part of them and letting forth. That a Bill is now depending in this House, by which the said Clause is intended to be repealed; and that if the said Clause should be repealed, those Disputes, which subsisted between the said Mayor and Aldermen and the Commons, in Common Council, before the passing the said Act, will be revived, and, consequently, the Proceedings in Common Council obstruded; and that the Petitioners conceive, the Assent of the Aldermen in making Acts, Orders, and Ordinances, is highly fit and reafoaable; and was therefore establishdd by Parliament, after the most deliberate Confederation 5 and that the Petitioners hope thgt this House will npt take away a Power from the Aldermen, which has not, in any In ft an ce, been misused since it was confirmed to them by the said Act: And therefore praying. this House to take the Premises into Confederation, and to give them such Relief against the said Bill, as rtxa.ll seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the said Bill be read a Second time.

THE Lord Perceval reported from the Committee, We(hni»far to whom the Petition of the Commissioners for Bridge, building Westminster Bridge was referred, That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, together with the Resolutions of the Committee thereupon, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerkrs

Table:

18 Geo. II.

14® Februa

75*

Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth 1

viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition,

Several Acts of Parliament, made in the Ninth, Tenth, Twelfth, and Thirteenth, Years of the Reign of his present Majesty, were produced; and several Parts of the said Acts being read, it appeared by the first-mentioned Act, that several Persons therein named were appointed Commissioners for building a Bridge cross the Rivet Thames, from the City of Westminster to the opposite Shore in the County of Surrey; and, by the subsequent Acts, were impowered to make, design, and layout, such Ways, Streets, and Passages, as they should find proper to make, open, and lay out, on each Side the River Thames, to and from the intended Bridge, the Courts of Justice, both Houses of Parliament, and the Parts adjacent; and to agree for, and purchase, such Houses and Ground within certain Limits by the said Acts prescribed, as they shall find necessary for them to be possessed of; and were likewise impowered to lett, fell, or dispose of, such Piece or Pieces of Ground, either together or in Parcels, as they should be possessed of, over and above what may be necessary for the Opening and Widening of the said Ways, Streets, and Passages, to such Person or Persons as should be willing to contract, agree for, or purchase, the fame.

Then the following Witnesses were called; viz

Sir Joseph Ayloffe Baronet, and Taylor White Esquire: Who, being severally examined, said, That the Commissioners for building the said Bridge have assigned and laid out several Ways, Streets, and Passages, to and from the said Bridge, and are desirous of preserving the fame, and the Buildings now erected, and hereafter to be erected, upon the said Pieces or Parcels of Ground, free from all Nuisances and Annoyances, and to preserve the Uniformity and Beauty thereof; and have agreed to dispose of some Part of the Premises, under such Agreements, Covenants, Limitations, and Refiridions, as are necessary for those Purposes, and for the Benefit of the Public in general.

And further said, That they apprehend, if the Commissioners were to grant the Lands in Fee, with Conditions or Covenants to restrain Nuisances and Annoyances, and preserve the Uniformity of the Buildings, they could not, for any Length of Time, enforce the Performance of such Conditions and Covenants, by reason the Premises might either be in the Hands of Persons not bound by those Conditions oV Covenants, as claiming no Estate under the Commissioners, or that the Heir of the Trustees to the Commissioners might not be found, in whole Name only any Advantage could be taken of the Breach of such Conditions; for if the Trustees should assign their Estates, their Assignees could not maintain an Action on any Breach of Conditions; for the Estate, which might revert in Breach thereof, is a mere Possibility, and not assignable in Law; therefore such Agreements, Covenants, Limitations, and Refiridions, cannot effectually be enforced, and perpetually remain a Lien on the Premises, without the Aid and Authority of Parliament.

Upon the whole Matter, the Committee came to the following Resolutions; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the Petitioners have fully proved the Allegations of their said Petition.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the House be moved for Leave to bring in a Bill for giving further Powers to the Commissioners for building a Bridge cross the River Thames, from the City of West-miufter to the opposite Shore in the County of Surrey, pursuant to the Petition.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for giving further Powers to the Commissioners for building a Bridge cross the River Thames, from the City of Westminster to the opposite Shore in the County of Surrey, pursuant to their laid Petition: And that the Lord Perceval and Mr. Plumptre, do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

Mr. Speaker reported, That the House had attended his Majesty in the House of Peers: Where his Majesty was pleased to give the Royal Assent to the several public Bills, and One private Bill, following; viz.

An Act for continuing the Duties upon Malt, Mum, Cyder, and Perry, in that Part of Great Britain called England; and for granting to his Majesty certain Duties upon Malt, Mum, Cyder, and Perry, in that Part of Great Britain called Scotland; for the Service of the Year One thousand Seven hundred and Forty-five:

An Act to enable the Parishioners of the Parish of Saint Margaret, within the Borough of King's Lynn, in the County of Norfolk, to raise Money, by Rates upon themselves, for finishing the Church of the said Parish: An Act for repairing the Road leading from the Town of Kingston upon Hull to and through the Town of Anlahy^ and from thence to the Town of Kirk Ella, in the County of the said Town of Kingston upon Hull:

An Act for confirming and establishing on John Pate Esquire, and his Issue Male, the Surname of Rose.

Speaker said, he had, to prevent Mi (lakes, obtained a Copy: Which he read to the House; and is as follow--eth; viz.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

It is with great Pleasure that I take this Opportunity to allure you of my intire Satisfaction in the Dispatch and Unanimity of your Proceedings in this Session of Parliament, and in the Zeal you have shewn for the common Cause, and for the Honour and truclnterefl: of Great Britain.

Gentlemen of the House of Commons,

I return you my Thanks for the Readiness and Chear-fulness with Vrhich you have already provided so considerable a Part of the Supplies; and I make no doubt, but the same Zeal and good Disposition will induce you to enable me to make good the Alliances I am already engaged in, and to concert such other Measures, in this important Conjuncture, as shall be judged necessary for the Support of the Queen of Hungary, and for carrying on the present War with Vigour, in order* to procure a safe and honourable Peace.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

I have, in conjunction with the Queen of Hungary and the States General, concluded a Treaty with the Kingo{Poland\ which I will order to be laid before you. Let me earnestly recommend to you the Continuance of the same Steadiness and Harmony in your Deliberations; which cannot fail to give great Encouragement to my Allies, and to add great W eight to our Efforts.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee* That a Sum, not exceeding Eight thousand Six hundred and Twenty Pounds, be granted to his Majesty, to make good his Majesty's Engagements with the Elector of Mentos, pursuant to Treaty.

Hungary, and Minister Plenipotentiary to the Court of his Polish Majesty: r

His Majesty the King of Poland, Elector of Saxony, the

Sieur Henry Cou n t deBnihl, Baron de and de Pfoerten, Knight of the Orders of the White Eagle, of St. Andrew, and of the Black Eagle, his Minister of Cabinet, Conference, and State, General of the Foot, Grand Matter of the Wardrobe, President of the Chamber of the Finances, Director General of the Taxes and Excise, Commandant of the Saxon Guards in Poland, and Colonel of a Regimenc of Foot:

And their High Mightinesses the States General, the Sieur Cornelius Calkoen, their M inifter Plenipotentiary to his Polish Majesty:

The said Ministers, after having communicated to e&ch other their respective full Powers, have agreed upon the following Articles.

1.

From this, and for all time to come, there shall be a firm, constant, and unalterable Friendship, Union, and Alliance, and a perfect and intimate Confidence and Correspondence, between his Majesty the King of Great Britain, her Majesty the Queen of Hungary and Bohemia, his Majesty the King of Poland, Elector of Saxony, and the Lords the States General of the United Provinces, their Kingdoms, States, Territories, and Subjects; and they shall be obliged, as well for themselves as for their Successors, to support and assist each other reciprocally, to have the same watchful Eye to their mutual Security, as to their own, to procure with Care and Affection all that shall be advantageous for them, and to remove and hinder, as much as shall be in their Power, all that might be prejudicial to them or to the common Cause.

2.

To this end* the high contracting Parties shall take and concert together, from this time, the most effectual Measures for re-establishing and (ecuring the Peace and good Order of Europe, and particularly* in the Empire; as also

to aflitl each other reciprocally ui protecting, preserving, and defending, all the Kingdoms, States, Countries, Provinces, Territories, Rights, and Possessions, which they now actually enjoy, or ought to enjoy, by virtue of the Treaties of Peace, Alliance, and Guaranty, that subsist among them, or any of them all whrch Treaties, and especially those of Alliance, Guaranty, and mutual Defence, shall remain in full Force, so far as they concern the high contracting Parties.

3- ,

His Polish Majesty, Elector of Saxony, moreover con-

firms and renews very expressly, and in a most solid and irrevocable Manner, as well for himself as for his Heirs and Successors, the Guaranty of the Order of Succession estabhflied in the most Serene House of Austria by the Pragmat ic Sanction; as his Britannic Majesty, and the Lords the States General, are engaged therein; and to which Order of Succession the Germanic Body have given their Guaranty and Sanction; promising to concur with all his Force, that no farther Attack dull ever be made upon fofalutary a Regulation, which isneccflary for the Security of the Empire, and for the Repose of in

general; and which mterefts so dlentially the Posterity of iris Polish Majesty, to whom the above-mentioned Regulation allures the said Succession after the Extinction of the Defendants of the late Emperor Charles the Sixth.

4-

And, for this Purpose, the Kingdom of Bohemia being actually attacked, his Polijh Majesty, Elector of Saxony, shall act immediately with an Army of Thirty thousand Men, as auxiliary Troops, for the Defence of the said Kingdom, and the Security of her Majesty the Queen of Hungary and Bohemia.

For defraying the Expences of so considerable an Armament, made in favour of the common Cause, his Britannic Majesty, and the Lords the States General, engage themselves to furn'rih his Polish Majesty, Elector of Saxony, as long as the Necessity shall require it, an annual Subsidy

Yoi. 24.

of One hundred and Fifty thousand Pounds Sterling, to commence from the First Day of January, in the Year 1745, N. S. and payable regularly from Three Months to Three Months; of which Subsidy his Britannic Majesty shall pay One hundred thousand Pounds Sterling, and the Lords the States General Fifty thousand Pounds, valued at the Sum of Five hundred and Fifty thousand Florins of Holland.

6.

As soon as all Danger shall cease on the Side of Bohemia and the Electorate of Saxony, to the Satisfaction of the contracting Parties, his Polish Majesty, Elector of Saxony, shall cause to march, at the first Requisition, and maintain at his own Expence, in consideration of the Continuance of a Subsidy of Ninety thousand Pounds Sterling, payable upon the Foot of the Sum specified in the preceding Article; viz. Sixty thousand Pounds Sterling on the Part of Great Britain, and Thirty thousand Pounds, valued at the Sum of Three hundred and Thirty* thousand Florins of Holland, on that of their High Migh-tinesses; a Body of Ten thousand of his Troops; viz. Two thousand Horle, and Eight thousand Foot, into the Netherlands, or elsewhere in the Empire, where his Britannic Majesty and the Lords the States General shall judge it necessary for the Good of the common Cause.

7-

If, in consequence of the Engagements that Lis Polish Majesty, Elector of Saxony, contracts by the present AI-. hance, his States in Germany should be attacked, besides the effective Assistance that the Allies shall give him for his immediate Defence, they shall use their utmost Efforts to procure hirii from the Aggressor full Satisfaction for the Damages that he may have thereby l'uftained; and, for this Purpose, in case any of his Countries should be seized upon, they shall not lay down their Arms until the same be fully restored to him; as his Polish Majesty, Elector of Saxony, shall, on his Part, persist inviolably in the same Engagements until a Peace iis concluded; and further, as long as there shall be in the States, whether of the Queen of Hungary and Bohemia, or in those of the high contracting Parties, any of the Enemy’s Troops, or Danger of their entering again into those State*, or into the Empire.

8.

If it should please God to bless the Measures and the Precautions that his Polish Majesty, Elector of Saxony, shall so concur in to take with the other high contracting Parties, for the present and future Security of Europe in general, and of the Empire in particular; in this Cafe, his Polish Majesty, Elector of ,shall partake of the Advantages that shall arise therefrom, by such Conveni-encics as shall be procured fdr him, and the high contracting Parties, promise, in general, to take, at the ensuing Pacification, all possible Care c f the Interests of his Polish Majesty, Elector of Saxony, and of his House.

9-

After the Peace is made, the high contracting Parties shall remain for everclofely united; and they shall then concert in what farther Manner they may be able to provide most effectually for their Security, and their reciprocal Advantage.

10.

Her Majesty the Empress of Russia and the Kingdoni and Republic of Poland are expressly, and from this time, invited to accede as principal contracting Parties to the present Alliance; and all Kings, Electors, Princes, and States, who have at Heart the Liberty and public Security, and the Preservation of the System of the Empire, and who are desirous of acceding to the present Alliance, shall be admitted thereto.

A Petition of the Merchants and others of Great Bri- Drawback tain and Ireland, Dealers and Manufacturers of Linens, on foreign Threads, and Tapes, made in Great Britain and Ireland, L’nCftb* whoseNamesare thereunto subscribed, on behalf of themselves, and many others, concerned and employed, in :the said Manufactures, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Manufactures of Linens, Threads, and Tapes, within the Kingdoms of Great Britain and Ireland, have, of late Years, been considerably improved and increased, and, if properly encouraged, might be brought to equal (which they now do in some Species), if not excel, all the like Manufactures of foreign Fabric now imported into these Kingdoms: That the Negroes, in several of the British Plantations, are chiefly cloathed with coarse Linens; the making whereof in these Kingdoms will contribute to lessen the Price of fine Linens, as it enables the Manufacturer to employ therein the coarse and refufi^Flax and Yam, which are unfit for making-fine Linens, and servesas a Nursery to introduce Hands, both old and-young,a’s Learners, which are now trfeless; who, as they grow perfect in Spinning, will make room for others to come in; and thereby, if encouraged, the Linen Manufactures in general, in a few Years, will necfcflarily be greatly extended: That the permitting the Duties$bn Linens, Threads, and Tapes, imported from foreign Coiin-tries, to be all,- except about Two per Cent.\drawn hack on their being exported, hath proved, a* verygreat Dii-couragement to the Exportation Of home-made Linens, *' 1

especially the Gparfe Sorts; and that, in the’Year. 1737, divers Merchants, and others, Dealprsin the fardManufactures, petitioned, this House, complaining of the DLfcou-,ragenaents the Linen Manufactures laboured under, by reason of the said Drawbacks allowed on Exportation of foreign Linens; and.that- the Committee, to whom the said Petition was rftfer-red, afterwards made their Report; whereby, among ocher things, it appears,'there aremade, in several Parts of these Kingdoms, a coarse Sort of Linen proper for cjoathing JSfegroes in the Plantations, which answers all the Purposes of Ofnaburghs; but that, by reason of the Drawback, foFeign coarse Linens were fold in the Plantations between Six and Seven per Gent, cheaper than the British or Irish Linens; and that, if this Drawback were not allowed, Brit if 1 and Irish Linens would be then fold near Six per Cent, cheaper than the foreign; and that, with proper Encouragement, diffident Quanti- ties of Linen might, in a short time, be made in Great Britain and Ireland, for the Service of the Plantations, in lieu of the foreign coarse Linen used there: That this House, on the 19th of April having ta/cen the said

Report into Consideration, came to;a Resolution, That the Manufactures of Linen, Threads, and Tape?, made in Great Britain and Ireland, were, of late Years, greatly improved and increased; whereby the Price of all such Manufactures of foreign and home Fabric had beencon-fidflTably reduced; and that the further Extension of such Manufactures would be attended with several national Ad-1 vantages;

i8 Geo. II.

250 Februarii.

771

vantages; and that all proper Support and Encouragement ought to be given towards the further Extension thereof: That, in the Year 1742, on a subsequent Application of the Persons concerned in the said Manufacture, this House came to a Rei'olurion, That the said Manufactures were greatly improved and increased; and that the Price of Linens, as well of foreign as of home Fabric, had been thereby considerably reduced; and that an Act of Parliament soon afterwards passed for granting a Bounty of One Peny per Yard upon British and Linens of the Value of Six Pence, and not exceeding Twelve Pence, a Yard; and of One Halfpeny a Yard upon all such Linens under the Value of Six Pence a Yard, upon the Exportation thereof; for the Payment whereof, an additional Duty vyas laid on foreign Cambricks imported into Great Britain: That the said Bounty hath not answered the Intentions of Parliament; it having proved but of small Encouragement to the Exportation of coarse Linen of our own Fabric; the same being usually exported to the Colonies by way of Afi'ortment only, and not lingly, or in large Quantities, at one time; and that as the Officers of the Customs require a separate Package, Entry, and Certificate, for every Parcel intitled to the Bounty, a great Part thereof is necessarily exhausted in Custom- house Fees, and other Charges4 by reason whereof, and of the MultiplicityofOaths.distant Payment, &c, many Persons decline being concerned in such Exportation; for which, among other Reasons, the Exports of foreign low-priced Linen have as yet been very little lessened: That, since the Year 1738, the Quantity of Linen made in Great Britain and Ireland, especially of the coarler Sorts, is greatly increased; leveraJ Persons having, since that time, applied themselves to the Manufacture thereof, particularly of Ofnaburghs, in which they have succeeded to the intire Satisfaction of the Planters; having made the same better in Quality, though not so low in Price, as those imported from abroad; but that while the Drawback is allowed on foreign Linens exported, the Manufacturers are discouraged from carrying on a general Manufacture of coarse Linens, there not being a sufficient Demand for them in England, unless for Exportation; whereas,

were the said Drawback taken off, the Linen Manufacture, in every Branch, would be greatly increased, many Thousands of useless Hands in both Kingdoms, who now want Employment, might be employed therein; Children, as well as Men and Women almost of all Ages, being fit and able to carry on the lame, especially in the coarler Branches thereof, and the Plantations might, in a short time, be supplied with coarse Linens manufactured in Great Britain and Irelandas cheap, if not cheaper, than what they now pay for foreign Linens; past Experience having made it certain, that, in proportion as the Linen Manufactures of these Kingdoms are encouraged, ' the Prices of Linens, as well of foreign as of home Fabric, are proportionality reduced: And therefore praying the House to take into Consideration this valuable Branch of Trade, which is of the greatest Consequence to both these Kingdoms; and to give the Petitioners such Relief in the Premises, as to this House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to a Committee.

A Motion was made, and the Question being put, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a select Committee: And that they do. examine, atad Rate to the House, the Matter of Fact contained in the said Petition;

Mr. Fane, according to Order, reported from the Com- Sandwick mittee of the whole House, to whom it was referred to Harbour, consider of the Report relating to the Harbour proposed to be made from Sandwich into the Downs, hear Sandown Castle, the Resolution, which the Committee had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth;

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee, That a safe and commodious Harbour may be made into the Downs, near Sandown Castle, fit for the Reception and Se-

curity of large Merchant Men, and Ships of War of Sixty and Seventy Guns, and be of great Use and Advantage to the naval Power of Great Britain, by preserving Ships in Distress, speedily refitting them for the Sea, and by saving the Lives of many of his Majesty’s Subjects; and, in Time of War more particularly, be a ready Means of bridling Dunkirk, of guarding the Mouth of the River, and protecting the Coasts from Invasion and Insults.

Your Committee having proceeded thus far in the Examination of the Matterof the said Pet it ions, recommended to the Parties concerned to endeavour to accommodate the Dispute between them, in relation to the Division of the Property of the Company; in consequence whereof, Two Proposals were delivered to the Committee, the one by the Agent for the Surgeons, and the other by the Agent for the Barbers; which were read; and are entered in the Appendix, N°6, 7.

At the same time, an Account of Contributions paid by the Surgeons and Barbers, and also an Account of the

several Receipts and Expences of the Company for Six Years pall, were delivered in by the Agent for the Barbers; and are entered in the Appendix; N# 8, 9.

And the said Agent being asked. How much the Income of the Estate in Ireland, belonging to the Company, amounted to, clear of all Deductions ? said, That, for Six Years past* the Company has received, communibus Amis, the Sum of £. 4a, upon Account of the said Estate.

The Committee came to the following Resolutions:

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Surgeons have made good the Allegations of their Petition.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Separation of the Corporation of Barbers and Surgeons, and making Two Corporations of the present united Company of Barbers and Surgeons, will contribute much to the Improvement of Surgery, and thereby become a Matter of public Utility.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Surgeons have made reasonable Propositions to the Barbers, touching the Property of the Estates now belonging to the united Company of Barbers and Surgeons.

Curia AJJiftentium, 29° 1675.

Mr. Edward Arris, a very worthy Member of this Company, having formerly settled, by Deed, £. 30 a Year, for a Diffeftion of a Body yearly, and Reading on the Muscles, desired that Deed might be delivered up to him, in Consideration of £. 500 he is willing to give the Company, to go on with that Work themselves: The Court thought fit to leave it to himself, to give what he thought fitting; and he offering freely to give them 10 more, the Court ordered the^. 510 to be accepted, and his Deed to be delivered up to him, and cancelled, and Counsel to be advised with, to draw up a Covenant for the Payment of £.30 yearly for the future, as formerly, by the Company.

Die Luna, vicesimo oE 1677.

Order about Dr. /fmQThe Court this Day heard read his Proposals. $ the Answer, which the Governors and some of the Assistants, not making a full Court, considered of on Monday the 14th of January last, about the Proposals in the Caule between Dr. Arris and this Court, of the 5th of December last 1677; and do agree and order, that that Answer, as amended by Counsel, and followeth verbatim, be the Answer of this Court, and delivered to the Master of the Rolls, Tomorrow in the Afternoon, by the Governors.

The Answer of the Matters, or Governor, of the Mystery and Commonalty of Barbers and Surgeons, London, to the Proposals made by Dr. Thomas Arris, in an Order dated the 5th Day of December 1677, at the Rolls, before the Honourable the Master of the,.Ralls.

This Court having heard and considered of the Proposals of the 5th of December abovesaid, in the Presence of the honourable the Master of the Rolls, in the Cause then depending in Chancery between Dr. Thomas , Plaintiff, and this Company, Defendants, do answer and say. That Mr. Edward Arris, deceased, the Plaintiff's Father, did voluntarily and of his own Accord, without any Request made to him by the Company, or any Person in their behalf, offer them £.510, to deliver up and cancel the Deed and Settlement of the Lands mentioned in the Proposals for Payment of the Rent Charge of^. 30 per Annum, fora muscular Diffeftion yearly; urging this as his Reason; viz.That his only Son and Heir, the now Doctor, had and did then receive the Profits of the said Lands to his own Use, upon Condition, and under Promise, to pay the said £. 30 per Annum, for the said Diffeftion; but he found that he did never pay One Peny of it, or ever would do, when he their Benefactor was dead, without Trouble and Suit; with some severe and (harp Expressions, which we will by no means mention, although they were the very Words of the Father spoken of the Son: And further we say, that Mr. , our pious Benefactor, did nor could expect any other Security from us for the Performance of the said muscular Diffec-tion, than a Covenant under our common Seal; for that he knew, being an antient Member, and sometimes Governor of the Society, that we could not secure it by any Lands of our own nor had we Stock enough to buy Lands sufficient to make any other Security; for the Five hundred and Ten Pounds, the Settlement we parted with, being really worth an Hundred Pounds more; and if we should, to pleasure the Plaintiff, although against his Father’s express Will and Intent, who was our Benefactor, return the said Five hundred and Ten Pounds again, it would be looked upon as a great Neglect, perhaps a Breach of our Trust, as we humby conceive, to agree to take other than the same Lands, and less than the Whole, which was formerly settled by the cancelled Deed; which Premises considered, we do hope, that the honourable the

Vox.. 24.

Master of the Rolls will give us that Credit, which the separate la-

Donor of this worthy Gift was earnest with us to do, when corporation alive, though his Son be not so willing to trust us; and of Sttrgoooot. that the Doctor may be decreed, without Return of the Money, to take a Covenant, under the Defendants common Seal, for securing the Trustrepofcdinus, according to the Agreement made with his Father, at a Court of Assistants, February the 29th, 1675; and likewise pay the Charges of the Company, which they have or shall be put to by this troublesome and unnecessary Suit; which doth so much shew what they must expect from him hereafter, if they should part with the Five hundred and Ten Pounds.

This Court hearing, that the College of Physicians are about the Renewing of their Charter, and Cpnfirming of 'it by Act of Parliament, do order, That the Master and Wardens, for the Time being, Mr. Serjeant Painter, Mr.

Arris, Mr. Boone, Mr. Davis, Mr. Serjeant Knight, Mr.

Allen, Mr. Stamford, Mr. Loe, Mr. , and Mr.

Wooddall, be a Committee to consider and advise with Counsel, how to prevent any Mifchricf which may come to the Surgeons of this Company by it.

7«^the 5th, 1689.

Ordered the Clerk to attend Mr. Trevor, and have it under his Hand, to answer the Two following Queries; viz.

Whether the Surgeons of London have Power by Law to give internal Medicines to their chjrrurgical Patients?

Quere, Whether the Bill, now patting in Parliament by the College of Physicians, be a Confirmation of their Acts of Parliament, and the Charters they now enjoy ? or whether it be prejudicial to the Chyrurgeons of London

Julykhe 23d, 1689.

A Committee.

Mr. Geo. Horfnell, \

Mr. Tho. Lichfield,)

It is agreed by the Persons present. That the next Court of Assistants be made acquainted. That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That all the Charters, Grants, and By-laws, by which the Company be left with Mr. Hollis the Counsel, and Order to draw a Bill for the betterestablishing the Company; which Bill, when drawn, to be presented to the House of Commons, and endeavour to get it passed into an Act; and also, amongst other Particulars to be mentioned in the said Bill, that these or the like Clauses may be inserted; viz. That it shall or may be lawful, at all times hereafter, that all and every Chyrurgeon, that be duly examined by Four or more of the Ten Examiners, in the Pretence of Two or more of the Masters or Governors of the said Company, for the Time being, and by them approved under the Seal of the same Company, shall and may, from time to time, and at all times hereafter, give all Sorts of internal Medicine to his or their chyrurgicalPatients, as he or they shall think most conducing to the Health and quicker Recovery of their laid Patient; any Act of Parliament or Letters Patents heretofore made or granted to the contrary in anywise notwithstanding; and that the giving internal Medicine, inall such Cases, shall be taken and deemed practising Chyrurgery; and that no Person or Persons whatsoever, for their own private Interest and Gain, at any time hereafter, shall undertake and practise the said Art of Chirur-gery within the Cities of London and Westminster, or within the Circuit of Seven Miles of the said City of London, unless he or they be first examined and admitted in Method and Form aforesaid, upon Pain of for every Month he or they shall practise the said Art, not being examined in Manner aforesaid:

That in case the Bishop of London, or Dean of St. Pauls, shall oppose the Company in having full Power and Authority in lfoenfing Chyrurgeons, that then Application^ 9 M bqf

And that no one of the College of Physicians of London shall, at any titne hereaftir, refuse to consult with any Chyrurgeon, so examined and approved, as aforesaid, in any same of Physic whatsoever.

At a Court of Assistants, May 7th, 1713

\ Whereas the Lord Bishop of London does pretend to a concurrent Power with jthe Governors of this Company to license Persons to practise Surgery; but the Inconve-. riience thereof having been represented to his Lordship, he has promised not to license any Persons for the future, except such as have been approved and examined by the Governor and Examiners of this Company: This Court, upon Consideration had thereof, and in order to prevent his Lordship from being misinformed touching the Qualifications of any Persons, who shall apply for his License, doth order. That Five Guineas shall, for this present Year, and also for so much time longer, as this Court shall take no order to the contrary, be paid unto his Lordship’s Register, as Caveat Money, and to prevent the Granting of Licenses by the Bishop of London to any Person or Persons to practise Surgery, but who have been examined and approved by the Governors and Examiners of this Company, for the Time being, under the Seal of the said Company, pursuant to the several Powers and Authorities granted to this Company, in that behalf, by the Kings and Queens of this Realm.

At a Court of Examinations, November 5th, 1713-

Ordered, That the Clerk do arrestand prosecute Mr. Rogers's Men, Mr. Bretton the Frenchman, in Spittlefields, anu all such others as practise Surgery without the Company’s Diplomas.

Court of Assistants, 24th June 1718.

The Master informing the Court, that the Theatre belonging to the Company flood in need of Repair, it was ' ordered that the same should forthwith be repaired: And it is hereby referred to the Discretion of the present Governors to cause the same to be repaired and beautified in such manner as they shall ttyink fit; and, when done, to pay the respective Workmen, whom they shall employ therein, their several Bills out of the public Stock of ther Company.

N°6.

The Surgeons propose, That the Annuity of Sixteen Pounds a Year, given by Dr. Gale for the Ofteology Lecture, and the Sum of £.510, paid to the Company by . Alderman Arris, for the Muscular Lecture, be vetted in the Company of Surgeons in Trust, to be applied to the Purposes of the Donors; and to relinquish to the Barber* all the rest of the real and personal Estate belonging to the united Company, except the Use of the Theatre, Diflfeding Room and Gallery, with the free Use of the common, Passage thereto, for One, Two, or Three Years, till the Surgons can provide themselves with proper Conveniences for their separate Use; they paying to the Barber* an Acknowledgment of One Guinea a Year for the fame.

N° 7.

The Barbers, upon considering the Proposals made by the Surgeons, beg Leave to give'this Answer:

That, in case of a Separation, allowing for the extraordinary Expences which are occasioned by the Businessof Surgery, and which will be saved, the Barbers will lose an Income of £. 249 per Annum, upon an Average, besides the personal Service of the Surgeons; but nevertheless, that they may not appear toobftrud any thing that may be thought for the public Good, they will not oppose a Separation, upon Condition, that ali the Property of the united Company (except Dr. Gale s Gift of £. 16 a Year* and Mr. Arris's Gift of £.510), shall remain to the Barbers:

That the Surgeons take a Lease of the Hall, Parlour, Theatre, &c, for such Days in the Year as they have commonly used the fame, at the Rent of £.80 a Year; which they conceive to be a reasonable Rent, considering that the Repairs and Taxes, which will fall upon the Barbers, amount, upon an Average, to £. 12$ per Annum, and are likely to increase; and that the Surgeons pay lqo towards the Expences the Barbers have been put to on this Occasion.

A Petition of Thomas Greenaway of Reading, in the County of Berks, Bargemaster, John Plumfed, and William Middleton, of Reading aforesaid, Maltsters, and Thomas Bishop of London, Cirizen and Salter, in behalf of themselves, and divers othei\Persons, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That in the Night, be- tjlc faicj gjj

tween the 31st Day of August and the First Day of September 1743, a Barge, belonging to the Petitioner Thomas Greenaway, laden with Flour, Malt, and divers other Goods belonging to the Petitioners John Plumsted, William Middleton, and Thomas Bishop, and divers other Persons, in passing through One of the Arches of the new Bridge at Westminster> ran upon a Pile, which was drove there for the carrying on the Works of the said Bridge; which Pile having been drove there in the Evening of the said 31st Day of August, and being covered with Water, could not be avoided by the Persons who navigated the said Barge; by which Accident the said Barge was funk, and the Goods therein greatly damaged; so that the Loss sustained by the Petitioners, and the rest of the Owners of the said Goods, amounted to the Value of Three hundred Pounds and upwards: And therefore, inaimuch as the said Loss happened without any Neglect or Default of the Petitioners, and was occasioned by the Works necessary for building the said Bridge, which Works were erected by the Authority of divers Acts of Parliament, so that the Petitioners can have no Remedy for the fame, unless by Authority of Parliament, and there is now a Bill depending in Parliament, for granting further Powers to the Commissioners for building a Bridge cross the River Thames, from the City of Westminster to the opposite Shore in the County of Surrey, praying, That a Clause or Clauses may be inserted in the said Bill, whereby the Petitioners, and the rest of the Sufferers, may be relieved in the Premises, in such Manner as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideradon of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

And it is referred to Mr. Strode, Mr. Blagrave, Mr.

Plumptre, Mr. Powney, I.ord Perceval, Mr. Pratty Mr.

A Petition of the several Persons, whose Names are Ditto, thereunto subscribed, being Traders in the Woollen Manufactory in the Town of Lavenham, in the County of Suffolk, was presented to the House* and read; fctcing forth, That the Petitioners, as the Laws already stand, ‘ are under great Hardships, upon account of what they are obliged to pay to the common Carriers for the Carriage of their Goods and Merchandizes: That the Petitioners conceive, if the Bill now before the House, intituled, A Bill to amend and render more effectual the Laws in being for the Preservation of the public Roads, should pass into a Law, the same would be a Means of raising the Price of the Carriage of Goods and Merchandizes all over the Kingdom of Great Britain, to the great Prejudice of the Petitioners, and all other the Inland Traders, and to the Detriment of the Trade in general of this Kingdom: And therefore praying, That the House will be pleased to take the Petitioners same into Consideration, and to give such Relief to the Petitioners as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table,

That the Petitioners had their Ships and Effects taken at Sea, and in Port, by the Spaniards, in the Year 1718, before the War was declared: That, in the Year 1721, there was a Peace concluded with the Crown of Spain; and it was expressly agreed, that all Goods, Merchandizes, Monies, Ships, or other Effects, which were seized or taken before War was declared between the Two Crowns, or since, should be immediately restored in the Species as they were seized or taken, or else there should be paid the just and true Value they were worth at the time they were seized or taken j and Orders were sent to the Intendants of several Provinces in Spain, &e. that what was stipulated might be complied with in every Particular:

That, in March j 7 28, the Petitioners petitioned this House; setting forth their great Losses, and proved many Particulars thereof at the Bar, in so plain and full a Manner, that the House, on the 3d of April following, came to the following Resolution: " That several Ships, Merchandize, and Ef-c< feds, belonging to the Petitioners, had been taken by the " Spaniards, in manifest Violation ot tre Treaties subsisting between the Two Crowns; for which no Restitution had yet been made, &c.* and aadrefled his Majesty thereon: That, in January 1729-30, an absolute Peace was made with Spain. and all former Conventions and Treaties, in favour of Trade and Navigation, were renewed and confirmed; and t hat a just and ample Recti-tution and Reparation foi all unlawful Seizures and Depre- dations

A Petition of the Factors and Dealers of London in Woollen Spanish Cloths, Cloth-serges, Druggets, Flannels, Shal- Manufk&ure, loons, and other Woollen Goods, was prefenced to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Exportation of Spanish Cloths, Cloth-serges, Druggets, Flannels, Shalloons, and other Woollen Goods, is greatly lessened of late Years, and many considerable Manufactures thereof are ruined, on account of the large Quantities of such-like Goods, which the French now manufacture, and.ori account of a Bounty allowed by France on Exportation^ which enables them to supply foreign Countries; which Countries were formerly largely supplied from the Manufactures of Great Britain; and that the Petitioners have great Reason to believe, that the Manufactures of Spanish Cloth in England will greatly decay, and that the Manufac-? tures of Cloth-serges, Druggets, Flannels, and other low-priced Woollen Goods, ill be inevitably ruined, unless the French are prevented from procuring the raw Wools of England and Ireland; and representing to the House,

That the Petitioners apprehend, that if a Law was made to prohibit the Importation of Spanish Wools into Ireland, and to give the People of Ireland a Liberty of exporting to foreign Countries, by way of England, under a Duty at Importation, to be drawn back on Re-exportation, such Camblets as they shall manufacture in Ireland, it would oblige them to work up so much of their own Wools, for their own Wear, and for Exportation, in Camblets, as would, together with what we shall yearly take from them in Wools, Worded, and Woollen Yarn, effectually prevent the French from procuring their Wools, and employ the Poor of Ireland more fully than they now are, or can be, by manufacturing Spanish Wool; which, the Petitioners apprehend, has been a great Cause of their having such Quantities of unmanufactured Wools yearly to fell, or to send to our Rivals the French: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into their Confederation, and grant to the Petitioners such Relief as to the House shall stem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom it is referred to consider further of the State of the Woollen Manufacture of Great Britain and Ireland.

Mr. Henry Archer reported From the Committee, who werfc appointed to inquire what Laws are expired, or near expiring; and to report their Opinion to the House* which of them are fit to be revived, or continued; That the Committee had inquired accordingly; and had come to several Resolutions, which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: YVhere the Resolutions of the Commictee were read; and are as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That an Act, made in the Fifth Year of the Reign of his present Majesty, intituled, An Act for encouraging the Growth of Coffee in his Majesty’s Plantations in America, which was to continue in Force from the 25th Day of March 1735, until the 25th Day of March 1739, and from thence to the End of the tfien next Session of Parliament; and which by an Act, made in the Eleventh Year of the Reign of his present Majesty, was further continued for Seven Years, and from thence to the End of the then nexc Session of Parliament; is near expiring, and fit to be continued.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That an Act, made in the Sixth Year of the Reign of his present Majesty, intituled, An Act for the better securing and encouraging the Trade of his Majesty’s Sugar Colonies in America, which was to continue in Force from the 24th Day o{June 1733, for Five Years, and from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament; and which by an Act, made in the Eleventh Year of the Reign of his present Majesty, was further continued for Seven Years, and from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament; is near expiring, and fit to be continued.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That an Act, made in the Sixth Year of the Reign of his present Majesty, intituled, An Act for the better Regulating of Laftage and Ballastage in the River Thames, which was to continue in Force from the First Day of June 17 33, for Five Years, and from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament; and which by an Act, made in the Eleventh Year of the Reign of his present Majesty, was further continued for Seven Years, and from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament; i$> near expiring, and fit to be continued.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That an Act, made in the Twelfth Year of the Reign of his present Majesty, intituled, An Act to continue the Duties for Encouragement of the Coinage of Money, which was to continue in Force for Seven Years, from the First Day of March 1738, and from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament; is near expiring, and fit to be continued.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition,

John Harding and John Perry, being severally examined, laid, Th^t the Barge, memioned in the Petition, belonged to the Petitioner Thomas Greenaway \ and that the fame, in endeavouring to pals through One of the Arches of the new Bridge at Westminster, (truck upon a Pile, which being under Water, and having no Mark or Guard Pile, could not be leen or avoided by the Persons navigating the said Barge: That they, the Witnesses, were on board the Barge at the time this Accident happened; and that the same Course was then held, which had been tftually kept for Two Years before.

Mr. Samuel Hawtyns and Mr. James King, being exa-ttnined as to the Damage occasioned by this Accident, said, in general. That the Lois sustained by the Petitioners was very contiderable; the Lading of the said Barge confiding chiefly of Malt and Flour; but no Evidence was produced to ascertain the Amount of that Loss.

Mr. Charles Labelye, being called, acquainted the Committee, that the said Pile was driven about the Dusk of the Evening, a few Hours before the Accident happened.
