A Petition of the several Merchants and Tradesmen of and within the City of York^ whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was presented to the House, and read; fe.tting forth, That the Petitioners have, for several Years paftj experienced the great Advantage, in their way of Trade, of Stage Waggons from that City to London, and so back again, which go and return every Week; whereby the several heavy and cumbersome Commodities the Peti- tioners deal in, are, with great Security and Certainty, brought and carried to and from Fork to London without any Loss, Damage, or Delay; Which Advantage to the Petitioners, as well as to the Trade in general in this Part of the Kingdom, would be greatly disttfrbed and incommoded, in case any Restraint, beyond what the Laws now in being have provided, should be iaid upon the*' Waggons, as to the Number of Worses necessarily employed in the conveying of those heavy Goods, which the Necessity of the Petitioners several Trades requires, and more especially at this time, when the Difficulties and Dangers of bringing those Goods by Sea are so very great, that, without a Convoy, the Petitioners cannot hazard so considerable a Property; and which they, in Order to have the Security of, have of late been frequently obliged to wait several Months for, although their Merchandize and' Goods have been as long lbipped, and thereby daily perishtng; and that as the Waggons for the Conveyance of such Goods are obliged to be made, to answer such Purposes, very substantial and strong, the very Draft whereof, when empty, is sufficient for, and is as much as, Two Horses can well draw; therefore, if the Number of Horles was to be confined to less than Three or Four, more than sufficient to draw the said Waggons when empty, the small Quantity of Goods, to be brought by such Waggons, could not possibly defray the Expence of the Waggoner; who therefore mud necessarily be obliged L5

to lay down his Waggon; whereby the Petitioners, and the Consumers of those Goods they severally deal in, will, by the Increase of the Price of such their Commodities, through the Scarcity and Hazard of removing them, as in Times of Peace, be greatly injured, and Trade in general greatly suffer thereby: And therefore praying. That the House will take the Premises into Consideration, as njot so far to restrain the Waggoners in their Carriage of Goods, as may either totally oblige them to desist from further carrying the fame, or else, by increasing the Rate of Carriage, load those Goods with Charges insupportable either by the Merchant or the Consumer.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read; letting forth, Th^t the Petitioners have tuffered very considerable Losses in Trade, by Seizures and Depredations committed by the Spaniards in the Years 1718, 1719, and 1720; the Accounts and Vouchers whereof were duly delivered by the Petitioners, according to public Notice, first to the Commissioners Plenipotentiaries from Great Britain at Cambry and Soijfons, and afterwards to the Commissioners for Trade and Plantations, when Commissaries went from Great Britain to Spain: That, some time ago, a Commission issued for the Distribution of such Sums as have arisen by Reprisals from the Spaniards, at the Commencement of the present War with Spain, amongst the Sufferers; but that the Commissioners, therein named, are only impowered to settle and adjust the Claims of such as have sustained Losses in the Year 1721, and from th^it time; so that those, who suffered before that time, are excluded any Relief, but by an Application to Parliament: That a Petition has been lately presented to the House by several Merchants of London, who have sustained Losses by Depredations of the Spaniards; praying a Relief for their Losses out of the Sixty thousand Pounds granted by Parliament; which Petition has been referred to a Committee of the House; and that the Petitioners conceive they are equally intitled to Relief as any other their Fellow Sufferers: That, on the 16th of April 1743, the preceding Part of the Petitioners Petition was presented to the House; and Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer, by his Majesty’s Command, acquainted the House, That his Majesty had been informed of the Contents of the said Petition, and recommended it to the Consideration of the House; which was then read, and was, by this House, referred to the Consideration of a Committee; and a Report was accordingly made from the said Committee to the House: And therefore praying the House to take the same of the Petitioners into their fur-therConsideration, and to grant, the Petitioners a Satisfaction out of the Sixty thgu&nd Poyndsgiven by Parliament, or in such other manner as to the House shall seem meet.

and was also delivered in at the same Rent by the Commit (loners Report to this House in 1716; for which, and several other Overcharges and Allowances, the said Company craved an Abatement out of the remaining Part of the Purchase Money; and, on the iftof June.1727, drew up an Account, and dated the Balance, witlrthe several Cravings, and laid the same before the then Lords Commissioners of his Majesty’s Treasury; by which the Balance remaining unpaid appeared to be £ 2,567. 12. i£; which Sum was paid into the Exchequer the 15th of the same June, as the real Balance then due to t|ie Public; but the said Lords Commissioners, on such Representation, declared, that however reasonable the Deductions might be, which were claimed by the Company, yet they had no Power over the fame; but referred it for the Determination of the Barons of the Court of Exchequer; for which Purpose, Suits were brought, in 1727, on behalf of the Crown, and on behalf of the Company, relating to what Allowances should be made in respect of such Overcharges, and for legal Conveyances to be made of such Estate: That, in January 1731, the Company, being considerably indebted on their Bonds for Money borrowed to pay for the Purchase of this and other forfeited Estates, did, as a further Security, convey the said Estate of the said late Lord Widdrinton to Trustees, to be sold for Payment of the said Bonds and Interest, amounting to a much greater Sum than the whole Value of the said Estate; and the said Company then depending, that the Balance due to the Public was, as aforesaid, fully discharged, covenanted that they were seised oft he said Estate as of a good Fee-Ample Estate, had good Right to convey; and that the same was free of all Incumbrances; and the Trustees were soon after put into Possession: That the Petitioners, claiming under the said Trust, preferred their Bill in Chancery for Sale of the said Estate, and a Satisfaction of their Debts; and, on the 24th of October 1740, the Lord High Chancellor was pleased to decree, That the Creditors were intitled to the Benefit of the said Trusts; and that an Account should be taken of their Debts; and that the said Estate should be sold for satis fying the lame, subject to the Demand of the Crown for what (if any thing) remained due of the Purchase Money; and that the Money arising by such Sale should (after setting apart £ 30,000, to answer the Demands of the Annuitants for Lives.charged on the Company’s Estates in Scotland) be applied'in satisfaction of what should appear to be really and bona Jide due to the Petitioners and other Creditors of the said Company: That the Petitioners, from 1731 (the Time of their being intitled under the said Tract), used all possible Diligence with the said Company, in order to obtain legal Conveyances of the said Estate;

but that the said Company, well knowing the said Estate would not be sufficient to discharge the Debts owing to the Petitioners, and that no Benefit could arile to themselves therefrom, refused or neglected all Endeavours for that Purpose, to the great Prejudice of the Petitioners: That the House, mentioned in the First Article of the said printed Rental, is a large antient Building, which, at the Time of the Purchase, was, and (till is, in a very ruinous Condition, and in Danger of falling, and uninhabitable, save only a small Part for the Use of the Steward to the said Estate; and the Park and the Demcfnes, mentioned in the same Article, are let to sundry Tenants at the utmost improved Rent; and though £.1,254 has been laid out in Repairs, Improvements, and building Tenants Houses, yet the Premises, comprised in the said First Article of the printed Rental, and thereby estimated at £ 5°°) have never produced more than £.250 per Annum: That, besides the Overcharges above-mentioned, there appears several other Overcharges in the said Rental, amounting to the yearly Value of £.54. 5J.; and also some Part of the Rents due at Martinmas 1720, to which the Company was intitled, were received' by Nicholas Tooke, then Agent to the Commissioners of forfeited Estates, and never accounted for to the Company: That the Petitioners, in 174.2, made Application to the said Company to use their Names, in order to procure a Hearing of the Cause in the Exchequer; which they refusing, the Court of Chancery was applied to, and, after great Opposition made by the Company, an Order was made for that Purpose: That the Petitioner, pursuant thereto, and, in order to obtain legal Conveyances of this Estate, procured the said Causesto be set down for Hearing; which came on in the Court of Exchequer on the 6th of June 1743, when the Hardshipsof the Petitioners were represented, and the Court was pleased to declare, That, with regard to such Hardships, they could not grant the Petitioners Relief for such Overcharges in the Rental, being bound by the drift Words of the Act of Parliament made for the Sale of the said Estate; and though the Court thought it a very hard Cafe, yet that the Petitioners had no other Way of obtaining Relief, but by an Application to the Legislature; and therefore the Court decreed the Agreement so made for Purchase of the said Estate to be carried into Execution, and an Account to be taken of what Money remained due to the Crown thereupon; whereby unless some Relief be obtained for the Petitioners, not only the Purchase-money on such Overcharges, but also a considerable Sum for accumulated Interest thereon, will remain chargeable on the said Estate, and thereby greatly leften the Petitioners Security, already very deficient: And therefore expressing the Hope of the Petitioners, that they maybe intitled to Relief, from the Justice and Favour of the House, not only in Consideration of the great Hardftiips of their Cafe, but also as the said Estate was purchased in the Year 1720, at so great a Price as near Two-and-thirty Years Purchase, by which the Public have already received a much larger Sum than could have been had for the same in any other Year, even if its real Rental had been equal to the estimated One, by which it was purchased: And further setting forth, That by an Act, made in the Fourth Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the First, impowering Commissioners to fell the forfeited Estates, no less than Four of the said Commissioners can execute Conveyances of the said Estates, as directed by the said Act; and the Number of Commissioners being now reduced to Four, some Difficulties may arile in making a proper Title, in case One or more of the said Commissioners should happen to die before the same is completed: And therefore praying the House will be pleated to take into Consideration the great Hardships and Difficulties the Petitioners labour under; and that an Allowance and Abatement may be made them in respect of the Overcharges above-mentioned, and the accumulated Interest arising thereon; and that the Powers of the said surviving Commissioners may be enlarged for making a legal Conveyance ot- the said Estate; or that the Petitioners may have such other Relief in the Premises, as to the House shall seem meet.

Woollen Ma- A Petition of the Clothiers arid Manufacturers of Cloth, fiutailure. Serges, Druggets, Dureys* Sagatces* and other Woollen Goods manufactured in the Town of Taunton, in the County of Scmerfef, Was presented to the House, and read; letting forth, That the Exportation of Cloth, Serges, Druggets, Duroys, Sagatees, and other Woollen Goods, is greatly Irlfcned of late Years* and that many considerable Manufacturers thereof are ruined, on Account of the large Quantities of such-like Sorts of Goods which the Frtncb now manufacture, and on a Bounty allowed by France thereon, which enables them to supply foreign Countries; which Countries were formerly largely supplied from the Manufactures of Great Britain; and chat the Petitioners have great reason to believe, that the Manufacturers or Cloth, Serges, Druggets, Duroys, and other kjW-priced Woollen Goods, will be inevitably ruined, unless the French arc prevented from procuring the raw Wools of England and Ireland; and representing to the House, That the Petitioners apprehend, that if a Law was made to prohibit the Importation of Spanish Wools into Ireland, and to give the People of Ireland a Liberty of exporting to foreign Countries, by way of England, under a Duty at Importation, to be drawn back on Re-exportation, such 'Cambists as they shall manufacture in Ireland, it would

oblige them to work up so much of their own Wools, for their own Wear, and for Exportation, as would (together with what we shall yearly take from them in Wools, Woffled, and Woollen Yarn) effectually prevent the French from procuring their Wools, and employ the Poor of Ireland more fully than they now are, or can be, by manufacturing Spanish Wools; which the Petitioners apprehend, has been a great Cause of their having such Quarts tities of unmanufactured Wool yearly to*fell, or to send to our Rivals the French: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into their Consideration, and to grant the Petitioners such Relief as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the ' Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom it is referred to consider further of the State of the

Woollen ManufaChire of Great Britain and Ireland.

Were severally presented to the House, and read* setting forth. That the Petitioners, as the Laws already Hand, are under great Hardships upon Account of what the Petitioners are obliged to pay to common Carriers for the Carriage of their Goods and Merchandizes: That the Petitioners conceive, that if the Bill now before the House, intituled, A Bill to amend and render more effectual the Laws in being for the Preservation of the public Roads, should pals into a Law, the same would be a Means of raising the Price of the Carriage of Goods and Merchandizes all over the Kingdom of Great Britain, to the great Prejudice of the Petitioners, and all other the Inland Traders, and to the Detriment of the Trade in general of this Kingdom: And therefore praying, That the House will be pleased to take the same of the Petitioners into Consideration, and give them such Relief as to the House shall seem meet.

And the said Petitions were severally ordered to lie upon the Table.

A Petition of the several Persons, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, Inhabitants of Stamford, in the County of Lincoln, and Places adjacent, was presented to

the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petidoners conceive, that if the Bill, now depending in the House, intituled, A Bill to amend and render more effectual the Laws in being for the Preservation of the public Roads, should pass into a Law, the same will not only tend to the Ruin of several Persons who now carry Goods for Hire (the Carriages now erected will, in a manner, be rendered useless to them), but put Thousands of his Majesty's indullrious Subjects under greater Difficulties than at present, and not answer the Purposes intended; and that as1 those Persons, who do now carry Goods for Hire, labour under greater Restraints, that is to say, they are obliged to; have the Wheels of their Carriages bound with Iron of a greater Breadth, and the same drawn by a lesser Number of Horses, than those who carry their own Goods only, the Petitioners apprehend, they cannot have their Goods! carried so reasonally as might be expc&ed^ were the

Wheels of all Persons Carriages bound wirh Iron of an equal Breadth, and such Carriages drawn by Horses not exceeding an equal Number; that the same will be a Means to put a Monopoly of Trade into the Hands of a few large Dealers; who, being under none of the aforesaid Restraints, will, in all Likelihood, by carrying their own Goods only, cut the Roads in a worse Manner, advance the Price of their Goods, with the Price of the Car-; riage of Goods and Merchandizes throughout the Kingdom, and occasion the Ruin of Numbers of fmal! Traders, who, by having their Goods bought at the belt Hand, and brought to them at a moderate Rate, do now support themselves and Families in a decent Manner: And therefore praying, That the House will be pleased to take the same of the Petitioners into Consideration, and give such Relief as shall be thought meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

that have been, and now are, yearly manufactured in Ireland (which the Manufacturers of England formerly supplied them with), and partly to the great Increase of Spanish Cloths manufactured in France, which, on account of a Bounty allowed on Exportation from France, and other Advantages, the French fell in Foreign Countries cheaper than the Manufacturers in England can afford to do; and that the Petitioners apprehend, that the House (when the Act was made to prohibit the Exportation of Fullers Earth, &c.) intended thereby to confine the foie Manufacturing of Woollen Cloths, particularly Superfine Spanish Cloths, to Great Britain only, and to preserve to its Manufacturers all Matcii.ls requisite for the better improving and enlarging that Manufacture; and that the Petitioners apprehend, if the Importation of Spanish Wool into Ireland was prohibited, it would be greatly advantageous to the Petitioners, and, in general, to the Manufacturers of Spanish Wool in Great Britain, and no way prejudicial to any other Branch of the Woollen Manq-fastures of this Kingdom: And therefore praying.

That a Bill may pass to prevent the Importation of Spanish Wool into Ireland, pr that such other Relief be granted in the Premises, as to the House shall seem meet.

Preservat!on ’ A Petition of several Merchants and Tradesmen of of Public Wakefield, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, wa3 Roads, presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioners have, for several Years past, experienced the great Advantage, in their Way of Trade, of Stage Waggons from that Town to Land so back again, which go and return every Week; whereby the several heavy and cumbcrlome Commodities the Petitioners deal in are, with great Security and Certainty, brought and carried to and from Wakefield to Lond without any Loss, Damage, or Delay; which Advantage to the Petitioners, as well as to the Trade in general in this Part of the Kingdom, would be greatly disturbed and incommoded, in case any Restraint, beyond what the Laws uow in being have provided, should be laid upon the Waggon as to the Number of Horses necessarily employed in the conveying of those heavy Goods, which the Necessity of the Petitioners several Trades requires, and more especially at this time, when the Difficulties and Dangers of bringing those Goods by Sea are so very great, that, without a Convoy, the Petitioners cannot hazard so considerable a Property j and which the\\ in order to have the Security of, have of late been frequently obliged to wait several Months for, although their Merchandize and Goods have been as long shipped, and thereby daily periffiing: and as the Waggons for the Conveyance of such Goods are obliged to be made, to answer such Purposes, very substantial and strong, the very Draft whereof, when empty, is sufficient for and as much as Two Horses can well draw; there- fore if the Number of Horses was to be confined to let's than Three or Four more than sufficient to draw the said Waggons when empty, the small Quantity of Goods, to be brought by such Waggons, could not possibly defray the Expence of the Waggoner, who mud therefore necessarily be obliged to lay down his Waggon; whereby the Petitioners, and the Consumers of those Goods they severally deal in; will, by the Increase of the Price of such their Commodities, through the Scarcity and Hazard of removing them, as in Time of Peace, be greatly injured, and-Trade in general suffer greatly thereby: And therefore praying the House will take the Premises into Consideration, as not so far to restrain the Waggoners in their Carriage of Goods, as may either totally oblige them to desist from further carrying the fame, or else by increasing the Rate of Carriage, load those Goods with Charges in-fopportable either by the Merchant or the Consumer.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

forth, That the Manufacture of Cloth in England

is greatly decayed; and that the Exportation of Cloth to foreign Countries is very much lessened of what it was about Twenty Years ago; which, the Petitioners apprehend, has been partly owing to the great Quantities of Spanish Cloths that have been, and now are, manufactured in Ireland, which the Manufacturers of England formerly supplied them with; and partly on Account of the great Quantities of it made in France-, they being, as the Petitioners are informed, by a Bounty allowed on the Expoit&tion of that Commodity, and other Advantages, enabled to undersell us at foreign Markets; and expressing the Desire of the Petitioners, that, as it hath always been the same of this House to encourage and provide for the Woollen Manufacture of this Kingdom, a Bill may pass to prevent the Importation of S Wool into Ireland; which, the Petitioners believe, will be greatly advantageous to them, and the rest of the Manufacturers of super-fine Spanish Cloths in Great Britain, and no-ways prejudicial to any other Branch of the Woollen Manufacture of this Kingdom: And therefore begging the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and grant the Petitioners tuen Relief therein as to the House shall seem meet.

That the Petitioner’s Testator suffered very great Losses by the Depredations of the Spaniards in the Years 1718, 1719, and 1720; the Accounts and Vouchers whereof were duly delivered, according to public Notice, first to the Commissioners Plenipotentiaries from Great Britain at Cambray and Soissons, and afterwards to the Lords of Trade, when Commissaries went from Great Britain to Spain: That, fbme time ago, a Commission iffvied for the Distribution of such Sums as have arisen by Reprisals from the Spaniards, at the Commencement of the present War with Spain, amongst the Suf- ferers; but that Commission' gives only a Power to settle and adjust the Claims of Losses in the Year 1721, and from that time; so that the Sufferers before that time' are excluded any Relief, but by an Application to Par-: stament: That a Petition has been lately presented to thfc1 House by several Merchants of London, who have fpf- tained Losses by Depredations, praying a Relief for their Losses out of the Sixty thousand Pounds granted by Parliament; which Petition has been'referred to a Committee: That the Petitioner conceives he is equally intitled to Relief as other Sufferers, having made the necessary and requisite Proof of the Losses before the' Persons who were authorized to make the Demand: And therefore praying the House to take the same of the Petitioner into Consideration, and to grant him a Satisfaction out of the Sixty thousand Pounds given by Parliament, or in such other manner as to the House shall seem meet.

A Petition of several Merchants and Tradesmen of and within the Town and Parish of Halifax, in the West Riding of the County of York> whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the said Town and Parish of Halifax, taken together, is a very considerable Place and Seat of Trade, but in a mountainous Part of the said Riding,

Twelve or Fourteen Miles distant from any Navigation; by reason whereof, the Petitioners have, for several Years, experienced great Benefit, in their way of Dealing, by Stage Waggons, and other Wheel Carriages, going and coming constantly in every Week from this Town and Parish of Halifax to London; whereby several heavy and bulky Commodities, the Petitioners severally deal in, are, with great Dispatch and Security, brought and carried to' and fro without Loss or Damage to the Owners thereof; which Benefit to the Petitioners in particular, as well as Trade in general in this Part of the Kingdom, would be greatly ditlurbed, if not intirely removed from the Petitioners, in case any greater Restraint, in respect to the Weight such Waggons should respectively carry, or Re* duftion of Horses, which should be so employed therein, be made beyond the Laws now in being to preserve the Roads in this Kingdom; more especially at a time when the Hazard and Danger of Carriage by Sea, without Convoys, are so very great, and such Convoys so difficult and uncertain to be obtained; the Petitioners having beenoften obliged, since the Commencement of the War, for the Reasons above, to wait several Months, after their Goods have been shipped, before they could have them go to London by Sea, to the great Damage of the Owners of such Goods, and the manifest Delay of Trade; and that as the Waggons for conveying such Goods are obliged to be made, to answer such Purposes, very substantial and strong, the Petitioners apprehend no less than Six Horses at the lead can be required, when leaded, to draw the same; the very Carriage itself, when empty, being enough for Two Horses to draw in that Country; so that if the Number of Horses for that Purpose should be reduced, or any greater Restraint be made with respect to Weight, the same will by far fall short of answering the good Ends and Designs of Trade; nay, will not even defray the necessary Expence and Charge of the Waggoner and his Horses; whereby he must of course be obliged to give off his Bu- . finess, and the Petitioners be deprived of the Opportunities of Land Carriage, and left to that single Remedy of removing their Traffick by Sea: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises so far into Consideration, as not to restrain the Waggoners so much in their Carriage of Goods, in respect to the Weight they are to carry, ox reduce the Horses so much in respect to the Number they are to employ, as may either oblige them totally to desist from carrying such Goods, or incxrease' t^e pte-

font

18 Geo. II. i &° MartiL 812

sent Prices or Rates of Carriage they are allowed by Law.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of the Gentlemen, principal Merchants* Drawback and Traders in the Wooilen Manufactures, in and about on foreigo the City of Exeter, was presented to the House, and read; Linens, setting forth, That the Petitioners have observed, by the Voles of this House, that a Petition hath been presented by sundry Persons, Dealers in, and Manufacturers of,

Linens, Threads, and Tapes, made in Great Britain and Ireland, praying further Encouragement to their Manufactures, particularly by taking off the Drawbacks payable at present on the Exportation of foreign Linens 5 and representing to the House, that such Linens are really the principal Part of the Returns for Woollen Goods manufactured by great Numbers of the industrious Poor in those Parts, as well as by many Thousands of British Subjects elsewhere, and exported into Germany and other Places, from whence the greatest Part of those Linens are brought into this Kingdom; and that particularly the almost intire Woollen Manufacture in and about the said City, amounting, according to the nearest Estimate, from One hundred and Fifty, to One hundred and Seventy, thousand Pounds per Annum, chiefly sent into the Circle of Westphalia and that Neighbourhood, is paid for by Bills on London, out of the Produce of those Linens; and that therefore the Petitioners are very apprehensive, that should their Importation be further clogged, by laying on of higher Duties, or the Drawbacks payable at present on them taken off (as those People have nothing else by' which they can make Returns to any considerable Value),

the Consequence must be the intire Ruin of the Woollen Manufacture in those Parts, by which means many Thou? sands of our Poor must ntceffarily be unemployed and starve, or become a Burthen on the Lands, and'our Wool at the same time lie rotting in the Grower’s Hands, or smuggled into foreign Parts, and manufactured there, and so the French, our formidable Rivals in Trade, would have

it in their Power to cut us out also of a great Part of our Trade with Spain and Portugal-, and further rcpre-fenting to the House, That the Petitioners apprehend . that

A Petition of the under-written Merchants, Planter, and others, trading to, and interested in, the Plantations in America, in behalf of themselves and many

others, was also presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That our Plantations are at present supplied from hence with great Quantities of foreign Linens for their own Comlumption, on which a considerable Profit remains to this Nation, and the Price comes already much dearer to our Planters, than if they were permitted a direct Importation from foreign Parts; and representing to the House, the Opinion of the Petitioners, that our Home Manufactures of Linen cannot as yet furnish the proper Sorts, nor in sufficient Quantities, to answer our Plantation Demands; and that if the Drawbacks should be taken off, the Price of Linens exported from hence would be so exorbitant, that it is much to be feared this valuable Branch of Trade would be loft, and the Inhabitants of our Colonies find out some other Methods of supplying themselves, either by Manufactures of their own, or by clandestine Importation from Foreigners: And therefore praying. That the Drawbacks on foreign Linens, exported to our Plantations, may be continued.

A Petition of the Linen Drapers of London, dealing in foreign, and in British and Linen for Home Consumption, and also for Exportation to all the Plantations, and the Northern Colonies, and to the Coast of , the Spani/k IV,eft Indies, i£c. was presented to the House, and read; setting forth. That the Petitioners perceive that an Application hath been made to the House, praying further Encouragements to the British and Irish Manufacture of Linen, and tending to take off the Drawbacks at prefen* allowed on the Re-exportation of foreign linens, and representing to the House,‘That the

and Irish Linens which are made and brought into this Kingdom, are free of Duty, and have many other Advantages, when, at the same Time, foreign Linens imported are charged according to their Breadths, with very high Duties, which alone is so great an Encouragement to the Home Manufacture, and the Demand is so great, that thrice the Quantity thereof might be fold, if the same could be made and bought for a reasonable Price; and that therefore the Petitioners conceive the Home Manufacturers cannot want a foreign Market before such Time (if ever) as they shall be able to supply this; and that the Quantity of low-priced Linens tqade in Great Britain and Ireland, under Twelve Pence the Yard, bears a small Proportion to the general Demand, it being well known, that more than Three-fourths of the narrow German Linen imported (of which there are annually about Twenty Millions of Yards imported), are consumed in this Kingdom, and amongst those many of the same Species which are exported to our Plantations; so that the Petitioners cannot but be surprized, that it should be represented that there was not a sufficient Demand for coarse Linens in England, unless for Exportation; and further setting forth, That the Encouragement to the Home Manufacture, which was desired of the Parliament in 1737, was prayed to be upon the coarse Linens, and it was then asserted, that if the Drawbacks on foreign Linens were taken oft', the Manufacture would greatly increase, and would be fold near Six per Cent, cheaper than the foreign; and that about Two Years ago a large Bounty was given (exceeding the Drawback upon foreign Linens) upon exporting such coarse Linens, whereupon the Petitioners hoped, that some of the promised Effects from that great Encouragement would have appeared; but that* notwithstanding such Encouragement, and the Advance in Price of Linens (and particularly those of North Britain) a very inconsiderable Part of that Bounty hath been applied to the Uses for which it was appropriated; from whence the Petitioners conceive, that the Home Manufacture of coarse Linen is very little, if at all, increased; and that if a foreign Trade also were necessary, the great Bounty so lately allowed on Exportation of British and Irish Linen, would be a sufficient Encouragement to export the same to the Plantations, the Coast of Africa, and the Spanish West Indies, if Quantities could be made so fit for those Countries, as what are supplied by foreign Linens: That the said particular Bounty allowed on Exportation of the Home Manufacture, not only exceeds the Drawback allowed on foreign Linen, but it is more easily and speedily to be obtained, and not attended with near the Expence, Delay, or Trouble, which the Exporters of foreign Linen are at, in order to receive the Drawback; neither are Home Linens under the Necessity of being under separate Packages from other Goods; and Jhe -Oaths on the exporting of them are only the common Securities required to be taken in all Cases of Bounties, to prevent Frauds upon the Revenue being otherwise committed: That many Sorts of foreign Linens are found to suit the Inhabitants in the Plantations, in Africa, and in the Spanish West Indies, better than the and Irish Linens; and that, should the Drawback be taken off those Linens, it would not only encourage, but necessitate, the African Merchants and others, to fend their Ships to Holland for their Linen Cargoes, to the great Prejudice of the Petitioners, of the India Company, and of many other Traders, who now gain by furnitliing those Cargoes here; besides which, as it is but too certain that a clandestine Trade is already carried on from the French and Dutch Settlements in the Neighbourhood of our Plantations, by the loading such foreign Linens, which should be exported from hence, that illicit Trade must increase, in proportion to the Encouragement it would receive from taking off the Drawback, at present payable on foreign Linens, whereby this valuable Branch of our Commerce would be in great measure loft to the Nation, to the Prejudice of the Petitioners in particular, as well as of the Kingdom in general: And therefore praying the House, That the Petitioners may have

Leave

i8 Geo. II. 21 821

Leave to he heard, by themselves or Counsel, before the said Drawbacks arc taken off, or any further Burthens are laid on the Re-exportation of foreign Linens.

Sir John Chapman reported from the Committee, to York whom the Petition of several Creditors of the Governor and Company of Undertakers for raising the Thames Water in York Buildings, whose Names are thereunto lub-feribed, on behalf of themselves, and other Creditors of the said Company, was referred, That the Committee had examined the Matter of Fad: contained in the said Pet ition; and had directed him to report a State thereof to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth;

That, on the 30th of March 1720, the fair! Company contracted with the Commissioners of forfeited Estates for the Purchase of the Estate of William late Lord Wid-dringtvn, in the County of Northumberland (which was mentioned in a printed Rental or Particular, produced to your Committee, to be of the annual Value of £1,808.

14J. id. at and for the Price of £57,100, being above the Kate of 31 Years and an Half Purchase; depending upon the Truth of the Rental or Particular:

That, by the Conditions of Sale, and the said Contract* your Committee find, that the Purchaser was to pay Ond Fifth-part of the Purchase-money on the 24th of June then following, and the remaining Four Fifths on thd 29th of September then next, with Intefeft at 5 from the said 30th of March to the several Days of Payment; and the Purchaser was to be intitled (pursuant to the C nditions of Sale) to the Rents accruing from Martinmas then last:

That on the 25th of June I’jlo, the said Company paid the Sum of £ 11,556. is. 1 being the Fifth-part of the Purchase-money, and Interest, into his Majesty’s Exchequer, and paid further, on Account thereof, by Instalments, several Sums, to the 13th of 1722, which, with the said Sum of £11,556. ir. 11 amounted to £49,404. 125. 8*<£; as appears by a Certificate under the Hand of One of the Officers of his Majesty’s Exchequer:

That the First Article of the printed Rental, by which the Company purchased the said Estate, is in the following Words: " A large House and Gardens, in good Order " and Repair, with convenient Outhouses, a large Park " well flocked, with Demesnes thereto, valued at about " £500 per Annum." notwithstanding which, it appears to your Committee, by the Report of the Commissioners for forfeited Estates, made to the House the 17th Day of January 1717, that the Premises comprised in the said Article were at that time let at no more than £250 pgr, Annum;and it also appeared by the Commissioners Receiver’s Account of the Rents of the said Estate, for the Half Year due the ill of May 1720, that the same was let at no more than after the Rate of £250 per Annum, subject to several Deductions and Allowances thereout for Taxes and Repairs, amounting to £82. ioj. per Annum:

That the House is a large antient Building, which, at the time of the Purchase, was in a very indifferent State of Repair, and is in a very ruinous Condition, and Part thereof in Danger of falling, and uninhabitable, and the Park and Demelnes therein mentioned are let to sundry Tenants at the utmost improved Rent; and though it appears, that £1,254 hath been laid out in Repairs and Improvements on that Part of the Estate mentioned in the First Article of the said Rental, yet the Premises therein comprised and estimated at £500 per Annum, have never produced, as appears to your Committee,

£250 per Annum.

And it further appeared, that several other Articles in the said Rental have proved deficient to the yearly Amount of £54. 5s. 2 id.; a particular Account whereof is hereunto annexed; and the Creditors, or their Trustees, have never received any Advantage therefrom since the Year 1731,when they first entered upon the said Estate; or did it appear, that the Company had received any Benefit thereby.

And your Committee find, that the Company craved an Abatement and Allowance out of the remaining Part of the Purchase-money, for Overcharges; and, on the 1 ft of June 1727, laid the same before the Right Honourable the then Lords Commissioners of his Majesty’s Treasury; whereby, after an Allowance of the said Overcharges, the Balance then remaining unpaid appeared to be£. 2,567* I2J. 1 \d. 5 which Sum the Company paid into the Exchequer the 15th of the same June-, and, upon such Application, the Lords of the Treasury declared, that however reasonable the Deductions might be, which were claimed by the Company, yet they had no Power - over the fame; but referred it for the Determination of the Barons of the Court of Exchequer; and your Committee find, that* in 1727, Suits in the Exchequer were brought for that Purpose, on behalf of the Crown and of the Company, relating to what Allowances should be made in respect of such Overcharges, and for legal Conveyances to be made of such Estate:

That the said Company being considerably indebted on their Bonds for Money borrowed to pay for the Purchase of this and other forfeited Estates, did, as a further Security to their Creditors, on the 18th of January 1731, convey the Estate of the said late Lord Widdrington to Trustees, to be sold for Payment of the said Bonds and Interest; on which there is now due for Principal and Interest, the Sum of 121,000, and upwards, being a much greater Sum than the whole Value of the said Estate 5 2nd the Company then depending, that the Balance due to the Public was, as aforesaid, fully discharged, covenanted, that they were seised of the said Estate as of a good Fee-simple Estate, had good Right to convey; and that the same was free of all Incumbrances; and the Trustees were soon after put in Possession.

And your Committee find, that the Creditors claiming under the said Trust preferred their Bill in Chancery for Sale of the said Estate, and a Satisfaction of their Debts; and, ondhe 24th of October 1740, it was decreed. That the Creditors were intitled to the Benefit of the said Trusts; and that an Account should be taken of their Debts; and that the said Estate should be sold for satisfying the fame, subject to the Demand of the Crown for what (if any thing) remained due of the Purchase-money; and that the Money arising by such Sale should, after v furring apart £. 30,000, to answer the Demands of the Annuitants for Lives charged on the Compares Estates in Scotland, be applied in Satisfaction of what should>Appear to be really, and bona fide, due to such Creditors of the said Company.

And your Committee also find, that the said Creditors, from 1731 (the Time of their being intitled under the said Trust), used all possible Diligence with the said Company, in order to obtain legal Conveyances of the said Estate; but the Company refused, or neglected, all Endeavours for that Purpose, to the Prejudice of the said Creditors; and it appeared by the Evidence of Mr. IVaddilove, Agent for the Creditors, that he has often applied to the late Solicitor to the Treasury, to have the Balance settled between the Crown and the Company, and to get the said Causes in the Exchequer set down for Hearing; that a legal Conveyance might be made of the said Estate; yet he could not obtain the fame; and no legal Conveyance hath as yet been made:

That, in 1742, the Creditors made Application to the Company, to use their Names, in order to procure a Hearing of the Causes in the Exchequer; which they refusing, Application was made, on their behalf, to the Court of Chancery; whereupon an Order was made for that Purpose on the 28th of October 1742:

That, pursuant thereto, and in order to obtain legal Conveyances of this Estate, the Creditors procured the It

said Causes to be set down for Hearing; which, on the 6th of June 1743, came on to be heard in the Court of Exchequer, when their HardIhips were represented; and, as it appeared to your Committee, the Court declared.

That, with regard to such Hard ships, they could not grant them Relief for such Overcharges in the Rental, being bound by the drift Words in the Act; of Parliament, made for the Sale of the said Estate; and that they had no other Way of obtaining Relief but by an Application to Parliament; and thereupon the Court decreed the Agreement, so made for Purchase of the said Estate, to be carried into Execution, and an Account to be taken of what Money remained due to the Crown thereupon.

And your Committee find, that, unless some Relief be obtained for the Creditors, not only the Purchase-money on such Overcharges, but also a considerable Sum for accumulated Interest thereon, will remain chargeable on the said Estate, and thereby greatly lessen the Creditors Security, already deficient.

And your Committee find, that the said Estate was purchased, in the Year 1720, at near 32 Years Purchase; by which the Public have already received a much larger Sum than could have been had for the same in any other Year, even if the real annual Value had been equal to the Value estimated in the Rental, by which it was purchased.

And your Committee find, that the Money which has been already paid into the Exchequer on Account of the said Purchase, amounts to the Sum of £. 51,972. lo d.; so that there remains unpaid of the principal Purchase-money of £. 57,100, contracted for, the Sum of £.5,127. 15* *d. exclusive of Interest.

That by an Act, made in the Fourth Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the First, for impowering Commissioners to fell the forfeited Estates, &V. no less than Four of the said Commissioners can execute Conveyances of the said Estate.

And your Committee find, that there now remains only Three of the said Commissioners living; so that no Conveyance can be made of the said Estate without the Assistance of Parliament.

A PETITION of the several Persons, whose names are thereunto subscribed, being Traders in the Town of Nottingham, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That as the Laws already stand, the Petitioners are under great Hardships upon Account of what they are obliged to pay to common Carriers for Carriage of their Goods and Merchandizes; and that the Petitioners conceive, that if the Bill, now depending before the House, intituled, A Bill to amend and render more effectual the Laws in being for Preservation of the public Roads, should pass into a Law, the same would be a Means to raise the Price of our Home Manufactures; so that they cannot be carried to foreign Markets upon an Equality with foreign Goods of the same Nature; and that the Stocking Weaving, the great and chief Manufactory of that Country, already lies under great Hard-{hips, by reason the French make up their Goods in a much (lighter Manner than we do, and of course fell them at a much lower Price; so that it is impossible for us to go to the foreign Markets upon an equal Footing; and that every Advance of Carriage (which mud of consequence follow the taking off the Number of Horses now allowed by Act of Parliament) will enhance the Prices of our Commodity at the foreign Markers; and that as to other Commodities which the Petitioners deal in, by reason of the Uncertainty of Convoys, they are, in a great measure, forced to make use of Land Carriage, which is already lenfibly felt by the Trader and Consumer: And therefore praying the House to take the same into Consideration, and to give the Petitioners such Relief as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Report from the Committee, to whom the said Bill was committed, be taken into further Consideration.

Ordered, That the proper Officer do lay before this House, an Account of what Sums of Money remain in the VOL. 24.

A Petition of Richard Partridge, Agent for John Green, Owner of the Sloop Endeavour, Giles Gibbs Matter, and Owner of Part of the Cargo on board her; as also Agent for Samuel Holmes, another Freighter in the said Sloop, taken by the Spaniards; being offered to be presented to the House:

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer, by his Majesty’s Command, acquainted the House, That his Majesty, having been informed of the Contents of the said Petition, recommends it to the ConGderation of the House.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read; setting forth, That the said Sloop Endeavour, Giles Gibbs Matter, was, on the 11th of February 1727-8, taken by a Spanish Guarda Costa, Nicholas Duan Commander, and carried into Baraco, on the I (land of Cuba, and afterwards to Saint Jago, where the said Sloop was condemned, together with all the Cargo on board (the Petitioners Interest therein), amounting in the whole to £. 800 Sterling dnd upwards, of which the Petitioner hath proper Proofs to produce, which he received but in the Year 1742: That the said John Green, Owner of the said Sloop Endeavour, and the other Freighter of Goods on board her, are his Majesty’s Subjects, living at Rhode-Island in New-England: That by the Commission lately ifi'ued by his Majesty, for distributing to the Sufferers by Spanish Depredations the Moiety of the Prizes taken from the Spaniards at the breaking out of the present War, it is therein provided, That, with respect to the Losses before the Treaty of Seville, bearing Date the 9th of November 1729, no Persons are intitled to any Share of the Prise

Money, whole Claims were not entered, and Proofs exhibited, before the 30th of June 1743, to the Commis-faries, or some proper Office in London; and thereby, through the Petitioner’s Inadvertency, they are excluded from any Benefit arising out of the said Moiety of Prize Money, in not exhibiting their Claim before the said 30th of June 1743, was occasioned by their not

knowing the Limitation of the Time for exhibiting of the said Claim: And therefore praying the House to take the unfortunate same of the said Sufferers into ConGderation, and to grant them Relief out of the Sixty thousand Pounds granted by Parliament, in the Year 1739, to answer what had been acknowleged to be due from Great Britain to Spain, upon the Convention between those Two Kingdoms, although the Petitioners have not gone through all the necessary Forms, as some other of the Sufferers have done.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee, to whom the Petition of several Merchants of London, trading to Portugal, Spain, and Italy, whose Names are thereunto subscribed; and also the Petition of Sir Daniel Lambert Knight; are referred: And that they do examine, and It ate to the House, the Matter of Fact contained in this Petition.

A Petition of John Stretch Merchant, together with an Account thereunto annexed, was presented to the House, and the said Petition was read; setting forth, That, upon the Embarkation of his Majesty’s Forces for Flanders, John Ellis Esquire was appointed Director General of the Hospital to be established for the Sick and Wounded, and appointed John IValmeJly and James Breme his Deputies: That an Hospital was established in Ghent, in September 1742, for the Reception of the said vSick and Wounded, and was supplied with Provisions and Necessaries by the said Deputies: That in the Month of March 1743, when the said Forces marched for Germany, a flying Hospital was ordered to attend the fame, and the said James Walmefly acted as Director to such Hospital, and employed the Petitioner as his Assistant: That the flying Hospital was first established at Nied* about Four Miles from Frankfort* and afterwards was ordered to Hannau, and then removed to Feckenheim and Bergball, and on the nth of June 1743, kid IValmefley employed the Petitioner as Purveyor, and from that Time, till the 20th of October following, the Petitioner acted as such, and disbursed several large Sums of Money for Provisions and Necessaries for the said Hospital, and received several Sums at different Times on account of his Disbursements, for which he always gave Receipts; and that there is now due to the Petitioner the Sum of £.3,058. 6. 8, as will appear by the annexed Account: That the Number of Men charged for in the said flying Hospital in Germany, from the 18th of May to the 20th of October following, reckoning the Men every Day in such Hospital, was 173,856 in the whole; and the Provisions bought for and expended by them, amounted only to £. 9,114. 5. 3; which makes the Charge of each Man Twelve Pence Halfpeny and One-Gxteenth Part of a Peny per Diem: That the said IValmefley gave the Petitioner the Specimen of an Account of the Expences of the Hospital at Ghent, from the 5th of September 1742, to the 24th of December following, both Days inclusive, whereby it will appear that each Man was charged, One with another, at the Rate of One Shilling and Ten Pence Halfpeny per Diem; and the said Walmesley inGfted, that the Petitioner should make out a general Account after that Rate, which the Petitioner absolutely refused to comply with, as he could not justify the same by his Vouchers; for that che same Number of Men charged at is, ioij per Diem each, would amount to £-16,299, which would be an Overcharge to the Public of £,7,184. 14. 9, at which Rate the said Wal-tnejley has declared to the Petitioner he would make out his Account, notwithstanding the Petitioner has all the Vouchers in his Custody: That the Number of Men charged for in the Hospital at Ghent, from the said Fifth fc of

To prove what was alleged in the First Petition, the ACta of Parliament recited therein were read; the First of which, being an Act made in the Second Year of the Reign of King William and Queen Mary, for the Encouraging of the Distilling of Brandy from Corn, recites. That by an Act, made in the First Year of their said Majesties Reign, for prohibiting Commerce with France, all Brandies, Aqua Vit*e, and Spirits, were prohibited to be imposed into this Kingdom; and that good and whole-fomt Brandies, Aqua Vitae, and Spirits, might be drawn from malted Corn; and therefore, for encouraging the Making of Brandies, strong Waters, and Spirits, from malted Corn, and for the greater Consumption of Corn, and the Advantage of Tillage in this Kingdom, imposed a Duty of One Peny only on every GaiJon of low Wines of the First Extraction, drawn from Drink brewed and made of any sort of malted Corn; and likewise imposed the several Duties of Eight Pence, Twelve Pence, and Three Pence, on every Gallon of low Wines made or drawn from the several other Materials therein mentioned; and makes Provision for obliging Distillers to draw their low W ines, or Spirits of the First Extraction, from clean and wholesome Drink made of malted Corn intirely, without any Mixture with any Melasses, Walh, or Tilts, or other Materials whatsoever; and, for encouraging the Exportation of Brandies or Spirits made from malted Corn, allows a Drawback of Three Pence for every Gallon of such Brandy or Spirits, without any Mixture with other Materials.

This Act was continued by another Act, made in the Seventh and Eighth Years of the Reign of King William.

And by the Act, made in the Thirteenth Year of the Reign of King William, for granting several n w Duties on low Wines, or Spirits of the First Extraction, the like Drawback of Three Pence upon the Exportation of

The Act, made in the Sixth Year of his present Majesty’s Reign, for the better Encouragement of Spirits drawn from Corn in Great Britain, allows a Drawback, upon Exportation, of £. 4. i8j. for every Tun of such Spirits drawn from Barley, Malt, or other Corn; and also, a Bounty of £. 1. 10s* when Barley is at 24 j. per Quarter, or under.

After which, several Witnesses were examined, with regard to that Part of the said Petition which complains of a Decrease in the Consumption of Corn, by Distillers uling Corn unmalted.

And the Evidence given to that Point was to the EffeCb following:

Mr. Stephen South, Dealer in Spirits, said. That Four Parts in Five of the Corn from which Distillers at present draw their Spirits are unmalted: That, in 1739, he saw an Instance of this Practice at a Distiller’s at Deptford, and counted the Sacks of malted and unmalted Corn, as they were emptied into the Tun.

Mr. William Harvest, Malt Distiller, said; That, during the Time he was concerned in the Business of Distilling, which was from 1726 to 1737, Two Parts in Three of the Corn used in drawing Spirits were generally malted; but that he had heard, that the greatest Part of the Corn used of Jate is unmalted*

He said likewise, That about Twelve Quarters of Barley produce One Tun of Spirits; which, if drawn from Malt, will require Fourteen Quarters, and thereby occasion an additional Expence of about £. 3. 12 s. each Tun; and that Spirits drawn from Barley are not, as he apprehends, so good as Spirits drawn from Malt.

Mr. Thomas "Waite, Farmer, said. That the Distillers never use worse Corn than the Maltsters: That they will not buy sprouted Corn, because their Spirits excel in Goodness proportionably to the Goodness of the Corn; and that therefore Corn, when it is bad, must be a great Loss to the Farmers, if they cannot fat Hogs with it.

Mr. John Parker, Farmer, said. That he grows 400 Quarters of Bailey in a Year: That he sold to a Distiller iome damaged Corn, that was capable of being malted, for 20 s, per Quarter, when the Price of other Corn was at 24 s. per Quarter:

That some Part of sprouted Corn is capable of being malted; but that not above One-half of mow-burnt Corn will malt, as had been found upon Trial.

Being asked the Question, he said. That if Distillers were prohibited the Use of unmalted Com, there would be a great Quantity yearly that could not be malted, from which Spirits might be drawn; but that the Farmers might, as he believed, use all of it themselves in feeding Hogs and Horses; and that the Consumption thereof this Way would be more beneficial than any Advantage they can make of it at present.

Mr. Timothy Child> Farmer, said, That Corn in wet Harvests is frequently very much sprouted; and that One-half of it will not then malt.

Which was also confirmed by Mr. Pope, Farmer, who grows Seven or Eight hundred Quarters of Barley in One Year, and fells the same to Maltsters; and who added likewise, that he never had any Corn incapable of being malted during the time he has been in Business, which is about Four Years; but that there is, in bad Harvests in England, Corn that cannot be malted; and that mow-burnt Com will not malt: That he has had Com very bad, with which he would have fed Hogs, had lie had Opportunity; and that other Farmers feed Hogs and Horses with damaged Corn: That he has offered to fell Corn to a Distiller; but he would not give the Price for it the Maltster would.

Mr. Ralph Porter, Maltster, said, That the Distillers using such a large Quantity of Corn unmalted, lessens the Consumption of Corn, diminishes the Malt Duty, and deprives the Maltsters of the Profit of the Manufactory; which he demonstrated in the following Manner.

He could give no satisfactory Answer, when lie was afkedr Whether 100 Quarters of Barley would make as much Spirit as-100 Quarters of Malt } but, in another Part of his Examination, he said, That he believed, if the Spirit could be got clean out of 10c Quarters of Barley, it would produce a Quantity equal to 137 Quarters Busheis of Malt, by reason the Weight of both is equal 5 and it is upon Weight that he grounded his Computation.’ He added further, That what Strength the Distiller doth not extra# in Spirit from Barley, when ground, remained in the Grains, which he gives to Hogs.

With regard to the additional Expence the Distillers would be at by the Use of malted Corn only; he said, he apprehended, that they are able to bear Part of that Expence; for that, before the late Duty was imposed, Distillers fold Spirits for£. 18 per Tun, but afterwards they made the Duty a Pretence for raising the Price to £. 24 per Tun.

Mr. William Harvest said. That he believed the additional Expence of Spirits, drawn from intire Malt, would be 7 d. per Gallon; but that the same would not necessarily occasion the Price to be raised; the present Profit of the Distillers being between Three and Four Pounds per Tun; though he doubted not they would raise the Price in proportion to their additional Expence; and that Spirits drawn from Malt would deserve an higher Price, being much better than those drawn from Barley.

Mr. South said. That One Tun of Malt Spirits, which is 252 Gallons, made into Gin, and retailed at Three Half-pence the Quarter of £. s. d. a Pint (which is 4s. per Gallon), amounts to 50. 8. —

That great Quantities of Gin are mixed One Third-part with Water, and is fold for 1 d. the Quarter of a Pint; which though it brings the Spirit to the same Price of £. 50. 8 s. per Tun, yet it occasions an Increase, for which no Com is con fumed, or any Duty paid:

That as the Profit upon every Tun of Spirits, drawn from Malt only, would (exclusive of the Distiller’s Profit) amount to/. *-9. 19J. per Tun, the Witness said, there would be no Reason tb apprehend, that any additional Expence would fall upon the Conl'umer; and consequently, that the Grower of Corn would sustain no Loss.

He ‘.aid, That unmalted Corn was at first made use of by the Distillers, under Pretence of making a Paste of it to put round the Tun, to prevent their Spirits from evaporating; from which Time the Use of it has gradually increased to the present Proportion:

That, at the time when Distillers used malted Corn intirely, they fold their Spirits at is. 1 od. per Gallon; but that, about Two Years since, they raised the Price of Spirits from £. 18 to £.24per Tun; and that they have at present a very large Profit, besides the Advantage of feeding Hogs.

Mr. John Butterfield, a Farmer, who rents £ 300 per Annum, said, That the Price of Corn was reduced at the time Distillers raised the Price of Spirits, as mentioned by Mr. South; and that, was Corn to be sold at 24J. per Quarter, the Profit of the Distillers is so large, that they would have no Occasion to raise the Price of Spirits.

He said further, That there has been no considerable Exportation of Corn for many Years; and that the Price at present is so low, that it is impossible for the most industrious Farmer to gain a Livelihood: That, when j 00,000 Quarters are exported in any One Year, the Price is raised considerably; and that if Distillers were obliged to draw their Spirits from Corn malted, it would occasion an Increase in the Consumption of 300,00a Quarters every Year; from which a great Benefit would arise; whereas the Distillers Trade at present is a great Detriment to the Farmers; but he owned, the Distillers must pay for the Increase of that Consumption:

That he hath had large Quantities of Corn, in some Years, incapable of being malted, which he could make use of in feeding Hogs; and that were the Distillers to* use malted Corn only, the Farmers could feed Hogs as cheap as they; but now, by reason the Distillers buy only the best Corn, the damaged Corn is useless to the Farmers; ii being not worth their while to fat Hogs with it.

Mr. Harvest said, That the Distillers cannot use bad Corn unmalted, because it gives their Spirits a Taste; but that £oarfe smutty Wheat and Barley, when malted, will make good Spirits: That Distillers buy both good and bad Corn at Bear Key; and that, at present, the Farmers give their bad Corn to their Horses.

And he and Butterfield said likewise, That, in case the Distillers used none but malted Corn, they would then be obliged to buy the Farmers damaged Corn to fat their Hogs.

And the said Butterfield being asked, Whether a further Imposition of 4d. per Gallon on Spirits at the Still Head would be an Advantage to the Grower of Corn ? he said, He believed it would be greatly injurious to the Farmers; for that it would not increase the Consumption of Corn, and they would still suffer.

Then, in order to prove that Hogs are fed with the Grains of unmalted Corn used by Distillers, and the

treat Detriment that Farmers sustain thereby, the Evidence given to the Committee was as follows: Mr. Thomas Waite said. That he has seen 2,000 Hogs fatting at one time in a Distillers Yard at Deptford: That they are not fed with Corn, but Distillers Wash, and other things by them used; whereby they are kept always drunk: That, by this Method, he said, a Hog will be fatted in about Twelve or Thirteen Weeks/; but that their Fat is only Greale or Tallow; and that he can, at the Market, distinguisti Hogs fed in this Manner from Hogs fed in the Country; and that he apprehends, the Flesh of Hogs fed by Distillers will not take Salt; but he never tried the Experiment:

That poor People, who have bought Distillers Hogs, have declared, they would rather give is. per Stone for Country-fed Hogs, than 14d. per Stone for those fed by Distillers; the latter of which, he laid, he could buy for that Price:

That this Practice of feeding Hogs is prejudicial to the Farmers, who cannot dispose of their Offal and damaged Corn, otherwise than by feeding Hogs and Fowls; which Hogs they cannot feed so cheap as the Distillers; nor is it possible to feed them without dry Meat; and that the best Bacon is the Bacon of Hogs fed with the best Pease.

Mr. John Butterfield said, That, in the Year 1722, he fatted a great many Hogs with Corn not capable of being malted; and the Price of Bacon was at that time 2 s. 4 d. per Stone to the Market, and 2s. 6d. perStone to private Families: That, the next Year, it was is. 6d. per Stone to Market, and is. 8d. per Stone to private Families: That, the succeeding Year, it fold for is. id. to Market, and is. 4d. per Stone to private Families; but he could not recollect what the Price of Com was at that time: That he afterwards fatted Hogs for some time 5 but when Pork was reduced to lod. per Stone, he left it off; and that that Sort of Corn he then fed Hogs with is now useless to him:

That many Farmers have left off Feeding and Breeding of Swine; for they may as well throw their Com away, as attempt to feed Swine upon an Average with the Distillers: That the sprouted Corn, with which the Witness used to feed Hogs, he makes very little Use of at present; some of it, he said, he had sold to a Person who grinds Corn for the Distillers, at 4s.per Quarter Ids than the Price he fold Corn to the Maltsters; and the Person who bought it, fold it again at $s. per Quarter Loss: That the Bacon of the Swine fed by the Distillers, when it comes to be boiled, wastes half away, and the Remainder of it is very soft and greasy; and that the keeping'many Swine confined together breeds Distempers amongst them: That he apprehends, if the Distillers were reirrained from feeding Hogs in this manner, it woifW be a great Advantage to the Farmers at a considerable Distance from London>z(\pecially those who have fenny Lands, or who live in inland Countries; for they then would feed many more Hogs, and might fend them to Market, when they could not fend their Corn:

That the very best fed Pork may now be bought for 20d. per Stone; and great Quantities are fold under that Price:

That several Persons in the West of England used to fend Hogs to Portsmouth, and would now, if they could get a Price for it upon an Average with the Distillers.

Being examined as to an Advertisement last Year from the Victualling Office, which expressed, That the Commissioners of the Victualling Office had dealt, and were willing to deal again, with the Farmers; he laid, he had beard of it; but that Proposals are always sent to the Commissioners, and the lowest Price is accepted; and that he believed the Victualling Office had not dealt with Farmers for many Years.

Mr. William Harvest said. That, during the time he was in the Business of the Distillery, Spirits being then drawn from Corn Two Parts malted to One unmalted, Vol. 24.

the Walh would feed, but not fat, Swiriey without a

That he took Four Hogs fed with Distillers Wash, and though he gave them each a Sack of Pease, yet, when their Flesh came to be boiled, the Fatfeparated from the Lean, and was so bad that his Servants could not eat it.

And he added, that, if the Distillers were to use no unmalted Corn, they could not feed Hogs without mixing coarle Com with their Walh.

Mr. John Parker said, That the Number of Hogs fatted by the Distillers has lessened the Value of Country Pork; and believes it to be the Cause of the Cheapness of all other Meat; and that it was likewise a great Detriment to the Graziers: That the Witness, in this Particular, had been a considerable Sufferer by it; having fed Cattle, and obliged to fell them for the same Price he bought them at:

That, were the Distillers to use no unmalted Corn, they could not then feed their Hogs without buying coarse Corn from the Farmers; and that the Farmers might consume ail their Corn that would not malt, by feeding their Hogs and Horses; which he said, he apprehended, would be a much more beneficial Way of disposing of it than any they have at present.

Mr. Timothy Child said, That he has been in the Business of Making of Bacon upwards of Twenty Years t That he has bought Hogs fatted by Farmers and by Distillers: That Pork and Bacon of Distillers Hogs is not near so good as the Farmers if kept any time; nor is the Flesh so firm when drest: That it wastes in the Dressing very much; and that Six Pounds of the Bacon fed in the Country will do as much Service as eight Pounds of what is fed by the Distillers:

That the Flesh of Distillers Hogs will take Salt, being of a soft Nature; but is unwholesome when kept in Salt or Pickle any time; and Haif of it will be rotten, when the Flesh of Farmers Hogs killed at the same time, will be very good; nor will the former keep so well as the latter in Summer, particularly in the Months of June, July, and August; during which time, the one is very good, and the other very rank and bafl: That his Customers, he laid, often complain to him that it is fish-fed; and that lie apprehends there is as much Difference between the one and the other as between a rotten Apple and a found one.

He laid, he gives about Two Pence a Stone more for the Country-fed Hogs than those the Distillers feed; but that he makes no Difference in the Price to hisCustomers: That he has had the Distillers Meat frequently returned, which he has changed for Meat fed in the Country; and those who have bought both Sorts, have found such a Difference, when boiled, that they afterwards have always asked for the latter.

Being further examined, he said, That the Meat of the Distillers Hogs is eatable inSummer; but it has frequently made People sick; and that he has heard that the Country-fed Meat is most in Esteem in private Families in London: That there is little Difference in Appearance between Farmers and Distillers Hogs at Market; but that he can distinguisti them.

He said further, that he apprehends $ie Pork and Bacon of Hogs fed by Distillers will not keep good in a Voyage to the Eafi or West Indies; and that if the Feeding of Hogs by the Farmers was encouraged, it would cause a great Consumption of Com.

Benjamin Rutland, Grazier, said, That the Fatting of Hogs by Distillers has been the cause of reducing the Rent of Marfii Lands which have lately fallen about Fifteen Shillings in Two Pounds, or Two Pounds Ten Shillings, a Year: That he formerly let a Piece of Marsh Land for j£. 120 per Annum, which is now rented for £. 80; and that he apprehends the Occasion of this Abatement is owing to Distillers feeding and jelling Hogs so cheap; whereby they have reduced the Price of other Meat; and which Practice, he said, he believed, encouraged the Breed of Hogs; but that, if it were otherwise,

That, at present, the Farmers feed their Servants with Bacon; but, if they could dispose of all they feed, they might buy Beef, and other Meat, for their Servants very reasonable:

Mr. John Jennings said. That he has been a Contractor in buying Hogs for the Victualling Office: That he has observed, that the Flesh of Hogs that are killed directly from feeding is grosser than the Flesh of those drove a Hundred Miles; and that the Hogs, that have faded for some time before they are killed, will take Salt better than those that are killed when they are full; and that the longer they fad, the better they will keep Salt, by reason, as he apprehends, that their Juices ferment the less after they are killed:

That Hogs fed byDidillers are often killed full; and that he has observed the Meat don't keep sweet so long as the Meat of Hogs fed ,in the Conn try: That, about Two Years ago, he bought Three hundred Hogs of a Distiller, the Flefti of which was tainted in the Summer-time, when the Pork fed in the Country was sweet; and that the Fledi of Hogs fed by Didiliers is more flabby than the other: But he said, that was the Meat of Hogs fed in the Country as fat as the Meat of those fed by the Didiliers, he believed it would be as soon tainted.

He added, that the Didiliers have entered into a Combination, and advanced a large Sum of Money, in order to prevent ocher Persons from contracting at the Victualling Office; and that because the Witness contracted for Hogs with some Farmers, the Didiliers afterwards refused to feil him any.

He said, that there was likewise a Complaint against him made to the Commissioners at the Victualling Office by the Didiliers, on account of his buying Country-fed Hogs, which, they said, were not so good as those fed by Didiliers; whereupon the said Commissioners made an Experiment, by salting some Meat of Hogs fed by the Didiliers, and some of those fed by the Farmers; and, after each had been barrelled Six Months, both were opened, and the Distillers was found to be great Part of it rotten, and the Farmers very good.

Mr. Anthony Ridley, who has been a Carcass Butcher near Forty Years, said, That the Distillers feeding of Hogs, and felling them so cheap, has greatly lessened the Consumption, and reduced the Price, of Beef and Mutton: That he formerly fold Four Hundred Sheep a Week, but now does not dispose of above Half that Number; and that many more Sheep come to London every Week than are fold.

Engles Prescot, a Carcass Butcher, said. That he formerly could fell Three hundred Sheep in a Week hetter than he can now fell an Hundred and Fifty; and that this Decrease is owing to the Distillers, who feed Hogs for little or nothing, and fell them very cheap; and that he is of Opinion this Practice of the Distillers mud, in time, ruin all the Farmers.

The Committee then proceeded to examine the Allegations of the Petition of the Yeomen and Farmers of East Kent; and the Evidence given by them to the Committee was as follows:

Mr. John Reynolds, a Farmer, occupying about Seven hundred Acres of Land in Kent, at the Rent of £. 300 per Annum, said, That he believes, if Distillers were obliged to draw their Spirits intirely from malted Corn, it would leflfen the Consumption of Corn: That he has seen, and considered, the Calculation made by Mr. Porter,

who was examined on behalf of the First Petition; and apprehends it to be a fallacious one; and that the same of the Farmers and Distillers is not truly dated:

That 100 Quarters of Barley will not only make 105 Quarters of Malt, as he, Porter, fays it will; but that it is the common Practice to make from that Quantity 140 Quarters of Malt, such as the Distillers use: That formerly, when he, the Witness, was an Officer in the Excise, the Custom of the Maltsters in Essex was to make Three or Four, and sometimes Five, Buftiels Increase in a Quarter of Barley, malted for the Use of the Distillers; and he believes the common Increase at this Time is Three Buftiels.

To this Fast of 140 Quarters of Malt being made from 100 Quarters of Barley, the said Mr. Porter said, he believed it was practicable; but that 100 Quarters of Barley, made into 103 Quarters of Malt, would weigh more, and, he believed, would produce more Spirit.

And the said Mr. Reynolds added further, That if Mr. Porter, by advancing in his Calculation, that 100 Quarters of Barley are equal in Weight to 131 Quarters of Barley malted, at the Increase of Five Quarters in the Hundred, intends to prove, that the same Quantity of Spirits may be drawn from the 100 Quarters of Barley, as from the 137 Quarters Four Bushels ot Malt, it is a false Conclusion, and cannot be done; for that One Quarter of Barley, made into Malt, will produce as much Spirit as One Quarter of raw Corn; and that therefore the Witness apprehended there would be no Increase in the Consumption of Corn by the Use of Malt only.

He further said, That suppofingit true, that 100 Quarters of Barley would produce the same Quantity of Spirits as might be drawn from 131 Quarters of Barley, made into Malt, at the Increase of Five Quarters in the Hundred, he apprehends, that the Use of malted Corn only would be a great Detriment to the Consumption of Spirits, and of consequence to the Consumption of Corn; for that Distillers would draw their Spirits at almost double the Expence they do at present; and that the Price of Spirits must be proportionably raised; so that if Spirits were now drawn for 1 s.per Gallon, they could not then be drawn under zs»; and the Distiller, in that case, would raise his Price to the Compounder in proportion, and the Compounder would probably take Advantage from thence of railing it to the Retailer above that Proportion; which Retailer would practise the same to his Customers; so that, by that means, the Price of Spirits might be raised to 4s.per Gallon.

The present Price of Spirits in the Retailers Shops, he said, was Six Pence per Pint; that is, 4s. per Gallon; and that the same would be raised, by the Use of malted Corn intirely, to Seven or Eight Shillings per Gallon; by which extravagant Price of Spirits, he said, he apprehended little or none would be drank:

Thzit, where he lives, he can buy Brandy for about 3J. 6d. or 4s. per Gallon; and has bought Ten Gallons of it for a Moidore:

That the Distillers have drawn Spirits cheaper since the Commencement of the War, because the Price of Corn has been falling; and that he is regulated in the Price of his Spirits by the Price of Corn:

That he thinks it is much the same thing to the Farmer, whether he uses his Corn in feeding Hogs, or fells it to the Distillers: That he believes if all the Hogs fed by them in a Year were to be distributed among the Farmers, it would not amount to One a piece.

Being asked, if it was the same thing to fell the Material of a Manufacture, or the Manufacture itself? he said, he conceives the Farmer is the best Judge what to do: That he did not know any Reason why the Contractors for the Navy could not buy Hogs fed in the Country as cheap as from the Distillers.

Mr. John Curling, Maltster and Farmer, said, That he rents 1,400 Acres of Land: That in the Barley, which he malts for Market, the Increase is Three Buftiels in a Quarter.
