Mr. John Nelson, a Hoyman, said, That most of the Malt, that is brought to Bear Key for the Use of Distillers, is manufactured after the Rate of Two and half and Three Bushels Increase in each Quarter of Barley, and, in pale Malt, rather a larger Increase:

That a great deal of Com grows in some Years, which is utterly incapable of being malted.

The laid Mr. Carling also said, That there is every ftfear a great Quantity of Corn produced in wet Lands, which will not malt; of which Sort, the Witnesssaid, he has some growing now, and has a great deal of it every Year:

That Three Parts in Four of the raw Corn, which he brings out of Kent is for the Use of the Distillers; and that the Price of Wheat is about 18 or 195. per Quarter; which, if malted, would come to a higher or less Rate, according to the Manner in which it was malted*

Mr. Charles Matson, a Farmer, renting £.700 a Year, said. That he apprehends, if the Distillers were to draw their Spirits from Malt, it would be the Ruin of the Farmers; for that it would lessen the Consumption of Corn, by increasing the Price of Spirits; and that the increasing the Price of Spirits will be an Encouragement to the Smugglers to run French Brandy.

Mr. Raynor, a Hoyman, said, That the Distillers make use of the best Corn that comes to Bear Key.

Mr. John Harrifoti said, That if Spirits were to be drawn intirely from malted Corn, it would raise the Price of those now fold for 4s. per Gallon to above 55.; and would be a great Encouragement for Smugglers to run French Brandy; which Brandy, he said, might be now bought for 4f. 6d. per Gallon; and that if People found they could buy it cheaper than home-made Spirits, they certainly would; which consequently must lessen the Consumption of home-made Spirits, and be detrimental both to the Farmer and Distiller; but that if the Importation of French Brandies could be intirely prevented, the Consumption of home-made Spirits would increase:

That he believes the Accounts at the Excise Office will prove, that the Duty upon Spirits has been increasing ever since the Act passed about Twenty Years ago, which impowered the Distillers to mix raw Corn with Malt.

And all the Witnesses examined on the behalf of this Petition concurred in their Evidence, That there is every Year a great Quantity of Corn incapable of being malted.

Then the Committee came to the following Resolutions:

Resolved, That it is the Opinion;of this Committee, That the Petitioners the Yeomen. Farmers, and Graziers, in the Counties of Middlesex, Surrey, and Kent, have proved the Allegations of their Petition.

Inland A Petition of the Dealers in Tea within the City of Duties on London, on behalf of themselves, and many others con-ea? c* cerned in the said Trade, was prefen ted to the House, and read; setting forth, That there was Reason to hope, the Interest of; the fair Trader in Tea would have effectually been secured by an Act, passed in the Tenth Year of his late Majesty; by which an Inland Duty of Four Shillings per Pound was laid on all Tea, without Distinction of Qua-. lity; but that notwithstanding the Regulations made by that Act, and the many Penalties the Smugglers of Tea, and their Accomplices, are liable to by Law, the clandestine Importation of Tea is so far from being prevented, that it is now carried to such a Height by the Smugglers, that the Petitioners have the strongest Reason to believe, that Three-fourths of the Teaconfumed in this Kingdom pay no Duty; and that the very high Duty of Four Shillings per Pound on all Teas, without distinguishing the Quality, is the principal Foundation for Smuggling; the coarser Sorts bearing too great a Proportion of the said Duty, and being bought abroad by the Smugglers at One-Vol. 24.

third of the Price it will stand the fair Trader in at home:

That, unless some speedy Remedy be applied to prevent this growing Evil, the Petitioners, and all fair Traders, will be under the greatest Difficiflties in carrying on their Trade, by reason of the Disadvantages they are under from the Practice of Smuggling; and that the Petitioners conceive, the most effectual Means to put a Stop to the clandestine Importation of Tea, would be to reduce the Inland Duty of ordinary Tea; and the Petitioners apprehend, that the paying a small Inland Duty for ordinary Tea would not only be a Means of enhancing the Revenue of Customs and Excise, but also of effectually preventing Smuggling, and keeping at home our Wool, as well as the current Coin of this Kingdom; large Quantities of both which are daily carried to France by the Smugglers of Tea, in open Defiance of the Laws made to the contrary: That the Smugglers are now become so numerous and outrageous, that the Civil Magistrates are intimidated, and unable to put the Laws in Execution against them and the Inhabitants of the Countries every-where through which they pass, are so alarmed with the Outrages and

Violences committed by them, that they live under a contin ual A pprehension of being robbed/tmd murdered: That the Petitioners, who have dealt largely in Tea, have been, for some Years, great Sufferers by the clandestine Importation of that Commodity, and are no longer able to carry on their Trades, without manifest Damage to themselves and Families; and must convert the remaining Part of their Fortunes into some other Employ, unless timely relieved by this House: And therefore praying.

That the House will take their same into Consideration, and give the Petitioners such Relief as to the House shall Teem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee of the whole House.

Resolved, That this House will, upon this Day Seven-night, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider of the said Petition.

A PETITION of the several Perfoi>s, whose Names Preservation are thereunto subscribed, being Traders in the Town of public ' of Yeovill, in the County of Somerset: And also. Roads.

A Petition of the several Persons, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, being Traders in the Town of Sherborne, in the County of Dorset, with Henftridge and Melborne, in the County of Somerset;

Were severally presented to the House, and read; fitting forth, That the Petitioners, as the Laws already stand, are under great Hardships upon Account of what they are obliged to pay to common Carriers for Carriage of their Goods and Merchandizes: That the Petitioners conceive, that if the Bill now before the House, intituled, A Bill to amend and render more effectual the Laws in being for the Preservation of the public Roads, should pass into a Law, the same would be a Means of railing the Price of the Carriage of Goods and Merchandize all over the Kingdom of Great Britain, to the great Prejudice of the Petitioners, and all other the Inland Traders, and to the Detriment of the Trade in general of this Kingdom: And therefore praying, That the House will be pleased to take the same of the Petitioners into Consideration, and give such Relief to the Petitioners as to the House shall seem meet.

A Petition of the principal Merchants and Traders in Drawback on Serges, and other Woollen Manufactures, in and about Foreign Ei-Barnstaple: And also, nCDS*

A Petition of the principal Merchants and Traders in Serges, and other Woollen Manufactures, in and about the Borough of East Looe, in the County of Cornwall',

Were severally presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That a Petition hath been presented by sundry Persons, Dealers in, and Manufacturers of.

Linens, Threads, and Tapes, made in Great Britain and Ireland; praying further Encouragements to their Manufactures, and particularly by taking off the Drawbacks payable at present on the Exportation of foreign* Linens; and representing to the House, that such Linens are (though indirectly, yet in reality) a Part of the Returns of British YVoolIen Manufactures wrought up by the Petitioners, and many Thousands other British Subjects, and exported to foreign Parts, to the great Advantage of this Kingdom; and that the Petitioners have btot too much Reason to apprehend, that if any further Burthen should be laid either on the Importation or Exportation ofthofe Linens (which are already charged with Duties greatly exceeding those payable on our Woollen Manufactures abroad) it may be a Means ofgivingOccasion for the like or greater Discouragements to such of our Woollen Manufactures as are exported to foreign Parts, and may be attended with other Consequences very prejudicial to the Woollen Manufactures of this Kingdom: And therefore praying the House, That the said Drawbacks may not be taken off, nor any further Discouragements given to the Importation of foreign Linens, Threads, and Tapes.

Merchants A Petition of the several Merchants, whose Names are gl^s on thereunto subscribed, in behalf of themselves and Part-p ' ners, being offered to be presented to the House;

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer, by his Majesty’s Command, acquainted the House, That his Majesty, having been informed of the Contents of the said Petition, recommends it to the Consideration of the House.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioners suffered very considerable Losses by Seizures and Depredations committed by the Spaniards in the Year 1718; the Accounts and Vouchers whereof were duly delivered by the Petitioners, according to public Notice, first to the Commissioners Plenipotentiaries from Great Britain at Cambray and Soissons, and afterwards to the Lords Commissioners for Trade and Plantations, when Commissaries went from Great Britain to Spain; and a Commission has lately issued for the Distribution of such Sums as have arisen by Reprisals from the Spaniards, at the Commencement of the present War with Spain, amongst the Sufferers; but that the Commissioners therein named were only impowered to settle and adjust the Claims of such as have sustained Lottes in the Year 1721, and from that time; so that those, whq suffered before that time, are excluded from any Relief, but by Application to Parliament: That a Petition hath been

lately presented to the House by several Merchants of London, who have sustained Losses by Depredations of the Spaniards, praying a Relief for their Losses out of the £. 60,000 granted by Parliament; and that the Petitioners conceive, they are equally intitled to Relief as any other their Fellow-sufferers: That, in the iaft Session of Parliament, the Petitioner John Buck, who is Executor to George Buck Esquire, deceased, in behalf of himself and Partners, and Richard Score, who isfince dead, in behalf of himself and Partners (of which the Petitioner George Strange wasr One, as Executor of his late Father George Strange, deceased), with some other Persons, applied to the House; and the then Chancellor of the Exchequer, by his Majesty’s Command, acquainted the House, That his Majesty had been informed of the Contents of the said Petition, and recommended it to Consideration; and chat a Report of the Petitioners same was accordingly made from a Committee to the House: And therefore praying, That the same of the Petitioners may be taken into Consideration; and that Satisfaction may be made to the Petitioners out of the £. 60,000 given by Parliament; or that such other Relief may be given them, as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee, to whom the Petition of several Merchants of London trading to Portugal, Spain, and Italy, whose Names are thereunto subscribed; and also the Petition of Sir Daniel Lambert Knight; are referred: And that they do examine, and state to the House, the Matter of Fast contained in this Petition.

A Petition of the Inhabitants of the Town of Newcastle under Line, in the County of Stafford, and of the Villages or Townships of Handley, Burslem, Shelton, and Fenton Culvert, in the same County, and other Places adjacent to the said Town and Villages, or Townships, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, Manufacturers cf earthen Pot Ware, and Traders and Dealers in the fame, and several other Sorts of Wares and Merchandizes, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioners, as the Laws already stand, labour under great Hardships upon Account of the Rates they are obliged to pay to common Carriers for Carriage of several Sorts of Goods and Merchandize; a great Part whereof is earthen Ware, of so small Value that the Carriage from these Parts *0 London, and other Places of the same Distance, to which they fend it in great Quantities, already exceeds the intrinsicValue by Sixty or Seventy Pounds per Centum, and, though of so small a Value, employs as great a Number of Hands as earthenWare of much larger Value: That the Petitioners conceive, that if the Bill, now before the House, to amend and render more effectual the Laws in being for the Preservation of the public Roads, should pass into a Law, the feme would be a Means of railing the Price of the Carriage in general so excessively high, as to render all Inland Traders, and the Petitioners in particular, utterly incapable of supplying foreign Markets upon as cheap Conditions as neighbouring Nations can serve them; by which means, this Kingdom will be deprived of the Sale of this and most other Sort of heavy Goods, to the Prejudice of the Petitioners, and all other Inland Traders, and their Families; which wiil increase the Number of the Poor, affectall Inland Estates, and be very detrimental to the Trade of this Nation in general: And therefore praying the House to take the same of the Petitioners into Consideration, and give them such Relief as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Report from the Committee, to whom the said Bill was committed, be taken into further Consideration.

Mr. Fane, according to Order, Reported from the Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred Duricgoa to consider of -ihe Petition of the Dealers in Tea, within T«a. the City of London, on behalf of themselves, and many others concerned in the said Trade; stnd also of the several other Petitions refered to the Consideration of the said Committee; the Resolutions which the Committee had directed him to report to the House; which he read In his Place; ana afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same were read; and are as followerh; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the Inland Duty of Four Shillings per Pound on all Tea consumed in Great Britain, granted by an Act of the Tenth Year of his late Majesty King George, shall, from and after the 24th Day of June next ensuing, ccafe, determine, and be no longer paid.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That, in lieu of the said Duty so to be determined, therfe be granted to his Majesty, from and after the said 24th Day of June, the Inland Duties of One Shilling per Pound, and Twenty-five Pounds per Cent, on the gross Price of all Teas, as sold at public Sale, and which shall be taken out of Warehouse; the said Duties of One Shilling per Pound, and Twenty five Pounds per Cent, to be appropriated and applied to the same Uses and Purposes, as by Law the present Duty of Four Shillings per Pound is appropriated and applied.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That, from and after the said 24th Day of June, the present Drawback of the Duty upon Tea do cease, and be no longer allowed.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the united Company of Merchants trading to the East Indies} be permitted to import Tea from any Part of Europe into Great Britain.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That, upon Failure of the said Company’s keeping this Market supplied with a sufficient Quantity of Tea, his Majesty be authorized to grant Licence to other Per Ions to import into this Kingdom Tea from any Part of Europe, under proper Limitations and Reftructions to be provided.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That all Tea Which shall be 16 imported from any Part

Claims on chant, Executor of Matthew Craufurd of Glasgow, Mer* Spain. chant, deceased, One of the Owner9 of the Ship Esther, of Glasgow, in behalf of himself, and of several other Merchants, Owners of the said Ship Esther, being offered to be presented to the House;

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read 5 setting forth, That the said Ship Esther, Eneas Campbell Matter, was pressed into the Service of the King of Spain, in the Beginning of the Year 1718, and was employed to carry Stores for him to MeJJina in Sicily, where (he delivered her Loading on the 12th of August 1718, and got a Receipt from the proper Officer there of that Date, having then been Two Months and Nineteen Days in the King of Spain*s Service, at the Rate of 600 Dollars per Month, which amounted to about £.400 Sterling, but that no Payment was ever received for the said Freight, occasioned by the War immediately breaking out with Spain: That, in the Beginning of the Year 1719, the said Ship being freighted to Smyrna, from thence to Civita Vecca and Leghorn, was attacked by a Spanish Privateer, and, after a ttout Resistance (having killed the Privateer Sixteen Men, and wounded Thirty-two), was taken by the said Privateer, and condemned as a legal Prize, the Value of the said Ship being £. 2,000, and the Freight due to her, for a very conllderable Cargo, upwards off. S00, which, including the Freight due by the King of Spain, makes the whole Loss amount to £.3,200. That, in the Year 1721, the Petitioners presented their Claim to the Lords of the Treasury, and to the Secretaries of State, and in the Year 1730, they likewise presented the same to the Court of Admiralty, pursuant to an Order made for that Purpose: I hat, in the said Year 1730, the Petitioners, by the Hands of Meflleurs John ana William Crawfurd Merchants, in London, gave their Claims and Papers relating to this Ship to John Crookjhanks Esquire, Secretary to the Commissaries who were appointed by his Majesty to go ro Spain, to adjust these Lottes 5 but that the said John Crookjhanks being since dead, and his Son, who was his Executor, being abroad in his Majesty’s Service, a Captain of a Man of War in the Mediterranean, and in whose Custodyall the said Mr. Crookjhank*s Papers are, the Petitioners have thereby been rendered unable to rake the proper Steps which other Merchants, under the like Circumstances, have done; and that several Merchants who were Sufferers, from the Year 1718 to the Year 1721, have applied to the House, that they may have Satisfaction for their Lottes out of the £. 60,000 granted by the House, the 14th Day of May 1739. to answer what had been acknowledged to be due from Great Britain to Spain: And therefore praying the House, That the Lottes of the Petitioners may be taken into Consideration, and that they may be infilled to the like Share of the said £. 60,000 as the House shall think fit to allot toother Merchants, although they have not gone through all the necessary Forms as some of them have done, or to grant them such other Relief as to the House shall seem meet.

The York Courant, printed for Cafar Ward, Bookseller, in Coney-fired, and dated Tuesday, February 26, 1744-5, (which Paper was, upon Friday the 8th Day of March last, brought up to the Table) being shewn to him at the Bar, he confellld that he printed the said Paper, and exprenbd his Sorrow for his printing therein an Account of the Proceedings of this House, declaring that he did not know the same to be an Offence, and would not have done it if he had, and promising not to be guilty of the like for the future.

Drawbacks A Petition of the principal Merchants, and Traders in on foreign Serges, and other Woollen Manufactures, in and about Linens, Borough of Mitchell, in the County of Cornwall,

was presented to the House, and read; letting forth, That a Petition hath been presented by sundry Persons, Dealers in, and Manufacturers of, Linens, Threads, and Tapes, made in Great Britain and Ireland, praying further Encouragements to their Manufactures, and particularly by taking off the Drawbacks payable at present on the Exportation of foreign Linens: That such Linens are, (though indirectly, yet in Reality) a Part of the Returns for British Woollen Manufactures, wrought up by the Petitioners, and many Thousands other British Subjects, and exported to foreign Parts, to the great Advantage of this Kingdom: And representing to the House, Thar the Petitioners have too much Reason to apprehend, that if any further Burthen should be laid, either on the Importation or Exportation of those Linens, which are already charged with Duties greatly exceeding those payable on our Woollen Manufactures abroad, it may be a.Means of giving Occasion for the like or greater Discourage-- ments, to such of our Woollen Manufactures as are exported to foreign Parts, and may be attended with other Consequences very prejudicial to the Woollen Manufacture of this Kingdom: And therefore praying, That the said Drawbacks may not be taken off nor any further Discouragements given to the Importation of foreign Linens, Threads, and Tapes.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Trtfervation A Petition of the several Persons, whose Names are of public thereunto subscribed, being Traders in the Town of Roads. Skept on Mallett, was presented to the House, and read;

setting forth, That the Petitioners, as the Laws already Hand, are under great Hardships upon Account of what they are obliged to pay to common Carriers for the Carriage of their Goods and Merchandizes: That the Petitioners conceive, that if the Bill, now before this House, intituled, A Bill to amend and render more effectual the Laws in being'for the Preservation of the public Roads, should pass into a Law, the same will be a Meam of railing the Price of the Carriage of Goods and Merchandize all over the Kingdom of Great Britain, to the great Prejudice of the Petitioners, and all other the inland Traders, and to the Detriment of the Trade in general of this Kingdom: And therefore praying the House to take the same of the Petitioners into Con toleration; and give them such Relief, as to the House shall seem meet.; (1

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Debate upon One of the Amendments, made to the said Bill by the Committee to whom the same was committed, be resumed.

Money given by Parliament, or in such other Manner as to the House shall seem meet.

The House was moved, That an Act, made in the 13th Year of the Reign of King Charles the Second, intituled, An Act for the establishing Articles and Orders for the regulating and better Government of his Majesty’s Navies, Ships of War, and Forces by Sea, might be read:

And the same being read accordingly;

Ordered, Nemine contradicente, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for explaining and amending an Act, made in the 13 th Year of the Reign of King Charles the Second, intituled, An Act for the establishing Articles and Orders for the regulating and better Government of his Majesty’s Navies, Ships of War, and Forces by Sea; and also for regulating the Proceedings upon Courts Martial in the Sea Service: And that Mr. George Grenville, Sir John Hind Cot ton, and the Lord Baltimore, do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

Resolved, That an humble Address be presented to his Majesty, That he will be gradually pleased to give Directions, that no Warrant be granted to muster complete any Regiment, Troop, Company, or Forces, under any Denomination, employed in any of his Majesty’s Wands or Colonies in America, until a Certificate be first had from the Comptrollers of the Accounts of the Army, that Proof hath been made, upon Oath, of the real Numbers of which such Regiment, Troop, Company, or Forces, did consist, during the Time or Times for which such Warrant shall be granted; and that, in such Certificate, there be also set forth to whac public Service in which the said Forces are employed, the Sums saved by the Pay of the non-effective Men have been applied; and that the said Certificate or Certificates be annexed to such Warrant to muster complete, and a Duplicate thereof lodged in the Office of the Secretary at War for the time being.

Ordered, That the said Address be presented to his Majesty by such Members of this House as are of his Majesty’s most honourable Privy Council.

A Petition of the principal Merchants and Traders in Serges, and other Woollen Manufactures, in and about the Borough of HelJloney in Cornwall, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That a Petition hath been presented by sundry Persons, Dealers in, and Manufacturers of Linens, Threads, and Tapes, made in Great Britain and Ireland, praying further Encouragements to their Manufactures, and particularly by taking off the Drawbacks payable at the present on the Exportation of foreign Linens: That such Linens are (though indirectly, yet in reality) a Part of the returns for British Woollen Manufactures, wrought up by the Petitioners, and many Thousands other British Subjects, and exported 'to foreign Parts, to the great advantage of this Kingdom: That the Petitioners have but too much Reason to apprehend, that if any further Burthen should be laid either on the Importation or Exportation of those Linens, which are already charged with Duties greatly exceeding those payable on our Woollen Manufactures abroad, it may be a means of giving Occasion for the like or greater Discouragements to such of our Woollen Manufactures as are exported to foreign Parts, and may be attended with other Consequences very prejudicial to the Woollen Manufacture of this Kingdom: And therefore praying the House, That the said Drawbacks may not be taken

Sandwich A Petition of divers Merchants, Commanders of Ships, and Ramsgate and others, whose Ships and Goods pass outwards and Harbours. homewards through the Downs, in behalf of themselves, and all others trading that Way, was presented to the House, and read* fetring forth, That a Report, and Estimate subjoined, with Plans annexed, hath been laid before the House, for making a safe and commodious Harbour into the Downs, near SandownCattk, fit for the Reception and Security of large Merchantmen, and Ships of War of Sixty or Seventy Guns; and that a further Estimate is to be prepared, of the Charge of purchasing. Lands proper for effecting this Scheme: That the Petitioners are tho-j-oughly sensible of the Necessity of a Harbour in or near the Dozens, for the Security of the Navigation of this Kingdom; and that their Views are only to have it at the fitted Place; and representing to the House the Opinion of the Petitioners, that a more convenient Harbour may be made at or near Ramsgate, capable of containing a greater Number of Merchantmen, and Ships of War of Sixty or Seventy Guns, on account of the advantageous Situation of the Place, and Setting of the Tides, where no Back-water will be wanted, and where Docks and Launches may be made on a natural and folkj Foundation; and that there will likewise be a Saving to the Public of several Hundred thousand Pounds, as the Petitioners verily believe: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, in order to have a Survey taken, and Report made, if a Harbour cannot be fixed at or near Ramsgate, more proper for answering the main Ends intended by that proposed near Sandown Castle, with an Estimate of the Charge, for the House to be fully informed which Situation of the Two will be most beneficial to the Navigation of this Kingdom.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of William Brooker, Master and chief Owner of the Ship called the Faro Merchant, being offered to be presented to the House;

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer, by his Majesty^ Command, acquainted the House, That his Majesty having been informed of the Contents of the said Petition, recommends it to the Consideration of the House.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read; setting forth. That the said Ship, going from New England to Bilboa in Spain, did, in October 1718, in her Passage, put into Castroy and that though no War was then declared between Great Britain and Spain, yet the Governor seized the said Ship and Cargo, consisting of 1,305 Quintals of dried Cod Fiffi, and 5,000 Hogshead Staves, on Freight, as appears by Bill of Lading; and that the Petitioner had also on board the said Ship 200 Quintals of dried Cod Fish for his own Account, over and above the 1,305 Quintals on Freight; which 200 Quintals of dried Cod Fish were then worth at lead £. 270 Sterling Money: That the said Ship (her Materials and Stores being all intirely new. One Voyage to Oporto only excepted) was really worth £.750 Sterling at the Time of Capture, when was also due, for Freight of the said Ship, ,£.380 Sterling; which made up the whole Loss sustained by the Petitioner, and those interested with him, the Sum of £. 1,400 Sterling; but that the Petitioner is himself by far the greatest: Sufferer: That, some time in April 1719, the Petitioner did, by Night, escape on board a Butch Ship, who, about the Nineteenth of the said Month, fell in with Admiral Norris's Squadron cruizing in the Mouth of the Channel; and the Petitioner being lent for on board the said Admiral, gave him an Account of his said Loss; and, in Two or Three Days after, the Petitioner was put on Shore at Portsmouthy and there directly made Oath of his said Loss: That, in June 1728, according to public Notice, the Petitioner did apply to the Commissioners of Trade and Plantations, and delivered in his Account of his said Loss, to be sent to Spain to the Commissaries there; but hath never had any Redress: And therefore praying. That he may be admitted to partake of the £. 60,000 granted by Parliament, and remaining undisposed of; or that he may have such other Relief as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Weight thereof, on a, l\fe‘cdium, li&'tlvYieen annually exported to New England, New York, Carolina, and other British Colonies in America the Exportatiop whereof^ the Exporters give Bonds to the Officers 6fthe Customs in* large Penalties conditioned; that such T$a shall not be re~ landed*\n Great Britain, and to produceproper Certificates, thereof within a Time therein limited fThat, with respect to Ireland, Tea pays a Duty, on its Impprfatjo.p there, of is. 9d. per Pound; and that the Drawback is not paid,' or the Bond delivered up here, until a Certificate trom' the Collector and Comptroller of the Calloms in Ireland, of the Landing of such Tea, and of its having paid the Irish Duty, be produced to t he Commissioners of the Customs here; and that the Checks to prevent Fraud between England and Ireland are so llrong, that there is no Inllance of any Seizure or Complaint of any such Tea having been run in between England and Ireland, or of the Officers in Ireland making any falle Certificate in respect to the Landing of Tea; it not being reasonable to expect they should, since they would thereby charge themselves with the Receipt of the Duty of u. 9d. per Pound to;. the Revenue, in order to deiraud the Revenue here of.. $?rd. per Pound, the Drawback payable here on the Exportation of low-priced Teas; of which kind moll of., those exported to Ireland art: That, by reason of the said. Duty of is. 9d. payable in Ireland, and the Freight, Commission, and other Charges attending the Exportation . thereof, low-priced Teas will come as dear to the Coufumer in Ireland, after an Allowance of the Drawback, and without paying the new Inland Duties, as the like Teas will, on the Foot of the new Inland Duties, be sold to the Con-lumer here; but that in case the same are to be charged with the new Inland Duties, and to have no Drawback allowed, the Duties payable thereon, including th? Irish Duty of is. yd. will amount, on low-priced Tea?, a Pound; which the Petitioners apprehend wiil, in a very

short

short Time, put a Stop to the exporting Tea from hence to Ireland, and will prove a very great Encouragement to the clandestine and fraudulent Importation thereof from France, and nccdfarily increase the Exportation of Wool from Ireland to foreign Parts: That, with respect to the Plantations, the Petitioners apprehend, that the charging all Teas that shall be exported thither with the said new Inland Duty, and the not allowing the Drawback' on Exportation, will produce the like Effects there, and encourage the clandestine Smuggling of Tea into those Parts, from the Dutch and French Settlements: And therefore praying the House to take the same of the Petitioners into Consideration; and that in the Bill, now depending before the House, for repealing the Inland Duty gf 4 s. per Pound Weight upon all Tea fold in Great Britain, and for granting to his Majesty certain other In-

Plenipotentiaries were appointed by both Crowns, in ordet to settle and adjust all Differences which had been raised on Account of Visiting, Searching, and Taking, of Vessels, 13 c. \ and it was agreed, that the King of Spain should cause to be paid to his Britannic Majesty the Sum of £.95,000, for a Balance which has been admitted as due to the Crown and Subjects of Great Britain, after Deduction made of the Demands of the Crown and Subjects of Spain, to the end that the above-mentioned Sum, together with the Amount of what has been acknowledged on the Part of Great Britain to be due to Spain on her Demands, may be employed by the King of Great Britain for the Satisfaction, Discharge, and Payment, of the Demands of the English Subjects upon the Crown of Spain* That, on the 14th May 1739, your Committee find, that the Sum of £.60,000, being the Sum acknowleged to be

A Petition of the under-signed Merchants," Importers of foreign Cambricks, in behalf of themselves, arid many others* was presented to the House, and read; submitting.to the Consideration of this House, whether the Bill to prohibit the Wear of Cambricks may not probably produce Conflquences prejudicial to this Kingdom, and its Manufactures; and fecting forth, That the Petitioners thought themselves encouraged to contrail for Quantities of Cambrick, from the Parliament having, scarcely Three Years ago, given the Duties payable upon that Commodity as a Fund for encouraging our Linen Manufactures, and not having prohibited the Importation thereof; and that the intended Prohibition hath been proposed so very late in the Sections, that the Merchants concerned in that

Trade (even the rtloft cautious of them) had but just finished their Orders for great Quantities, for their Stocks, before this Prohibition was heard of (the Season of the Year admitting of no longer Delay); and their Goods are now bleaching; which is what the Petitioners would most certainly have avoided, had any such Prohibition been expected by them; That the Quantities already in the Merchants and Dealers Hands, together with the ad*-ditional Quantities so lately contracted for, and coming in, mull, at all Events, occasion a considerable Loss to his Majesty’s Subjects, upon any Prohibition, which will be greatly increased, without the Indulgence of this House, in granting proper Times to enter the said Goods under the p re salt Duties, and to vend the same again, after they are imported; there being no Place to which the same can be exported, but at a heavy Loss: And therefore, in-as much as the Petitioners conceive it is nor intended to lay any Hardfnips upon them, in respect of those Goods which they have very lawfully bought and paid greac Sums for, as well for the First Purchase, as for the Duties to the Crown; praying. That the Petitioners may be heard upon the said Bill, with respect to the Commencement of any additional Duties, and the Time tfo be allowed for Wear and Consumption of the present lapge Stock; and that this House will make such other. Pro virions in the said Bill, as may do the lead Prejudice to the fair Trade.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of the under-signed Linen-drapers, and Dealers in Cambrick, in behalf of t hemselves, and many others, was presented to the House, and read; fecting forth, That Cambricks having been a pretty general-Wear, and no Prohibition laid thereon at the Commencement of the Frencbf\N-dr, the Petitioners have laid out large Sums in purchasing their Stocks of the fame; and are highly affected by the Bill to prohibit the Wear thereof, as there is no Place to which they can fepd them, but at.great Loft: That, in case this House shall shink it convenient to pass a Law of that Sort, while the Petitioners have such large Quantities by them, and without any previous Notice Qf such Intention, the Petitioners must greatly suffer in their Property: And therefore praying Leave to be heard, upon the said Bill as to the Time to be allowed for the Wear of Cambricks.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Running of A Petition of Thomas Lowndes was presented to the Wool. House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioner has framed a Scheme, which, if executed, he doubts not, will effectually hinder the Running of Wool from Ireland to France, and to other foreign Parts: That the Petitioner has in View the mutual Benefit of Great Britain and Ireland, without die least Tendency to a Register, or to any other chargeable, oppressive, or vexatious Method: That though this Performance has cost this Petitioner’a great deal of Study and Pains for very many Years, -attended with the Expence of a considerable Sum of Money, yet the Petitioner proposes no Terms; the known/Justice and Equity of the House, being the strongest Assurances to the Petitioner, that he, or his Representatives, (Hall be suit-ably rewarded for this Service, in case the said Scheme, 'when made public, be in the main approved of; which he is ready to communicate, when, and in such manner, as the House shall think proper.

Ordered, That the said petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom it is referred to consider further of the State of the Woollen Manufacture of Great Britain and Ireland: And that the Petitioner be heard, before the said Committee, if he thinks fit.

Mr. Carew accordingly reported from the said Committee, the Resolution, which they had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Proceedings of the Court Martial, assembled on board his Majesty’s Ship Torbay, begun the 28th of January 1744, and ending the 5th of February following, pursuant to an Order from the Commissioners for executing the Office of Lord High Admiral of Great Britain, bearing Date the 28th of November 1744, to Vice Admiral Rowley, for inquiring into the Conduct and Be-

haviour of Captain Richard Norris in the Engagement between the English Fleet, under the Command of Admiral Mathews, and the united Fleets of France and

Spain, in the Mediterranean, on the I ith of February 1743, were partial, arbitrary, and illegal.

The said Resolution, being read a Second time, was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed toby the House.

And then the House adjourned till Tomorrow Morning, Nine of the Clock.

After which, his Majesty was pleated to make a moll The KJng’i gracious Speech to both Houses of Parliament, as fol- petc*1, loweth; viz.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

THE Zeal, Unanimity, and Dispatch, of your Proceedings, having brought the public Business to a happy Conclusion; and the Seaton of the Year being so far advanced, it is necessary that I should put an End to this Session of Parliament.

It is a particular Satisfaction to me to be able to acquaint you, that, since the Beginning of it, the Postureof Affairs abroad has received a very considerable Alteration, to the Advantage of the common Cause. The late Successes of the Aujirittn Arms in Germand the Conclu-

fion of an Accommodation between the Queen of Hungary and the Elector of Bavaria, have laid the bell Foundations for a further happy Progrefe. By these Events, the Influence of France in the Empire is much weakened and diminished, and a Way is opened to restore that Strength and Power to our antient and natural Allies, which will tend greatly to the He-establishment and Security of the Balance of Europe.

The Resolutions which have been taken by my good Friends the States General of the United Provinces, for exerting their Efforts in concert with me, and the Engagements they have entered into for settling the Proportions of Forces and Expence, cannot fail to give Spirit and Vigour to the Operations of our Armies. From these good Beginnings, 1 hope, by the Blessing of God on the Justice of our Cause, this Campaign will be attended with such Succefe, as to defeat the ambitious and dellruftive Projects of the House of Bourbon, formed against the Liberties of Europe, and particularly levelled against my Kingdoms. In this View, I am determined, in conjunction with my Allies, vigorously to prosecute this just and necessary War, in order to the procuring a Cife and honourable Peace.

Gentlemen of the House of Commons,

I return you my hearty Thanks for the ample Supplies which you have so chearfully granted for the Service of the current Year; and which, you may be afTur-d, Hiatt be strictly applied to those great and national Ends for which they were given.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

I intirely rely on your Duty, Fidelity, and good Affections, of which 1 have had so many convincing Proofs.

Let it be your Care to cultivate and promote the feme good Dispositions in your several Countries, to support my Government, an5 to preserve the Peace and g>od Order of the Kingdom; as it shall ever be mine to advance and secure your lading Prosperity and Happiness.

And afterwards, the Lord Chancellor, by his Majesty’s parlfamrni Command, laid, prorogued.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

It is his Majesty’s Royal Will and Pleasure, That this Parliament be prorogued to Thursday the Twentieth Day of June next, to be then here held: And this Parliament is accordingly prorogued to Thursday the Twentieth Day

of June next.
